○ Commentary on the Introduction Chapter:

This commentary on the text is broadly divided into two parts. First, a general explanation; second, a specific explanation. Within the initial general explanation, the text is further divided into three sections.

First, it explains that ancient scholars directly interpreted the scriptural text without dividing it into sections, chapters, or paragraphs. Second, [it discusses] the general [implications] following the division of sections...

Regarding the intent of the topical divisions (*lun-fen-chieh*): "Third, the current division" refers to the present school’s analysis of the text. The initial phrase, "the preceding generations," etc., briefly indicates the period prior to the Liang dynasty, as no specific sections were established therein. As for the term "generations" (*tai*): [The text continues: ...it refers to the successive dynasties. Specifically, it denotes the various eras from the time of the Buddha’s passing until the end of the Liang dynasty. "The preceding generations" refers to the period prior to the Liang dynasty; "the later generations" refers to the period following the Liang dynasty. Furthermore, "the preceding generations" refers to the era before the Sui dynasty, while "the later generations" refers to the era beginning with the Tang dynasty. Moreover, "the preceding generations" refers to the period before the Tiantai school arose, while "the later generations" refers to the period after the Tiantai school arose. Although the *Yi* (Meaning) was established thirty years ago, it is now being replaced by the *Gai* (Alternative), which represents a different era’s interpretation. The propagation of the Dharma across successive generations has always existed;
hence, it is called "generations" (*dai*). The various schools differ in their divisions and sections, some being extensive and others concise, and some having topical outlines while others do not.

What is valued is grasping the intended meaning. As the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra* is difficult to fathom, one must explain its profound mystery and wondrousness through the ten fascicles, expounding upon the two gates of the Original and the Traces.

In the Buddha’s intention, this sutra is likewise so. One must clarify the essential purport of the sutra—its revelation and its application to the final age—and understand that its inclusive intent is to equally manifest the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the subsequent text stating "Xiaoshan Yao," this refers to Dharma Master Yao of Xiaoshan Temple in Wucheng, Wuxing.
As for "Peng of Guannei," this refers to Dharma Master Peng of Guanzhong. These are used as the criteria for dividing the sections.
The variations in expansion and contraction are as detailed in the following text; they may be divided into two, three, or four categories, all of which involve orchids and chrysanthemums.
If one adheres to these with partiality, there will be no threefold benefit, and one will lose the single path and the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*.

Regarding Emperor Wu of Liang and others: whenever the Liang Emperor descended from court, he would wear a plain woolen cap and don a *kāṣāya* robe to ascend the throne himself and lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
He divided the text of this sūtra into three parts—forenoon, noon, and afternoon. Therefore, the following passage refutes him by asking:
"At dusk and at midnight, with which part of the text do you then align?"
Kaishan [Dharmakṣema] established only the "Preface" and the "Correct" sections, because he considered the "Circulation" section to pertain to future generations.
Guangzhai [Huijian] was the one who established the "Circulation" section; since the time of Master Tanyan of Miyan, all sutras, whether large or small, have been divided into these three parts.
Regarding "Lingwei" and so forth: Lingwei is the name of a temple. Dharma Master Baogao composed this commentary on the text.

As for the question concerning the causal origin (*nidāna*): it arose from Cunda’s offering of food, whereby the Tathāgata revealed the eternal and taught that the five fruits of the eternally abiding [Dharma] are without distinction.
Cunda then posed a question, which subsequently led to a discussion with Mañjuśrī as the causal origin. Later, Kāśyapa raised three [questions].
There are fourteen questions, all of which concern dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Regarding the response concerning "having residual power" (*sāvaśeṣa-vega*): the direct answers extend from the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly" through fourteen chapters.
From the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" onwards, the five modes of conduct and ten merits are fully discussed; even up to King Siṃhaguṇa, all possess residual power.
Regarding the "Five Gates of Hexi": the Dharma Master Lang of Hexi and the current school’s textual division share the same names.
As for Vasubandhu, he is also called Bandhudatta; this is translated as Tianqin (Heavenly Relative). He composed the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*, which is divided into seven sections.
Regarding the "Eight Gates of Xinghuang": Xinghuang is the name of a monastery. Dharma Master Lang was known by his contemporaries as "Subduing-Tiger Lang.
He divided the *Changgan Deyi* and other texts into eight gates.

Regarding the prohibition in the Sūtra and the allowance in the Śāstra: the "Sūtra" refers to the present Sūtra; the "Śāstra" refers to the Great Śāstra. As for the prohibition in the Sūtra, it is as described in the subsequent passage:
from the cowherd woman adding water up to the women of the city adding it four times, it is therefore prohibited. As for the allowance in the Śāstra:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) explains the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* by means of eight gates. Why? Because the *Prajñāpāramitā* is profound, it is divided into eight gates.
This is like a deep body of water that is difficult to cross, which is divided to make it shallow; or like a person carrying a heavy load, who breaks it down to make it light.
Therefore, it is said that [the treatise] "opens" [the sūtra]. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is as described in the third fascicle of the *Zhiguan ji* (Record of Stopping and Contemplation).
Now, the section on the "Correct Explanation" is divided into five chapters, beginning with the invocation of the assembly and extending to its application up to *nirvāṇa*;
each of these clarifies the meaning of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Furthermore, these seven meanings explain the five chapters.

First, regarding the invocation of the assembly for *nirvāṇa*: the fifty-two assemblies all gathered at Kuśinagara; those who are provisional (*upāya*) should be invited, while those who are ultimate (*tattva*) must be summoned. Second...
1. Expounding the gift of *nirvāṇa*: "Expounding" refers exclusively to the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
2. Demonstrating the practice of *nirvāṇa*: This refers to the five practices and ten merits. 3. Questioning and answering the meaning of *nirvāṇa*:

The Lion’s Roar (*Siṃhanāda*) uses six layers of question-and-answer to clarify the meaning of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), beginning with the clarification of the single essence of the Three Jewels and extending through the six causes and effects. 4. Subduing and gathering through refutation.
Regarding the application of *nirvāṇa*: from the "Kāśyapa Chapter" through the end of the sutra up to the "Ājñātakauṇḍinya Chapter," all clarify this application.
As for the principle that "the Way does not operate in isolation," there are two kinds of Way: first, the Way of self-cultivation; second, the Way of benefiting sentient beings.
Self-cultivation proceeds from cause to fruit, while benefiting others proceeds from fruit to cause.
Regarding "waiting for the time, the place, and the assembly": "time" refers to the moment at dawn on the fifteenth day of the second month when light was emitted from the face;
it also symbolizes that the oral teachings shall never be interrupted, which is why they were emitted from the mouth. "Place" refers to the site of the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara;
all Buddhas of the three periods enter nirvana in this same manner. "Assembly" refers to the fifty-two groups of followers.
Furthermore, "to illuminate" (*qizhao*) means that "to initiate" (*qi*) is like "to open," and "illumination" (*zhao*) is light.

Regarding "emitting sounds according to the species": from the dung beetles (*qieqiang*) at the lowest level up to the fifty-two classes of beings, all are moved by these vocal teachings to gather here.
It is the corpse.
That which is called "summoning" by means of conditions refers, in the distant sense, to the remote past; in the proximate sense, it refers to the five flavors of this present life.
These are capable of opening up the eternally abiding Buddha-nature as a condition; thus, it is truly the person who is summoned.
"Summoning and inviting" (*zhāozhì*) means "to request. "Summoning" (*zhāo*) refers to the superior enabling the subordinate to act; "inviting" (*zhì*) is synonymous with "attaining.

This is because the light of the Great Nirvāṇa causes both the provisional and the real to benefit all beings, such that even Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) still attain the benefit of a portion of the Dharma-body.

"Those who rush together from the ten directions" means they leap forward with joy. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states: "At the Tathāgata’s single command, they rush and leap from the four quarters.
"All manifest it" means that now the secret treasury of Buddha-nature is opened and fully realized; both those of provisional and ultimate [teachings] thereby attain nirvana.
Cultivating the gates of liberation is what is called "universality" (*xian*). Exhausting the entire treasury of the Dharma is why it is said there is "no stinginess.

However, the statement that "not all are able to receive it" explains the meaning of "no stinginess" by referring to the provisional teachings; it means they were not yet capable of hearing the Great [Vehicle].
Regarding the "poison smeared at the very beginning": although the name "milk" is the same, there is a distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox.

At first, the poison of impermanence is used to sever the milk of heterodox permanence; subsequently, one takes up the poison of impermanence to wash away that [poison] itself, thereby explaining the milk of true permanence.
Thus, while the names of the initial and final milks are identical, their meanings differ.

Regarding "the same at the beginning and different at the end": because various bodhisattvas initially shared in the view of false permanence, but later, when their faculties were matured, [the Buddha] preached impermanence for them;

this is called being "different at the end. Initially [he preached] impermanence, and later he preached true permanence; this constitutes two layers of "the same at the beginning and different at the end," all of which was done to observe the capacities of beings and await the proper time.

Regarding "bestowing the gift of eternal physical strength," it means that one first bestows impermanent physical strength; this is because one now opens up the previously bestowed impermanent physical strength to bestow it as eternally abiding physical strength.
Regarding "due to the bhikṣu’s request to remain," this refers to the bhikṣu who practices the threefold cultivation and adheres to the teaching of impermanence, requesting the Tathāgata to remain.
"Throughout the world for one kalpa or half a kalpa, do not enter nirvana.
To "reject the false and discuss the true" means to reject the three types of false cultivation and to explain the superior cultivation, which is termed "the true."

"Exhorting with earnestness" means as explained extensively in the following text. He exhorted him to inquire about the precepts with eloquence and skillful means, repeating his request again and again;
hence it is called "earnest."

Regarding "bestowing in accordance with questions": beginning from Kāśyapa’s inquiry in the *Dīrghāyuṣka-parivarta* (Chapter on Long Life) and extending through fourteen chapters, [the Buddha] extensively answers those questions, causing all to realize impermanence and ensuring that the Dharma is not obstructed; this is termed "bestowing."
"The dharma-rain overflowing" means that one's own practice is internally full, while transforming others constitutes the overflow.
"Filling the city of Kuśinagara" means that the fifty-two assemblies all received the flavor of the Dharma within this city;
thus it is called "filling."
Regarding skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*): the Tathāgata, manifesting illness by assuming a sick body, extensively taught the state of being without illness.
He caused [beings] to advance in the practice of the five modes of conduct and the ten virtues; therefore, it is called "prior."
"Kāśyapa’s threefold entreaty" refers to the passage in the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" (Xiànbìng pǐn) where Kāśyapa thrice urges and thrice requests the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma.
"Fused and joyful" (*róng yì*) means joyfully pleased.

"Explaining the three to indicate the one" means explaining three types of sick people: first, those who slander the Mahāyāna; second, those who commit the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*); and third...
The icchantika—such a disease is certainly incurable. "Pointing to one" refers to pointing to a person who can be cured;
whether they encounter a caregiver or not, they will all be healed.
"Vast and inexhaustible" means immense and great. The essence of nirvāṇa pervades all places; since the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual, it is said to be inexhaustible.
Regarding the phrase "to cite one and it encompasses all": "one" refers to Buddha-nature. Since Buddha-nature subsumes everything throughout the ten directions, it is said that it "encompasses all.

This is like pointing to saltiness when speaking of the ocean: the ocean possesses manifold virtues, and though the myriad streams all converge there, they share the single taste of salt. This is the metaphor.
The Buddha is like the ocean. All sentient beings alike return to the ocean of the Buddha-nature within *nirvāṇa*, wherein there is nothing that is not fully encompassed.
As for the meaning of *nirvāṇa*, it is simply the Buddha-nature; all sentient beings possess it entirely, and this is what is called *nirvāṇa*.
This is because of the underlying principle.
Regarding the statement that "the substance of Buddha-nature is neither good nor evil," etc.: the principle of the direct cause (zhengyin) does not pertain to good or evil;
rather, its nature permeates both good and evil. Now, speaking from the perspective of this principle, it is designated as "neither."
Regarding "pervasive and boundless": its essence and its function permeate all phenomena; thus it is called "boundless.
The essence of Buddha-nature is like empty space, and its radiant color-form likewise pervades all things, for both its two functions—good and evil—also pervade all things.

Regarding the phrase "encompassing" (*nang-kòu*) and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "It is like a treasure within a bag; if it is not extracted and shown to others, no one will know of it. The Buddha-nature is likewise.
Like the treasure in the bag, it is now revealed throughout both good and evil. Here, "encompassing" (*kuài*) means to bind together or summarize;

"broadly" (*gài*) means to outline or provide a general summary. The *Zhìguānjì* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*) states: "That which has a bottom is called a 'bag' (*náng*); that which has no bottom is called a 'sack' (*náng*)."
Regarding those who act with goodness: all sentient beings are like Rāhula; they are all the true sons of the Buddha.
Regarding those who act with evil: the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was a son of the Bodhisattva, yet he constantly sought out the faults of the Buddha and became an icchantika.
In the assembly at the Nirvana, they were granted their predictions of enlightenment.
Since these two sons are thus, they are both the sons of the Tathāgata—whether virtuous or non-virtuous—and equally possess the functioning of Buddha-nature.
Regarding the phrase "employing both the heterodox and the orthodox": "employing" has the same meaning [as "transformative function"].

It also carries the sense of "transformative activity. As for "the heterodox followers of the ten outsiders": "heterodox" refers to the followers of the Six Heretical Teachers; "outsiders" refers to the ten types of non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas).

"The middle is also analogous to this" means that among the three flavors—the partial, the great, and the perfect—the intermediate ones involve the refutation of the small and the entry into the great; thus, they constitute the meanings of "present" and "past.

Regarding "the inverse and the compliant are mutually dependent," the inverse depends upon the compliant, and the compliant depends upon the inverse; therefore, they are said to be "mutually dependent" (*xiang*).

"Beginningless yet beginning, ending in the endless": the essence of *nirvāṇa* is fundamentally without beginning or end; it is now divided into five chapters, hence the mention of "beginning and end.

Regarding "the exhaustion of evil and the perfection of good," the exhaustion of evil refers to both the provisional and the profound levels, while the perfection of good refers to the ultimate stage of realization. This should also be understood accordingly.
Dividing this according to the six identities (*liu ji*), it is called the "exhaustion of evil.
When both subduing and gathering have ceased, the period of transformation is complete; yet if there are those not yet saved, one further establishes the conditions for them to attain liberation.
Regarding the teaching of the beginning, middle, and end: this refers to the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination. The "beginning" refers to addressing the assembly;

because there is giving by the assembly, and because one practices based on that giving, the practice through which one realizes the principle is called the "middle. That which has utility regarding the principle is called the "end."
Regarding the general discussion that every word and every deed is bestowed upon sentient beings: "words" refers to the teaching of *nirvāṇa*, as the subsequent text states:
"If one hears the two characters 'eternal-abiding,' one will not fall into the evil realms," and so forth. "Deeds" refers to the activity of transforming people through cause and effect.

This means that the five practices are the cause and the ten virtues are the fruit. Sentient beings—namely, the fifty-two classes of beings, down to the dung beetle—are all given the gift of buddha-nature.
Regarding the "separate questions and conditions": thirty-four questions serve as the conditions, and the Buddha provides extensive answers in fourteen chapters;
therefore, it is said that he "bestows" them.
That the text is extensive means that it answers the questions at length.

That the matters are clear means that Cunda’s offering of the three constant virtues and four merits, the three dots of the letter *i*, and Kāśyapa’s subsequent inquiry regarding giving are all elucidated;
therefore, it is said to be "clear."

The compass and square: the compass makes circles and the square makes rectangles. If one explains partiality and gradualness as being like the square, and explains the Great [Vehicle] as being like the circle, then by using the square to assist the circle, the Dharma can be grasped;
practicing in accordance with it accords with principle, and thus it is called "practice."

This sutra elucidates the Buddha-nature from beginning to end because it clarifies the Buddha-nature, the various aspects of the Buddha-nature, its bestowal, and even the functioning of the Buddha-nature.
As for the separate presentation of one round of question and answer, this refers to the six rounds of clarifying the meaning of the Buddha-nature by Siṃhanāda in the following text. As for...

There are six layers; however, because they are discussed collectively as six sections, it is said to be "one. Alternatively, although there are five chapters, they are clarified within a single chapter, and thus it is said to be "one."
Regarding the phrase "like the grasses and trees of the great earth": the great earth is like the Buddha-nature, and sentient beings are like the grasses and trees.

Therefore, within the *Lotus Sūtra*, there are the three types of grasses and two types of trees; the five vehicles and seven virtues all grow by means of this great earth. Hence, it is called "function."
"My teaching is also like this" means that the Dharma of Buddha-nature pervades both good and evil; therefore, it is called "universal.

When discussed specifically regarding its inclusion of evil and its inclusion of heterodoxy, such evil and heterodoxy do not go beyond the four *siddhāntas*. The fact that evil and heterodoxy are not identical constitutes the *loka-saṃvṛti* (worldly) standpoint.
Turning the mind toward it is the arising of goodness; destroying evil is the application of the remedy; entering into principle is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the citation of scriptural evidence, according to the text there are both general and specific applications: multiple passages constitute the general, while a single passage constitutes the specific.

Regarding the invocation of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions: this is spoken because they are currently at a lower stage; thus, there is the word "invocation. By means of provisional skillful means, they are led toward the ultimate reality, so that they may simply receive benefit.
As for the "Great Lion’s Roar," it refers to definitive teaching. A Bodhisattva is like a lion cub, and their roar is like the birth of a lion.
Therefore, it is called "great.

It was fortunate that there were many who could bestow gifts upon us. The Tathāgata clarified permanence from beginning to end, and Cunda filled the great assembly with eight *droṇas* of sugarcane syrup;
thus, it is said there were "many. Because the gift of food clarifies permanence, it is said they "could [bestow]."

Furthermore, those who cultivate with single-minded devotion do so with the mind set on Great Nirvana, practicing the five modes of conduct (*pañca-kṛtya*) and the non-sequential [practices], and so forth.

Regarding the attainment of the ten merits: since "merits" refer to realization (*adhigama*) and the "five modes of conduct" refer to cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the Buddha-nature is elucidated through the meaning of realization.
This is the meaning.
As for the "six phrases," they simply refer to six rounds of question and answer. The Tathāgata fully answers these six phrases.

Regarding the citation of a passage from a single location, it clarifies that the five kinds of Buddha-nature correspond to the five chapters; specifically, the Śūraṅgama corresponds to the invocation.

The *saṃgha* corresponds to giving (*dāna*); the *vajra* corresponds to conduct (*caryā*); the "lion's roar" corresponds to meaning (*artha*); and buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) corresponds to function (*vṛtti*).
These four are the means of realization, while buddha-nature is that which is realized. This is because both the subject (the means) and the object (that which is realized) are mutually dependent.
As for the statement that "the Buddha-nature is not one," if in principle there is not even one, how could there be five?
It is now designated by these five names in order to lead one to understand the principle that it is not five.
All of them were companions and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the Tathāgata, such as Mañjuśrī and others; they were all his teachers in the past, while now they are his disciples.

At the time when he was practicing the causes [of Buddhahood], they were his fellow practitioners; or, having already attained realization or being about to attain it, they assisted the Buddha in his transformative activities.
Therefore, they are called "spiritual friends."
Regarding "universally illuminating the principle" (zhōujiǎo jīlǐ): it is called "universal" (zhōu) because the knowledge of all modes (zhòngzhì) fully encompasses both the provisional and the real.

There are two kinds of principles: first, the principle that is realized; second, the principle of the way. Both are capable of being the illuminator and the illuminated, thereby forming the conditions for spiritual capacity (jīyuán).

Regarding "excavating the treasury of enlightenment" (*bodhigarbha*): "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) refers to the Buddha. The principle of the Buddha-nature treasury exists within the bodies of sentient beings, yet people do not know it.
The Tathāgata reveals it; this is illustrated by the metaphor of "excavation. Therefore, the subsequent passage speaks of "weeding out the weeds and filth.
"Treasury" (*garbha*) carries the meaning of "containing" or "storing."
If one follows the one who establishes the teaching, the teaching is spoken by virtue of wisdom; now, from the perspective of the teaching, it is called "giving.
Regarding the phrase "the five are not swayed": the five refer to sequential practice, while the one refers to non-sequential practice.

By means of the one, the five are guided so that they are all made harmonious, upright, and free from all crookedness or deviation, just as empty space cannot be tilted or disturbed by partiality or narrowness.
It is movement.
As for "shattering and dispersing afflictions": afflictions are as firm and solid as a diamond (*vajra*), and can only be destroyed by the horn of a sheep or the shell of a tortoise.
These "delusions" refer to the three delusions; here they are spoken of collectively, hence the phrase "the bonds of delusion are completely dispersed."
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to that which is signified by names. A name is that which can express; thus, the principle underlying the name is taken as the "signified.
This signified is precisely the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. It does not transcend the secret treasury of the Buddha-nature and the three virtues, all of which ultimately converge in eternal quiescence.
Regarding this meaning of "sovereignty," it pervades all places.

As for the mutual identity of essence and function: in the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), the stages prior to the [first] ground constitute function external to the essence; thus, they have not yet attained such identity.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao), function is identical to the essence, because one returns to the essence from within function.
Regarding the statement that "within all phenomena there is the nature of peace and bliss": peace and bliss are none other than nirvana.
All phenomena do not transcend the ten realms of the dependent and the primary; thus, they all possess the nature of nirvana.
"All returning to the upright and good" means gathering the evil into the good and gathering the deviant into the upright.
Regarding "the words and meanings having a basis": where there are both words and meaning, the wise employ them; where there are words but no meaning, the ordinary person employs them;

where there are neither words nor meaning, the fool employs them. Now, these five chapters are all supported by textual evidence; following the texts [is as follows]: [The text continues with the specific citations.]
This interpretation is also consistent with the sūtras; it does not differ from the local people who close their eyes and stubbornly dig away at the truth.

Seventh, regarding those who present divergent interpretations: first, I shall refute the Liang Emperor (Wu). As in the *Lotus Sūtra*, he was first refuted by Guangzhai, while other schools were intimidated by his reputation.
At the hour of dusk and midnight, I further refute He Wen. When the Tathāgata preached the sūtra, it reached the middle of the night.
[The Buddha] entered parinirvāṇa. How can one exclusively divide the middle period into two parts—the middle morning and the middle afternoon?
Regarding the "Invitations to the Sangha" (Ju-si qing-seng), there are two fascicles which I have not yet examined.
As for the current division into chapters according to the Dharma, "Dharma" refers to the scriptural text as previously described; all of these are fully supported by authoritative sources.
Regarding the phrase "merely using a small portion of the chapters": our school (Jinjia) takes the two chapters from Kāśyapa to Cundabhadrī as the "application" (yòng);
Guangzhai’s *Líutōng* (Circulation) uses only the single chapter on Cundabhadrī, and thus it is called "small."

Regarding the "spiritual flavor" (*lingwei*) and so forth: the text is divided into four sections. The question constitutes one part; the *nidāna* (origination) constitutes two; the answer constitutes three; and the residual force constitutes four. Now, as for the intent of this refutation:
within the text, there are thirty-four formal questions answered up to the "Chapter on the Great Assembly.

Subsequently, from the "Virtuous King’s Lion’s Roar" down to Ājñātakauṇḍinya, there are further questions and answers. Why, then, do you single out only the preceding portion as being the "residual force"?
Regarding the "Gate of Past and Present Causes and Conditions": the past refers to the Deer Park, and the present refers to this sutra;
these serve as the causes and conditions. As for "attaining the real and losing the provisional": it may be that those who came from the Deer Park attained the real;

yet, having been matured through various stages by the three samādhis during the intermediate period, and having entered stage by stage with sharp faculties, they must still await the present conditions. Furthermore, this is because the provisional is able to lead toward the real. Now...
The phrase "breaking it down beneath" means to refute [the opponent's position].
Regarding the "abbreviated and extensive gates," the question is abbreviated while the answer is extensive; this merely refers to breaking it down beneath.

As for now combining these into the chapter on "Practice" (xing): since practice encompasses both cause and fruit, why would one need the latter two? Now, they are combined to break down what lies beneath.

Regarding the phrase "difficult to resolve due to being mixed": this is because the essence and function of the Buddha-nature are inseparable; the following section now analyzes them separately to refute [the opposing view]. As for the "Master of the Ground" (Dishī):
previously it was mentioned that Vasubandhu provided this explanation, and here he is called the "Master of the Ground.

This title should be understood as referring to him based on his composition of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*. Even though Tianqin (Vasubandhu) composed a thousand treatises, what prevents him from having such a name?
Regarding "the division of manifesting supernatural powers in reverse": this refers to arising from the Truth to manifest function, wherein the high demonstrates the low traces.
All fifty-two assemblies are defined by their supernatural powers; this is called "breaking down from below."
Regarding "the lineage that severs doubt": Cunda attains the five fruits of permanence as his lineage. This lineage is simply the Buddha-nature.

As for "severing doubt," [Cunda] raised difficulties concerning the five fruits of the past and present to the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata then provided answers in order to cause him to have no further doubts.
Regarding the section on the true meaning of the True Dharma (*saddharma-tattvārtha*): the Middle Way is the True Dharma; this Dharma is itself reality.
Because this reality is the meaning elucidated by the teaching below, it is called "true meaning" (*tattvārtha*).
Regarding the "stages of cultivation through skillful means" (*upāya-bhāvanā-aṅga*): the five practices constitute the skillful means, while the ten virtues constitute the completion of cultivation.

As for the phrase "the ability to complete such cultivation," it is redundant because the meaning of "completion of cultivation" is identical to that of "entry into realization. Therefore, it is said to be superfluous.
What follows now is the correct explanation.
Regarding the section on "Abiding in Compassion": Kāśyapa Bodhisattva established extensive refutations for the sake of the final age, so that the multitude might attain understanding;
therefore, it is called "compassion."
Regarding the manifestation of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect): it causes the deviant to return to the correct; thus, its characteristic is "manifestation.
The phrase "holding evil and turning toward the good" explains the reason for this.

As for the difference between the "opening" and "closing" of the Hexi [master], the Hexi master synthesizes while the Xinghuang master analyzes; this is merely a distinction between analysis and synthesis.
[This is] the Ear. In the earlier division by Xinghuang, eight gates were established; however, the subsequent explanations of the "Gate of Practice" and the "Gate of Stages" were still combined.
One should have stated them as the "Fifth Gate of Stages" and the "Sixth Gate of the Middle Way," etc. (The details remain unclear).
Regarding the second part, the detailed explanation, this is the correct interpretation of our own school. First, the general introduction is explained; next, the specific introduction is explained.
Within the initial general introduction, first the meaning is explained, and then the text is explained.

Regarding the initial reference to the "Chapter on Invocation": "Chapter" (zhang) refers to a formal section or division. As the *Shijing* says: "The words of those gentlemen of the capital formed complete chapters.

As for "the Way of the three periods being the same": the sūtras spoken by all Buddhas of the three periods invariably conclude with these words [evam mayā śrutam], which distinguishes them from non-Buddhist teachings.
The two characters for "Dao" (the Way) and "A-ou" (Āyu) are identical; thus, their paths are the same.

Regarding the distinction between the faculties of the teaching gates: since the teaching itself is the gate, it is called the "teaching gate. The first three teachings differ in terms of time and place, and are therefore termed "distinct.
Although the *Lotus Sūtra* is the same as the *Amṛta* (Butter) stage, the text of this sūtra further addresses the faculties of beings in the final age. It is complete.
There are four teachings; hence it is said that the capacities [of sentient beings] are distinct.

Regarding the phrase "the sutras, the paths, and the supports are each distinct": this refers to the merging of the canopies and the manifestation of transformations in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*; the donning of robes and holding of alms bowls in the *Vajracchedikā*;
and the rain of the four kinds of flowers in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

These words, being exhortations to inspire faith, are intended to engender wholesome roots; they should fully clarify the four *siddhāntas*. The distinction between the general and the specific corresponds to the *loka-saṃvṛti* (worldly) intention.

The two characters "Ā" and "U" used to refute the non-Buddhists correspond to the *pratipakṣa* (remedial) intention. The fact that the Way is the same throughout the three periods of time corresponds to the *anuśaṃsā* (beneficial) intention.
The essence of the Dharma as it is heard is the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth). For now, we shall discuss this in terms of engendering [wholesome roots].
This is because it is spoken from the perspective of the "virtuous side.
Next, the text is explained. First, regarding the phrase "the principle transmitted": "principle" refers to the essence of the Dharma heard;
the secret treasury of the three virtues is that which is transmitted. This specifically identifies Ānanda as the person who transmits it.
Regarding "conforming to the opportunity and the principle": when the capacity is perfect and the principle is perfect, such that the capacity accords with the principle, it is called "conformity.
That the fifty-two assemblies all know [the Buddha] as eternally abiding is what is called the "principle."
Regarding the "master from whom one receives [the teaching]": the Buddha is the Master who is the source of what is received, and the sentient being is the person who is capable of receiving it.
Regarding the "place where it is heard": the "place" refers to that upon which one relies; the *nirvāṇa* of the three virtues is that which is heard.
Regarding "mutually verifying one another": from the person who hears [the teaching] verifying the principle heard, up to the assembly of fellow listeners, it is thus called "mutual verification.
"Wishing to cause those of the future" means that this sutra is intended for the capacities of beings in the final age; "will" (jāng) refers to the future.

Furthermore, the "various sūtras, both great and small" refers to a classification according to the teachings (*jiao*). "Small" refers to the Three Piṭakas; "Great" refers to the Shared and Distinct [teachings].

This is because there is a difference between what is transmitted and that which transmits within the two teachings and the Three Piṭakas. Based on the previous explanation which categorized them according to the arising of goodness through causes and conditions, this explanation categorizes them according to the teachings.

Regarding the *honji-suijaku* (original and trace) contemplation of the mind, this refers specifically to the *Lotus Sūtra*. If one establishes the principles of essence and function (*tǐyòng*) through *honji-suijaku*, why would the constant contemplation of *nirvāṇa* while practicing the path not also be valid?
However, it does not equal the thoroughness and detail of the fourfold interpretation found in that [Lotus] text.

If one says that understanding merges with the Truth, then understanding is that which can transmit, and what is transmitted is the Truth—just as it is said that "form is itself emptiness" and so forth.

Regarding "the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom is stilled": the reduction of the body to ashes refers to the initial stage of the Hīnayāna, while the stilling of wisdom refers to the Shared Teaching; these differ in that the former involves the destruction of form, whereas the latter involves the negation of emptiness.
Furthermore, if one says that "conforming to capacity" (jì) constitutes "suchness" (rú), this refers to the emptiness of the preceding two teachings.

Regarding "the phenomenal being contrary while the principle is conforming": prior to the stages (bhūmi), entering the stage of food (i.e., the stage of practice) is "contrary"; ascending to the stages and realizing the principle is "conforming. Moreover, regarding the ten practices (daśa-pratipatti)...

Engaging in the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) to benefit sentient beings while remaining within the conventional world is "contrary" [to the ultimate], whereas practicing contemplation based on the principle is "conformable.
Regarding such passages as "Thus have I heard," one should provide the fourfold explanation as previously established; the text here is abbreviated.
For a detailed account, refer to the four types of Ānanda who did not hear [the teaching] in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding what is commonly heard in the world, although it is said to be "constant," one must still distinguish its differences.

As detailed in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), each and every passage therein employs four types of interpretation: based on causes and conditions (*yinyuan*), based on the teaching (*jiao*), based on the primary and secondary traces (*benji*), and based on the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*).

These differ from the establishment of "causes and conditions" and "based on the teaching" according to the meaning in this present text; the names of the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold truths) appear in the latter two [sections].
Thus, it is non-existent.

Now, to clarify this, the following section provides an extensive explanation in five chapters, which is further divided into two parts: first, a general correspondence; second, a detailed individual correspondence.
Regarding "not different" (*bù yì*) meaning "as if non-existent," and "not 'is'" meaning "this": the fifty-two assemblies are all assemblies of the *nirvāṇa* of these three virtues.
As for "different" meaning "definitely different," it means that the fifty-two assemblies are each distinct from one another.
Those who have realized this meaning are all Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body. Their diverse species and extraordinary forms are, in essence, the same as the Buddha-nature they have heard.
"Diverse species" (詭類) refers to the strange and anomalous; that is, the multitude of strange anomalies. Therefore, it is said they are "variegated and mixed. "Mixed" (雜) also implies difference.
Regarding "the coarse and the refined reflecting and supplanting one another": humans and the like are considered coarse, while devas and the like are considered refined.
As they reflect and supplant one another, the subsequent passage states: "twice as superior as before," and so forth.
If one views them with the eyes of an ox or a sheep—that is, what is seen by the fleshly eyes of an ordinary person—the fifty-two assemblies are no different from what an ox or a sheep sees.
If one views them with the Buddha-eye, abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.
To realize that they are neither different nor not different is to understand that they share the same Buddha-nature.

My previous failure to hear [this] refers to the fact that the first three teachings provisionally revealed the reality; whereas what I have now heard is that all [teachings] reveal the secret treasury.
Regarding the statement that "the fruits of the two kinds of giving are equal," both past giving and present giving are heard to be eternally abiding.
Therefore, Cunda cites the past to challenge the present, while the Tathāgata cites the present in response; thus, there is no difference between the two types of giving.
The "various flavors of the Dharma" refers to the flavors of both the ultimate and provisional teachings; it is also the flavor of the four teachings and five periods.

Regarding the phrase "the practice of a single period," this "single period" differs from the previous "single period"; in all cases, it refers to the complete perfection of the round (perfect) practice.

All practices are simultaneous. Because the realization of a single moment is equal in its merit and other qualities, the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom all conclude with the stages of attainment;
they are not realized sequentially.
"In a single thought-moment" means that at the time of realizing the Dharma-body, one is immediately able to teach and transform sentient beings within the hundred realms;
hence it is said, "manifesting bodies in the five destinies," and so forth.
"The body of return and cessation" refers to the locus of reliance, which signifies the Dharma-body; therefore, the subsequent text says, "placing all..."
Within my secret treasury, I too shall not long remain; thus it is called a "dwelling.
As for "driving out the heterodox and leading in the evil," this means driving away all non-Buddhists so that they leave the six great cities and all head toward Kuśinagara;
both the heterodox and the orthodox are all delivered, causing them to enter the secret treasury.
"Whether it be another or oneself": "another" refers to the various sons who are established in the secret treasury; "oneself" refers to [the father] who will also dwell therein before long.
Regarding the teaching that the three sons together constitute the three fields, as in the passage below concerning the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and icchantikas...
The essence of their minds is entirely equal. "Three fields" refers to the superior, middling, and inferior fields.
As for the statement that "the multitudes do not exceed the eight Buddhas," it means that all fifty-two classes of beings possess the nature of the true cause;
therefore, it is said they do not exceed equality. Regarding the "eight": the past constitutes one, the present ten directions constitute one, and the six [stages] are collectively termed as one.

The Buddhas are thus six; these constitute the eight Buddhas. Alternatively, it is said that the past and present Buddhas constitute seven, and with the future Buddha added, they become eight (the source of this latter account remains to be verified).
"Nothing surpasses it" means that among all sentient beings, the Buddha is supreme; therefore, it is said to be unsurpassed.
Regarding "the five fruits undergo transition," both the five fruits of the mundane world and the five fruits of the supramundane world are subject to transition.
Thus, the subsequent passage poses the objection: "This is an impermanent body, a body sustained by various foods; how can the retributions of the two kinds of giving be equal?"
This is the distinction.
As for the winding and meandering of rivers and streams, the three previous teachings were circuitous and differed in their skillfulness or clumsiness;
the present teaching is like a straight cord leading directly into the Western Sea.
If one who has not yet realized emptiness still perceives manifestations, how much more so for those with the fleshly eye?
How much more so for one who can perceive the nature—the Buddha-nature of the Middle Way?

As for one who sees it with complete clarity and distinctness, this refers to the person of perfect cultivation; such a person may also be analyzed according to the six stages of attainment, meaning they have partially attained it.
It is clear, even unto ultimate clarity. As the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* states:
"That is to say, when the faculty of the eye is complete and unimpaired, through cultivation, one sees with distinct clarity," and so forth.

Regarding what is now heard concerning the "low-mi" spirit-turtle: "low-mi" refers to a wicked fish, while the "spirit-turtle" is a sacred turtle. Whereas [the former] was on land, they are now both together in the water;
this is a metaphor for the fact that within the river of *nirvāṇa*, the Buddha-nature of the seven kinds of sentient beings is one and the same.
"To turn toward the place where the Buddha dwells" refers to the locus of the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*).
"Bestowing it upon the multitude" means returning that locus of the three virtues to bestow it upon sentient beings;
this is the intended meaning of what is explained (*vācya*), for both the giver and the recipient are none other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Regarding "attracting the heterodox and gathering the wicked," it should be read as "attracting the heterodox and gathering the wicked," meaning they are brought together to return to one's own abode.
Thus, this general introduction of the three points proceeds from the broad to the narrow; because the essence of the Dharma heard possesses the three virtues, they are called the "three points."
I have heard that the "Thus Have I Heard" (evam mayā śrutam) serves as the introduction to the Prajñāpāramitā because it pertains to the initial stage of hearing.
The "At one time" (ekasmin samaye) serves as the introduction to liberation because wisdom is the principle that supports the raft.
The "Together with [the assembly]" serves as the introduction to the three dots (the three seals of existence) being non-void, for it provides companions who testify to the faith.
When I hear of the joy of the sequence, it is the joy of extensive learning and discernment; this is precisely Great Nirvāṇa.
When one attains purity through the sequence at a single moment, one practices in accordance with the principle, such that delusions and karma are both extinguished.
The "Preface on Abiding" refers to the eternal abiding of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The "Preface on Hearing Together" means that all who hear together take the sovereign True Self (*ātman*) as their companion.

The "Preface on the Five Prefaces" sets forth the essential meaning of the sutra; this essential meaning is simply the Buddha-nature, the three virtues, and the Nirvana of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Purity is taken as the essential point.
"The first is the method of enumeration" refers to the numerical method; from one to ten, all are methods of counting.

"It is merely a worldly meaning" means that in the Tripitaka teachings, Bodhisattvas have not yet severed their afflictions and are thus the same as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). As for the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), they have severed [the afflictions].
Delusion is itself not the mundane world.
That emptiness is "one" refers to the meaning of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). Although the preceding teaching is empty, it is still merely an emptiness achieved through analytical reduction.

Regarding the unification of the True and the Conventional: in the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), the first stage (Prathamabhūmi) of the Bodhisattva is the True, while the ten practices (Daśabhūmika-pūrvaṅgama-caryā) are the Conventional; upon reaching the stages (Bhūmis), one realizes their unity.
Therefore, it is called "convergence.

"The one is all" means that within the ultimate (the true), there is the conventional; "all is one" means that within the conventional, there is the ultimate. This is both the simultaneous negation and the simultaneous illumination of both.
All of these manifest the Middle Way: permanence and impermanence, neither permanence nor impermanence, both permanent and impermanent, and so forth.
According to this principle, one contains three, and three are nine; yet nine are simply one. That they are neither three nor one is precisely because each and every one is itself.

Regarding the three bodies and four meanings: "four" refers to the four teachings. In the first two teachings, the response body (nirmāṇakāya) is the same, yet there remains a distinction of superiority and inferiority.

In the distinct teaching (biejiao), the recompense body (saṃbhogakāya) further possesses the difference between being for one's own use or for the use of others. This is because, in the perfect teaching (yuanjiao), the dharma body (dharmakāya) is the reality.
The phrase "the subsequent meaning lies in the present" refers to its classification as belonging to the Perfect [Teaching].
"That is, the people of the land" means that because people are born in this place, it is called their "native land.

"Their union resembles entwined branches" refers to the name for *liánlǐ* (entwined) trees; for instance, when a family possesses righteousness, the trees may be moved by this virtue and grow together in such a manner.
The sweet-tasting *táng* tree is planted to manifest virtue.
As for its resemblance to "yielding to one another," it is like the yielding between the noble and the humble in the world, where the withered and the flourishing mutually concede to each other.

This alone is the explanation through the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*) regarding the city below. The various [interpretations] correspond to the differences among the four views, as will be fully explained below.
Following the previous [method], one should explain this by combining it with the four *siddhāntas*: the different names for the city correspond to the *laukika* (worldly) level;

the arising of goodness in those who see [the city] corresponds to the *pauruṣeya* (human/beneficial) level; the resolve of the strongman corresponds to the *pratipakṣa* (remedial/destroying evil) level; and the non-duality of withering and flourishing corresponds to the *paramārtha* (ultimate) level.
Regarding "showing compassion to people": boundless compassion that pervades the entire dharma-realm is what is meant by "showing to people.
Regarding "using a city to symbolize permanence": the city of the three virtues cannot be shaken or overturned, and is therefore permanent.
The Mallas represent me because, being sovereign, they have no one to whom they are subject.
The auspicious river represents purity; it is also called the River of Golden Sand. Because its sand is pure, it can extinguish the defilements of sin; thus, it represents purity.
Regarding the trees representing bliss: because trees provide coolness and many people delight in them, they symbolize the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the city being indestructible representing permanence: since destruction is impermanence, being indestructible symbolizes permanence.
"Abundance expresses bliss": as worldly abundance is itself bliss, so too is nirvana, being fully endowed with the eight flavors.
"Arrogance toward adversaries expresses the self": arrogance necessarily implies sovereignty.
Regarding "the absence of difficulty in manifesting purity": the eight worldly winds (*aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ*) cannot defile it.
Regarding "the *rishi* (powerful one) manifesting permanence without attachment": previously it was said that he manifests the self; now it is said that he manifests permanence. Why?

Because the interpretation of the meaning within this school is perfectly comprehensive and sovereign. Furthermore, within each of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), every single virtue is endowed with the four virtues (*caturguṇa*). As explained at length...
In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the ten kinds of triads all possess the four virtues.
"The eternal flow symbolizes permanence" means that because it is eternal, it is permanent.
"The pair in the east symbolizes permanence" means that the eastern direction belongs to wood; wood takes flourishing and luxuriance as its meaning, and it is also the foremost among all directions.
Because it is the head, it is eternal. According to this principle, one should also say "eternal and non-eternal," and so forth; however, only one side has been mentioned for now.
The meaning of the bird metaphor appearing in the subsequent text—where both aspects are presented—is precisely this point.
The two pillars in the south symbolize music (*yue*). The south corresponds to fire; since fire can bring all things to completion, it represents music.
The two pillars in the west symbolize the self (*wo*). The west corresponds to metal; just as when people possess gold, they have mastery over its use, so too does the self exercise sovereignty.
Regarding the north representing purity: the north belongs to water, and water takes purity as its essential meaning; this meaning is most manifest there.
The center belongs to earth, which presides over the four directions.

Regarding the phrase "if one can [distinguish] the general and the specific": the former refers to the general, while the latter refers specifically to the four virtues. These four virtues are in fact the three virtues;
these three virtues are precisely the dwelling place of the Buddha.

If it is said that the following is an explanation according to the teachings: "those in birth and death" refers to what is seen by those of the Tripitaka [teaching], as they contemplate impermanence;
"what is seen by the followers of the Two Vehicles" refers to the Two Vehicles of the Shared Teaching; and "what is seen by those who have ascended to the stages" refers to the Distinct Teaching.
Regarding the "eight Buddhas among the nine Buddhas": the eight Buddhas are as previously described; by adding the current Teacher, they become nine.

If one interprets every sentence in this manner, it serves as a model for the subsequent passages, all of which are explained according to the Four Teachings. It may be omitted here as the text is abbreviated.
"Regarding 'I say': this is the interpretation composed by my late teacher Miaole.
This difference in perspective concerns the distinction between the analytical [teaching] and the essence [of the teaching].
'The Way of Mahāyāna' refers to the path of the Great Vehicle, which differs from the paths of the two vehicles according to the analytical teaching. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*..."
He rebuts this, saying: "It is like a narrow path that cannot accommodate two people walking side by side" (and so forth).
Regarding "the precepts, the mind, and the realization of the Path": the precepts refer to the ten precepts, the fivefold precepts, and so on; the mind refers to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
"Seeing" refers to the three truths in their sequential order; "the Path" refers to the three paths of liberation. To speak of these five aspects is like playing music that one does not hear.
Regarding the two types—the place and the time—one does not perceive the form of the Honored One with Distinctive Features, as if a candle had been extinguished and could no longer be seen.

"Furthermore, that which is not shared with the previous Buddhas" is provisionally determined by comparison with the Tripiṭaka: the form of one *zhàng* and six *cun* is comparable to the image of a *bhikṣu*.
"When the revelation is completed" refers to the completion of the revelation in the *Lotus Sūtra*. This sūtra itself states: "Eight thousand *bodhisattvas*..."
"Receiving the prediction of enlightenment amidst flowers" refers to the attainment of the prophecy.
Regarding "the Great One praises his virtues," there is no separate textual passage; thus, the character "Great" (Dà) is employed to extol him.
"Mastery of the four Āgamas and the Tripiṭaka" means a comprehensive understanding of both internal (Buddhist) and external (non-Buddhist) scriptures.
Regarding "surpassing the ninety-five kinds": there are ninety-six paths and scriptures; since one path belongs to the correct [teaching], it is said that there are "five" [kinds of heterodox paths].
Some say that the six founders of the non-Buddhist paths each had fifteen disciples, and including the original teachers themselves, this makes ninety-six.
However, this should not be taken as a definitive enumeration.
Those who are revered by the worthy and noble are precisely the worthy and noble ones within the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.

Those who have attained mastery over the provisional and real dharma-gates: the provisional refers to the four flavors, while the real is this present sutra; the provisional is itself the real, and the real is itself the provisional.

Regarding the "assembly of those destined for certainty" (niyata-gaṇa): it refers to the ultimate perfection of the Vehicle, wherein the five periods of teaching have reached their conclusion; thus it is called "destined.
As for the manifestation of great transformative power as previously described, this is the explanation according to the classification of teachings (yōkyō-shaku) as found in the preceding text.

Regarding "not looking upward" and so forth: these refer to being free from the four types of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). "Looking upward" means gazing at the stars; "downward" refers to cultivating fields and gardens;
"square" means engaging in the dispatching of messengers; and "horizontal" refers to various other forms of wrong livelihood for one's own sustenance.
This is called "one who destroys evil. One destroys evil by means of the three trainings.
That which sustains the life of wisdom is the wisdom of emptiness; emptiness-wisdom is the life-force.
Furthermore, there is no knower; the knower is also empty.
Regarding "one who cannot be terrified or delighted": because it is empty, there is neither terror nor delight.
Regarding "that which is entirely equal within all dharmas": within the ten realms, the Buddha-nature is the self-sustaining, eternally abiding life-force.

Regarding the phrase "the latter two monks, etc.": the treatise bases itself on the stage of the inner ordinary person (*ābhyantarapṛthagjana*) to designate them as "possessing shame" (*hrīmattva*). Here, however, we advance to take those of the "thin ground" (*tanubhūmi*) who possess purity as being "possessing shame.
As for the phrase "the other two bhikṣus, in whose teachings it exists": this refers to the "mute sheep" (*mūka-eḍaka*) who violate the precepts, which pertains to all four *yāna* teachings.

Furthermore, there are four meanings: first, the manifestation of images is exclusively true; second, one should accept [the teaching] according to the advancement or retreat of those present; third, it is for the purpose of establishing karmic connections;
and fourth, it is for those monks who possess a sense of shame.
Therefore, regarding the phrase "the various assemblies" with its sub-commentary (etc.), within each assembly there are further four assemblies, which together constitute sixteen.
This is explained in detail as in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra). Alternatively, "counting the people" is an explanation based on the teaching (*jiao*).

Regarding "surrounded before and after": "surrounding" refers to the deportment of standing, while "circling" refers to the deportment of walking; these should also be understood according to the differences in the deportments of the four teachings (*catur-yāna*).
As for "with reverence through the three karmas," this is because both walking and standing are defined in terms of the three karmas (body, speech, and mind).
This explains the separate preface. Regarding the initial passage stating that "sound and time manifest the Dharma": "Sound" refers to the teaching of sound;
"time" indicates the moment when light arises and darkness ceases. The "zhong" (middle) month stands between the "meng" (first) and "ji" (last) months, symbolizing the Middle Way.
"On the day of the full moon" refers, as explained in the subsequent text, to the day when the Moon-Love Samādhi (*candravimala-samādhi*) reaches its perfection.
"Without waiting and not exceeding [the time]" means that the Tathāgata knows the proper timing and thus avoids the error of missing the capacity of sentient beings.
Now, precisely at the moment of approaching *nirvāṇa*, he gives rise to the Perfect and Eternal Dharma to simultaneously benefit those of the final age; thus, it does not miss their capacity.
As for those who attain liberation, their karmic conditions for the Path have ripened; hearing the Dharma of eternal abiding, they attain liberation.
As for those not yet liberated, this serves as the causal condition for their future liberation.
"Taking supernatural power as the root" means that, as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the lifespan chapter reveals the root of long duration;
therefore, he manifests supernatural power by stroking [the disciple's] head and entrusting him.
"Taking the great sound as the branch" means that what is now being taught is the teaching of the perfect and eternal Great Nirvāṇa, which is taken as the branch.
"Cause them to realize that there is neither beginning nor end" refers to realization in terms of principle (*li*).
Furthermore, "emptiness-wisdom as the basis," and so forth, refers to an explanation based on the teachings (*jiao*). In the two preceding teachings, the essence is analyzed to reveal emptiness;
"all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñā*) is specific [to the third teaching], while "true reality" (*bhūtatathatā*) pertains to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).
The note (and so forth) instructs that the four teachings be explained as all being the fundamental and derivative aspects of essence and function (*tǐyòng*).

Some interpret the power of formless concentration (*ārūpya-samādhi*) as intending to cite scriptural evidence to prove that formless concentration can give rise to transformations (*nirmāṇa*) in both the desire and form realms;

how then could such a state be without a body? Furthermore, the phrase "making offerings to the Buddha" and so forth belongs to the terminology of our own school; this [interpretation] is merely capable of being challenged.
The intention here is to permit the citation of texts such as the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (Renwang jing) to prove the existence of a body.

As for the phrase "the summit of the three realms of existence" (*tridhātu-agra*), if explained according to the teachings (*yōkyō*), the stages of "no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*) and so forth correspond to the two preceding teachings,
while the stage of "wondrous enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and so forth correspond to the latter two teachings.
Regarding "one who is invited": this may refer to an earthen Buddha, who is invited because the auxiliary Dharma has not yet arrived.

Since this meaning is broad, it refutes other interpretations; for now, the four teachings—provisional and real—are all pervasive, being fully endowed both horizontally and vertically, and thus it is called "broad."
Thus, those who are moved are not uniform; being not uniform, they comprise the fifty-two assemblies.
That the response to the universal proclamation is non-dual means that although there are two, they are non-dual—this is called "universal. Although non-dual, they appear as two.
"Universally reaching all capacities so that they may all now hear [it] is why it is called 'proclaiming' (*gao*).

To praise [the Buddha] so as to inspire veneration means: he is the Lord of the three realms, the Father of Great Compassion, and the Teacher who has appeared in the world; thus, one should universally revere and look up to him.
To proclaim [him] so as to inspire sorrowful longing is for the purpose of generating wholesome roots."
Regarding the mere recitation of the three titles: these three titles universally encompass all dharmas; therefore, they are frequently invoked in various sutras.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "If I were to analyze the meaning of these three phrases, I could not exhaust them even in immeasurable kalpas."
To clarify the three matters: they refer to the sovereign, one's parents, and one's teacher.
"Truly identical to all Buddhas" means that the foremost of the ten titles of the Buddhas of the ten directions is all called *Tathāgata*. "Truly" (*yun*) signifies "to accord with" (*he*).

"He is the Father of the World" means that the Father of the World dwells in a position of supreme honor; because he is comparable to a father who has transcended the world, he is called "Venerable and Exalted.

"He is the Lord of the World" means that, like a sovereign of a nation, he takes loyalty and filial piety as his kinship; he is able to give rise to the worldly rites between ruler and subject as a wholesome karma.
Now, the Lord who has transcended the world is able to give rise to the wholesome karmas of the Great and Small, the Partial and the Perfect, which is termed "Supreme Blessing."
It is a field.
Regarding those who are "World Teachers" (*lokaguru*): as for the term "teacher" (*śāstṛ*), one who is able to provide a model and standard for others is called a teacher.

Now, the World Teacher of the supramundane is able to sever the doubts of those with partial or limited views and bring about the realization of all-encompassing wisdom; therefore, he is called a "Teacher. Thus...
The passage from the *Cunda* [Sūtra] concerning "having no master" (*amukhya-guru*) explains the meaning of reverent devotion; this is precisely the sense of being "without a teacher.
The Sūtra states, "Today," which refers exactly to the morning of the fifteenth day of the second month.
The "Original Father-Master" refers to the father with whom one formed a karmic connection in the past; thus, he is called "Original.
"If even one were lost, the great vow would remain unfulfilled" means that because there was the power of a great vow in the past, [the Buddha] now pulls them out and bestows [liberation] upon them.
Because his mind is universal, it is called "regarding all equally."
Regarding the "binding of the three titles": it is because children return to their father, subjects return to their ruler, and disciples return to their teacher.

Regarding the "binding of the four immeasurables" (*catvāry apramāṇāni*): just as a house in the world can cover everything, so now, through unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*), one universally covers the entire *dharmadhātu*.
Since compassion is the root, they are called the "four immeasurables."

First, regarding the instruction to resolve doubts: as the subsequent text states, "If there are any doubts, you may now ask about them all," this encourages inquiries concerning the precepts and simultaneously addresses the uncertainties of those in later generations.

As for "expounding and elucidating": for over forty years, [the Buddha] had not yet been able to reveal and expound [this teaching]. Now, he fulfills the Buddha’s intent; thus, the five fruits are revealed first.
Regarding "the new *i* is now manifested": teachings of heterodox permanence are termed "old," while the meaning of the three dots (*am*) is termed "new."
The Great Awakened One is precisely the Omniscient One. "Awakened" (jue) means knowing; "Great" (da) means pervasive.
Regarding the phrase "the enlightened master is the lord and so forth": since there is a master, he is like the lord of his subjects or the father of his children;
one is thus three.

Regarding the mutual citation of one side: by citing the latter, one knows the former, hence it is called "Great Enlightenment" (Mahābodhi); by citing the former, one knows the latter, hence it is called "Tathāgata.
"Great" (Mahā) encompasses all ten titles [of the Buddha].

Regarding the clarification of the four meanings in each section: this refers to the meanings of the Four Teachings. Within each individual meaning, the three roles of Master, Parent, and Teacher are all fully present;
however, their explanations differ, which is why it is said that they are "in every section."
"At the time of the rising dawn": "Rising" (xu) means brightness; it refers to the time of the bright morning.
"Manifesting the arising of wisdom-brightness" means that at the moment the sun of the Great Nirvana first rises, the darkness of the three delusions is extinguished.
Regarding "the face and the mouth": the mouth symbolizes that the teaching shall continue unceasingly into the future; the "gate" (mouth) signifies the ability to connect cause and effect.
Therefore, light issues forth from the mouth.
This symbolizes that Buddha-nature is not identical to the six dharmas; that is to say, the nature of the true cause—the self and the five aggregates—is neither identical to nor separate from them.
Because it is free [from such things], it is represented by the mouth.
As for the "great ocean of *mahāparinirvāṇa*," it signifies that the Buddha-nature is vast and expansive, just as the ocean possesses manifold virtues.
As for "beings with great bodies," this represents the "greatness" of the dwelling place of sentient beings within the ten dharma-realms. The various tortoises...

The fish represent the primary retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*), while the precious jewels represent the secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*). Because these ten dharmas differ in terms of both the primary and secondary retributions, they are described as "various.

Because they share the same Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), it is said that their light pervades all. The Sūtra states that the radiance is of mixed colors to symbolize the differences among the six realms of existence.
The six kinds of form constitute the "mixture.
To deliver the Six Perfections is to uproot the suffering of the Three Realms; to purify the Six Faculties is to bestow the bliss of the Three Realms.
The Lotus Sūtra represents the semblance stage, while the Avataṃsaka Sūtra represents the true stage—the ten kinds of the Six Faculties.
Next, the four sections of text—from "explaining the luminous place" up to "emitting the six colors"—each fully embody the four *siddhāntas* (purposes of teaching);
this may be seen by examining their interpretation.
Regarding the mutual manifestation of height and breadth: height is subsumed within breadth, and breadth is subsumed within height, thereby avoiding prolixity in the text.
Regarding the mention of "among them," this refers specifically to within the three thousandfold world system and throughout the ten directions.

As for the six realms of existence being "obstructions of retribution," from the perspective of supramundane dharmas, all three realms—namely those of humans, devas, and so forth—are termed obstructions.

Regarding "obstacles removed and goodness produced": it is like when a person’s mind is free from anxiety and distress, they do not produce mental karma; if they do not utter sounds, they do not produce verbal karma;
if they do not raise their hands, they do not produce bodily karma. Now, as the three karmas receive this [teaching], the conditions are activated and obstacles are removed.
The light summons those who practice for *nirvāṇa*; the light manifests the teaching, for one practices in accordance with the teaching.
Regarding the mutual dependence of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*): ignorance is like the earth, while craving and views are like water; water depends upon the earth.
Now that all three delusions have been shattered, the earth shakes to manifest this.
"Those with conditions of delusion and craving": "delusion" is ignorance (*avidyā*), and "craving" is affliction (*kleśa*); since both arise from conditions, they are called "existent.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "at one time," although the wording suggests a sequence, the intended meaning is simultaneity.
How could one possibly dismiss the interpretations of others?
The scripture states, "At that time, all sentient beings," which refers precisely to the moment of the voice, light, and earthquake. "All" implies plurality;
it refers specifically to the fifty-two assemblies. Therefore, it is termed "collective."
The Sūtra says, "Each should exercise restraint. "Restraint" (cai) means to measure and deliberate; "restraint" (yi) means to suppress and endure.
Why did the Tathāgata emit light and cause the earth to tremble? It was because one should go to where the Buddha is; if one does not go, there will be no six benefits.

Regarding the statement that "the father, teacher, or master does not suffer at the time of death," it should properly include terms such as "lord" (*prabhu*) and so forth; however, the text is abbreviated.
Since one is born from a biological parent, the term "father" is used; yet, the "lord" is what constitutes the basis of support.
Regarding the "great kalpa" (*mahākalpa*): eighty *lu-lu* (a unit of time) constitute one great kalpa.
The meaning of "kalpa" is manifold (and so forth). As for "obstructing the subsequent Buddhas": in the Bhadrakalpa, there are one thousand Buddhas, yet only four have appeared thus far.
How could it be that nine hundred and ninety-six Buddhas have not yet arisen? Therefore, it is said they are "obstructed."
As for those who grasp hands: it is the height of sorrow, yet it is also the height of joy. Just as when worldly people reach the extreme of either sorrow or joy, they all grasp one another's hands.
Regarding the invitation of the Tathāgata-Father: just as in the world, when a father departs from his house, the house becomes empty; thus it is called "empty space" (ākāśa).
Since the intent of the invitation is such, one cannot be without any one of these three—the host, the kinsman, or the teacher—and therefore they must be invited.
The Sūtra says, "Go quickly. "Go quickly" is a term used to urge and seize [the deceased].
"Releasing the suffering" means explaining the suffering of the master, parents, or teacher who has passed away.
"Thus revolving" refers to proceeding from the past toward the future; losing even one [link] is not permissible, just as a world without a ruler is a state of chaos.

[This] refutes [the objection]. Without a kinsman, the family perishes; without a teacher, there is no ground for resolving doubts. Now that the Master of the Text is no more, where shall one find a teacher?
With the Dharma extinguished, there is nowhere to rely. As the three sufferings weigh upon his heart, he speaks thus of "doubt and confusion."
Regarding those who have both the actual matter (*vastu*) and the outward manifestation (*pradarśana*): "matter" refers to the *śrāvakas*, who constantly follow the World-Honored One;

therefore, they are placed at the front. The forms of the *bodhisattvas* lack a fixed standard; they may be either close or distant, and thus they occupy the middle position. As for the "mixed assembly," their forms are distant and they remain far from the Buddha;

therefore, they are placed at the rear. Regarding those with outward manifestations: if the *śrāvakas* represent the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the mixed assembly represents the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), and the *bodhisattvas* represent the middle, they are thus situated accordingly.
This is the distinction between the elder and the younger brothers.
Now, my intention is as before; I rely on the previous division of the father’s estate, which differs from other interpretations.

Regarding the phrase "startling those who ask later": "startling" (*hai*) means to cause surprise, shaking their ordinary sentiments. It means that one does not take physical proximity as the basis for closeness.

"Remote": this refers to remoteness in terms of the capacity of the audience (*indriya*). Because their capacity has not yet been activated, in terms of principle (*artha*), they are considered remote; therefore, it is necessary to summon them.

Furthermore, regarding "because of the majority": perhaps the assembly near the Buddha is small while those coming from outside are numerous; speaking according to the majority, it is said that they are summoned.
Regarding the number already established above— eighty billion hundred thousand people and so forth—

the reason for singling out a single individual is that while a son is honored by his father and a younger brother yields to his elder brother, the term "disciple" here refers specifically to one person alone.
One admires their virtue and conduct, not their age. Thus, the Vinaya states: "Those who are called elders do not necessarily have to be advanced in years.
Knowing that [the youth] would come to know future matters, the Māra King feared he might usurp his own seat; therefore, he exhorted him to leave the household life. This is what is manifested here.
Regarding the eighteen transformations and so forth:
now, to briefly eliminate obstacles and preserve what is wholesome—once the wholesome has arisen, obstacles will necessarily be removed.

To distinguish these according to the Four Teachings: from the response, "This is the [teaching] below," refers to the Hīnayāna (Zàngjiào). Furthermore, from "to show" below, it indicates the meaning of the Shared Teaching (Tōngyì).
The eighth stage emerges from the provisional to observe the path of the dual [truths], thereby being able to transform sentient beings; thus it is called a "model.

Furthermore, the phrase "separate delusions" refers to a specific meaning, namely that those prior to the stages have not yet severed separate delusions. The phrase "grief and sorrow" refers to the perfect [teaching]; therefore, a scriptural passage is cited to establish this proof.
If interpreted according to the four *siddhāntas*, it corresponds to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
