This raises the distinction in order to inquire about the non-distinction. By citing the distinctions among the four castes and nine realms, one inquires about the non-distinction of the three causes as being of a single essence.

Regarding "partially eliminating afflictions only to a small extent": this refers to the Bodhisattvas of skillful means and the aforementioned Śrāvakas who eliminate [afflictions] only within the realm of desire;
they are called "partial" because, when viewed from the perspective of the Perfect [Vehicle], their elimination is merely "to a small extent."

"Only longing for the rain from heaven" refers to the Dharma-rain of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-cheng) of the Ultimate Truth Heaven (Diyi-yitian); hence it says "only longing. "Longing" (*xi*) is synonymous with "seeking" (*qiu*).

Regarding the general and specific requests made in accordance with the capacities and conditions of the audience: this refers to the passage in the preceding section on the Dharma-exposition where [the disciples] desire to request the Tathāgata, and so forth; that is the first.
The three [aspects] are, in essence, one body; this is termed "universal" (tong). Within the analogy of the three distinct invitations, they are likewise one within the three;
this is termed "particular" (bie). In discussing their single essence, it is simply because the capacities and conditions of sentient beings differ that these universals and particulars exist.

The subsequent response by the Tathāgata anticipates the following passage to present the three current meanings, thereby ensuring that the preceding and succeeding sections are interrelated so that the textual flow and meaning are complete.
As for the manifestation of the nature of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*): since it is said to "remove poverty," it bestows honor and prosperity.

Regarding the nature of the revealing cause (*vyañjanahetu*): the "Dharma rain" refers to the teachings of the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*), for the Dharma is able to instruct and thereby bring about the perfection of *prajñā*.

Regarding the manifestation of the direct cause (*saddhetu*): it is that which can directly give birth and nourish, causing growth in the *dharmakāya*; this is precisely what is meant by permitting the secret treasury.
The meaning is that [the father] can protect all his children.
These three—ruler, parent, and teacher—are of one essence and without distinction; therefore, they are said to be "as one.
The Classic says, "A person's life rests upon three; serve them as one. This is precisely the meaning.
Regarding this interpretation, others may think: "The *Siṃhanāda-parivarta* begins by extensively discussing the meaning of the three causes of Buddha-nature;
since this belongs to the section on giving (*dāna*), how can such an interpretation be justified?"

The meaning of my current response is as follows: Buddha-nature is eternal. This sutra, from beginning to end, clarifies only the doctrine of permanence (*nityatā*). There is a specific basis for this sequence;

therefore, it is said that "if it were not opened at the outset. "Opening" refers to opening up the teaching of permanence. As for the question, "What would there be to follow upon later?"—this is a refutation of the opponent's position.
To bestow upon them constant life means to abide eternally in the life of wisdom. To bestow upon them the lord of constant peace means to be able to bring peace to the people.
To bestow upon them constant discernment means that the teacher is able to explain and analyze.

Regarding "self and others, internal and external, etc.": one's own body is the internal; the bodies of others are the external. According to the text of the invocation, this also refers to the nine realms as external and the Buddha-realm as internal.
Because the environment and its inhabitants (the *niśraya* and *āśrita*) are non-dual, it is said that they are equal and without distinction.
"From humans and devas up to bodhisattvas of skillful means" refers to those at the seven stages of skillful means (*saptavidha-upāya*).
"Those who labor as farmers" means employing physical strength to acquire wealth, and employing evil to serve the good.

The analogy of the three bodhisattvas refers to the Triplet, the Distinct, and the Perfect [Teachings]. In the Perfect Teaching, from the stage prior to the Ten Abidings up through the Seven Faiths and above, one is precisely eliminating the "dust-like sands" [of afflictions];
therefore, it is called "three."
As for the manifestation of the Buddha-nature, it refers to the manifestation of the three causes of Buddha-nature.
"Precisely residing herein" intends the triad of master, parent, and teacher.

That all are "poor" means that those in the stages prior to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) have not yet realized the Dharma-body; in this sense, they are said to be poor, as the secret treasury has not yet been revealed.
This is because they are opened.

Although there are slight differences— namely, that humans, devas, and bodhisattvas are all analogized as being within the realm, which is why they are called "slight"— the distinction lies in their superiority or inferiority and their different celestial states.
As for the intention behind these [statements]: from the shallow to the profound, this applies even to humans and devas, let alone Bodhisattvas.
Yet, because it is not fixed, they are expressed as alternatives.
The *Sūtra* refers to it as "sha-lu" (the character for *lu* is pronounced with the *lǚ* tone). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that *lu* refers to a salty soil in a harsh region;

thus, the character is composed of the "west" radical (*xi*) below, which represents the shape of salt. That which is produced by Heaven is called *lu*; that which is produced by man is called *yán* (salt). Salt is located in the western direction.

"First, regarding those who pass through the stages in accordance with the Dharma: this refers to passing through the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). Furthermore, those who do not accord with the human or celestial realms are omitted;
for these are places where the capacities for the three vehicles arise, and they do not pertain to the supramundane dharmas of the two vehicles or of bodhisattvas."

The Sūtra speaks of the "Amṛta rain of Dharma. While the term "Dharma-rain" applies generally to all teachings, "Amṛta" refers exclusively to the Perfect and Ever-Abiding teaching, just as celestial amṛta is the medicine of immortality.
Regarding "the essence possessing precepts": the essence of the three virtues of *nirvāṇa* consists of unconditioned *śīla*, the fivefold precepts (*pañca-śīla*), and so forth.

Concentration (*samādhi*) is the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*; wisdom (*prajñā*) is the wisdom of the three types of knowledge (*trividya*). Although they are of one essence, they are here described according to their personified aspects.
These are still merely the limited and partial precepts, concentrations, and wisdom; hence they are called "minor virtues.
When the sutra says "rescuing and extending to the immeasurable," it refers to the sentient beings of the nine realms and the four castes.
As for "abundant yet sufficient": because the many are one, they suffice for the few; because the one is many, it encompasses the many.
It cannot be grasped by a single patience, nor can it be conceived by manifold thoughts; thus it is called an "inconceivable offering," an offering made to an inconceivable assembly.
Regarding "serving the three as one": I and all sentient beings are the same as Rāhula; we are all his only sons.
As for the passage concerning the World-Honored One’s granting of the titles of lord and so forth: a lord bestows emolument, a teacher bestows accomplishment, and a parent bestows birth.
Therefore, it is said that the three pursuits were successfully accomplished.
That "serving fire" (shì huǒ) signifies "the teacher" (shī): fire can transform all things, just as a teacher instructs his disciples.
That "honoring Śakra" (fèng shì) signifies "the principle" (yì): just as Śakra is the lord of the thirty-three heavens and is honored by all the devas.
This is a respectful offering; thus, the commentary states as follows.
Regarding "the study" and so forth: this refers to the two vehicles of the preceding two teachings.
As for the Jewel Mountain Sumeru, it is composed of four treasures, which serve as a metaphor for the four bodhisattvas.

The metaphors of the sandalwood forest and the lion, which illustrate morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), draw upon the meaning of the preceding passage to demonstrate that the master and disciple together possess the three trainings in their entirety:
the sandalwood forest represents morality, the lion represents wisdom, and the mountain represents concentration.

That which is revered and honored by the world is precisely what is intended here: because he is revered and honored by the four types of bodhisattvas of the three preceding teachings, he is titled "World-Honored One" (Lokanātha).

Regarding "pervading all": this refers to the basis and the supported of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which corresponds to all objects of cognition because the nine elements (*dhātu*) differ from one another.
It is called "Buddha" because the knowledge of all modes is that which possesses the capacity for awakening.
Regarding the two requests concerning the Dharma and the analogy, there is one "Excellent! seal for the request concerning the Dharma and one "Excellent! seal for the request concerning the analogy.
Since both fully embody the meanings of lord, relative, and teacher, it is said: "Excellent! Excellent! (sādhu sādhu).

Regarding the passage "permitted three times, etc.," the text omits the word "intimate" (*qīn*). Since "constant life" (*cháng mìng*) carries the meaning of "intimate," it says, "I now bestow [life] upon you.
Regarding the "seven hundred [kalpas], etc.," the lifespan of the Buddha in the East is the same as that of Śākyamuni.

"Even so, these are impermanent" refers to the interpretation of Guangzhai. His intention was that although the title of this chapter is "Immeasurable Life," [the Buddha] is still a Buddha of limited measure because he is the future successor (upapadya).
Thus, he is the same as Amitābha—whose name means "Immeasurable Life"—who likewise has Avalokiteśvara as his successor;
both are therefore impermanent. The following refutation addresses such a claim.
Regarding the partial citations from various sutras: the Vaipulya, Śūraṅgama, and Prajñāpāramitā sutras are not just one; thus they are called "various.
Furthermore, he cites the explicit teachings of the Lotus Sutra, which likewise lead back to impermanence.

Regarding the loss of both paths: according to your interpretation, you lose the permanence that is concurrently associated with the Mahāyāna within the previous two teachings, and you also lose the permanence revealed by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Furthermore, you fail to grasp the meaning of "neither permanent nor impermanent" in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
It is because the *Nirvāṇa* is contrasted with the preceding teachings that these are called the "two paths."
As for the Mother Prajñā, she is the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), for she is able to give birth to all things.
As for the Buddha’s Teacher, it is the Dharma which is the teacher of all Buddhas; the Dharma of the Buddha-nature serves as the teacher.
Regarding the three Buddhas of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, they share the same Dharma-body.
As for the question of how the One Vehicle could refute the One Vehicle: it is by means of the One Vehicle of Buddha-nature that the One Vehicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is refuted.
Therefore, we know that those who are confused regarding the provisional means (*upāya*) are ignorant of both the internal essence and the external manifestation;

this is precisely to be deluded regarding both the provisional and the real. As for being deluded regarding the "sections" (*bhāga*) of the teachings: "sections" encompass the teachings, but the teachings do not encompass the sections. For example, the Vaipulya section contains all four teachings, while the Prajñāpāramitā section contains three.
It is for this reason that the Great Master (Chih-i) judged them as "combined," "single," "confrontational," and "interlaced. This applies to both the Vaipulya and the Prajñāpāramitā.
If the "presently constant" were no different from *nirvāṇa*,
then the "constant of the future and present" would refer to both the constant nature of presently existing *buddha-nature* and the constant nature of that which is yet to arise.
That there is "no interval" between them means that both the constant and the impermanent are fully endowed with the secret treasury of the three virtues (or four virtues).
It pervades all places; how could there be any interval between them?
It is like one who avoids space while seeking space: that which is immediately before one is impermanence, which is itself permanence; there is no need to avoid it.
This also reveals the esoteric teachings of skillful means. In the past, they were perpetually concealed; because the eternal and so forth had not yet been disclosed, it was called "esoteric" (mi).
Now that the impermanent is revealed as being precisely the eternal, it is called "revealed" (ha). "Revealing" (ha) carries the meaning of "disclosing" (kai);
therefore, it is termed "manifest revelation" (ken-ha).

Regarding the "throat" and "collar" of this teaching: just as for a person, nothing is more essential than the throat, and for clothing, nothing is more fundamental than the collar, so too is the constant meaning [of this teaching].

Regarding the "heart" and "head" of all sutras: just as the body takes the heart and head as its primary organs, so too does this teaching universally encompass all dharmas; such is the constant meaning.
"Thus. It pervades the heads of all minds.
As for "cave-dwelling," it refers to the secret treasury of the three virtues, which serves as the abode of Great Nirvana.
If one were to regard it as a fixed and eternal entity, then one would be violating the various sutras by establishing Nirvana alone as a fixed and eternal thing.
"Fundamentally, this concerns a great matter": when the Tathāgata appears in the world, his transformative activity through cause and effect is termed a "matter";
therefore, it is explained by analyzing the characters.
"The constant stimulus and the constant response" refers to inconceivable resonance and response, which serve as the causes and conditions.

"Always establishing all dharmas": "establishing" means to set up or found. It refers to the essence of the One Vehicle, which is what is apprehended through cause and effect; therefore, it is called a "phenomenon" (*vastu*).
"Master and disciple are both eternal": Eternity is the Buddha as master, and the Buddha is the disciple. Since master and disciple are non-dual, they are said to be "both."
It is permanent.
As for "the immovable retribution," it refers to the fruit of eternal abiding.
Regarding "purity as the true dharma," it is because *prajñā* (wisdom) constitutes the true dharma, as it is capable of generating gnosis.

Regarding the characteristics of the four dharmas previously cultivated: this refers to the textual passage that refutes the three types of cultivation; namely, impermanence, selflessness, and so forth, which constitute the four dharmas.

As for "remedying the fundamental illness": taking what is truly eternal and permanent to be an object of false interpretation is called "illness. This is explained based on that fundamental [misconception].
Therefore, it is called the "fundamental illness.
Regarding the "non-dual yet dual functioning": this means that the functioning is identical to the essence; hence, it is called "dual.
Regarding the "uninterruptedness of the four *siddhāntas*": this refers to the universal inclusion of all phenomena and their free exposition.
The four *siddhāntas* are constantly interspersed below [the text], all of which are inconceivable. The structure of the text does not follow a sequential order:
the first is the worldly (*loka*), the second—the wondrous principle—is the ultimate (*paramārtha*), the third is for the person (*pudgala*), and the fourth is remedial (*pratipakṣa*).
This also demonstrates that while they are discussed out of sequence, they are nonetheless presented as a sequence; thus, they are called the "constant four *siddhāntas*."
Regarding the phrase "burying the perfect capacity and so forth": it refers to burying the four *siddhāntas* and destroying all notions of permanence.
Since the discussion of permanence is precisely the *Śāstra*, both contain the meaning of "double negation" (*ubhayapratiṣedha*); therefore, it is said that [the former] "harms" [the latter].
"Difficult to destroy" means it cannot be destroyed by the partial and limited [realms] of the six paths of existence.

Regarding the statement that there are three periods of time: phenomena (dharma) possess the three periods of time, but principle (li) does not possess the three periods of time. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* cites that which is "not called bodhi," and so forth.
Bodhi is termed the fruit; nirvāṇa is termed the fruit of fruits. Thus, they do not belong to the three periods of time.
Those who would attain the essential meaning are those referred to by the four verses appearing below.

These are presented in four locations—“There is no such place where dharmas exist in the three periods of time,” and so forth—and are thus called the "Four Appearances. The ancients also termed them the "Four Pillars of Nirvāṇa.
Just as a house collapses if it lacks pillars, so too is the significance of Nirvāṇa.
Next, I shall now explain for you the passage below, which enumerates each of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) one by one, as in the text.
Regarding the phrase "prior to this": it is Kāśyapa’s own account of how, before he heard the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, his views were all partial and distorted;
therefore, they are termed "erroneous" (*mithyā*). This does not mean that they were identical to the errors of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
"Opening all those with remainder" means that the seven stages of expedient means all open the way for entry into the state of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
"Acting as a kinsman to open the correct" means causing the birth of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). "Acting as a master to open the conditions" means that the conditions manifest the correct.

"Acting as a teacher to open understanding" means that the three causes are fully possessed. Therefore, they are able to flourish, give birth, and bring to completion, so that all enter together into the secret treasury.

Regarding "opening up the nature of the objective realm": the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) of the six realms of existence constitute the causal nature; therefore, they are called the "objective realm.
Furthermore, because one requests that the five kinds of Buddha-nature be opened up, it is called the "fruition nature," and so forth.

Regarding "which persons": "persons" refers to those at the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*); "dharmas" refers to the dharmas of the seven stages of expedient means; "teaching and practice" and so forth are all inverted.

Regarding "which stage": it is the stage of realization and attainment. Regarding "what is the purpose": it is the purpose of those at the various stages of expedient means in transforming sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding "good and evil": humans and devas constitute good, while the four realms of existence (the *caturgati*) constitute evil.
Regarding "vertically deep and horizontally vast," etc.: those on the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) are all inverted. The bottom of *nirvāṇa* is called "deep";
because it horizontally encompasses the good and evil of the nine realms, it is called "vast. Because it is vast, it is boundless; because it is deep, it is bottomless.
"One who can establish the Great Meaning" takes the meaning of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) as "Great.
Regarding "fully encompassing cause and effect," the causes are the three causes, and the effects are the three virtues and four virtues. The functioning of these effects is inexhaustible.
Therefore, it is compared to the myriad virtues.
As for the five dharmas being simultaneously eternal, they are headed by "eternal," meaning there is nothing that is not eternal.
Regarding "that which is not form acting as form": the Dharma-body is formless, while the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) manifests as form.
Regarding "the inexhaustible application": the application of good and evil differs across the nine realms; therefore, it is inexhaustible.
As for the Buddha possessing these five and bestowing them upon others: this is solely because sentient beings equally possess these five within their own bodies.

Thus, the manifestation of these five is called "bestowal" (*dāna*); it does not mean that something else is bestowed separately. Therefore, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the equal granting of the great chariots is said to be for the sake of the children.
The reason it is called "equal" is that because the fruit is inexhaustible, the giving is also inexhaustible.
Regarding what can be known from the middle period: after the Deer Park and before the Nirvāṇa, the two *Sūtra* sections constitute the middle;
both contain the meanings of permanence and impermanence, yet it has not been stated that there is no difference between the two fruits. Therefore, it is said that they can be known [to be equal].
This seal of the eternal Dharma is the seal of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Like empty space, it universally seals all phenomena; there is nothing that is not eternal.

This is precisely what it means to practice the eternal: both the initial and subsequent acts of giving are *dānapāramitā*. When the six perfections are fully complete, this is called [the perfection of giving].
It is indeed so.
There must be such persons; both the giver and the recipient are the constant nature of humanity.
Regarding the various meanings, they are as explained in the following response. "Good son, the Tathāgata has already, throughout immeasurable [aeons]... [He has delivered them].
This answers the meaning of the three bodies and four bodies; hence it says "various.

Regarding the statements that at the beginning and end they all receive, all eat, and all do not eat: at the beginning, "all eat" refers to impermanence, while "not eating" refers to the Dharma-body, which is the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*).
At the end, "all eat" refers to the opening of the eternal, while "all do not eat" refers to the eternal body.
This is because they equally enter the secret treasury. Opening up what was previously "not eating" is equivalent to what follows regarding "not eating"; thus, it is said they are "equal.

Furthermore, this is based on two layers of initial and final stages. If the *Avataṃsaka*—as seen through the great conditions—is taken as the beginning, then receiving office upon the lotus pedestal and receiving light upon the crown of the head constitutes receiving food upon the crown;
the latter refers to the present sutra, which opens the eternal principle and receives the pure [Dharma].

To bestow [food] is called "eating. To enter parinirvāṇa is precisely "not eating. Therefore, at the time of his initial appearance in the world, he received milk porridge and this was called "eating.
Later, when he went to Cunda’s house and ate the *tandula* (rice) and meat broth before entering parinirvāṇa, this was called "not eating.
This is what is perceived through limited conditions; thus, there are both great and small conditions, and both exist.
"Eating and not eating" refers to equality.
If one follows the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and judges according to the classification by teaching, it is because the middle two *sūtras* are both empty, and so forth.

In the Mahāyāna gate, form is itself emptiness; therefore, from form and mind at the beginning up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) at the end, there is nothing that is not emptiness. Hence, it is called "equality."
If one relies on the *Śāstra* to provide further proof for the teaching of Prajñā, "the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena" refers to the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) Prajñā;
therefore, it is said to be "equal. If it refers to the common (*sādhāraṇa*) Prajñā, it is equal because it is identical to the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the Mahāyāna gates mentioned previously.

Since the true reality of the uncommon Prajñā is no different from that of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it does not specifically mention the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* shares the same flavor as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*. With...
"Nirvana is constant," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "pervading all dharmas": "dharmas" refers here to the dharmas of the nine realms; "teachings" refers to the persons of the seven stages of expedient means.
Since these are all the principle of the double negation, it is said to be "equal."
The three fingers being distinct represents the seeing of nature through the Middle Way. In this context, that which is neither eternal nor impermanent is called the Middle Way.
In the texts on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, this is illustrated by the three contemplations; the Middle Contemplation corresponds to the Middle Way, wherein subject and object are non-dual.
Regarding "Great Awakening" (Mahābodhi): "Great" (mahat) is a specific name for "wondrous" (miao); "great" is itself "wondrous.

As for these various "constants," although there are six distinct types, all are termed "constant"; therefore, they are referred to as "various" (zhū). The term "six" serves to exclude redundancy, while "that which is" (ji) excludes separation;
thus, they are categorized based on the permanence of the Perfect and Complete [Teachings].

Regarding the statement that "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi can be known by its translation," this is translated as the "Unsurpassed Way" (anuttara-mārga) and is also called "Fruitional Wisdom" (phala-jñāna).
Regarding "the Dharma-principle is fully complete": "Dharma" refers to the teaching (śāsana), while "principle" refers to the principle of Nirvana consisting of the three virtues (triguṇa).

This opens up the partial teachings and partial principles of the previous [vehicles], causing them all to enter the perfect and eternal; therefore, it is said to be "complete. This means that when one is opened, all are opened, and so forth. If this were not stated...
"All" does not yet signify "complete.
When one practices giving based on this, it is through the unconditioned *dāna* of the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is called "complete."

Regarding the scriptural passage stating "attaining bodhi," etc.: *bodhi* is the fruit; *nirvāṇa* is the fruit of the fruit. Their names are identical in the secret treasury, hence it is said they are "fully endowed.
As for the initial general negation that this is not so: it is because what precedes is inferior and what follows is superior.
Yecheng is the name of a monastery. Dharma Master Xiu was there, possessing unsurpassed understanding; Dharma Master Zang of Kaishan was also present there.
As for the difference in their names, I have not yet seen any textual evidence for it.

Regarding "first, having wisdom and abandonment": as long as afflictions are not yet exhausted, there is no abandonment; as long as the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is not yet attained, there is no wisdom.
The subsequent giving refers to the difficulty of being fully endowed with both wisdom and abandonment.

Regarding the phrase "possessing the title of Sage" (*ārya-nāman*): sentient beings do not possess the title of sage; the Buddha is a sage. Because he is equal to the "God among Gods," he possesses the title of Sage.
Regarding the phrase "endowed with the eyes of deliverance" (*pāramitā-cakṣus*): "deliverance" refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and "eyes" refers to the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*).
The Sūtra states, "up to and including the wisdom-eye," but does not mention the deva-eye (divine eye). The intention is that the deva-eye is identical to the fleshly eye;
the only distinction lies in the presence or absence of obstructions.
Regarding those who attain the five fruits and those who do not: if one holds to the small vehicle while hoping for the great, the Mahāyāna will not accept it;
these are merely worldly fruits, and thus it is said that they are "undigestible," and so forth.

The Sūtra says, “digestion” (huāxiào; the first character is read as either *hūguā* or *hūbà*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that “huà” means transformation (*biàn*). This refers to the fact that [the body] is subject to constant change and impermanence.

Regarding the phrase “first, having fully enumerated”: this first section clarifies both self and others, while the subsequent four sections all combine them. Since the textual treatment of self and others is already complete, it is simply stated here as “this” for the sake of brevity, avoiding further elaboration in the text.

Regarding "difficult to resolve due to its crisscrossing angles": when minor conditions are placed at the beginning and major conditions are placed at the end, or when the latter and the former are juxtaposed, the words and meanings intersect and form angles;
thus it is said to be "difficult to resolve. The character *jì* (pronounced *qí jì*) is the name of a type of grass.
Regarding the "bodhisattvas who are his retinue," they take Śākyamuni as their retinue; this should be understood as being spoken prior to his [Śākyamuni's] completion [of Buddhahood].
The great disciples he dispatched are none other than the Bodhisattva Anantagātra.
Thus, the Jing and Wei rivers appear distinct; as for their clarity and turbidity, they are differentiated by the perspectives of those who see them—whether their vision is broad or narrow.
As for the *Suvikrāntavikramin-paripṛcchā* (The Inquiry of the Victorious Heavenly King) and other such texts, their four characteristics differ, yet they all testify to the first [stage].
The *Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma* establishes that even the subsequent nirvāṇa possesses four characteristics.
Since the Great Master [Tiantai] judged and compiled the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he has cited it here.
Regarding the phrase "now further addressing the Teachers of the Schools" and so forth: the Teachers of the four teachings differ from one another.
"Possessing the six supernormal powers and the three insights" refers to the six *abhijñās* and the three *vidyās*.
"Able to benefit others in five ways" means that accepting the offering of milk porridge is itself a way of benefiting others.
Regarding "becoming [an Arhat] for the first time as difficult": this refers to the moment when the thirty-four moments of mind sever the fetters.

Regarding "entering the stage of a sage" (*ārya*): this occurs upon reaching the seventh ground; because one abandons the dharmas of the external ordinary person and realizes the stage of an Arhat, they are called "sages.
However, they have not yet received the name "God among Gods," as they have not reached the stage of a Buddha.
"It is not that which is the impermanent body" refers to the Bodhisattva Hīnadhātu (Heterogeneous Treasury); thus it is said "not.

"Having already perfected the threefold extinction of the three [aspects of] giving" means that because the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty, both the giver and the object given are extinguished;
as the *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā* says, this is "giving without abiding in signs."
Those who have not yet attained the Buddha-eye attain the stages of a bodhisattva because they have not yet reached the stage of a Buddha.
When the Buddha says, "I have become a Buddha for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas," this refers to the passage on the revelation of the provisional to reveal the real,
and the revelation of the trace to reveal the fundamental, concerning the lifespan found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Regarding the statement that "the initial manifestation and initial reception, and the subsequent manifestation and subsequent reception" refer to what is perceived by the two conditions of the Great and Small [vehicles]:
this means that the traces of the two stages—initial and subsequent—are designated as "initial" and "subsequent."

How can it be that what was seen at the beginning of inferiority—the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka—is the same as what was seen after the stage of Difficult Victory (*durjayā*), which is the vision through great conditions following *nirvāṇa*?

The meaning of this is clear. The five fruits of the past are opened up to become the five fruits of the present, just as in the *Lotus Sūtra* the hired laborer is pointed out as being the elder’s own son;
there is no other path. Therefore, it is said they are equal and without difference.
This is a distinction.
Regarding the body having separation and union: although the previous objection separated it into four, their union is impermanent.

The Buddha’s answer states that although the five bodies are separated, the *vajra* is used as a metaphor for the two eternal bodies; therefore, he speaks of "four bodies," "five bodies," and so forth.
The sutra omits the word "no" (wu) and prefixes it to "afflicted body" (fannao shen). "No" signifies negation; it negates the four bodies, hence it says "no final body" (wou hou bian shen).
Since the "final" is impermanent, it only negates the three bodies. Impermanence is itself permanence, which constitutes a dual application;
therefore, the sutra does not explicitly state it.
"Always being the head of this teaching" means that by sharing the same offering as Cunda, he opened up its fundamental doctrine of permanence; thus he was truly at its head.
"Nearly extinguished" (*dai jue*): *dai* here means perilous or imminent. Hence, the Book of Documents says, "Human life is nearly gone."
"Radiance" is identical to "wisdom. To cite the passage from the later section, the *Guṇarājaparivarta*:
"This is the great condition for first receiving the food of the crown-radiance," and so forth.
"Those for whom it is not now the first time they have severed [the afflictions]" refers to those such as myself who have already done so throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Regarding "neither large nor small, neither both nor neither," all these manifest the Middle Way. That the body is neither eating nor non-eating, and that it is neither non-eating nor a permanent body, are both extremes;
the same applies to the Vajra-body. That which is profound and yet more profound—
The great and the small, both being neither, constitute one mystery. With respect to its long duration, it is not a trace and thus does not "eat"; this is another mystery.
Therefore, it is called "again" (fu).
"The non-differentiation is clear" concludes the intent of the response. Why does Cunda insist upon impermanence and challenge permanence?
All other challenges follow this pattern.

The same applies to the Buddhas. If we discuss Bodhisattvas, there is a distinction between those who have severed [ignorance] and those who have not; this is because at the time of realizing the fruit, they have all as yet not seen their nature.

As for those who enter the Vajra-samādhi, it refers to the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-sambodhi), who severs the final grade of ignorance and immediately enters Sublime Enlightenment (Suyukta-buddha). Therefore, it is said:
This refers to clearly seeing the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the statement that "wisdom and abandonment are not distinct, but their names differ according to the time": in the Mahāyāna, when first realizing Bodhi, wisdom also attains abandonment;
later, upon entering Nirvāṇa, both wisdom and abandonment are fully present. Thus, they are merely designated by different names.

One who possesses the marks of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) is a "god among men. Although such a king of men travels throughout the four continents, he is also called a "sovereign emperor who flies through the air";
hence, he is described as a "god among men."

That is to say, from the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) up until one cannot become a "pure-heaven" deity (*śuddhāvāsa-deva*), refers to those who are persons of the three fruits [of the *anāgāmin*] among the Pure Abode Heavens (*śuddhāvāsa*).
The phrase "up until" (*yāvat*) indicates that they have transcended the second fruit.
Those who are still "ordinary beings" have not yet severed their afflictions and are thus equal to common worldlings.

Those who have attained the bodhisattva path, from the first stage (bhūmi) and the first dwelling (vihāra), destroy the demons of affliction within the realm of desire through their causal practice and attain the dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya).
"Destroying the aggregates and the demon of death" refers to the analytical destruction of the two types of death.
"Attaining the immovable samādhi" refers to the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment entering the Vajra-samādhi, which directly destroys the celestial demon (māra).
Regarding the "demons of the four inversions such as impermanence," it should properly be stated as the "demons of the eight inversions such as permanence and impermanence.
As for "giving that does not see the principle," such giving is not complete and cannot reach the other shore.
"Those who have already attained thorough penetration" refers to the twelve divisions of the Dharma, which universally encompass the six perfections, the five eyes, and all phenomena.
Regarding "wealth, Dharma, affairs, and principle": *dāna* (generosity) pertains to affairs; since one realizes the principle through the very phenomenon itself, it is called "Dharma."
Those who surpass humans, devas, and the two vehicles are the practitioners of the seven stages of preparation (saptavidha-prayoga).
They have partially attained the Buddha-eye and see what is perceived from the stages (bhūmi) upward.

Now, regarding the Buddha’s answer concerning the single matter of the Dharma-gift (dharma-dāna), it refers to the Mahāyāna teachings of the twelve divisions of scripture, which he bestows upon others.
Sentient beings are themselves *dāna* (giving).

As for "the remaining perfections and the five eyes": the five perfections correspond to the four eyes. "Perfection" (*pāramitā*) refers to practice, while "eye" (*cakṣus*) refers to the truths; therefore, they are called the "perfections and the eyes."
As for the scripture’s statement, "In truth, he does not eat," it is because the Dharma fundamentally has no food; it was only for the sake of sentient beings that he accepted Cunda's offering.
Regarding the request to remain until [the teaching] had been fully set forth: since the assembly of fifty-two [thousand] had not yet received permission, they did not dare to make such a request.

Those who have not yet attained realization perceive only the manifested traces (*nirmāṇakāya*) and have not yet reached the fundamental essence of the *dharmakāya*; therefore, it is said to be "profound and mysterious.
Now, the word "as for" (*fu*, 夫) serves to refute the interpretations of others, referring to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions; hence, it is called "as for. Fundamentally, there is no going.
Abiding is the very essence of the body and mind of the Dharma. This alone is abiding. Sentient beings see it as departing; the Buddhas see it as abiding.
That which remains eternally present despite its appearance of departure is what is called "signs" when the Buddha manifests *nirvāṇa* and displays his passing away between the twin śāla trees.
That which is eternally present is, in reality, not extinguished. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The multitude see the end of the kalpa," and so forth;
yet [the Buddha] constantly dwells on Vulture Peak and in other various abodes. This is precisely the manifestation of extinction while being non-extinguished.
"Abiding in the mark yet constantly departing": the Tathāgata’s manifestation of birth in a royal palace, his renunciation of the world, and so forth, are termed "marks.

As for "constantly departing," as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says, "Sentient beings are unable to conceive the thought that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter, and they harbor a heart of constant indulgence";
this is precisely not being born while manifesting birth.

If that is so, the following is the intent of the current objection: To refute the [notions of] going and staying held by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, what benefit is there in the Tathāgata being present among the assembly—namely, the fifty-two groups as well as Cunda and the others?
The phrase "as explained above" refers to the meaning of the objection. The refutation of immeasurable evils is as set forth in the subsequent text;

the refutation of the heterodox and entry into the orthodox, etc., all constitute the severing of afflictions. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Those who should attain liberation through the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa shall thereby attain it.
This is precisely that meaning. Furthermore, by taking the single individual Cunda as an example, one sees that he possesses the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*.
"All serve as conditions for the ears and so forth" means that one should know Cunda was able to act as the condition for the fifty-two assemblies to obtain benefit through the four *siddhāntas*;
he was their dwelling-condition (*pratiṣṭhā-hetu*).

Regarding "both departing and abiding": the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) should be seen as departing, while the dharma body (*dharmakāya*) is eternally abiding; it is appropriate to see them as both departing and abiding, for all thereby obtain benefit.
That they neither depart nor abide is stated according to the underlying principle.
That an auspicious name is established first is "good. That auspicious omens manifest first is why it is called the "wondrous meaning" (*miao-yi*).

That it is vertically bottomless and boundless refers to the aforementioned ten meanings, reaching the ultimate limit of the causes and fruits of one's own practice, as well as the subject and object of transforming others.
Those who are peerless and surpass all the world consist of the fifty-two assemblies; they cannot be matched by anyone else.

Those who have attained great fame and benefit: "fame" refers to the ten subtle mysteries, and "benefit" refers to the five fruits. Because they bring benefit to both oneself and others, it is called "great."

Regarding "yielding to take the place behind": this means remaining at the rear of the great assembly. While the five fruits (the recipients) should take precedence, although [the donor] yields by staying behind, they should actually be the first to receive the offerings.

As for "fulfilling the perfection of giving" (*dānapāramitā*): it refers to the function of benefiting others, causing the generosity of the multitude to reach fulfillment; this is what is called "virtue."
Regarding "satisfying because the four aforementioned [conditions] are fully possessed": this means that merit, virtue, and so forth are all fulfilled.

To further cite the six difficulties: as the sutra says, being human, observing the precepts, encountering a Buddha, practicing wholesome deeds, hearing the Dharma, and making offerings—each subsequent condition is more difficult than the preceding one;
therefore, it is said that they are "even more difficult than these."

Regarding the "Flower-Tablet Wheel-Turning King" (Huabiao Lunwang): the Flower Principle (Huaili) appears once every three thousand years. When it appears, the road of the Great Ocean Wheel-Turning King manifests;
because the Wheel-Turning King is about to emerge, it is called a "tablet" (biao).
Regarding the one who acts as a Dharma King: since his virtue and vows are already fulfilled, he shares the auspicious signs of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin);

therefore, it is said that he will certainly become a Dharma King. As for the difficulty for others: this refers to those who do not encounter a Buddha, and thus it is said that Cunda’s [attainment] was easy.
That "none among the multitude can precede it" expresses the sense of being solitary and brilliant, standing out uniquely.
That "the name accords with the Dharma" means that since it is called "wondrous," the wondrous is the true mark (dharmatā), which accords with the Jewel of the Dharma.
Regarding "the mind merging with the Buddha": because the inconceivable mind is fully endowed with the three wisdoms, it merges with the Buddha. This is called merging with the Sangha.
When wisdom accords with its object, this harmony is called the Sangha. Thus, the Three Jewels as a single essence are no different from the Buddha.
To praise one for having attained a master’s mind like the Buddha’s mind is like praising a loyal minister who is able to accord with his sovereign’s mind.
Cunda stands at the head of the assembly; his mind is identical to the Buddha’s mind.

Regarding the phrase "equal to the Brahma King": the Brahma King is the one who invites the Buddha; his invitation to the Buddha is identical in intent to that of Cunda’s, and thus they are said to be equal.
As for the phrase "one who is preeminent," it refers to being the foremost among the multitude because one is uniquely so; thus it says, "Mañjuśrī is the head," and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the expression "yet another one who yields": since there were ten previously, the word "yet" (fu) is added again, thereby making eleven in total.
Regarding "those who have departed from what is beneficial": having attained the precepts, they spontaneously depart from the four evil destinies.
Regarding "the Buddha is unstained by worldly dharmas": he is not moved by the eight worldly concerns.
Because this Dharma is taught by one who is unstained by such things, it is said that "hearing the Dharma is difficult."
"Not desiring any existence" means not seeking the twenty-five states of existence, such as those of humans or devas.

To explain generally the benefits of the Three Jewels: the Tathāgata is the Jewel of the Buddha; that which is within the Saṃgha is the Jewel of the Saṃgha; and the exposition of the teachings is the Jewel of the Dharma.
Therefore, it is said that they provide benefit.

This refers to the benefit of skillful means (*upāya*). The metaphor of the cloud corresponds to power; once the cloud of wisdom has arisen, afflictions are suddenly exhausted, and thus it is called "cooling.
This clarifies the direct benefit: true wisdom is the mother, and skillful wisdom is the father.
Regarding "dispelling chaos and rectifying what is contrary": all deviant tendencies return to their source.
When ignorance and darkness disturb the practitioner, the Sun of the Sage hangs high and this great night is illuminated. Thus it is said that the Master benefits [all].
Now, as for these six difficulties that are mutually dependent upon one another: obtaining a human body is due to the observance of the precepts;
having obtained a human body, one is then able to see a Buddha appear in the world; because a Buddha has appeared in the world, one encounters the Buddha, gives rise to faith, and hears the Dharma;
and because of hearing the Dharma, one makes offerings to the Buddha at the time of his parinirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement that these three exist even when there is no Buddha: the three factors of human birth, maintaining the precepts, and hearing the Dharma also exist when a Buddha has not appeared in the world;

this is because one may hear the Dharma from a Pratyekabuddha. Yet, one loses one's own benefit by failing to attain the five fruits, and furthermore, one obstructs others by preventing them from attaining the five fruits.
"Your own spear and shield" refers to a contradiction in one's words. To "offer" is to depart; yet now you again request to remain.
Because the former and latter are inconsistent, it is called a "spear and shield. A detailed explanation of the "spear and shield" is provided in the *Zhiguan ji* (Commentary on the Mohe Zhiguan).

Regarding the phrases "the more it exists, the more it perishes" and "the more it perishes, the more it exists": abiding is existence, while departing is perishing. From the perspective of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), one sees departure;
from the perspective of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body), one sees abiding. As the Sūtra says, "This body of mine is itself the dharma body," and thus it is said to exist ever more fully (*mí cún*).

That all say "reaching" (*zhì*) means that, fundamentally, there is neither departure nor abiding; it is only for the sake of sentient beings that departure and abiding are spoken of. This is the nature of the Tathāgata’s...
The body should neither go nor stay; therefore, it is said to be "neither existent nor non-existent. This is explained in terms of the three truths and the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Above, its existence and non-existence were discussed in relation to the three bodies; here, its abiding and non-abiding are discussed in relation to the three truths.
As for those who speak with stammering tongues, it cannot be discussed verbally;

this refers to Vimalakīrti’s silence. As for those who grasp at it, they miss the mark; it cannot be conceived by the intellect. If one grasps at "abiding," one loses "going"; if one grasps at "going," one loses "abiding.
Since both going and abiding vanish, it is said that one must sever all emotional concerns and discursive thought.
Regarding the statement "there are six kinds of knowing" and so forth, it should be understood that one knows them precisely as they are through the six objects of focus.

Cunda abides in the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), which is knowledge of partial truth (*viśuddha-satya*); it is not yet ultimate knowledge. This is the intended meaning of the phrase "obstructed by the objective realm."
Below, they personally ceased their expectations. Since Cunda had raised the request on behalf of the assembly, and Cunda himself was still subject to restraint, the assembly then desisted.
Regarding the manifestation or concealment according to capacity: departing is concealment; remaining is manifestation. At times he employs remaining, and at other times he employs non-remaining.
The permanent is sometimes used as the departing; the permanently functioning is impermanent, yet it takes that very [impermanence] as its essence.

Impermanence is the permanent, being function within the essence; permanence is impermanence, being essence within the function. When both essence and function are quiescent, it is neither permanent nor impermanent;

when essence and function are both illuminated, they are both functioning without any [fixed] impermanence. The two birds fly together and both come to rest—the meaning lies herein. From beginning to end, this sutra...
The three truths emerge from this; Zhiyi’s (Zhang’an) application of them deeply captures their essential meaning.
That all phenomena are universally opened up as eternal means that, beginning from the Avīci Hell and ending with the stage of Equal Enlightenment, there is nothing that is not permanently abiding;
therefore, it is called "all. How could it be fixed that "self" is superior and "other" is inferior? It is said that they are eternally non-dual.
Regarding "constant" and so forth: if one dogmatically clings to the other, one loses the self; if one dogmatically clings to the self, one loses the other.
Now, since the self is precisely the other, it is said that it can perform such a supreme function.
If it were used because of permanence, there would be no need for an invitation, for permanence is itself abiding.
If it were used because of impermanence, there likewise would be no need for an invitation, for impermanence is departure; what benefit, then, would an invitation provide?

Therefore, regarding the mention of "two functions": the realm of all Buddhas is the function of permanence, while the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the function of impermanence;
hence, it is said there are two.
As for the prohibitive statement that they "should not," this means that both the permanent and the impermanent functions should not be requested.

Regarding the contemplation of suffering as a single mark (*ekavidha-duḥkhatā-vipaśyanā*): the scripture states, "Sentient beings are suffering," which precisely indicates the contemplation of suffering; "wandering in saṃsāra" describes the characteristic of that suffering;
and the section beginning with "the three realms" provides the formal explanation of the contemplation of suffering.
The Sūtra says: "There is the nature and characteristic of the Way. "Existence" (you) refers to the three realms of existence, the twenty-five states of existence, and so forth.

"The Way" (dao) is the fundamental nature of the six destinies. Nature (xing) refers to that which is internal; it is the nature of the fundamental source. Characteristic (xiang) refers to that which is external; it is the manifest form of the fundamental source. These can be distinguished by grasping them.
Because one can thoroughly understand this fundamental source, it is said to be empty and non-existent.

Regarding the next two lines on the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*): the Sūtra states that one is "enveloped and shrouded by afflictions" (*kleśa*). Generally speaking, the term "self" (*ātman*) carries the meaning of sovereignty.
Since one is now enveloped and shrouded, one lacks such sovereignty; therefore, it is said to be "non-self."
Regarding "ultimately without remainder": Nirvana is precisely the essence of impermanence.

As for "crossing from this shore to that shore," it refers to crossing from the "this" and "that" of birth-and-death and the nirvana of the Lesser Vehicle to reach the "other shore" of the Middle Way Nirvana.
Regarding "all such 'this' and 'that,'" this refers to the various teachings on Nirvana which employ both the principle of "neither of the two" and the application of "both."
All these are sovereign.

Regarding the statements that "the three truths are one truth" and "one truth is the three truths," this refers to the mutual identity of essence and function: when functioning, it is the essence, such that the three truths are one truth;
when being the essence, it is the function, such that one truth is the three truths. When both essence and function are quiescent, they are neither three nor one.
Essence and function are both illuminated; they are three yet one.
As for the statement, "If one is empty, all are empty—why then do you request that I remain? emptiness has no characteristic of abiding, and there is likewise no going when departing;
thus it is said, "all. The phrase "and so forth" (*nāi-zhì*) is an abbreviation of the text; one should say, "if one is provisional, all are provisional. Since the provisional is not real...
Regarding the phrase "how can one request him to remain," etc.: since the principle of the Middle Way is that there should be neither going nor remaining, why would one now request it?
Therefore, this [request] is negated.
What follows is a brief refutation of other interpretations, intended to clarify this meaning—that is, to reveal the intent regarding the Buddha’s realm.
To clarify that "the one is empty, and all are empty" means that the permanent is itself impermanent; to clarify that "the one is provisional, and all are provisional" means that the impermanent...

Because it is eternal. Regarding "one being within all," this refers to the simultaneous application of both eternity and impermanence; thus, it is said to be the intended meaning of the objective realm (*viṣaya*).

As for the further explanation provided later, it is as detailed in the subsequent text, specifically within the discussion between Mañjuśrī and others concerning how the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent, and so forth.
"Truly as the Holy One has spoken" refers to the intent of refuting the six difficulties.

"The fetter of stinginess is severed from outflows" is a term that remains general; it signifies the partial severance of the subtle delusions of ignorance, whereby the virtue of abandonment is accomplished.
The "equally great bodhisattvas" refers to those such as Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince.
Those who have been pulled from beneath the depths of the abyss are like children; those who dwell atop the clouds and mists are the "equally great bodhisattvas."

The phrase "expressing gratitude for that which is not used" precisely refers to the profound meaning of *nirvāṇa* upon the neck [of the Buddha]. Because it is that which is not used, he expresses his gratitude with it.

Regarding the statement "the suffering of the great assembly has reached its limit, while the Tathāgata has not yet [passed away]," this was because Cunda had finished making his request and further showed himself most earnestly. All...
"To withhold what has not been promised" means to assent.
"Never to change one's word" means that when sentient beings request [the Buddha] to remain, he does not give rise to a mind of weariness or aversion.
That which must not be taken up one-sidedly refers to both the Buddha and sentient beings, who are alike like those suffering from hunger and thirst;
the intentions of these two types of beings benefit whether they depart or remain, and there is never any weariness or indolence. For this reason, it is used as a metaphor.
At that time, those in the assembly who did not yet understand were unaware of the meaning of the "twofold movement" and the "twofold negation.

Those who contemplated it through the four *siddhāntas* saw that the conditioned and the unconditioned are not the same; this was because the assembly had not yet understood how to generate wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*).
Expedient means served as a secondary support, provisionally manifesting a dialogue in which Mañjuśrī concealed the unconditioned while extensively explaining it.

The conditioned is precisely skillful means; it serves to refute Cunda’s remedial perspective. To state that the two functions are secondary is to correctly reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of the Tathāgata’s realm.
To "destroy the abiding by means of non-abiding" means to destroy permanence by means of impermanence.
To be "confused and deluded within oneself" means to cling to the two extremes and consequently give rise to understanding through words, without yet knowing how to employ both simultaneously.

Regarding "those who resist and dispute in confusion": Mañjuśrī resisted and opposed Cunda; because their contentious arguments were difficult to resolve, it is said that they shall be set aside for now.
Regarding "pointing distantly to the Tathāgata": this refers to the *Aishan-pin* (Chapter on Sorrowful Lamentation), where the three types of cultivation are extensively refuted.
"Exemplifying the correct to reveal the incorrect" means exemplifying the correctness of the Middle Way to reveal the incorrectness of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
"Being able to question and being able to answer" means being endowed with the two types of adornment.
Victory is non-victory; permanence is impermanence. Defeat is non-defeat; impermanence is permanence. This reveals the "neither-nor" [of the tetralemma], which is why it is called "equality."

Regarding these matters and principles: Mañjuśrī addresses the phenomenal aspect (*dharma*), while Cunda addresses the noumenal principle (*tattva*); this may also be considered a complementary perspective.
As for Mañjuśrī’s elucidation of the *śūnyatā-samādhi*: Mañjuśrī is an ancient Buddha; the text clarifies the Mahāyāna as he engages in dialogue with Vimalakīrti.
All [these passages] discuss the inconceivable emptiness (*acintya-śūnyatā*). Cunda is a worldly person; that is, he exists within the realm of existence (*bhava*).
As such, his words are merely relative expressions and have not yet established the ultimate meaning. Therefore, it is said that he should still be considered existent.

Regarding the statement, "There is going and no returning; to obtain this 'non-existence'": it means that by clinging to the existence of the Small Vehicle, one now encounters the non-existence of the Mahāyāna.

Because there is no longer the existence of the Small Vehicle, it is called "no non-existence. Within the text, one should further state that "the non-existent has existence," which would then establish the existence [of the Mahāyāna].

That which is appropriate to the nature of things is manifested as "Carrying" when it is appropriate to see Manjusri as Carrying, and manifested as "Victorious" when it is appropriate to see Manjusri as Victorious;
this does not mean that Manjusri conforms to being carried.
Regarding the mutual striking of the anvil and the hammer: Mañjuśrī is the anvil and Cunda is the hammer; this is for the purpose of perfecting the vessel of the Dharma.
As for the simultaneous relinquishing of victory and defeat: it was precisely at this moment that he urged the offering of alms, thereby manifesting the essence of the Middle Way’s eternal abiding.

Regarding the statement that each possesses two functions which manifest the essence as being both [permanent and impermanent]: the non-permanent takes the permanent as its essence, and the permanent takes the non-permanent as its essence;
therefore, it is said that they "are" [both].
Regarding "injury to both substance and function": to cling to impermanence is to injure the substance of permanence; to cling to permanence is to injure the functioning substance of impermanence.
Therefore, it is called "neither."
Regarding the differentiation of essence and function: that which is non-constant takes the non-constant as its essence, while that which is constant takes the constant as its essence.
This is because the essence itself constitutes what is "is," whereas that which is not used constitutes what is "is not. Therefore, it is said that one is "is" and the other is "is not."
"That which is neither both nor neither" means that it is not the "is" of the preceding "both," nor is it the "neither" of the preceding "both"; hence it is called "neither-neither.

This reveals that it is simultaneously both "is" and "is. Within the text, one should further state "the essence is identical to the function," though this is omitted and can be understood by implication.
Second, "returning to the fundamental principle" refers to returning to the fundamental principle of making offerings.
Regarding "sharing the same inferiority": the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is supreme, yet it shares the same inferiority as all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in being impermanent.
Regarding "the weariness of the multitude of existences": this refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), which burden the practitioner.
Regarding "those who see three and hear one": those at a distance hear it, while those nearby see it; thus, the "Non-ideation" [heaven] is cited.
Those who are deluded regarding the higher dharmas are equal to fools, for they do not distinguish between the superior and the inferior.
Regarding the method of blending: taking the superior and blending it with the inferior is what is called "blending.
Regarding the loss of a superior name: this refers to being titled "God among Gods" (Devātideva). As for the most honored and supreme Dharma: this is the eternal Dharma.
If one were to equate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) [with the Buddha], it would be to drag the lower down to the level of the higher, thereby dishonoring his exalted title.

As for sentient beings receiving the Buddha’s grace, as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* where the four great śrāvakas express their realization, there are ten kinds of grace that are difficult to repay.
These range from the grace of extracting them from suffering and bestowing upon them happiness, up to the grace of universally pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*. For now, I shall speak of four.
This is merely a matter of ritual offering.
As for those who do not possess the strength of Nārāyaṇa, the Buddha does not derive his power from karmic retribution.
Now, using the daughter as a metaphor for compassion means that through unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*), one is able to give rise to genuine understanding.
The phrase "addressing those above to admonish those below" implies that by looking toward Mañjuśrī, one has already recognized the assembly present.
The phrase "those on the broad ground receive no benefit" means that those of the lowest ignorance cannot be forcibly made virtuous.
"The most holy do not require the labor of exhortation" means that those of superior wisdom cannot be made ignorant;
therefore, it is said they are "neither above nor below," which refers to those of middling capacity.

Regarding those who have already resolved their minds but have not yet reached fulfillment: one interpretation holds that from the stages above the Dwelling Grounds (bhūmi) up to, but not including, Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), all must be exhorted and admonished.
A second interpretation holds that this refers to those from the stage of the mere name of the initial resolution of mind upward, up to the stage prior to the Dwelling Grounds.
This is called being "insufficient.
There is no one living at home who has attained the five fruits; that is to say, there is no household of the Mahāyāna. A "household" (kula) is that upon which the body relies;
it is the embodiment of the three virtues that constitutes a household.

Although a woman may be poor and sickly, she possesses the principle of giving birth to a child; likewise, although one is shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), there exists within wisdom and severance the principle of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

"Beggar" (the character *gǐ* is pronounced with the *gǔ* and *lài* finals): according to the *Cāngpiān*, "begging" means to go about requesting. According to the *Tōngsùwén*, to pray for something is called "gai" (*qiúyuàn yuē gài*). This is its essential meaning.
"Following people and following death" means that when people die, one goes out to beg for alms.
"Being oppressed by delusion and distraction": lack of wisdom is called delusion; lack of concentration is called distraction.
Regarding "plain silk is easily dyed": "plain silk" refers to names; "easily dyed" refers to contemplative practice (*guanxing*).
As for "directions and corners": a corner is defined as a four-sided angle. Names and contemplative practice provide a partial understanding of the Middle Way, which is termed a "direction.
Furthermore, it is said that the "round" constitutes the "direction," while the three preceding teachings constitute the "corners."
One who contemplates the five aggregates as a transient lodging realizes that this dwelling is empty, like a guest’s stay. The five aggregates arise from ignorance like a gathering of travelers;
their moment-to-moment succession of aging and death is like a morning dispersal.
"Fan Zhuo takes pity on him. "Zhuo" means clarity. A person of wisdom who enters the contemplation of the Dharma practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) alongside it;
therefore, he takes pity on him.

This may be compared to one who is pregnant. Thus, when the three types of wisdom within the mind cultivate both phenomena and principle in a perfect manner, it is called "entering the holy womb" (*āryagarbha*).

"One who gives rise to pure understanding" is one who can contemplate that the three paths are themselves the three virtues (*triguṇa*). That the six sense faculties function interchangeably is called "pure understanding.
"Compassion has already been manifested" means that with a single wondrous voice, it pervades the trichiliocosm, reaching toward all Buddhas. This is called...
Regarding "this being manifest":
for those who possess all obstacles and difficulties, the three obstructions and four maras arise in chaotic competition prior to reaching the stage of semblance (*sāmya*).

Regarding "compassion fully subdues": upon reaching the stage of semblance, one has already severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*), which is termed "subduing" (*vinīta*); however, ignorance (*avidyā*) remains.
"Breaking" refers to dependence; it may mean that compassion is strong while ignorance is weak, and so forth.

Internal karmic obstacles refer to the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), while external karmic obstacles refer to the "sands and dust" [afflictions]. This is because they constitute obstacles both internally and externally.

The Ganges represents the afflictive hindrances; it is a metaphor for subtle ignorance. Having already broken one grade [of delusion] through partial realization of truth, it is said that "he has crossed over.

"Not abandoning the correct teaching" means being able to contemplate the three hindrances as being identical to the three virtues; therefore, it is said that he "teaches the aggregates, elements, and sense bases."
Thus, suffering is the Dharmakāya—neither permanent nor impermanent; karmic bondage is liberation—neither bound nor liberated;
and afflictions are Prajñā—neither light nor darkness.

Regarding "attaining birth in the Brahma Heaven": this refers to the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*). It is partially attained at the initial stage of abiding and perfected at the ultimate stage of wondrous enlightenment; hence, it is called the "two types of compassion.
"One should not apply them unilaterally" means that one's contemplation must not fail to contemplate the Tathāgata and so forth.

The Sūtra states: "There are none who have not yet attained the eye of wisdom. This refers to the ultimate eye of wisdom of the Mahāyāna, as the Sūtra says: "May I obtain, like the World-Honored One, the foremost purity of the eye of wisdom.

That which deviates from principle and cannot be explained in a partial manner is precisely the conditioned and the unconditioned; this reveals the principle of the Middle Way within the Great Teaching.
Furthermore,
regarding the three passages herein that extensively refute [certain views], these apply to the preceding four types of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) alike; since none may be taken as partial,
they are called "extensive" because they manifest and establish the correct principle.

First, regarding the opening of the partial teaching: the Sūtra says, "One should say that the Tathāgata is definitively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This "unconditioned" is precisely the partial [teaching].
Next, explaining the observation of capacities: the Sūtra asks, "For what reason is he able to produce wholesome dharmas for sentient beings? This refers solely to the Great Nirvāṇa.
The mind is settled; there is also the compassion that takes no object. Thus, the analogy of the "man" is joined together.
As for the title of the sixth fascicle, "The Parable of the Man," the meaning is that a man is able to travel a great distance.
Regarding "the principle is quiescent yet illuminating": the nature of reality (dharmatā) possesses the three virtues. The dharma-body is at peace, which is termed "quiescence.
Prajñā is internally luminous, hence it is said to be "illuminating. Liberation accords with conditions, which is termed "practice."

The statement that "the two intervals from beginning to end are collectively termed 'the middle'" means that from the stage of "identity with principle" (*li-ji*) up to the "ultimate" (*chui-jing*), there are the four intermediate stages of identity;
thus they are called "the two intervals. They are designated as "two" because they are viewed in relation to what precedes and what follows.
Regarding "constrained and oppressed by birth and death": not yet having emerged from the triple world is called "constraint"; the cyclical wandering through the six realms is called "oppression.
Regarding "humbly requesting instruction": being situated at the level of names and concepts is called "humility"; seeking understanding in accordance with principle is called "requesting."

Regarding the five desires being "not one's own" and "belonging to another": this refers to delusion arising from principle; thus they are said to be "not one's own. Since they do not exist inherently, they are said to "belong to another.

To metaphorically entrust them to the aggregates and sense-bases (skandhas and āyatanas) is like [entrusting things] to a house; it means that one can contemplate the three paths and know that they are all unreal, thereby treating them as a provisional entrustment. Furthermore, it is with... [the body].
Because the aggregates (skandhas) dwell therein, it is said to be like a house.
Being oppressed by ignorance is like one who is lying down; the coarse state of lying down in ignorance is merely a state of suppression. Regarding "sinking and not waking from sleep," and so forth:
Because ignorance has not yet been shattered, one lies down and falls back into sleep; hence it is said that one does not awaken.
As for the phrase "suddenly rising," the law of impermanence departs without a destination, signifying that there is no path [to follow]; hence it is said that one suddenly rises.
This is merely a brief mention of one; it is simply a condensation of the text. Since there is retribution, there must necessarily be karma;
since karma arises from afflictions, by mentioning one, all three are encompassed.
"Those who previously had not attained it" refers to the period before the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*); this is designated as "previously.
Because they have attained a semblance of understanding in which the six sense faculties function interchangeably, it is called "startled. As this semblance deepens, it becomes "awakening."

It is like entering the ocean and seeing level ground. Borrowing from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: it is like a person entering the ocean who sees only the appearance of levelness and no mountains or forests;
as they gradually go deeper, they certainly know they are moving away [from land]. Similarly, when a person at this stage knows that they will certainly shatter ignorance, this is called "death."

However, regarding those who possess pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*), the purity of the six sense faculties is called "white dharma. The five stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) are called "black dharma.
Upon reaching the stage of partial realization (*bhūta-tathatā*), it is neither white nor black; this is precisely the meaning of the three truths (*tri-satya*).

This is what is shameful. A person without shame or remorse is like the contemplation of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), such as the description in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* of having a "wasted and emaciated body.

One who is born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven represents the stage of the first *bhūmi* of partial realization, wherein one attests to the principle of the natural (*t'ien-jan*) and shatters one grade of ignorance.

It is clear that through the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*), one naturally reaches the ultimate stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*). Therefore, it is said that "this analogy establishes both.
When the Sūtra states, "successively and constantly being born in places of peace and bliss," this "peace and bliss" is none other than the secret treasury of the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*.

The "Treasury" (the *Abhidharmakośa*) begins from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) and concludes with the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*). Hence, it is said that they "proceed successively.
When the Sutra says, "for this reason," it refers to the conditions (*pratyaya*) of these six stages.

The Sūtra says, "those who possess a sense of shame and dread": they feel shame before the *paramārtha-deva* (the ultimate truth) and dread before the sages; this refers to the stage of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).
The Sūtra says, "a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts": this refers to upholding the ultimate precepts of the Mahāyāna. Since Mañjuśrī...
Having long upheld the Mahāyāna, one should not speak of impermanence.
A sutra states that those who [harbor such views] within their own homes shall fall into the Avīci Hell, from which there is no time of escape.
If that is so, the following objection from another party is raised: "The thirty-two [marks] are joined with the subjects, yet it is not permitted for them to be joined with the sovereign;

therefore, one cites the eighty secondary marks to challenge the status of the sovereign. Now, by employing the thirty-two marks as the position of the 'joined division of reality' (*satyabhāga*), these likewise constitute the sovereign through the eighty [marks], which is precisely the joining with the ultimate sovereign.

Regarding the causes and conditions for long life: long life is the fruit, while causes and conditions are the cause. It is through these causes and conditions that the fruit of long life is brought to completion.
As for Mañjuśrī’s single-word reprimand and exhortation, it is as stated in the preceding text: "You should not now utter such words."
This is a form of reproof. "One should train thus" and so forth is an exhortation.

As for the statement that the Noble One speaks only of his own Dharma and not the Dharmas of others: since Cunda already occupies the rank of the tenth stage (daśabhūmi), [he is not subject to such reproof].
It speaks of the six types of loving-kindness; therefore, it refers to them as "one's own dharma. The preliminary teachings are called "the dharma of others.
Even when those at the stage of non-realization speak of the noble dharma, it is likewise called "the dharma of others."

Regarding the phrase "obstructing the Great [Vehicle] at the end while refuting the Small [Vehicle] at the beginning," the intended meaning is as follows: if Cunda did not cling to the Small Vehicle at the beginning, it would have been difficult to refute it with the Great Vehicle at the end;
thus, the Tathāgata would have been unable to use the Great to refute the Small. Furthermore, those who cling to the Small in future ages would likewise not be refuted.
Because there are these two implications, it is said that [Cunda's position] "obstructs" [the teaching].

This refers to those who are new to the assembly; it is precisely the gathering for *nirvāṇa*. These newly arrived individuals have not passed through the five flavors [of the Dharma], yet they hear of the eternal abiding (*nitya*) while still clinging to the Lesser Vehicle.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* cites how even a hair’s breadth of goodness does not perish, and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* itself points to the eight thousand followers and others.

"Except for those after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa" means that this exemption prevents the charge of conceit (abhimāna). This refers to those who, after the parinirvāṇa, adhere to the Lesser Vehicle while performing rituals;
they are subsequently refuted by means of the Great [Vehicle]. Thus it is said, "after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa."
