"He is no ordinary person" refers to the fact that Cunda was originally of high station. As explained in the *Fahua shu* regarding Nanda:
he was the nephew of King Śuddhodana, the second son of King Droṇodana, the cousin of the World-Honored One, the elder brother of Ānanda, and the uncle of Rāhula;
he was certainly no ordinary man. Thus, Zhou Gong raised an objection, saying:
I am the son of King Wen, the younger brother of King Wu, and the uncle of King Cheng. I am no lowly man of the world.

When I speak all day long of "existence," that existence is not [true] existence; it is for the sake of the conventional use of the world. Therefore, it is said that it is not a state of total exhaustion.

Regarding "those who all day long speak of non-existence": non-existence is not truly non-existent, because it is eternally inexhaustible. Since the principle of the "double negation" (neither-nor) is ultimate, it is beyond the reach of words.
As for "this is the time of initial departure," the meaning is that among all times, the time of departure is considered supreme.
"Regarding 'the time when things are new,' it means that giving must be timely.
As for Mañjuśrī sharing the same views as others, these are the views of the Hīnayāna.
As for the assembly saying that Cunda’s practice was shallow, since Cunda was the son of a skilled artisan within the city, he was like those of the secular world."
It is of the same stream. The Tathāgata seals and praises it, and all doubts are thereby extinguished.
As for the scripture’s statement, “it likewise gladdens all sentient beings”: since all beings possess the three causal natures of the Principle (li), they share the same principle as myself;
thus, it is said that “all sentient beings” are addressed.
Regarding "the two gates aligned together," this refers to the simultaneous alignment of both the inverse and the direct. The first alignment states:

"If the Tathāgata delights sentient beings, he should likewise delight me. If he does not delight me, then he does not delight sentient beings; for I am included within the number of all sentient beings.
Thus, it is said that perfect delight would be destroyed [if this were not so].
"To prostrate oneself side-by-side" means: since the Tathāgata does not find me pleasing, you likewise are not found pleasing;
yet if he were to please you alone, it would constitute favoritism and aversion on the part of a Buddha.

First, regarding those who are untainted by outflows (*anāsrava*): if one competes with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) for the sake of what is pleasing, it instead becomes the deep-seated affliction of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Therefore, it is said: "You should not say that the Tathāgata finds pleasure [in such things]."

Second, regarding the explanation of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*): it clarifies that the Buddha has no attachment or delight, because both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are equally inverted.

Second, regarding the illustration used to clarify this: the intent is to show that one should have no affectionate attachment toward either the conditioned or the unconditioned, just as a dairy cow feels affection for her calf.
It is explained that there is that which is universally pure and pleasing. As the sutra says, "regarding all equally" is called "universal.
The wisdom of the Buddhas is precisely this purity. One should not speak of it as being exclusively conditioned or unconditioned;
rather, the very essence of the term "unconditioned" inherently possesses the three virtues. This is something that brings joy to both you and all sentient beings alike.
The metaphor of "possessing ignorance" refers to the waters of ignorance and craving.

Regarding the phrase "because it is the practice of a bodhisattva, it is not yet clear": if one discusses the sequence of the bodhisattva path, as stated in the subsequent text, even a bodhisattva of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) has not yet attained full clarity.
Regarding "the Buddha does not proceed": he abides in ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), like the garuḍa; thus, ignorance is exhausted. Kaishan says:
"The former refers to the lower being able to know the higher, which is like riding a donkey; the latter refers to the higher being able to know the lower."

"A bird ascending into the sky" and "the two analogies of the iron-smith at Yecheng" mean: [the first] intends to show that those of inferior wisdom initially do not know the superior intellect; the donkey’s vehicle represents wisdom that is inferior to that of a horse.
A fine horse is compared to a gentleman, and is therefore termed "superior intellect. The subsequent analogy concerns fish, turtles, and their like, who do not know how to ascend into the sky.
Therefore, it is called the "supreme realm.

Regarding the phrase "the essence of spiritual flavor," this is the name of a monastery. As for the passage stating that one initially does not know the *dharmakāya* and later does not know the *nirmāṇakāya*, it is as the sutra says, "For example, like a king," which is a metaphor for the Dharma King.
The subsequent section should read "subtle, secret, and profound," and so forth. This is...
This is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The subsequent analogy, which speaks of looking down at the great ocean, refers to the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Because it responds to the ocean of birth and death of all sentient beings, it is said that "one sees all forms and images."

Regarding the phrase "note: as stated above," this means to provide an explanation. Since there is currently no refutation [of these views], each of the explanations provided above possesses its own logic.

As for the phrase "clearing away the meaning of the single path of self-clinging," "clearing away" (fù) means to eliminate. Clinging to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) constitutes what is called a "single path."
This view is not ultimate.
If you claim it is not real, I shall likewise test you; it is not my own definitive teaching. Therefore, it is said to be "a view of a single path," and so forth.
Regarding what you have not yet fully understood: it is as the sutra says, that one cannot fathom the wisdom of the Tathāgata and so forth.

As for "examining the subtle and investigating the ultimate," this merely refers to analyzing, scrutinizing, and investigating doctrinal points in accordance with principle; it is simply termed "inconceivable."
"Explaining that all contemplations are quiescent" means that the preceding two layers of reproof explain how both speech and contemplation are utterly ceased.
"The various auspicious omens mentioned above" refers to the nine omens found in the previous section on invocation.
Therefore, we know that this light is precisely intended to urge the offering. The light symbolizes the Middle Way, while the offering symbolizes the opening of the eternal;
thus, their meanings regarding the Middle Way are identical.
As for the stern rebukes and reproaches, they condemn greed and the like, as well as the three faults of being untimely, too fast, and so forth.

To "harmonize the teaching with the capacities" means to preach the dharma of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), harmonizing the present teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) with the capacities of the assembly at that time;
when these accord like a seal and its impression, it is called "harmony. To support those above and transform those below, the intention is no different from that of Cunda.

The manifestation of the Middle Way through light is identical in its pedagogical intent to the assembly at the meeting with Cunda. The command for Cunda to prepare the offerings is likewise a skillful means to transform those of inferior capacity;
thus, the assembly of these two individuals is entirely due to the Buddha’s power.
"To know this matter immediately" means to take the causes and effects of the three virtues of *nirvāṇa* as that matter.
"To know the mind by seeing the form" refers to the perspective of the Hīnayāna, which is not far-reaching; it is not refuted within the text.
When Mañjuśrī beheld the light, his intention was already far-reaching, signifying that the eternal [nature] was about to be revealed; thus, he understood the Buddha’s intent.
The Sūtra states that it is not without causes and conditions; there are two kinds of causes and conditions: first, the cause and condition for the offering of alms;
second, the cause and condition for the Buddha’s entry into nirvāṇa.
The "one who weeps out of urgency" refers to the Buddha entering *nirvāṇa*.
The "one who remains silent because no promise has been made" means that [the Buddha] has not yet dared to manifest this [event].

Next, regarding the "weeping with grief": having heard the three urgent exhortations, the matter reached its ultimate limit and the principle was exhausted; thus, sorrow and suffering dwelt within his breast, and his mind...
"Unable to restrain himself," means he raised his voice and wept piteously.
As for "first stopping the disorder," it refers not only to Cunda, but to the fifty-two assemblies as well; the intention here is to have them contemplate the five gates.
Regarding the three analogies for impurity: as stated in the *Sūtra on the Dying Prisoner*, such things as ripe fruit and pieces of meat are all foul and filthy objects.
Because the prisoner dwells in an impure place, these are used as analogies for impurity. The text omits the contemplation of suffering (*duḥkhānupaśyanā*);

however, in the concluding passage below, it states that one should contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Since conditioned phenomena are themselves suffering, the five gates are thus fully complete.

This is like the contemplation of non-self. As the sutra says: "It is like the up-and-down motion of a pestle. Generally speaking, that which is called "self" takes sovereignty as its defining characteristic.
Since there is both "up" and "down," there is no self.
The Sūtra says, "It is like food mixed with poison. The five [aspects] such as impermanence are each distinct from one another;
this is termed "mixed. All of them harm the practitioner through afflictions; this is termed "poison."
I enter parinirvāṇa out of compassion; this is precisely the objectless loving-kindness (*apraṇihita-maitrī*).
It causes you and all sentient beings to together attain the Dharma of the secret treasury of the three virtues. Had I not entered nirvāṇa, you would not have been able to obtain it;
therefore, I enter parinirvāṇa.
The scripture states, "and all," which refers to the fifty-two assemblies.

That "the teachings of all Buddhas are likewise" means that the Tathāgata appears for the sake of the assemblies and enters [parinirvāṇa] for the sake of the assemblies; this is because the conditions and circumstances differ.
It is indeed distressing and sorrowful.

As for the meaning of this verse being the same as that of the two verses below, it is like the verses of the Snow Mountain Youth (*Himavat-kumāra*) in the following text, such as "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" (*sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "cannot help but feel sorrow" and so forth, the intended meaning is: although I know that the Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa, I feel sorrow for the sake of sentient beings, and I make this request for the sake of sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "unable not to deliver [beings]" and so forth: it is a cause for celebration because the Tathāgata has enabled me to attain the five fruits; it is a cause for joy because he enables sentient beings to attain them as well.
This is like the analogy that the provisional and the real cannot be separated from one another; they are the constant and the non-constant applications.

Those who employ skillful means according to the occasion can utilize both the permanent and the impermanent; these are all for the sake of sentient beings who differ from one another, and now they all abide in nirvāṇa.
The "immovable fruit" refers to the fruit of the three virtues of nirvāṇa.
Regarding "practicing together": this refers to the practice of the dual flow. Nirvana is impermanence; that which is not nirvana is permanence.

○ Commentary on the Third Chapter, "Lamentation":
To explain it in detail, there are four distinct aspects (*siddhi*), hence it is called "detailed.

That which is "lamented" refers to the corruption of the wholesome that has already arisen; this means that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma gradually becomes diluted and corrupt. This is fully explained as set forth in the sutra.
Regarding the praise for not yet having produced the "blindness" of evil: it is because [the Buddha] causes that blindness not to arise.
"Exclusively by means of the secret dharma" refers to the dharma of the three virtues and nirvana; thus, he concludes with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

In the preceding chapter, those addressed were worldly people; speaking in general terms, this was not without reference to the Path, for even among the fifty-two assemblies there are those who possess the Path.
In the present chapter, those addressed are the bhikṣus of inferior cultivation mentioned in the text below.
In this present chapter, there is no one who offers a meal; it concerns the three types of bhikṣus who practice cultivation.
In the preceding chapter, there was a dual invitation: an invitation to receive offerings and an invitation to remain in the world.
In this present chapter, there is a single invitation: an invitation to the newly realized Dharma.
In the preceding chapter, the person was the cause; because the great assembly offered praise, Cunda conveyed their request. In this chapter, the self is the primary cause;
there is no great assembly, as it concerns only the three types of cultivation.
In the preceding chapter, the Buddha-nature was briefly elucidated; it discussed only the five fruits of permanence, and thus was concise.
In that previous chapter, the present teaching was discussed by extensively citing the permanent body, the dharma-body, and so forth, in order to refute the past [teachings].
In this chapter, both the present and the past are presented together to use the superior to disparage the inferior; the "inferior" refers precisely to the past.
In the preceding chapter, the two interlocutors were Mañjuśrī and Cunda.
In the present chapter, the interlocutors are the three bhikṣus who practiced cultivation; they employ extensive analogies in their discourse with the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "those who moved by attachment in the previous chapter gave rise to doubt": this means that the attachments of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) were moved, thereby giving rise to the doubts addressed in the present chapter.
As for the distinction between the general and the specific: specifically, the previous chapter was directed toward the mundane and so forth;

generally speaking, the previous chapter was also directed toward Mañjuśrī, which pertains to the Path (*mārga*). Since the present chapter clarifies the eternal through Cunda, it pertains to the mundane (*laukika*) below.
Each of these nine phrases has its own specific meaning; this is the explanation of their general and particular senses.
As for the "three requests," they are: first, the request out of compassion; second, the request through prayer; and third, the request according to the capacity of the practitioner.
"It is not that he does not teach at all" means that, since the previous section discussed permanence based on Cunda’s discourse, the essential meaning has already been heard in brief;
this [section] shall now explain it extensively. Therefore, it says: "From now until the end, you all... and so forth.
"We who possess poisonous bodies" refers to Arhats; because they have not yet severed ignorance, they are said to have "poisonous bodies," for [ignorance] is able to destroy their wisdom.
"Departing while constantly abiding" means that impermanence is itself permanence. "Abiding while constantly departing" means that permanence is itself impermanence.
If you do not understand, you do not understand the simultaneous wandering of going and staying, nor their common entry into the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*).

As for your illness having a sequence of before and after: first is the illness of the heterodox and eternal; later is the illness of the impermanent. When the teaching of the impermanent arises, the teaching of the heterodox and eternal is abolished.

When the teaching of the eternal and so forth arises, the teaching of the impermanent is abolished. A detailed discussion of the arising and abolishing of the five periods is fully set forth in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This is the explanation from the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text).
"Winding around the Tathāgata, etc. refers to the pedagogical methods throughout the Buddha’s lifetime, following the five periods of teaching.
"Whether early or late depends on you" means that if one attains awakening within the *Avataṃsaka*, it is called "early"; as for you now, you have not yet awakened.
It is always so; it is only now that he enters, which is termed "late. Therefore, Śāriputra’s realization states:

"He did not wait for what was before, nor did he wait for what was after; this is our own fault, not the World-Honored One's. Thus it is said: "The fault lies with us, as it were, toward the Tathāgata."

"Who could possibly be the agent? means that there is no presiding master.
"Furthermore, it is the power of the Buddha's body" refers to the essence of the Dharmakāya.

"It is also [the power of] Cunda, Mañjuśrī, and others" refers to the great bodhisattvas of the Dharmakāya who constitute the assembly that initiates [the teaching]; they also possess the three powers.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that the conditions for causing an earthquake are immeasurable in meaning: this refers to how, upon attaining the three bodies (*trikāya*), the four *siddhārthas*, the primary and attendant [deities], and the fifty-two assemblies, there are various responsive inducements and causal conditions;
therefore, it is said to be "immeasurable. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* is cited to explain this through the four...
"Xi" (悉) means "to fully realize and establish.

as stated in the aforementioned scripture, "Cunda, you should not contemplate whether the various Buddhas are long-lived or short-lived, nor even the realm of the Tathāgata. Second, the Tathāgata’s skillful means may appear long...

The meaning is that the Buddha’s wisdom is like the tip of a finger; it does not know what is distant. As for the Tathāgata being "fourfold indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*):
since he lacks the wisdom of reflexive illumination, he likewise does not know [in the same way as ordinary cognition] whether others are good or evil, remaining thus like something indeterminate.

This would lead to an infinite regress: the wisdom that reflects back would require another wisdom to illuminate it, and that illuminating wisdom would require yet another reflection of wisdom, and so on, as they would continue to illuminate one another in succession.

Regarding "immediately harming both houses": it is said that by asserting the Buddha has no "reversal" (no retribution), one harms the Kaishan school; because the Kaishan school maintains [the existence of] karma, they hold that wisdom exists inherently.
By this, one also harms the Guangzhai school; hence, it is called "both."
One may challenge the Guangzhai school on the grounds that [the Buddha] lacks the capacity to illuminate himself and, furthermore, to illuminate others.
One may challenge the Kaishan school on the grounds that there is no distinct wisdom of "reflexive illumination" (fanzhào) to avoid the fault of infinite regress.
As for those who find it difficult to accept the Master’s view: one does not necessarily [attain] one, nor do three necessarily [attain] three;

"Praying that the Buddha may remain and grant his light" means to entreat him. It is a prayer for the benefit of his radiance.
First, regarding the explanation of previous commentators: since their interpretations are without fault, I shall employ them here as before, condensing the five similes into three.

This refers to those such as masters, parents, and teachers. As for "criticizing the invitation," it means criticizing and judging that the Tathāgata has no beginning or end [in his compassion, teachings, and instructions].
The following extensive passage provides the analogy.

there were Bodhisattvas who attained entry at every stage and even those who shattered ignorance. How can it be judged that [the teaching] only reached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* before entrusting the Dharma to those such as the Caṇḍālas?

Therefore, it is called an obstruction. Now, taking the Two Vehicles as the correct interpretation is also a matter of residual habituation (*vāsanā*), specifically the residual habituation of the Mahāyāna.
It is simply another name for ignorance; thus, it is said "also.
"Not exhausting the remaining afflictions" means that one has not yet shattered ignorance.
"Official business arising and responding" refers to propagating the Dharma and transforming others; as this is not a private matter, it is called "official business."
For example, those who enter the cycle of birth and death suffer together with sentient beings, just as if they were in prison.
Now, regarding the phrase "taking the mechanical device as a bystander": the arrival of the device is like a Buddha, and its meaning is like a question.

Regarding "attaining a portion of the Buddha-dharma," this refers to the passage in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* where Śāriputra expresses his realization; it is precisely the dharma-portion of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Mahāyāna.

Since this is used as an analogy for the two vehicles (*śrāvaka-yāna* and *pratyekabuddha-yāna*), it is likewise a "small portion" that constitutes their dharma-portion. Thus, they are said to be "born from the mouth of the Buddha."
This is like having a semblance of a child but not yet having obtained the true child. "The student" refers to one who contemplates afflictions.

"The people who have means of livelihood" refers to those practicing the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). "The people who are despondent and lack a livelihood" refers to those whose ignorance (*avidyā*) has not yet been destroyed.

First, regarding "it rests with me alone": by using the virtuous king as a metaphor for the Dharma King, it is shown that when sentient beings commit offenses, the responsibility lies solely with me, the sovereign.
As for citing the example of Mañjuśrī: the bhikṣu’s intention was that both Mañjuśrī and Cunda have realized eternal bliss, whereas he alone has been instructed [otherwise].
...and so forth, thereby realizing impermanence.
Yet those who are ashamed of traveling perilous paths do not show me the level road. This "level road" is none other than the Eightfold Path to Nirvana.
The "eight winds" for ordinary beings consist of the four pairs of adverse and favorable conditions.
That one should not grieve over what has been lost refers to the passing away of the Tathāgata;
that one should not rejoice over what has been gained refers to his not entering into *nirvāṇa*. At these two extremes of abundance, ordinary beings—
To harbor anxiety or joy is to lose the Dharmakāya; there is neither this nor that attainment.
Regarding those such as "the minister's son" and so forth: in the ultimate truth there is no conceptualization. Who is the minister of the sovereign?
Who is the son of the kinsman? Who is the disciple of the teacher?
"Who goes and who crosses over?"—the former refers to the response (the teaching), and the latter refers to the capacity (the recipient). That both say "who" implies there is no sovereign master.
"Silent and without trace (*wén*)," where "trace" (*wén*) means a footprint; it is also said to mean "self" (*wǒ*), signifying that there are no tracks or signs.

Therefore it is said, "He remains silent. Therefore it is said, "The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus.
That one cannot proceed in a single direction means that because of the cessation of sorrow there is joy, and because of joy there is the cessation of sorrow.

Regarding "reproaching the ordinary while praising the noble": this stops the grief of humans and devas and causes them to cultivate right mindfulness.

Regarding "the praise and entreaty": within the context of praising and praying, the rising sun and the rising mountain are used as metaphors for the Buddha; the Buddha then responds to these praises.

they have not yet returned to the great ocean of nirvāṇa. Since they neither see nor enter it, what benefit would there be in requesting them to remain? Therefore:
The meaning is as stated in the Sūtra: "One cannot obtain the priceless jewel without entering the great ocean.

even such pairs as duality and non-duality are all instances of such therapeutic counteraction.

Xinghuang says that because the subsequent text fully contains this meaning, he does not permit the preceding section to be understood as exclusively referring to the past, nor the second question as exclusively referring to the present.

Furthermore, regarding the inclusion of various inquiries: the thirty-four questions in the subsequent text, as well as the "Lion’s Roar" and others, collectively comprise the entire work as the basis for these inquiries.
Regarding the statement that "the Śākyas are without fault," our school cites the text in terms of the past, the present, and the negation of both, none of which lose their logical consistency;
thus it says, "Among all various dharmas, I shall accord with them," and so forth.
Regarding the further summary in three ways: since this was already explained previously, the word "further" is used merely as a transition; it is, in fact, an explanation based on the Three Truths.
Furthermore, regarding the summary in four ways: this adopts the sense of "simultaneous illumination," thereby comprehensively encompassing both the present and the past.
Regarding the phrase "extensively analyzed, as noted in the commentary," the intent is to explain that the five flavors and four teachings are all interpreted in this same manner.

As for the "three gates" and "four gates": the three gates refer to the three truths; the four gates refer to emptiness, existence, and so forth. Among the four teachings, this pertains to the [Tripitaka] Teaching.
The teachings all consist of four gates.
Xinghuang says that these constitute eight stages; "stages" refers to levels, meaning that the sequences differ.
"Next, showing" refers to the causes and effects of the present and the past. "Finally, bestowing" reveals the new *i* (the letter I).
"Those who possess wisdom but lack the precepts" refers to those who lack the ultimate ten precepts of the Mahāyāna and the wisdom of single-mindedness in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
they are not true renunciants, nor have they departed from the house of the two deaths.
Regarding the question, "How can this body be the Dharma-nature body? the intention is that partial truth (pratisaṃvid-satya) is taken as the Dharma-nature;
thus, Śāriputra said, "We have all entered the Dharma-nature together."
"To be of one and the same intent" means to attain the five absences of difficulty, which is precisely to be free from the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*).
"To be complete in both text and meaning" means to consolidate the eight stages into three; this fulfills the meanings of the master, the parent, and the teacher, respectively.
"Being able to leave behind" refers to attaining the five absences and being free from the eight difficulties.
"Not praising the renunciation of those who sever their attachments" refers to passages in the sūtra such as "being able to endure what is difficult to endure."

He does not praise the final act of giving because, for those who have left the household life, the precepts are easy to maintain while giving is difficult; for laypeople, giving is easy while the precepts are difficult.

Next, he cites the analogies of gold sand and the udumbara flower: the purity of the substance of the gold sand represents a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts and realizes the fruit of arhatship, thereby escaping the eight difficulties.
The udumbara flower represents the difficulty of obtaining a human body.
"One should not let it pass in vain" means causing one to attain the newly revealed secret treasury (*guhyakośa*).
"One should not recognize the Buddha through intimacy" intends to censure those bhikṣus, for they have not yet recognized the Buddha.
What follows explains the intent behind this recognition.
Those who do not recognize the Buddha do not recognize the Buddha as their own one-body; they are also not true children of the Bodhisattva-Buddha.
How, then, could they recognize the Buddha as their own kin, being merely like worldly princes?
I do not dare refuse what I find as sweet as shepherd’s purse; for while shepherd’s purse is sweet and tea is bitter, the latter is used to lead one toward the former.
As for the "unsurpassed skillful means," these are the skillful means of the Tathāgata’s identical essence and the gateway to the Nirvāṇa of the Three Virtues;
therefore, it is said that they are not small. Within the *Avataṃsaka*, they are not received, nor have they been practiced since the time of the Deer Park.
"One who is unwilling to perform tasks" refers to one who does not cultivate the unconditioned precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
"Pointing to the mountains and pointing to the earth" means: "That which I have relinquished—my own bodily bones—are as vast as the Mount Vipula."
Regarding the statement "pointing to the sea and pointing to the river": the amount of mother’s milk one has drunk is equal to the four great oceans;

all such matters are included therein. As for those who are heedless and shameless: from the perspective of the Two Vehicles, [the Great Vehicle] is called "heedless" [in comparison], yet because they remain heedless, they feel no shame before the Heaven of Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-deva*).
Being bound within the realm of *pariṇāmi-śarīra* (transformation-bodies) is termed "prison"; because they have not yet emerged from it, they do not attain the Great [Vehicle].
They ride upon liberation. This is your own fault; it is not that I am unkind.
As for the "various māras and bands of thieves," these refer to the four māras within the realm and the four māras outside the realm, none of whom dare to cause harm.
Regarding the phrase "profound, vast, and surging waves," the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is called the King of Samādhis because all samādhis are contained within it;
thus, it is termed "vast. It penetrates to the very bottom of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa); thus, it is termed "profound.
"Waves" is an alternative name for the waters of all samādhis.
*Pìní* (睥睨): The upper character is read as *pǔ* (普末反) and the lower as *wǔjì* (五計反). The *Guǎngyǎ* states: "Bìnì, tié, núqiáng, bì.
The *Cāngjiě* says it refers to the small parapets atop city walls. The *Shìmíng* explains: "It means to peer (*bìnì*) through the openings for matters that are not routine.
Privately speaking, 'bì' implies assisting in the height of the city wall."
For one who is profoundly versed in both the ancient and the present, the city of Nirvana has existed inherently from the beginning; it is not something that has only recently come into being.
Therefore, it is said that his realization is far-reaching. Being fully endowed with the three types of wisdom is itself clarity and understanding; thus, my city is such as this.
What is it that is not awe-inspiring, and what is it that is to be feared? Internal enemies, which are the afflictions (*kleśa*), are called "awe-inspiring";
external subjugation of all Māras is called "fear."

"Both inside and outside are jewels" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment of the Mahāyāna’s unconditioned practice (*anabhisaṃskāra*), which serve as its adornment; thus they are called "jewels.
Filling the interior and overflowing to the exterior, through one's own practice and the transformation of others, their function pervades the entire Dharma-realm, manifesting in brilliant splendor.
"Furthermore, 'without obstruction or deficiency' means that a single dharma possesses all dharmas.
'Grasping at false pebbles' refers to those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), as illustrated by the metaphor of the spring pond in the subsequent text."

"You who have a humble mind and are content" means that, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is like a poor person who, having obtained a little, considers himself satisfied and no longer aspires to anything better;
therefore, it is called "dwelling in little. Because one practices only a small amount of the Dharma, it is called "abiding in the lower."
"Not being weary of rag-robes" refers to the dust-like sands of ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Not delighting in jeweled necklaces" refers to the Mahāyāna precepts and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that adorn the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

"Begging for food at many places" means seeking sustenance by traversing all phenomena; it is the practice of contemplation within ordinary households, fully traversing the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
This is the Middle Way.
"Not delighting in superior flavors" refers to the *amṛta* (nectar) of the three virtues of *nirvāṇa* as the superior flavor.
"Not delighting in great illumination" refers to the threefold wisdom within the single mind.

Regarding "hesitating on a narrow path": the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) disparages those of the two vehicles by comparing them to a narrow path that cannot accommodate two people walking side-by-side;
"hesitating" (*pan-huan*) describes the state of not advancing.

To briefly clarify "not being able to be separated from that which cannot be left": one cannot attain the secret treasury of the Mahāyāna, yet one does not depart from the impermanence of the Hīnayāna.
Regarding "not entering the ranks of the multitude": when phenomena and principle are in harmony, they constitute the Three Jewels as a single essence; this is termed the Saṃgha.
Since the Saṃgha is itself a multitude, it is said here that one does not "enter" based on the perspective of principle.
"One must not be without difficulties" means that even if one is outside the boundaries of the realm (*dhātu*), one may still lack the "difficulties" of being beyond the two vehicles (*yāna*).

Seeing, cultivation, and the state of no-more-learning—these three stages for those of the two vehicles constitute the difficulty of entering and exiting meditative concentration with deliberate intent, which is the difficulty of being before or after a Buddha.

The principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the difficulty of the long-lived heavens (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*). Not possessing the ten kinds of six sense faculties constitutes the difficulty of incomplete faculties (*vyaṅga-indriya*).

The partial truth of the cessation-nirvāṇa is the difficulty regarding the Northern Continent; the possession of all-encompassing wisdom alone is the difficulty regarding worldly wisdom and eloquence.
This is explained at length in the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā* (and so forth).
"Not attaining the true fruit" refers to the fruit of Great Nirvana (*mahāparinirvāṇa*).
"The preliminary expedient means of the Path" refers here to the period prior to realizing the fruit according to the Hīnayāna; this is termed "prior to the Path.

This is not the same as the Mahāyāna treatises' discussion of "prior to the Path," "subsequent to the Path," and so forth. If discussed generally, everything prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes the period "prior to the Path. [End of middle section]
Regarding the two flavors [of the Separate Teaching and the Shared Teaching], both possess the stages prior to the Path and subsequent to the Path, and so forth.
When it is said that "the stage prior to the Path is the Perfect cause," this refers to opening up the preceding expedient means (*upāya*), all of which constitute the Perfect cause;

this is discussed in terms of the Mahāyāna, referring to the period prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*) and the abidings (*vihāra*). From the first abiding upward is called the stage subsequent to the Path. The stage subsequent to the Path is the Perfect...
"Function" (*yòng*) refers to function as discussed in relation to the essence (*tǐ*).
"True, good, and wondrous form" refers to the essence; "producing wondrous goodness" refers to practice (*xíng*).
"Amṛta-perfection" means the medicine of eternal immortality; because it is fully endowed with the three virtues, it is called "perfect. There is no lack.
This refers to the determination [of the meaning].

Originally, those named the Sangha on account of the merit of cause and effect are as follows: the Mahāyāna cause is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and the Mahāyāna fruit is likewise the true reality of all phenomena;
these are all of one essence within the Triple Gem and are thus called the Sangha. Therefore, it is refuted by saying: "As for your..."
Cause and effect are the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle; they are not ultimate.
"Not a slayer" refers to ignorance beyond the realms, which is treated as the thief.

"Non-arising" refers to the non-arising of the transformation-body (*pariṇāma*). It is not that the character "non-" is placed below the word "arising"; it does not emerge from falsehood. Such is the characteristic of the Buddha-dharma.
The body sixteen feet tall and all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing are entirely false.
That which does not reach is liberation; being able to shatter the eight "reaching" states, such as permanence and impermanence, is itself liberation.

That "the Buddha and the Sangha are likewise" means that within a single jewel all three virtues are fully present. For example, just as the Sangha possesses the Dharma-nature, permanence, and so forth, the Tathāgata is likewise endowed with these three virtues.
The Buddha is named "Awakened" (Buddha); when this awakening and non-awakening are in harmony, they constitute the Sangha.
The third is also complete.

Regarding "neither arising nor not arising": this is the ground of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). In principle, it is fundamentally non-arising; yet, it can also give rise to the medicinal herbs of the five vehicles and the seven kinds of goodness.
The growth of medicinal herbs does not depart from that which enables their growth—the earth. The earth, as the source of growth, possesses the nature of solidity;
the medicinal herbs that grow there likewise possess the nature of solidity. Therefore, it is said that they do not depart from it.
"Karma that summons the great earth" refers to karma that is neither outflowing (*āsrava*) nor non-outflowing.
"Merit that brings forth medicinal herbs" refers to the merit of precepts and meditative concentration.
"The three kinds of revolving" refers to the triad of the great earth, medicinal herbs, and sentient beings; thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says, "All are one ground."
Because all things produced are equally moistened by a single rain, it is said that they cannot be separated from one another.
"Wan" (宛) refers to a shape where the edges are low and the center is high.
As for "possessing all things," nothing exists outside of the five vehicles, the seven virtues, and the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates. Furthermore...
It is said that there are eighty-four thousand gates of affliction (*kleśa*), and it is also said that there are eighty-four thousand gates of various samādhis;
because they contain and preserve all dharmas, they are called "treasuries" (*piṭaka*).
Regarding the phrase "citing the three dharma-bodies and so forth," this is explained in detail as the ten kinds of triads in the *Zhiguan* section of the *Fahua xuanyi*.
As for "transcendent conjunction," it refers to using what follows to correspond with what precedes.

Regarding "all see the Buddha-nature": from the initial arousal of the bodhicitta until the ultimate stage of wondrous enlightenment, every single instance therein involves the realization of the three causes of Buddha-nature; therefore, it is said that "all" see it.

Regarding the phrase "the six stages of discernment," etc., the intent is to explain that there are differences between the entry into the principle (*yuli*), the entry into names (*mingzi*), and the entry into contemplation (*guan*).
Now, according to the meaning of the text, that which constitutes the entry into the ultimate truth of the true nature (*zhenyi*) is termed "seeing" (*jian*).

The followers of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* say that the *ālaya-vijñāna*, when referred to as the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*) within the realm of delusion, clarifies that the seeds of both good and evil are contained and stored therein.

The followers of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Dharmatrāta’s school) say that it refers to the future fruit of Buddhahood and so forth; this is an interpretation of the Hīnayāna, which is entirely distinct [from the former].
Because sentient beings are themselves [the Tathāgata], they are called "mysterious. The Sūtra states: "Within the bodies of sentient beings, the Tathāgata sits cross-legged.
This refers to the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-guṇa*); it is the Tathāgata in the sense of principle (*li-ji*). Since the three causes are fully present, it is said to be so.

This treatise refutes [other views] because they do not coincide with one another. Furthermore, this treatise is merely a name for its own *nirvāṇa*, just as the term "deformed person" is used [to refute others].
It is like the treatises of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which do not allow people to see the meaning, being like a hidden treasury.
Regarding "like the moon dwelling in the sky": the moon of true permanence is shrouded by clouds;
now, as this sutra reveals it, it points out that these very afflictions are themselves bodhi—just like seeing the moon alone in the sky once the clouds have parted.
Regarding the phrase "sentient beings do not understand," this refers to those who have not yet attained awakening.

As for "the Dharma-realm encompasses all," it means that the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, the three thousandfold world, and the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants are fully and perfectly manifested; therefore, it is called a "treasury" (garbha).
When a great wind sweeps away the mist and the Milky Way shines brightly, it is because the heavy clouds obscuring the Great Clarity have been cleared away by a long wind.
The secret treasury of the Three Virtues shines as brightly as the sun; "bright" (bǐng) also means "clear" (míng).
Regarding the phrase "as stated in the sutras," this likewise refutes others as previously mentioned.
"The three combined with the three virtues" refers to combining the two preceding metaphors.

"This is entering the principle through phenomena" means that the first two concern phenomena (*dharma*), while the latter one concerns principle (*tattva*). This pertains to spiritual practice; [it is] the eye.

It belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*). Wisdom is itself the eye. When non-Buddhists worship deities and are likewise able to bring merit to others, this is included within [the category of] conduct (*caryā*).
Regarding the statement that "the three virtues are the Teacher of the Buddhas," it refers to the Dharma, which is that upon which all Buddhas rely as their teacher.

Regarding the "seal" (mudrā) applied to teaching and practice: the true reality (*tathatā*) of the Mahāyāna serves as this seal. When applied to teaching and practice, they likewise become the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
As for all verbal expressions and the like, such as those in the "Chapter on Letters," there are no mundane letters nor supramundane dharmas.
It is not permanent; therefore, it is said to be "corresponding.

As for "cultivating correspondence," as stated in the subsequent text: "If this person hears the two characters 'permanent,' they shall not fall for seven kalpas"—this is precisely what is meant by correspondence.
Regarding "attaining correspondence": this refers to attaining the principle of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) once one has ascended above the stages of abiding.
That the Dharma-body is both illumination and sovereignty means that illumination is prajñā and sovereignty is liberation;
these three are not distinct from one another.
That "three yet one, and one yet three" exists because they are mutually interfused.
If the three were fixed as three and the one were fixed as one, it would merely revert to the ancient teachings' explanations of verticality and horizontality.
Regarding the extensive establishment of questions and answers: the sixfold series of questions and answers by the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda extensively discusses the meaning of Buddha-nature;
it is nothing other than these three virtues of the present, which are no different from the three dots of the syllable *i*.
"Vast and inexhaustible" describes the appearance of water. Since the Buddha-nature is like the ocean, how can it be described?

"What is its ultimate destination? Nirvāṇa takes the three virtues as its destination; therefore, following the text on "Arousing the Mind through Stopping and Contemplation," this is clarified by means of the six stages of realization (*liujie*).
Within this, the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the three virtues are likewise used as the destination. Thus, the destination is itself the three.
"Virtue. To what destination does it point? It is to enter together into the Secret Treasury, and so forth.
That which can adorn the celestial countenance and act as the sovereign of the world—by means of these three days, it is able to illuminate the great trichiliocosm.

Whether extended vertically or horizontally, [ordinary] functions are not its utility. Internally, it corresponds to the Tathāgata, the Sovereign Dharma King, who is able to possess the three virtues as his adornment.
Yan: Taking the aspect of illumination is *prajñā* (wisdom); taking the aspect of severing evil is *vimukti* (liberation).
Through the power of concentration and wisdom, everything is accomplished. It is like the vision of the gods: everything is accomplished.
Regarding the summary that encompasses all: these three dharmas subsume all phenomena without exception. The Dharma-body is also threefold;
Prajñā is also threefold; and Liberation is also threefold. These three sets of three make nine, yet the nine are simply one.
Since this one is not fixed as one, it is said that it is also not nirvāṇa.

Regarding the mutual inclusion of the vast and the minute: the ten directions are the vast, while form and so forth are the minute; yet form and so forth are the vast, while the ten directions are the minute—and in both cases, neither is constricted.
Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible," etc.: the term "etc. includes wisdom, which is likewise so; this refers to *prajñā* (wisdom).

That all phenomena are eternally abiding refers to the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body), because form is itself liberation. Since these three virtues are fully possessed, they are cited here to testify to the third [aspect], the *dharmakāya*.
"Neither knowing nor letters": "neither knowing" refers to contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*), while "not letters" refers to written words. Prajñā is the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Because it is not a form of knowing, one's deliberations and discriminations cannot be stirred; this is the essence of luminous observation, which is not moved by afflictions (*kleśa*).
It cannot be conceived through ordinary sentiments or discursive thought.
It cannot be expressed in words or written upon the *shen*. The *shen* is the large ceremonial sash.

For instance, whenever the Master spoke a word or performed an act, Zizhang heard it from across the wall and recorded it all upon his sash to ensure its completion. These written characters are all beyond words.
It is said that this cannot be inscribed upon one's girdle.
That which is not identical with the pervasion of space has no expressive signification.

That ordinary beings and sages are equally illuminated refers to the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of sages; as these pervade the ten realms, it is said they are "equally illuminated."
The mundane and supramundane are the "half-syllables" (ardhakṣara).
The supramundane of the highest order is the "full-syllable" (pūrṇakṣara). Furthermore, according to the meaning of transformation, both possess the half and the full:
the Hīnayāna is the half, and the Mahāyāna is the full. If one speaks purely of the Great [Vehicle], this is the full within the full. If categorized according to the five periods... [the middle]...

Regarding the two types of *su* (intermediate): those that possess half-light and fullness, and those that possess both half-light and fullness; the *Lotus Sūtra* possesses only fullness, and so forth.

Furthermore, in terms of the three kinds of worlds (*trividha-loka*) corresponding to the four lands: the Land of Common Residence corresponds to the mundane world; the Land of Expedient Means corresponds to the supramundane;
and the Land of True Reward and the Land of Peaceful Light correspond to the supreme supramundane, and so on.

Regarding the "flowing forth of the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-pravāha*): as stated in the *Cunda-parivarta* cited above, "The unsurpassed rain of Dharma falls upon the field of your body"—this is precisely the meaning of "flowing forth."
Regarding "like a cascading river and surging from the sea": the teaching bestowed upon those below is like a cascading river; compassionate transformation of others is like the sea;
and the universal proclamation of the distinct and perfect sounds is therefore said to be inexhaustible.
Regarding the phrase "neither clamor nor stillness," it is not the clamor within the realm of conditioned existence, nor is it the stillness beyond that realm;
it is neither the bondage of ordinary beings, nor the liberation of those of the Two Vehicles.

"The ten knowledges that cannot be rendered void" refers to the enumeration of the ten knowledges of the Hīnayāna, as explained in detail in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) under the section on "Wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "bound by non-Buddhists," this refers to skillfully demonstrating bondage within what is actually not bondage, as in the case of the layman Vimalakīrti and others.
"All the māras and non-Buddhists are my attendants. This refers to those who were initially identical [to me] but later became different, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "though base, one must bestow," the character *shī* (施) is pronounced with a level tone (*píngshēng*). Here, "bestowing" (*shī*) means "transformative manifestation" (*shīhuà*).
Entering brothels to demonstrate the faults of desire and the like are all instances of base and defiled places.
"Untainted and unattached" means that, like a lotus flower which is not defiled, or like a physician who is not attached, the Tathāgata is likewise.

As a Great King of Physicians, although he treats all manner of illnesses, he administers medicine according to the ailment; he is like the celestial moon, which appears in water in whatever shape the vessel may be—whether square or round—and there is nowhere it does not manifest.
Regarding the statement that the Buddha’s verbal action (*vākkarman*) is subsumed within *prajñā*: *Prajñā* is wisdom (*jñāna*). Wisdom arises from teaching, and teaching is speech.

Regarding the statement that his mental action (*manaskarman*) is subsumed within liberation (*vimukti*): the mind is simply the heart-mind (*citta*). This mind is capable of both good and evil, yet the Tathāgata is able to employ it.
Therefore, it is called liberation.

As for the adornment of the Tathāgata, this refers to the realization of the Dharmakāya; by employing the power of meditative concentration and wisdom as adornments, he thereby delivers sentient beings.

Regarding the purification of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*): from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) upward, one is fully endowed with the six organs as described in the ten kinds of six organs in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Each single organ possesses all ten, and they are all capable of mutual function, thereby realizing the virtue of inconceivable liberation (*acintyavimokṣaguṇa*).
As for Prajñā, it is as previously explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* regarding the purity of form (*rūpa-viśuddhi*) and so forth.
Regarding the inclusion of both the general and the specific, as well as phenomena and principle: Nirvāṇa is the general; the three virtues are the specific.
Phenomena refer to liberation, while principle refers to the Dharma-body.

Regarding the statement that "the concise encompasses the extensive without exceeding the three virtues": in the concise sense, a single virtue possesses all three; in the extensive sense, within one there are immeasurable [virtues].

As for "desiring to study and requesting [instruction]," this refers to the period of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings when [the Buddha] used censure and critique; this is what is meant by "desiring to study."
As for why one is false and the other is true: if the former teaching were not true, it would not have been taught in the past; if the present teaching is true, why was it not taught in the past?
The Sūtra says, "All were filled with sorrow," and there are two reasons for this sorrow: first, they grieved because they heard that the Buddha had entered Nirvāṇa.
Second, they grieve because they hear their own falsehoods exposed; thus the text says, "They do not contemplate the meaning of abiding in peace," and so forth.
As for the arising of the understanding that one must "leave this" and "abide in that": "leaving this" refers to impermanence, and "abiding in that" refers to the partial truth of *nirvāṇa*.
This is the underlying principle.
As for the phrase "the Master has never said," the intent is to refute the ancients; since the *Lotus Sūtra*, where has the Buddha ever preached teachings such as impermanence?
This is what is meant by "reciting the Dharma as heard."
When the Venerable One speaks of what is "swift," he holds to these teachings on impermanence and so forth, claiming they accord solely with his own intent.
When he speaks of what is "superior" among progressive practices, he refers to the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā, which rebukes and supersedes gradual progress.
"Perception is the initial gateway to wisdom" refers to the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness; thus it is called "initial.

When it says "not [yet] spoken of as prior," it does not mean that the delusions of views have not been addressed. One first severs the delusions of views and subsequently exhausts the delusions of cultivation;
therefore, it is said that "when the delusions depart, wisdom perishes."
Regarding "that which is appropriate within this principle": it refers to the middle way that is neither partial truth nor dual negation, namely, the middle between annihilation and permanence.

As for the phrase "able to sever all delusions," the intended meaning is: although the severing of delusions is achieved by means of this principle, both I and the Tathāgata have equally realized this principle;
how then can you dismiss it by calling it false? Therefore, it says, "How could it be so regarding this?"
Regarding the difficulty in perceiving the meaning of the text: the intention is simply that it does not reach the middle way of "neither-nor.

As for the praise of the three preceding attachments, these refer to teaching, practice, and principle. Regarding the frequent use of the analogy of a relative in the fourth section on censure and request:

in the five analogies of the preceding text, ancient commentators interpreted them exclusively as relatives; therefore, it is said they are "frequent" [in that sense]. Now, however, I divide them into three categories: master, relative, and teacher.
The five analogies and two [analogies] for three are also based on ancient works as a close commentary; these are likewise numerous.
As for the Buddha’s censure that they are not true, it is because he censures their failure to recognize the single essence of the Triple Gem, and thus returns the blame back to them.
"Those who provide unified instruction" refers to the masters who provide unified instruction.
"Those who raise distinct delusions" refers to ignorance and nescience.
Regarding the "five sets of five hindrances," this explains the aforementioned five. It simply means that by combining the five, the ten, and the seven, they constitute fifty.
These are the seven afflictions (*kleśa*). They mostly pertain to the delusions of thought (*sahakleśa*).
Regarding the "seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and seven outflows (*āsrava*)" that pervade the mind, these will be explained extensively in the following text.

As for the "treatise master," this refers to the interpretation of the masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* (Sarvāstivāda) school of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). "Together with ignorance (*avidyā*)" refers specifically to the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*).

Regarding the statement that "each one has three inversions," this refers to the three inversions to be remedied by the contemplations of the five gates. These are called "inversions" because they do not aspire to the Mahāyāna.
As the Sūtra says, "those whose illness has not yet been cured" refers to Arhats who still possess the illness of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Regarding "the four [afflictions] of seeing the truths and the one of cultivation": each of the Four Truths has its own afflictions of seeing and so forth, making four;

together with the one of cultivation, they form five, which are also called the five classes of afflictions (*pañca-varga-kleśa*). Regarding "the five practices" (*pañca-carita*): "practice" (*carita*) refers to the manifestation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding those who commit evil through the three types of action: as the sutra states, "being deluded, wild, and licentious" refers to mental action (*manas-karman*); "loose speech and negligence" refers to verbal action (*vāk-karman*);

and "lying amidst impurity" refers to physical action (*kāya-karman*). Intoxication applies to both ordinary persons and sages; while ignorance differs in its coarseness or subtlety, the effects of taking medicine or vomiting may likewise differ in their severity.
The analogies of the plantain tree and so forth all signify a lack of substantiality. Just as dregs have no flavor and medicine has no fragrance, all things are universally devoid of self.
If there were a self, all things would necessarily possess substantiality.
To say that such a thing is impossible is to hold a view identical to that of the non-Buddhists, recklessly conceiving of a self.
To speak of the existence of a self is precisely to describe the supreme, true, and ultimate self.
Regarding the "three meanings above," these refer to the differences in the respective attachments to teaching, practice, and principle.
As for "the nature of question and answer," it means that the questions and answers correspond appropriately; such correspondence is naturally excellent, and for this reason they are praised.
Furthermore, it is because they accord with the four *siddhāntas* according to the occasion, and thus are praised. The four *siddhāntas* should be matched to the sequence of the text as it appears.
That which lacks substantial reality is precisely what is currently excelled over by the three cultivations; this is what is called "reality.
That which is not true speech refers to speech that is merely instruction.
First, regarding "perversion and confusion": to take the impermanent as permanent is called perversion, like being intoxicated and disoriented. Second, regarding "contrary to goodness":
this means contrary to true goodness.
As for "not knowing its meaning," this is intended to rebuke you for merely obtaining the names "impermanence" and "non-self" without understanding their actual significance here.
The constant application of the household's resources constitutes righteousness.
There are also those who speak of it from their own perspective, like a drunken man; they merely have words, but no factual record.
They speak only of impermanence, yet there is no reality to it.

"Listening to others' transmigration" refers to the teaching that washing away permanence is called "transmigration. Since permanence and so forth are not intoxication, why is it called "transmigration"?
Therefore, it is said to be "of others."
The Sūtra states that "those who transmigrate through birth and death" refers to the two kinds of birth and death: those within and those beyond the realms (*dhātu*).
As for "sentient beings," this refers to those who have not yet destroyed ignorance; even when they reach the fruit of Buddhahood, they are still termed sentient beings.
That which you deem wrong is not actually wrong; this means that taking "permanence" as wrong and "impermanence" as right is precisely to mistake what is right for what is wrong.
Nirvana is without sensation, meaning it is devoid of the three types of sensation, such as suffering, pleasure, and so forth.
The Dharma is itself unstained; there is no staining by the two extremes and so forth.

Alternatively, there are different formulations such as the ten gates, the eight inversions, and the six practices. Regarding the ten gates, they are as found in the first fascicle, in the chapter on the *upāsaka* (lay follower), under the thirteen antidotes;
here we shall briefly mention these ten. As for the six practices, there are three superior and three inferior, which constitute their differences.

Sixth. Here, we only contrast them with three; thus, mentioning only three is the concise version, while the ten gates are the extensive version. Therefore, it is said that "the meanings have both extensive and concise [explanations].
As for "clarifying the eight inversions together," this refers to speaking by contrasting ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles; hence, it is called "clarifying them together. Furthermore...
Regarding the four inverted views that grasp at emptiness: in the Mahāyāna, the contemplation of non-self has no further distinct meaning other than the discussion of emptiness itself;
therefore, it is not refuted. Furthermore, among the three types of cultivation, one does not grasp at the impure because the impure is not a rational contemplation (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
However, in the case of the Hīnayāna, since the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is its initial gateway, it is grasped.
For one who correctly cultivates all dharmas, not even a single form or a single fragrance is devoid of the four virtues such as impermanence and so forth.
If they were to offer a defense by saying, "If this were to reach [the ultimate state]," the intent of that defense—since it rejects impermanence—is identical to that of the worldly [view].
What is meant by "permanence and so forth"?

To resolve this objection: it is precisely because you hold such views that you have fallen into error; you simply do not realize that both the mundane and the supramundane are characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Therefore, "one who lacks virtue" means one who lacks the four virtues. "One who lacks its meaning" refers to the meaning of the three virtues of nirvana.
"The conscious mind is inverted" refers to the sixth consciousness, according to the doctrine of the Sarvāstivādins.
"Consciousness whose mind is non-erroneous" refers to its being the primary among the eight consciousnesses. Furthermore, "all that possesses mind" is a general clarification.
"Capable of universal discernment" means it is the most clearly cognizant.
The so-called "exhaustion of the mind" refers to the exhaustion of the afflictions to be abandoned by wisdom through their eradication. "Emptiness of the untainted mind" is the arrival of the mind;
"conception" is the arrival of conception; and "view" is the inversion of vision.
"Arriving at the fourfold endowment" refers to the four [attributes] beginning with impermanence.
"Unsurpassed skillful means" refers to employing both permanence and impermanence for the sake of sentient beings upon the stage of fruition;
this is precisely the unsurpassed supramundane skillful means.

The question regarding "having a name but no meaning," with its accompanying commentary (*yùnyún*), explains through the fourfold logical analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) all instances where there is both a name and a meaning—whether mundane or supramundane, limited or great, partial or perfect.
"Having a name but no meaning" refers to mundane beings, ordinary worldlings, and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
"Having both a name and a meaning" refers to the supramundane, such as the bliss (*sukha*) of the Tathāgata and so forth. "Both having a name and having a meaning" [refers to...]
Regarding "the arising of worldly applications and so forth," the phrase "without name or meaning" is because the principle of *nirvāṇa* is not properly subject to names or meanings.

As for the instruction to "distinguish each according to the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*)," this follows the previous example: the worldly is neither attainment nor virtue, while the supramundane is virtue but not attainment.

"Attainment" (*prāpta*) refers to both "virtue" (*guṇa*) and "attainment" (*prāpti*) in the mundane world; for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), it is called "attainment," while for the application (*prayoga*), it is called "virtue.
In the supramundane, it is neither virtue nor attainment, as explained according to principle. The same applies to superiority and inferiority; therefore, it is said that they are "both [aspects]."
This refers to the virtue of the world’s inversion. It is precisely the virtue of accomplishment through the non-attainment of dualistic discourse, because there is no grasping.
Since the functioning of skillful means arises as both constant and non-constant, it is called "transcending the world."
Regarding those who practice in isolation: "inferior" refers to the four [contemplations] such as impermanence and so forth.
Regarding those who practice both together: "superior" refers to the simultaneous application of both permanence and impermanence and so forth.
Furthermore, the phrase "neither dual nor partial, but perfect" is stated in terms of the ultimate principle.
Regarding "with whom does one differentiate": this excludes those who are improper, without specifying particular individuals.
"Those who exclusively cultivate excellence" refers to those who manifest the gradual stages; they have resolved their minds and know the eternal.
Those who possess both [views] are persons of indeterminate nature; they may be superior or inferior.

Regarding those "fully possessed of all faults," within the context of non-self (*anātman*), this refers to the fact that throughout the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they are entirely bound by attachment, suffering, and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that [this view] is particularly to be refuted. The subsequent refutations follow the same pattern.
Regarding those Śrāvakas who further advance: within the Vaipulya [sūtras], being rebuked by the Prajñāpāramitā and undergoing refinement are all instances of advancing.
As in the Lotus Sūtra, those who did not enter must undergo further refinement; even coming to the Parinirvāṇa is an instance of advancing.
"Purity is the unconditioned" refers to the principle of *nirvāṇa* as naturally pure through non-activity; therefore, it is designated as the *dharmadhātu* which encompasses all things.
When the Sūtra says, "One should not speak such words," it means one should not say, "Now I too shall fall away," for I am for the sake of the multitude.
Śāriputra said, "There is coming and staying. Your going would be of no benefit; why then do you follow me into parinirvāṇa?
One who cannot know the coming and going of a Buddha is like this: for the sake of sentient beings he comes, and when the capacity of sentient beings has ceased, he goes.
The dharma of coming and staying is not within your realm; therefore it is said, 'How could you possibly follow him in his departure,' and so forth."
Regarding the beginning of the arising of delusion: it is because at the end of the season, when things are new, delusion arises toward objects.
Furthermore, regarding the arising of understanding based on delusion: the cessation of that understanding also occurs at this same time.
Regarding "one who has sunk into deep water": the Buddha-nature exists within the bodies of sentient beings; because craving and attachment act as water, it is said to be "within.
Regarding "not lost forever": later, a wise person will still be able to recover it; therefore, it is not permanent loss.

Clods of earth and stones are used as metaphors for that which causes harm, namely suffering. Clods and stones are coarse and heavy objects; just as when a person is harmed by them, it constitutes suffering.
Because they are empty and unreal, they are devoid of self.
"Separation and dispersal at every moment" refers to impermanence in every thought-instant.

"The end of partial cultivation" refers to the gradual transition from the provisional toward the perfect; this is also called the "end" because it signifies the ultimate limit. Thus, it is termed "the final stage."
Regarding the second point, by the power of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*): first is the power of internal permeation; second is the power of relying on superior cultivation.

As for causing sentient beings to awaken: it is by the power of the Buddha-nature that the waters all become clear. However, because this involves the sense of becoming clear, it is not itself awakening.
The analogy of "seeing" refers to the discussion in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* regarding seeing the son from afar within the Lotus Sūtra;
thus it is said that he has not yet been able to seize him.
As for "dwelling in birth and death as if in nirvāṇa," this means being able to remain far removed from birth and death while abiding in nirvāṇa.

In this context, the scriptural passages that serve as focal points for the practitioner’s attention include the "Three Virtues of the New Yi," the "Rejection of the False and Discourse on the True," the "Secret Treasury of Buddha-nature," and the "Two Birds Flying Together.
These are all places where the practitioner should fix their mind; therefore, one should take joy in them.
Beyond these, what else could possibly be said? If one does not fix the mind upon them, it remains the same as mere rubble; one has not attained the truth.
Those who have not yet believed in the Buddha as eternal do so because they regard the Three Jewels as being of a single substance (*eka-rasa*).

As for the statement that "though they verbally request the new [teachings] and so forth," this refers to the *vaipulya* (extensive) teachings which censure and reject [the old], which is the "requesting of the new.

In the *Prajñāpāramitā*, however, the entrustment of the Dharma-treasure still retains the old [perspective]. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says, "They still dwell in their original place"; this is the textual evidence for that. Herein, the following section explains the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).
This is difficult.
Regarding "each being a condition for the three and one": the inferior consists of the three, while the superior is but one.
As for "transforming delusion to give rise to faith," what you previously stated was merely your own delusion, claiming that you saw the sun and moon revolving.
Because of such conceptualization, it must be corrected.
Regarding "the true Dharma is unstained": if one lacks faith, the mind will not be unstained by dharmas. Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit.
All dharmas arise from this; therefore, it causes the arising of faith.
Those who are negligent are a general metaphor for ordinary persons and those of the two vehicles.
"Riding upon various karmas" refers to both tainted karma and untainted karma.
Regarding "clinging to desirable fruits": this is because ordinary beings cling to birth and death (*saṃsāra*), while those of the Two Vehicles cling to *nirvāṇa*.
The analogy for "lack of understanding" is as follows: a pearl was originally present, but due to conditions it was thought lost; therefore, there is no understanding [of its presence].
The phrase "due to dissipation" explains the aforementioned meaning of losing the pearl.
Regarding "breaking one's practice leads to loss as an immediate consequence": because of dissipation, there is no practice at all.

As for "it is not that one first understands and later loses [the pearl]": this refers, for the time being, to the period after one has regressed from the Mahāyāna during the process of transmigration. If we rely on...
The formation of karmic connections through great penetration is still resolved first. What is now called "forgetting in the interim" refers to the pleasure of birth and death;
it is merely a figurative expression for losing [the realization].
As for praising the Buddha, this is presenting one's own realization, such as the joyful cultivation of non-self and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "together seeking and attaining it," this does not mean taking up the sense of losing a treasure. It refers to the pearl that has been inherently present, which is intentionally explained together [with the seeker].
As for the "clumsy contemplation" of those who seek it out, these are bhikṣus practicing the three types of cultivation who have not yet heard the principle of perfection.
Regarding "knowing the words and knowing the meaning": the words are the teaching that expresses, and the meaning is the principle that is expressed.
Hearing this Perfect Vehicle enables one to accord with this principle; it enables one to accord with this principle.
That the expressive [words] are like the expressed [meaning] is because of the liberation of letters;

that the expressed [meaning] is like the expressive [words] is because the teaching accords with the principle. If one knows that the Tathāgata never preaches the Dharma, this is precisely what is meant by "much learning. This is its significance.

The full moon is a metaphor for "resemblance to bliss" (*sādṛśya-sukha*): because it is perfectly round and complete without any deficiency, and there is nothing further to be attained, it is called "bliss.
The moonlight is a metaphor for "purity" (*viśuddhi*): the sovereign moon resides in the sky, while the pearl resides in the water. The moon is likened to the pearl;
because the form of the pearl resembles the moon and is unimpeded above and below, it serves as a metaphor for the "self" (*ātman*).
Regarding the phrase "a person attains its gate": Heaven attains the One and thereby finds tranquility; Earth attains the One and thereby finds clarity;
the sovereign attains the One and thereby governs the world. Thus, a "person who attains the One" refers to one who has realized a portion of the single path of purity;
hence it is said that "the person attains its gate. "Gate" (mén) carries the meaning of being able to pass through; it leads one through to the principle of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

This is capable of destroying one grade of ignorance. It is also as explained in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) and the *Shier buermen* (Ten Gates of Non-duality); these are likewise one and the same meaning.
"Perfect cultivation prior to the Way" refers to the period before the five grades, the six faculties, and the first dwelling (*prathama-bhūmi*). "Tranquil and gradual" follows the ancient exegesis.
Regarding the phrase "the water of the teaching is not turbid and the waves of the mind do not stir": the water of the teaching is not turbid because the teaching is itself the mind;
the waves of the mind do not stir because the entire mind is water. Since wave and water are non-dual, it is said that this accords with principle.

Those who traverse all dharmas do not go beyond the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus). Although the flavors of the teachings differ, they all possess degrees of superiority and inferiority.

"In every place" refers to the intent behind the transformation throughout the entire period of the Buddha’s career—encompassing the Great and Small Vehicles, the Partial and Complete Teachings, and the Gradual and Sudden approaches;
hence it is said, "How could this apply only to the present sutra? and so forth.

Regarding "not limited to a single realm": beginning from form and mind and culminating in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), throughout the successive sublime objects of experience, there is nothing that is not the Middle Way.

Furthermore, concerning the six stages where the ultimate is not yet clarified: the teaching of our school differs from other interpretations; both the path of teaching (*śrutamārga*) and the path of realization (*bhāvanāmārga*) reside in the initial stage of the mind.
Upon entering the state of non-effort (*anābhoga*), one spontaneously attains thorough penetration. Thus, the Great Master’s *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:
Regarding the phrase "sending the practitioner": this refers to arriving at that stage of Bodhi-megha (Cloud of Enlightenment). This is the initial stage of the "True Position" (*bhūmi*).

It is interpreted in this way either because it corresponds to this [described] state, or for the sake of following the scriptural text. As for the fear of delusion and so forth: having investigated its arising and ceasing, one may harbor doubts regarding this point;
thus, I have briefly outlined the general principles, as I have not yet attained profound insight. All other details remain unexplained.
"Departing from the function of self-conceit (*māna*) and so forth" refers precisely to the function of the practitioner. "Self" refers to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the like;
"conceit" refers to the affliction of discursive thought (*manasikāra-kleśa*).

As for "the force of the words being mutually established," the principle of practice has already been refuted previously; now it is cited here to establish this teaching. Thus it is said: "Correctly..."
The intent lies in the teaching.

Regarding the note at the end of the passage "not explained early on" (and so forth): previously, it was extensively clarified that if the former teaching were not the Buddha’s, he should not have spoken it;
and if the former teaching were indeed the Buddha’s, it should not be considered non-equal [to the latter]. This merely cites one side by way of contrasting the present and the past.
This is divided into two parts. The answer is simply that it is a refutation.

Regarding the first, the "disease of inversion": "the one" refers to the sovereign or king, who belongs to those who cling to false views; his lack of clarity regarding false teachings is called "internal darkness."
