Regarding "those who outwardly display my majesty": the King, having obtained sovereign power, uses it to lead them on; they act perversely according to their own whims.
Therefore, it is said that "seeking pleasure" refers to perverse pleasure.
The Sūtra says "wán-yín" (頑嚚). In the *Guǎngyá*, "wán" means dull-witted; in the *Cāngxié Piān*, "xiáo" (囂) means wicked.

The *Zuozhuan* states: "A mind that cannot fathom the principles of virtue and righteousness is called 'obstinate' (*wán*); a mouth that does not speak words of loyalty and good faith is called 'dumb' (*yín*).
This refers to those who believe in heterodox arts, taking the "four inversions" to be their practice.
Those who are "greedy and moist" take themselves as the self; they are attached to existence and non-existence because they possess a sense of autonomy.
The Sūtra says, "Not knowing the root source from which illness arises," which describes an understanding of permanence and bliss that is purely a belief in false permanence.
The Sūtra states that "knowing the good and bad, the wholesome and unwholesome, etc. means that correct pleasure is good and wholesome, while perverse pleasure is ugly and unwholesome.
Regarding the meaning of a "king" as one who leads and governs:
this is an analogy for sentient beings who, after receiving false teachings, proceed to lead their own followers.
Furthermore, regarding "sentient beings who insistently entreat": before the Buddha appeared in the world, various non-Buddhist teachers each transformed sentient beings.

Regarding "lacking true understanding within": this refers to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). Regarding "lacking skillful exposition without": this refers to the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) of the Buddha.
"Few medicines" refers to [remedies for] such things as heterodoxy and the constant [afflictions]. "Many illnesses" refers to the illnesses of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
"Due to grasping at characteristics" refers to the characteristics of the views, afflictions, and ignorance;
among these, attachment to the view of self is the most powerful, and it is also termed a "characteristic."
These are those who do not know medicine; though they know its name, they do not understand its meaning.
Regarding the passage "green, white, etc., as detailed below" (and so forth), it is explained extensively as follows.

Regarding "the medicine being applied inappropriately": this refers to using the medicine of impermanence for those who are constantly ill, or using the medicine of true permanence for those who are ill with impermanence;
both are termed "being applied inappropriately.
Regarding "the conditions for curing illness": first they are the same, and later they differ; this constitutes the condition.
The Buddha’s knowledge of the Eightfold Noble Path refers to the unconditioned (anabhisamskāra) Eightfold Noble Path of the Mahāyāna.
It is capable of curing the eight inversions and can employ the impermanence of the former two teachings and the permanence of the latter two teachings as its eight methods.
Among the ten,
the first refers to the non-Buddhist practitioners with views of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*), who deny all cause and effect and extensively commit various evils.
"The life-force of wisdom also dies" means that the impermanent, eternal, and untainted life-force of wisdom perishes.
Those who commonly follow external paths (tīrthikas) are those who seek rebirth in the heavens or in such realms as the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Those who sever the fetters (saṃyojana) through external paths are those who employ mundane wisdom (laukikajñāna) to sever the afflictions of the lower eight stages.

Regarding those who are able to be both comprehensive and inclusive: the Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections take the four gates as their comprehensive scope and the transformation of others as their inclusive practice.
Those who lack skillful exposition have not yet severed their afflictions, yet they perform the act of giving (dāna).
To treat those with incurable illnesses is to shatter ignorance (*avidyā*). To treat those without pain or affliction is to realize that phenomena are themselves emptiness.
Being unable to treat those who are destined to die is because the followers of the Two Vehicles have not yet shattered ignorance.
That which cannot cause one to return to the origin has not yet entered realization.

That which cannot cause one to transcend the origin refers to those who have not yet reached the second stage (*dvitīya-bhūmi*) and beyond; therefore, it is said they "transcend. The first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) is taken as the origin.

Even reaching the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), one cannot transcend the origin of Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata*). If formulated as four propositions, the origin is low while the trace is high.
There is a profound meaning here.
"Discoursing on military affairs" and so forth refers to public lectures. For instance, it is like the Crown Prince taking up King Wen’s bow and personally [scaling] the ninefold Iron Ring Mountains.

Regarding "removing his crown and dismissing his horse," this refers to the Crown Prince’s journey through the four gates of the city, where he grew weary of the world and left the household life; the name of the slave was... [name missing].
Chanda and the horse named Kaṇṭhaka were sent back to the palace.
"Only this body attains Buddhahood" refers to the six-foot-tall physical body.
"The remaining two years" refers to the period from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* until the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
"Each has six aspects of practice" refers to clarity through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
The scripture’s phrase "coming from afar" signifies that the response arises from the Truth (*tathatā*), which is why it is called "far.
"Those who lack the wisdom to contemplate the capacity [of beings]" refers to the capacities of both the present and the past.
"Those who possess supernatural powers" refers only to those with mundane, out-flowing (sāsrava) powers.
"The threefold refuge for the scaly-textured" refers to the first bestowal of the three refuges upon the Dragon Kings.

As for the scripture’s statement, "Now is precisely the right time," although it speaks of the initial teaching, its intent is addressed within the context of those possessing great spiritual capacity (mahā-indriya). Therefore...
"Clouds" refers to time.
"Roots and conditions meeting in obscurity" means that within the capacity [of the practitioner], there is an obscure distinction between small and great according to their specific circumstances.

"The other realms are likened to the various delusions" refers to those of the Initial Teaching (śīkṣā), who are fully possessed of the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the delusions of dust and sand (*rajas-aṃśu*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
This refers to delusion. That which involves much harmful activity is so called because it can give rise to all afflictions within and without the realms.
This is termed "dying by transgression": when false delusions obstruct right understanding, such that the life-force of wisdom fails to arise, this is designated as "death."

That "those of the superior, middling, and inferior capacities all attain enlightenment" refers here to individuals of the three capacities within the Hīnayāna. The one of superior capacity is Ājñātakauṇḍinya, who serves as the foremost.
As for "sentient beings who do not understand," they do not understand the provisional teaching of impermanence; their intent lies in the ultimate reality.
As for those who hold that "non-being" is the horse, they say, "The Way is not this horse; where else could it be? This is a reprimand.

This affliction is easy to see: the fruit of Buddhahood is fundamentally eternal, yet they arbitrarily claim it is impermanent. If one says it is eternal, they perceive the impermanence of birth and death.

This disease is difficult to perceive because that which is fundamentally true and eternal is now described as impermanent. Those afflicted by the attachment to impermanence do not recognize it as eternal;
therefore, it is said to be "difficult."
"The roots and conditions knocking at the Buddha's gate" refers to the arising of great capacity.
"Sending a messenger to summon a physician" takes that capacity as the messenger.
When the Sūtra says, "One should take milk," it refers precisely to the milk of the True, Constant, and Eternal.
Regarding the "opening of the provisional" (*kaishen*): as the sutra says, "these are not true words. Words are merely teachings; what was previously taught was not the ultimate truth.
Regarding the analogy of the "great impermanence": as in the preceding passage, bitter and salty medicines can all cause a fever if one clings to them, thereby falling ill.
"That which can burn the world" refers to burning the world outside the realms (*dhātu*).
As for "using the past to mock the present," it is as the sutra says: "You previously said it was poison; why do you now take it? This is a mockery of the present True Permanence (*bhūtanityatā*).
Regarding the phrase "now that they have been made to take [the medicine]," it means they are returning to taking the milk of true permanence today and censuring the poison of the past;
as the present and the past are contrasted with one another, they form a pair.
"To again fulfill the previous intention" means to fulfill the intention expressed in the preceding "double surprise.
Regarding the statement that "the entire body of this passage is a metaphor," the preceding text opens with four metaphors;
here, it corresponds to the fourth, which employs the medicine of the four virtues, and is therefore called the "essence of the Way."
It is not that one understands the principle; "principle" (li) here has the meaning of "constant" or "low.

"Mai yi" (麥䴬)—the character *yi* is pronounced *shi*—refers to wheat chaff. This term does not appear in various other books; it appears only in the *Zhao Shu*, where there was a person surnamed Yao named Yi who created this character.
The section beginning with "Next, having removed this milk" and below is how the ancients divided the chapters.
Regarding the phrase "the two birds fly together, which is acting in accordance with what is appropriate": when it is time to employ them, they act; when it is time to set them aside, they hide.
Thus it is said they "attain their proper place," as in the passage in the text below where it says "both hide and both rest."

Regarding "the scripture and its meaning being in accord": the "scripture" refers to the present sutra; the "meaning" refers to the meaning of permanence and bliss. These correspond naturally with one another.
As for "those of superior faculties," those such as Śāriputra in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are considered superior; through the "Teaching of the Dharma," they all attained awakening together.

The Sūtra says: "That which is medicine and that which is not medicine. Although the name "milk" is the same, for non-Buddhists it is not medicine, whereas for the Tathāgata it is medicine, capable of curing impermanence.
*Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra-śikṣā* (Private Notes), Fascicle Three, Part One, End.
Private Notes on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra Commentary* of Tiantai, Scroll Four (Part Two).
Compiled by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Xingman.
○ Explanation of Chapter Four: The Chapter on Longevity.
Regarding the first three chapters that Yan and Guan established, these were already completed by Dharmakṣema’s translation and subsequently edited and finalized by Master Xie.
Yan and Guan divided this single chapter into three—namely, the Preface and the other two sections—and thus it is said they "established" them.
One can thus know with certainty that Dharmakṣema and Master Xie each held their own respective portions [of the work].
Regarding the preservation of this chapter: because the preceding three chapters were all titled "Chapter on Life Span" (*āyus-paryāya*), the original Sanskrit term has now been retained here.
As for the translator’s adjustment of the characters: "life span" (*shòu*) has now been moved to the lower position and changed to "longevity" (*cháng*) in the upper position.

This is because in the Western regions (India), the left corresponds to what is considered the "upper" position in this land (China); thus, it is said that he adjusted them "left and right. It is just as when a person from the East refers to the West as "right"—the person [from the East]... [text ends].
Regarding the statement that "in the West, east is called left," this is because things have no separate essence.

The word "fearing" (*kōng*) likely refers to the preceding passage; it is the intention of our school to explain that, for instance, as in the case of Cunda obtaining the five fruits of merit, the extensive exposition of the three bodies and four bodies all constitutes texts concerning longevity. Therefore, it says "fearing."

"Long" (āyuṣmat) always occurs in the vocative case. The question asks for the reason why. "Constant" (*nitya*) and so forth are the bases from which [the name] follows; "long life" (*āyuṣmat*) is the name established based upon those bases.
Therefore, it is that which is derived from the basis.
"Being identical with the Dharma-body of all Buddhas" means that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same Dharma-body;
because they are one body and one wisdom, etc., it is said that they are "all entirely equal. This explains the intent of the four *siddhāntas* of this chapter.
That the Buddhas are not different is the *loka-saṃvṛti-siddhānta*.
Second, regarding those who delight in the long and loathe the short: "things" refers to persons.

Furthermore, because the capacities of these beings have unequal inclinations toward joy and aversion, they should be shown longevity so that their mental states may become wholesome; this is the "knowledge of others' minds" (pudgala-jñāna).

Third, regarding the refutation of the ineptitude of practicing exclusively on impermanence and so forth: this is explained in detail above in the section on the mutual remediation of superior and inferior qualities;

it refers to the transformation of biased attachments, which is precisely the meaning of "remedy" (*pratipakṣa*). Fourth, the synthesis of the preceding three [categories] as all equally contributing to long life is the "ultimate sense" (*paramārtha-siddhi*).

Regarding the third pair, the assembly of bodhisattvas: whereas the preceding "Cunda Chapter" addressed the mixed assembly and the "Lamentation Chapter" addressed the śrāvakas, this chapter addresses the bodhisattvas.
Throughout the various questions and answers, "Long Life" (Āyuṣmat) is placed first as the introductory title for each discourse.
Regarding the statement "the Buddha-dharma reaches three [occasions]": this refers to the first exhortation by the Buddha, the second instruction, and the third address to the bhikṣus.

As for the fact that the initial joy was followed by silence once doubts were exhausted: this is precisely the passage found in the *Upamā-saṃyukta* section of the sutra, where it says, "At that time, the śrāvakas remained silent.
It is merely that the compiler of the sutra has placed this account later in the sequence.
Regarding the phrase "later exhortation implies," it means that [the text] infers that the various bodhisattvas possess the merit of both self-cultivation and the transformation of others.

As for the statement "above, having already questioned the sūtra," the intent is that Cunda raised examples such as the impermanence of the physical body to pose his questions, while the Buddha answered with the eternal body and so forth;
the extensive discussion of superiority and inferiority within the three types of cultivation all constitutes the textual content of these questions.
Regarding the claim that the Sūtras are profound while the Vinaya is shallow, this is now refuted and not permitted.

Furthermore, if one discusses depth and shallowness based on the phenomena themselves, if one cultivates with the mind of *nirvāṇa*, how could there be any distinction between depth and shallowness as being intended for the final age? Therefore, it is asked: "Why wait for exhortation?"

Furthermore, the claim that the core essence (*śāstra*) of this present sutra lies therein is also incorrect. When the ancients saw the words exhorting questions regarding the precepts (*vinaya*), they took them to be the core of the sutra.

According to our current interpretation and based on the Great Master’s [Tiantai] classification of the teachings (*panjiao*), this sutra is a discourse on the permanence [of the Buddha-nature] within the context of the precepts;
it is also called "The Precious Treasure for Redeeming Life. Why? Because the Tathāgata saw that among the bhikṣus of the final dharma age (*mofa*), there would be many who violate [the precepts].
Regarding the precepts: [the practice of] keeping the eight impure things and [relying on] permanent property (sangha-vastu) causes one to be submerged in afflictions.
Fearing the loss of the life of wisdom, one would use these precepts to ransom this life—just as when a person is in prison and is offered much wealth and treasure to secure their release.
Therefore, that is not the primary tenet [of our school]. Now, we take the eternally abiding Buddha-nature as the primary tenet of the sutras.

Now, examining the scripture which says, "Regarding all the precepts and disciplines" (*śīla-vinaya*): since it says "regarding all," one should inquire not only about the *vinaya*, but fully inquire about meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Although the word "all" (*sarva*) does not appear at the beginning of this scripture, it may have been present in an earlier version; we now take the phrase "regarding all" from the subsequent passage.

Regarding the statement that both the path of restraint (*saṃvara-mārga*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are called "precepts" (*śīla*): "concentration" refers to the precepts co-arising with concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*), and "path" refers to the precepts co-arising with the path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*), and so forth.
The plural expression "all" (*sarva*) refers collectively to the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).

The "simultaneous illumination of the two truths" refers to the exhortation to inquire about the conventional; this implies that the ultimate is contained within the conventional, as explained in detail in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) within the section on the sevenfold two truths.
Furthermore, it is said that one must not claim that the Tathāgata cultivates only emptiness and quiescence. One should simply take the words "emptiness" and "quiescence" as referring to oneself;
this, in turn, refers to the Middle Way, which is the emptiness and quiescence of the dual negation of the two truths.
"To explain in full as above" means to fully exhort [others] regarding the Threefold Training (triśikṣā).

Therefore, using the precepts and discipline (vinaya) as the basis for exhortation implies that by citing the vinaya, one simultaneously encompasses concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā); furthermore, this is because it fully integrates both the Vehicle (yāna) and the Precepts (śīla).
Regarding the "realm of the Tathāgata," this is explained from the perspective of principle (*li*). The Buddhas of the three periods arise from the Truth (*zhen*) to manifest in response (*ying*);

they ride upon the path of reality (*rushi dao*) to attain perfect enlightenment, and are thus called "Tathāgatas" (Thus-Come Ones). Therefore, it is said that they are in full accord with all Buddhas.
"All those who possess meditative concentrations" refers to practice; it is the inconceivable concentration.
"The instructions they expound" refers to the teaching; it is the inconceivable teaching.
Regarding "this path and non-path": the nine dharma-realms are termed non-path, while the Buddha-realm is termed the path. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"Practicing within the non-path, one attains penetration into the Buddha-path," and so forth.

Regarding "those who lack the three types of knowledge": because the śrāvakas of the two vehicles have not yet perfected the three knowledges, they are unable to inquire about the three truths and so forth.

Third, regarding "the śrāvakas being forced to receive the entrustment": this means that their mental capacity and verbal ability were insufficient, and thus the Tathāgata compelled them to accept it.

"From the past to the present, there are one hundred and twenty [links]" means that, taking the ten links in their entirety, the future birth, aging, death, and so forth have not yet been discussed, because they exist in the present and have not yet arisen in the future.
Since each link has twelve [sub-factors], there are one hundred and twenty [in total]. (As stated above:
"Like those who cannot remain," refers to the śrāvakas who enter parinirvāṇa; they are unable to perpetuate the lineage of the Triple Gem and cause the Buddha-lineage to endure for a long time.
Therefore, it is called "dwelling.

Thus, it is said that a wealthy person is like the "elder" (śreṣṭhin) described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Possessing immeasurable wealth and treasures, they practice for themselves and transform others;

being full within and followed by others without, they are termed "wealthy. When one intends to act based on conditions, if the conditions in this place have ceased, one should respond in another place.
Thus it is said that he "adapts to transformation.
As for "riding upon Suchness to give rise to response": this refers to the Dharma-body; from the stage of the Dharma-body, it gives rise to [manifestations] for the sake of other sentient beings.
"One hundred *jin* (gold)" refers to the "one hundred phrases of liberation.
In the *Hanshu*, it is stated that ten thousand units constitute one *jin*; thus, one hundred *jin* would be one million.
The "one hundred phrases of liberation" are explained in detail below. During the summer retreat at Lingshi Temple, the Great Master lectured on these one hundred phrases of liberation.
Each phrase is explained through one hundred interpretations, such that ten thousand dharma-gates serve as its retinue; this is what it means to "meet with this.

Regarding the statement that among humans he is the tenth and among devas the twentieth: this is calculated based on the Buddha’s presence within the realms of humans and devas as he teaches the Dharma.
This is a transformation.

To say that the exhaustion of both pervasive and specific delusions is the time of "return" means that one realizes Great Nirvana, which is like returning to one's native land; therefore, it is called "return."
"To take refuge in me" means that within one's own body there is inherently the Three Jewels as a single entity; therefore, it is said to be "taking refuge in me.
This interpretation is somewhat more convenient than the previous explanation.
Regarding the "son of faith": as for the term "son," it refers to one who can succeed to and carry on the family lineage.
Since there is no such successor, the Mahāyāna will perish and be lost.
One who employs this provisional expression should not call the Buddha a "foolish person"; therefore, it is called a "provisional assumption.
If one were to ultimately harbor the underlying intention that the act of entrusting constitutes being a foolish person, one should not say "the Buddha."
As for the scripture’s question, "What should one ask?"—not asking is the very loss of the Dharma-treasure.
"Vigorous and handsome" refers to being able to transform oneself and others through mastery of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Regarding "all samādhis enter into it": the Bodhisattva realizes twenty-five samādhis and destroys the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
This is called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the king of all samādhis; it is also called the *Ghaṇṭā-lakṣaṇa* (Bell-characteristic) Samādhi, for all samādhis enter into it.

Regarding the three truths having one truth as their mother: this is the single reality-truth (*ekābhisaṃbodhi-satya*). As the sutra says, "The Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the mother of Bodhisattvas";
this likewise means that the three wisdoms are, in fact, a single wisdom.
Regarding "the One Truth and Three Truths as the Father": the provisional means (*upāya*) of the same essence serves as the father; this is the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyajñāna*).
As for the scripture stating "as if it were one's own," it means that when a Bodhisattva realizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), they share the same essence as all Buddhas;
therefore, it is said to be "one's own."
The Sūtra says, "At that time, there was someone who came. This refers to Śākyamuni seeing a bhikṣu whose mind had turned toward awakening;
the movement of his spiritual capacity moved the Buddha, which is why it is said he "came.
"To forget oneself and attribute merit [to others]" means that while śrāvakas are unable to attribute merit to bodhisattvas, [the Buddha] is well able to do so.
The questions and answers are all derived from the preceding text, such as the passage from "two conditions" up to "abiding for a long time," and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding cases where the examples appear similar but the underlying intent differs: the Bodhisattvas have long since attained understanding, yet they manifest as if they have questions; the Śrāvakas, however, have newly severed their defilements, and thus it is said they are "without doubt.
To say that [the Bodhisattvas] cannot take credit for this is precisely what constitutes the difference in intent.
To briefly cite those who agree: this concerns the meaning and application of practice.
If one asks about "life," it refers to the life-span of the ultimate reality (paramārtha-dhātu), which is the eternally abiding heaven of the practitioner.

The question regarding the discernment of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is as follows: Wisdom and discernment reside in teaching, while compassion is the foundation. Because the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) constitute the holy life, one asks about it;
thus, it is addressed in terms of giving (*dāna*).

If it is asked why taking refuge in the precepts (*śaraṇagamana-śīla*) is explained as the "noble practice" (*ārya-caryā*) and so forth: it is because the precepts themselves constitute the noble practice of morality.

"Taking refuge" refers to the wholesome states of ordinary beings, humans, and devas, such as those illustrated in the subsequent text by the analogies of the wooden ox, the wooden horse, and the yellow leaves; therefore, they belong to the category of taking refuge.

Regarding the opening of the precepts for those practicing due to illness when they would otherwise be obstructed by them: since illness is an evil, and evil is that which is to be prevented, while the precepts are that which prevent it, this is explained in terms of practice.

Regarding "adorned with the immeasurable": this refers to the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. That is, precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth serve as the adornments, while the city of *nirvāṇa* serves as that which is adorned.
Because these adornments and the object adorned are inexhaustible for the benefit of others, it is called "immeasurable."
"That there is nothing further to inquire about" refers to the ultimate principle.
"Inquiry and discernment are the adornment of joy" refers to the joy of extensive learning and analytical discrimination.
"Inquiry and taking refuge are the adornment of the self" means that by overturning and eliminating false notions of self, one realizes the true self.
Regarding the fourth [category], the Tathāgata as donor, it concerns application.

This refers to using the "constant life" (*nityajīvita*) to subdue those who are evil. Here, "life" (*jīva*) refers to the precepts (*śīla*). Since one maintains the precepts and does not kill, one thereby attains life.

The reason these three types are raised as the starting point for inquiry is that they take up such matters as the discourse on lifespan, the exposition of the precepts, and the taking of refuge as their primary subjects.

Furthermore, regarding the question, "Is life itself eternal life? and so forth, this applies to the preceding two chapters; as for "eternal life," it pertains to the preceding section concerning Cunda. If...
Regarding the four virtues, this generally refers back to the preceding expression of lamentation. As for "questioning and discernment being ordinary speech," speech is simply discernment.
When the *Śāstra* says, "At twelve years of age, he was able to question and answer," it refers to the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*, concerning the youth Kāśyapa, who had reached the age of twelve.

The "four intentions" refer to the four *siddhāntas* (the fourfold causes and conditions). For example, as in the text, the distinction between persons and dharmas corresponds to the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly perspective);
the cultivation of goodness and the destruction of evil, and so forth, may be understood accordingly.
Regarding "giving birth to virtuous bhikṣus": it is so that all bhikṣus may turn their minds toward entering the Mahāyāna.

Regarding "subduing those with haughty hearts": it is so that bodhisattvas who consider themselves to be of high station, upon seeing a youth capable of questioning them, will all give rise to a heart of reverence.
The ninth dwelling refers to the stage of the Youthful (Kumārabhūta).
As for the summit of the ten stages, it occupies the pinnacle of all subduing [stages]; being equal to Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, it is designated as the "Youthful."
Regarding those of noble lineage here, it refers to the Six Jia clans as the foremost; that is, these superior clans occupy the first rank.
"May I be permitted to ask? means: "The great assembly is like the ocean; I do not know if you will allow this humble youth to question you.
Thus he speaks these preliminary words, which also manifest the virtues of the youth.
The Sūtra says, "Causing you to rejoice," because it accords with their capacities; hence it is called "rejoicing.
The statement that "the Buddha’s form is great because his wisdom is great" means that the container and its contents are in perfect correspondence.

If one were to discuss matters great and small without first declaring that one’s own voice should be silenced, then I, with my shallow knowledge and at such a young age, compared to the assembly of great Bodhisattvas whose virtues are towering and magnificent, ought indeed to remain silent.
How could I possibly have anything to ask? Therefore, it is said that I rely upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
"Relying on assistance" means requesting the Buddha’s protection; it is like borrowing. The Buddha lends it, and the great assembly assists it;
thus it is called "relying on assistance.
As for the question regarding "the remaining momentum," this refers to the final four verses.
"Those who give rise to the various chapters" refers to the subsequent chapters from which these questions arise.
"To cause the spiritual faculties to become correct" means to entrust them to a Dharma Master of Righteousness.

Regarding the phrase "becoming the refuge for the multitude," this refers to the passage at the end of the previous "Chapter on Lamentation" (Śokavarga), where, due to the request made through threefold cultivation,
[the Buddha] asks him to remain and entrusts the Dharma to Mahākāśyapa and others.
The first verse is combined into two questions, which are then expanded into four questions; each of these corresponds to one of the two pairs of cause and effect.

The single verse concerning the celestial Māra Pāpīyas is combined into one question because the celestial Māra Pāpīyas is identical [to the preceding case], and thus it corresponds to the text of the "Chapter on the Correct Nature" (Yan-zheng-pin) below.
If one simply counts [the verses], why are there thirty-two questions? It is because the nineteen lines of verse together comprise thirty-two.
Furthermore, if one counts the verses including the introductory verse, there are likewise only thirty-two questions; thus, the introductory verse is combined [with the others].
Second, by combining the celestial Māra with [the previous] as one, there are thirty-two questions in total.
If the verses are counted separately, there are thirty-four questions; including the celestial Māra as separate, this makes thirty-five questions.
Regarding "those whose doubt and attachment have already been destroyed": as stated above, this refers to those for whom [doubt] has already been eliminated through lamentation.

As for the rescue-argument that "doubt arises because of conditions," it means that due to the specific capacities and circumstances [of the audience], these bodhisattvas necessarily experience doubt.
Furthermore, it is said that the various commentaries below differ.
The answer, "The Buddha in the past listened to the Dharma with a sincere mind," refers to the causes practiced in the past.
As for the "original cause," it is as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "In my original practice of the bodhisattva path, the lifespan I have accomplished is now..."
It is still not yet exhausted; this is precisely the cause.
That which is fundamentally and infinitely inexhaustible is because it has departed for a long time, having departed for a long time.

Regarding "eternally and eternally inexhaustible" and so forth, they are explained extensively in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the three periods of time. In the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, there are ten kinds of the three periods of time.

They are not the same. As for the claim that [the dharmakāya] can be pointed out as belonging to the past: the dharmakāya is an eternal cause and an eternal fruit, and thus is not subsumed within the three periods of time. It is only by way of conventional designation (*saṃvṛti*) that it is said to be "pointed out" [as past].
Therefore, it is called "provisional" (*prajñapti*).
"Please answer regarding the nature of peace and bliss" refers to the principle of manifest nirvāṇa.
"Opening it in the future" refers to its existence within the *dharmadhātu* (the fundamental nature) of all sentient beings.

As for the four questions beginning with "How does one attain long life," the first two questions concern the dual fruits, while the latter part of the question concerns the cause. How does one attain [these]?
The single phrase "Great Firm Power" is the application of the fruition.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Merits of Names," it is explained through seven points.
As for "in reality not an Arhat," this refers to an original Bodhisattva of the Four Reliances manifesting in the form of an Arhat.

"To be able to see the nature that is difficult to see" refers to the fruit of the realized portion (*darśana-bhāga*). These two questions are answered by a single chapter; hence, they are said to be "conjoined.

As for the conclusion of the fifteen questions: this opens up the first four questions, which constitute the answers to the two questions concerning "how" and "the causes and fruits of the wholesome."
The original verse provides no answer. However, as seen in the subsequent text, there is a question such as: "If pleasure has not yet arisen, how can it be called the experience of pleasure?
Together with this one question, there are thirteen questions in total.
Regarding the "repeated request of the great assembly": this refers to the five lines below, which do not relate to the preceding meaning; it serves to exhaustively answer the questions.
As for "lion's roar," it refers to the inquiry into the meaning of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

This refers to the beginning of what is explained later; that is, the three types of sick persons mentioned in the subsequent "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" (*Vyādhikathana-parivarta*) serve as the starting point.

As for the fact that the preceding questions are numerous while the fascicles are few: from the initial thirty-four questions and answers up to the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly," there are only seven fascicles of sutra text; hence it is said to be "few."

Regarding the statement that "fewer questions should not result in many scrolls," this refers to the final four verses. While others count the number of questions, the intention here is to refute that;
how could there be only four questions? The answer lies in the subsequent textual passages of the various sūtras.
Regarding those who faced the Indic texts from Hexi and so forth, these were the individuals who translated the scriptures concurrently with him.
However, seeing that they were young, their age was twelve at the time. This refers to the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold intentions), wherein the depth of merit differs according to the world (*loka*).
"Everyone gave rise to a most extraordinary mind" means that by praising the fruit of Buddhahood through the perspective of the causal stage, one causes [beings] to generate wholesome roots.
"Able to inquire about the Great Matter" refers to the matter of cause and effect; even a small cause can accord with the ultimate fruit, hence it is called "Great.
This is the sense of applying an antidote.
"All that accords with principle" means that when one investigates the reality, it is non-dual; this is termed "accordance.

From the initial exhortation and inquiry regarding the precepts up to the point of taking refuge, all are what the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* calls the "correct essence. Investigation is itself reality; it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The phrase "as proposed below, etc. refers here to the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*.

"Already attained, not beginning now" means that it is not as if [the Buddha's response] is first accomplished in this present life; rather, it is like the long-standing original beginning described in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Now, as for praising him further: having first requested that the Buddha augment the power of the great assembly, he now praises him;
this is no different from [praising] the All-Knowing One himself.

Regarding "citing the initial accomplishment to establish the subsequent": the assembly’s initial attainment of Buddhahood is its constant cause; the present attainment of the constant fruit is the matter concerning which they are able to inquire.
Regarding "acting as a refuge for the assembly": the Bodhisattvas of the four refuges in the future will be able to serve as refuges for sentient beings.
Regarding those who speak of the "partial and indeterminate teachings," our school explains that there are two kinds of indeterminacy:

first, secret indeterminacy, wherein the Buddha responds universally to the capacities of all beings with a single voice, yet sentient beings are unaware of one another’s experiences; this is called "secret.
Second, manifest indeterminacy, wherein sentient beings are aware of one another, and they receive either great or small benefits according to their differences.
Regarding what is called the "Esoteric Teaching" (guhyaka): if it is the esoteric [teaching] transmitted solely by the Buddha himself, the compilers of the scriptures did not record it;
if it is the indeterminate esoteric [teaching], it is not subsumed under the exoteric.

Regarding that which is not the site of the expedient means (*upāya-maṇḍala*): from the time of his long-ago true accomplishment until the present day—specifically, the period prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—all is termed "expedient means."
One should not disparage the old interpretation as being incorrect.
As for "those who cannot reach it vertically," this is because the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is profound, like the great ocean.
In the initial response concerning the causes of long life, the two characters "how" (*katham*) constitute the inquiry into the cause.
The subsequent inquiry regarding the "fruit of long life" consists of the three characters "attaining long life.
If one speaks of "opening the secret of cause and effect," this refers to opening the cause and effect of the preceding three teachings.
If, for the sake of manifesting nirvāṇa, one speaks of both cause and effect, it means that while the primary intent concerns the essence of nirvāṇa,
one also clarifies the function of cause and effect to demonstrate that it is neither cause nor effect.
Nirvana is not cause or effect; it is spoken of as cause and effect only as a skillful means (*upāya*).

The essence of nirvana does not correspond to cause or effect, yet for the sake of the multitudes, it is said to be cause and effect by way of skillful means. The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra* states:

"The cause of the Mahayana is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; the fruit of the Mahayana is likewise the true reality of all phenomena. This refers to that which is neither cause nor effect, while nevertheless discussing cause.
Indeed it is so.

To allow for indulgence while suppressing [the practice] is to take the fruit as the essence while discussing causes in various treatises, or to take the cause as the essence while cultivating the fruit;

this is not a case where cause and fruit are merely sequential. If they were merely sequential, the cause would simply be the cause and the fruit would certainly be the fruit. However, this is not so.
This is because they rely upon one another.

Regarding "manifesting the True Dharma": the essence of the secret treasury is called the True Dharma. From the initial generation of the mind of awakening, one constantly contemplates *nirvāṇa* while practicing the path;
until reaching Buddhahood, one is able to manifest this principle.
To designate these four names as cause and effect refers to cultivating the causes for Great Nirvana and thereby eliciting its fruit;
that is, it manifests the arising of goodness, the destruction of evil, and the entry into principle within the mundane world, which are not [inherently] cause and effect.

The preceding passage, "it is not that the fruit and so forth are not clarified," explains the two passages concerning cause and effect. The intent of the sutra is, for the time being, to discuss cause and effect from the perspective of the majority and the primary meaning.
As for "the wondrous medicine of ambrosia," this refers to the secret treasury of the three eternally abiding virtues; it is designated as "medicine."
If it is said that "if the vessel is overturned, one does not hear [the Dharma], and thus both reflection and cultivation are lost," it should be stated as "overturned, leaking, defiled, and mixed.
This means that the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) of the Mahāyāna do not arise; the Dharma-texts do not enter [the mind], which is called "overturned" (*āvṛta*).

Being unable to reflect is "leaking" (*asrava*), and being unable to cultivate is "defiled and mixed" (*saṃkliṣṭa*). This is explained in detail in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the text is extensively analyzed and clarified. For now, however—
Because it arises from hearing, it is said that if one is obscured or confused, it is not a case of failing to contemplate or practice; rather, all three types of wisdom (trividya) are lost.

Therefore, the *Śāstra* is cited to establish these three wisdoms: "One who regards and listens to the Dharma with the intensity of one drinking water in thirst, entering single-mindedly into the words and meanings, and rejoicing with exultation upon hearing the Dharma—to such a person one may speak."
If one lacks such karma, yet observes the precept against killing and listens to the Dharma with a sincere mind as a cause for nirvana, this constitutes the cultivation of the karma for long life.
If karma that is a fixed cause cannot produce its fruit, this refers to the karma of the nine realms, which cannot attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
That which cannot function as a cause refers to the fruits of the nine realms; these are not the Buddha’s perfect cause, for this provisional cause is fixed in its nature as cause and fruit.
Regarding that which is neither cause nor fruit and so forth: all sentient beings are *mahāparinirvāṇa*; they are neither cause nor fruit, yet they are capable of [attaining it].
Because it is cause and effect, even though one allows for indulgence or suppression and maintains a state of composure, the essence itself is not cause and effect.
To rely upon this to distinguish cause and effect is precisely what is "not cause and effect," and yet it is the fruit and so forth; therefore, it is called "indulgence."

Regarding the statement that "even Bodhisattvas of Diligence cannot know," this is first explained in terms of specific matters: within the Tripiṭaka teaching, Bodhisattvas are designated as "Diligent.

However, if discussed comprehensively, it means that Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching and those in the stages prior to the Grounds of the Distinct Teaching all know the principle of the Perfect [Teaching];
therefore, it is said that they "cannot know" [it].
Being unable to refrain, I have recorded what I have heard. This is the Master [Jizang] employing the meaning of the Great Teacher [Nāgārjuna] to establish these words of praise and narration.

The intent is as follows: first, that he did not personally receive instruction from the Great Teacher due to the latter’s parinirvāṇa; second, that this Dharma is profound and abstruse, yet he has nonetheless ventured to set it down in writing.
This is explained in detail in the *Nirvāṇa Xuanyan* (Profound Meaning of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra), in the "Preface to the Composition of the Commentary" (*Chao shu yuanqi*), and so forth.
If there is karma that can destroy karma, it is because inconceivable karma can destroy the karma of the nine realms.

All karmas are established from non-abiding karma; the aggregates (skandhas) and realms (dhātus) are the secret treasury, the aggregates and realms are non-abiding, and the secret treasury is the aggregates and realms—this is how all karmas are established.

To say "one" and thereby lose the function means that "one" is the essence (*tǐ*) of the functional; it is three within being one. To say "three" and thereby harm the essence means that "three" is the function of the essential;
it is one within being three. Only when essence and function are mutually identical can they be called non-dual (*advaya*), which constitutes the essence of *nirvāṇa*.
This is also a discussion of activity (*karma*) in terms of the Three Truths; hence it is said that "three is one," and so forth.

That which is extensively explained to others regarding the essence and function prior to the Way refers to the stage from the first abode (*prathamabhūmi*) up to, but not including, the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

This "prior to the Way" is both one and three: it is the essence and function of self-cultivation and the transformation of others, as well as the path of diverse skillful means (*upāya*) prior to the Way.
"By the power of the jewel" refers to the power of Buddha-nature. Buddha-nature is the essence (*tǐ*), while clarity and purity are its function (*yòng*).
Therefore, it is said that "function is identical to essence. Thus, the cited passage serves to verify this relationship between essence and function.
"By 'I have practiced' [it means] that he immediately cites the causes and effects of the distant past.
Therefore, one should know that the subsequent clarification of the Dharma-gate of the past is a brief refutation of others who do not interpret the text according to the three periods of time."
The phrase "resembling those who precede the Path" is not a definitive judgment.
The phrase "arousing the causes of evil" refers specifically to arousing the ten unwholesome karmas, which are the causes that destroy equality.

"Evil fruits" refers to the fruits of the three miserable realms (*trāya*). "The nature and its qualities are mutually related" means that the principle of the natural state of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is the same.

Regarding the statement "there are those who possess Buddha-nature and those who do not": when one is a prince, one possesses Buddha-nature; yet, having committed evil and fallen into hell to become an icchantika, one then lacks Buddha-nature.
This refers to the Buddha-nature of conditions and understanding (*pratyaya* and *pariniṣpanna*). Therefore, the following passage likens it to a king.
This is true even for [the stage of] the "Son" (Ekayāna);

how much more so for those who realize function within the very essence? To cite the shallow as an illustration of the profound: if this is the case even at the stage of the "One-Son" (Ekayāna), how much more so at the ultimate fruition?
When the sutra speaks of "great kindness and great compassion," it refers precisely to the four great vows and the immeasurable mind of non-action.
That which uproots the causes of suffering refers to the nine realms as causes. That which bestows the fruit of bliss refers to the fruit of Great Nirvana.
Regarding the analogy applied universally to the Four Noble Truths, it means that the four types of Four Noble Truths collectively constitute the realm of the Unconditioned (anabhisamskāra).
It is not only those in the four realms of existence who take the unconditioned Four Noble Truths as their manifest objects throughout the mundane realm;
because these truths uproot the suffering of the nine dharma-realms, they are said to be "universal."
It is not merely that the ten evil deeds are eliminated; the three delusions are universally removed.
It is not merely that the goodness of the precepts is maintained; one universally studies the factors of the path and the *asaṃskṛta* (unconditioned) dharmas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"Non-extinction" refers to realizing the principle of cessation—the nirvāṇa of the three virtues—and abiding in the secret treasury.
"That which is likened to the fruit-retribution" refers to the fruit-retribution of Great Nirvāṇa.
The Scripture says, "I am unable to understand," which is precisely why he raises an objection; he uses his lack of understanding to challenge [the teaching] in order to seek comprehension.
Regarding "correcting partiality that deviates from compassion": when one repeatedly challenges those who are good and corrects those who are evil, such correction is termed "partial."
Regarding "both being contrary to the essence": impartial regard (*samacittatā*) is contrary to both malice (*vyāpāda*) and the treatment of those one loves.
Regarding "mutually obstructing one another": loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and its remedy are mutually contradictory.
To answer these three points with a single statement: all sentient beings are like Rāhula; they are equally the sons of the Buddha.
This answers the three intentions regarding the compassion of the single essence.
"Not the compassion of defiled attachment" answers the two intentions from above concerning equal regard and the administration of punishment.
"Compassion is likewise so" means that its essence is equal regard, which is the thought of regarding [others] as one's own child, while its function is the administration of punishment.
This is the compassion that is without conditions; its function pervades the entire dharma-realm. As for the application of punishment, where does it reside? Punishment is entirely equal.
That there is no difference between the preceding and the succeeding is because there is no distinction in essence between cause and effect.
Regarding "supreme compassion and supreme skill": supreme compassion is the essence, while supreme skill is the function; it is solely through compassion that one is able to transform others.
As for the interpretation that [the Buddha] perceived the situation but nonetheless harmed five hundred practitioners of pure conduct, this is as explained in the following passage.
Furthermore, King Sireyu killed five hundred Brahmins because he perceived their [true] nature, as detailed extensively in the following passage.
If one interprets this in light of the following passage, the present objection serves to incite the arousal of the resolve for enlightenment; therefore, it is said that there is no harm.
As for "the mind being constantly equal," it is as the Sūtra says: "generating a heart of compassion toward all"—this is precisely what is meant by equality.
"Raising what is non-orthodox to reveal what is orthodox" means that by citing the non-orthodoxy of national laws, one reveals that the Buddha-dharma is different; this is precisely what is meant.
Regarding the "fourteen administrative officers," these refer to the thirty-five matters and so forth omitted from the Vinaya; they are explained in detail as found in the Vinaya.
Regarding the statement that the bhikṣu Uttara was "for" (wei) the householder Citta: Uttara was the master of the Āmra-vihāra. Since the two were close friends, it says "for.
The character *wei* is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that in the *Caturvarga-vinaya* he is called the bhikṣu Kalyāṇadharma.
Previously, he was acquainted with the householder and constantly received his offerings; later, the householder invited him...
Upasena was making offerings at his house. According to the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra*), Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were two Dharma-leaders.

A lay devotee prepared a hundred portions of food for them. Later, the bhikṣu Sudhana saw this and became resentful, remarking that there were only a few *mṛdvīkā* (raisins) and *modaka* (sweetmeats).

[The Buddha explained: This lay devotee’s family had previously been poor; for three generations they had practiced this occupation. However, the lay devotee possesses the power of past merit and a long life-span.

Regarding the discussion of bhikṣus: it is like a chicken and a crow producing offspring together; the respective mothers of those bhikṣus are distinct—namely, the *pṛthagjana* (ordinary person) and the *arhat*—just as the chicken and the crow reside together [in one nest]. (And so forth.)
"Taking the constant radiance as one" refers to following that constant radiance. "That which is not radiance" all has something signified.
"Each dwelling and each studying" means each residing in a monastery and each pursuing their respective studies; thus, the five schools differ from one another.
Regarding the severance of the delusions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsa-kleśa*), the ultimate and conventional truths are each distinct.

Regarding the severance of the delusions as numerous as motes of dust (*rajas-sama-kleśa*), these motes of dust can obstruct the path of transformation (*nirmāṇa-mārga*) and cause the principle of the truths (*satya-tattva*) to remain obscure,
like a poisonous tree within a house.
Regarding the statement "this [previous] claim is erroneous": the Buddha himself stated in the sūtras that "anointing and cutting are equal.
If he now inflicts punishment, his own words would be erroneous.
Regarding the statement "that [current] claim is false": one should challenge it by citing other sūtras.
The differences in the arising of faith refer to the distinctions among the capacities of the four teachings.
As for the claim that this would be too chaotic, it is because there is no differentiation between the Great and Small Vehicles within the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, those who refute the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) belong to the three preceding vehicles.
Regarding the former practice of designating four groups as the "four children," some say these are the bhikṣus and so forth, while others say they are humans, devas, nāgas, and ghosts.
Therefore, [the author] rebukes them by asking, "Which group do you intend to kill with your staff? and so on.
"Partial mindfulness and partial treatment" refers to the children of the three preceding teachings.
"Practicing various forms of filial piety" is as explained regarding the causes for long life.
When the sutra says that parents are a "noble field of merit," it treats those who have broken the precepts; they are like parents, for their bodies possess the Buddha.
By nature, [the Buddha] is a fertile field of merit.
As for those whose words and deeds are inconsistent, their three karmas are all in discord.
Regarding inconsistency in physical conduct: he preached the causes for long life, yet his own life was short, ending in parinirvāṇa at the age of eighty.
"Contradiction in mental activity" refers to the contradiction between loving-kindness and enmity.
"Contradiction in verbal activity" refers to regarding others as one's own child while simultaneously treating them with or without discipline.
When the Buddha asks about "what is constant," he is refuting other interpretations, such as the four kinds of constancy mentioned in the subsequent text. [He teaches] impermanence.
This is likewise fourfold. Both [of these] are worldly views that have not yet severed the notion of permanence regarding life.
When you seek the cause through the effect, it is the effect of arising and ceasing—impermanence—that you use to seek the present cause.
As for your question, "Why do you not investigate the effect by means of the cause? it is because the cause of long life clarifies the effect of the longevity of *nirvāṇa*.

"Permanence not due to enumeration" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nityatā*) refers to the permanence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state of cessation through non-enumeration (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The third is the permanence of the unconditioned state of space (*ākāśa*).
"That which is the wondrous existence" refers to the wondrous existence of the Tripitaka that is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, which is taken as "constant.
Furthermore, "there is no responsive illumination" because the partial truth of *nirvāṇa* has not yet reached the stage of practical application.
"Originally possessed" means that the principle of partial truth (*ekāntika-satya*) is originally possessed [by all], because form is itself emptiness; therefore, there is no opposition.

"Transcending the permanent and the impermanent" means transcending the permanence of the two preceding teachings; hence it is called "transcending. Upon reaching the stage of the *bhūmis*, it is singular...

It clarifies that [the Buddha] is neither permanent nor non-existent; since there is as yet no function of illumination, it is said: "Directly, the single cause is transcendent; the single fruit is not fused," and so forth.

First, the permanence of the Buddha Jewel is clarified; next, the permanence of the Three Jewels is clarified. This means that the initial Buddha Jewel also possesses the three aspects of the one essence (*ekakāya-trisvabhāva*).
It is a treasure.
Regarding the Buddha’s response with four similes, no other schools offer such an interpretation.
As for the river of birth-and-death and lifespan entering the river of *nirvāṇa*, it is because all sentient beings are themselves Great *Nirvāṇa*.
"The River of Nirvana emerges from the River of Birth-and-Death" refers to the cultivation of causes leading to the realization of the fruit.

"Neither birth-and-death nor nirvana," and so forth, is discussed in terms of the essential substance (tǐ). Since both possess the functions of illumination and application, it is said that they give rise to birth-and-death and the like.
Now, regarding what is called "among humans, in the heavens, on the earth, and in space," etc.: "humans" refers to the four continents; "heavens" refers to the six celestial realms;

and "earth" refers to those dwelling upon the earth as well as those in space. All sentient beings possess both the *jāti-skandha* (the aggregates of birth) and the *antarābhava-skandha* (the intermediate aggregates).

Regarding the statement "all shall become Buddhas," some commentators say that a portion of sentient beings will not become Buddhas because there are no beings among them who can serve as vessels for transformation.
However, the intended meaning of the present text is that all shall indeed attain it.
Regarding the statement that "four rivers flow from Lake Anavatapta": *An-ava* means "non-existent" (*an*), and it also refers to the "Lake Without Affliction or Heat" (*Anavatapta*).
From each of its four sides, a river issues forth, encircles the lake once, and flows into one of the oceans. A detailed explanation is as found in the *Fashu Ji* (Commentary on the Dharma).

Regarding the phrase "by means of prajñā," etc.: true-mark prajñā (bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā) can give rise to the four kinds of spiritual lineages (*gotra*) and also encompasses sentient beings of the nine realms.

As for the statement "from the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established": the non-abiding of ignorance is precisely the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*). This secret treasury is... [incomplete]
Abiding is precisely ignorance; therefore, it is said that all phenomena are established [therein]. If the three paths are non-abiding, then principle is able to give rise to all phenomena.
Regarding the question of how one can truly enter and emerge from meditative concentration: the nine realms constitute emergence, and nirvāṇa constitutes entry.
Such entering and emerging are, in truth, neither entering nor emerging. One emerges for the sake of sentient beings and enters the secret treasury together with them; this is what is called "entry."
The Sūtra states that regarding sentient beings and their life-span, those who are foremost are precisely the sentient beings of the nine realms of existence;
all of them attain this foremost state.
Those who are able to enter the *amṛta* (the essence of clarified butter) are supreme among all flavors, for they enable the preceding four flavors to likewise enter the *amṛta*. Nirvāṇa...
"Parinirvāṇa is the foremost of all lifespans.

Regarding "Kāśyapa follows the fundamental principle to make his request": Kāśyapa follows the aforementioned principle of the eternal lifespan and thus formulates a difficult question to entreat [the Buddha] to remain.

The sūtra states, "like pouring down a great rain," which refers to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). This is also like the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) evaluation of the four types of Dharma masters;
since this [master] possesses both wisdom and learning, it is called "great rain."
Regarding the initial objection that the two teachings are not different: as the Sūtra says, "The world also speaks [of this]," and so forth. "Speaking" refers precisely to teaching.
Because external principles are false, they do not manifest; they merely steal the name of "eternity" without possessing its actual meaning.
This is what is meant by "falsehood," and for this reason, they do not manifest.
Regarding "the various forms of color": the various teachings differ. Regarding "belonging to the same group": the principles of the various teachings are identical.
Regarding "benefiting through transformation according to capacity": this refers to the capacities for the partial and the perfect.
Regarding "those who do not seek milk or curd": humans and devas are called "milk" because, when compared to the first [stage], their physical forms have not yet changed.
The followers of the Two Vehicles are like "curd," for they are all impermanent.

As for the practitioner who propagates the sutra benefiting themselves: because those in the final age will not accept [the teachings], they arise from what is extraordinary; thus, they consume it themselves.
This is also the dedication of the merit of transformation back to oneself.
Regarding those who lack a mind of compassion: non-Buddhists do not take great compassion as the foundation for unsurpassed bodhi;
they only seek the worldly views of permanence and annihilation. For this reason, they lack it.
As for those who have attained benefit, it is not that they possess a mind of attainment regarding the transformation of others;
we who lack such capacity are merely subjects of discourse within the context of our spiritual potential, for in truth, we do not yet know.
If one is able to uphold the precepts, all shall be reborn in the heavens; therefore, it is said that they "abide eternally.
The analogy of the gruel refers to humans and devas: gruel is the dregs of curd, for it does not equal the curd itself. Such is the fruit of the realms of humans and devas.
This is because they are rejected by the Mahāyāna.
Curd is a metaphor for those who resemble the Path; it refers to the cultivation of the fourfold equanimity.
Ghee is a metaphor for the True Path; it refers to the non-conceptualization of nirvāṇa.
Regarding the phrase "self, person, knowledge, and views," etc., the "etc. includes the sixteen types of knowledge and views.

There are some practitioners of the holy life who, while practicing the precepts and so forth, truly do not understand the cause within the Buddha-dharma, asserting instead that [awakening] is obtained through meditative concentration and liberation.
The Sūtra states: "Though it is preached, they do not truly know it. This means that although they know the names, they do not understand the meaning.

The analogy of the Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) for the present Buddha refers to his initial manifestation as a response to those of great capacity, wherein he still preaches the teaching of permanence.
"The ox does not lose its life" means it does not lose its eternally abiding life.
"Returning fully complete" means that the eternal name and the eternal meaning are fully possessed without loss; this is what is called "returning."
The Sūtra states: "Among all sentient beings, there are none who do not suffer from illness and pain; there is no suffering of the causes and effects of the two kinds of death.
Regarding the entrustment to those who propagate the Sūtra: this refers to the period after the Tathāgata has passed away, when the Dharma is entrusted to the Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances.
The scripture states, "For this reason," which concludes the discussion by returning to the orthodox: it is because all [these] are termed true and eternal.
The scripture states, "It is not other dharmas," meaning that they are not the dharmas of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and so forth.
The Sūtra states: "One who knows the body of the Tathāgata" refers to the eternal body, the Dharma-body, which is not like the bodies of worldly beings such as Brahmā.
"Reaching the place where I have reached" means that I and my sons enter together; this secret treasury is designated as the "place."
The cessation of contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) is *nirvāṇa* as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The cessation of uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This is because [the sūtra] explains that since wisdom is impermanent, wisdom ceases. Non-analytical cessation occurs by taking the body as a condition;
when the body is reduced to ashes, the uncontaminated wisdom does not function due to the deficiency of its conditions. Because it obstructs what is to arise, it is not grasped.
It is for the sake of *nirvāṇa*. This refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Since there is both "is" and "is not," the extinction of outflows (*āsrava*) is "is," while untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is not "extinction.
As for this side being "not," it means not grasping at the side of wisdom.
Regarding the existence of "is" and "is not": the body is *nirvāṇa*, while wisdom is not *nirvāṇa*.
The Master Guan says that this should not be so, for both body and wisdom are extinguished.

Therefore, regarding those who argue that the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is difficult to reconcile with the body: the *dharmakāya* is the eternal body, yet *dharmatā* is impermanent while the body is existent.
How can this be known?
The Sūtra states: "As for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is a term of universal application; the words do not speak of extinction. Now, this is not so:
the essence of *nirvāṇa* is inherently subject to arising and ceasing. What is now called "extinction" is that which ceases due to conditions, and is thus termed *nirvāṇa*.
It is the extinction of the body and wisdom.
Regarding "arising from the fetter of craving": because one encounters this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "craving.
Regarding "the accomplishment of the bliss of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-sukha*): this refers to the attainment of the fruit of concentration.
Regarding "the intermediate state that is neither form nor mind": this refers to the retributive dharma (*vipāka-dharma*).
"Appearing as if there were no subtle mind" means that the mind does exist; it is called "appearing as if" because the mind is so subtle.
The reason it is not separately referred to as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is to follow the intent of the subsequent passage, which maintains that there are only four aggregates.
Regarding the accomplishment of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it is said that its dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is not extinguished.
As for the absence of the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), this means that now there is no extinction.

When the Sūtra speaks of the Tathāgata’s extinction of dharmas, it refers to the manifestation of extinction by the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) does not undergo extinction.
The Sūtra states that "various skillful means" refers to manifesting the bodies of the ten realms within a single body, with each individual body demonstrating birth and extinction;
since there is nothing that is not the secret treasury, it is called "inconceivable."

Regarding the statement that one cannot attain the precepts because the three dharmas have distinct characteristics: this is spoken in reference to the "three jewels as one essence" (*ekakāya-triratna*) according to the present sutra.
Therefore, the sutra says, "one will ultimately be unable to realize [it]," referring to the realization of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth; these are precisely the Mahāyāna śrāvakas.
If this were not the case, why would they not have attained realization prior to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*? Thus, it is said that they do not attain the precepts.
Therefore, the subsequent objection asks: "Why not receive [the precepts] again, and so forth?
Regarding the "pure three refuges," this refers to the single essence of the Three Jewels in the present sutra; it is what is meant by the term "pure."

The Sūtra states: "If one can [realize] this inconceivable [reality], it is precisely the Three Jewels as a single essence. Therefore, it says that there is a place of refuge. The Sūtra further states:
"Because of the tree, there is the shadow of the tree. The tree is the Dharma-body as a single essence; the shadow is the Three Jewels to which one returns.
It is a treasure.
The Sūtra says: "If your father and mother were each distinct [and separate], it would be like a tree without a shadow; the single entity would not be established, and thus no child would be born.
If the tree has a shadow, it can give birth to the sons of the Dharma-King of the Mahāyāna, who shall succeed to the long life of their parents."
The latter part [of this chapter] must be understood.
○ Commentary on the "Chapter on the Vajra Body," Number Five:
Regarding the four meanings of "vajra," these four *siddhāntas* explain this vajra from one through four, along with the following analogies.
It pervades all places, thereby corresponding to the four *siddhāntas*.
As for the "foundation of the world": when the world was first formed, a golden wheel resided below, upon which there was a vajra pedestal.
It was here that the Tathāgata sat to attain enlightenment and preached the Dharma; therefore, it is called the foundation.
That which is used for its sharp and piercing power can destroy all things.
Therefore, regarding the "Chapter on the Vajra Body": the vajra is the metaphor (the means of comparison), and the Dharma-body is the object of the metaphor.
Furthermore, both the subject and the object are mentioned together to form this chapter.
Although the thirty-four questions above share a single underlying intent, this is explained according to their specific distinctions. It is by virtue of the vajra that one possesses longevity;
it is by virtue of the vajra that one is able to preach this sutra; it is by virtue of the vajra that one can [subdue] celestial and māra demons;
and so on, even down to the subsequent requests for instruction, all of which are due to the vajra. However, this first question contains four meanings within itself. How so?
The Longevity [Question] asks about the fruit; the Vajra [Question] asks about the fruit. Furthermore, for what reason and by what conditions does it again ask about the cause?
The single phrase "firm power" (dṛḍhabala) is simply the function of the fruit. If one were to discuss only cause and fruit, there would be only two questions.
If one understands that longevity is identical to the vajra and so forth, it is because the vajra itself is universally designated as longevity.
To explain this further through detailed analysis: since those who possess wisdom attain understanding by means of analogies, it is said that the vajra-body [is longevity].
This serves as an analogy.
"Not that there is no distinct meaning" means that while it is general, it is also specific; "specific" refers precisely to the *vajra*.
The subsequent passage, "specific while being general," means that within each individual question, the *vajra* is fully present.
If penetration were not penetration, then penetration would not be penetration, for they are each distinct from one another.
That which is neither penetration nor distinction is the essence of nirvana;
that which is both penetration and distinction is the function of nirvana.
Now, regarding the response from a distinct perspective: this answers the question by treating the general as specific.
"The Dharma adheres to the person" clarifies that there is a person who possesses the Dharma; this person has a self (ātmagrāha), and thus the Dharma they possess is a Dharma characterized by a self.
"Power is its function" means that it is the function of the essence of the human dharma. "The initial brief explanation" refers to the *Cundā-parivarta*.
"The merit of the name is itself eternal peace" means that upon hearing this name, the mind is able to find peace within the principle of the Truths (*satya*).
If one does not deeply contemplate these two characters, how could one attain such things as "not falling [into the evil realms] for seven kalpas"?
As for "whether bound or scattered" and so forth: if spoken of collectively, it refers simply to the five fruits that are eternally abiding;
if spoken of distributively, they are dispersed throughout various texts.
Regarding "situated outside both sides," it means being situated outside of both [the internal and external].
That which is "honor" (glory) is precisely the True One; that the True is all-true refers to ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
That the One is conventional and all is conventional refers to the inconceivable conventional (*acintya-saṃvṛti*). It is said that in all cases, the three truths are mutually interfused.
Regarding "that which cannot be destroyed": a single phrase is identical to all phrases, and thus it cannot be refuted; all phrases are identical to a single phrase, and thus it cannot be demolished.

As for the statement that "first the fruit of the Dharmakāya is clarified, followed by the causes of the Dharmakāya," this means that the preceding [section] concerns longevity, wherein the cause comes first and the fruit follows.
This response regarding "the effect preceding and the cause following" intends to clarify that the cause is the cause of the effect, and the effect is the effect of the cause;
thus, cause and effect are non-dual. Nevertheless, when discussing cause and effect, their temporal sequence is not fixed, which is termed "inconceivable."
Regarding "attaining the name through detachment": this refers to attaining the name by virtue of being able to detach from that which is subject to destruction and mixed with food.
As for the explanation of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) now presented, it is simply as previously explained in the *Vajra-parivarta*: the four meanings of the *vajra*.
"All should embody" means that a single phrase possesses four meanings.
"The primary intent employs this" means that the title of the chapter is now established by taking both the Dharma and its metaphor as its designation.
Regarding the passage "that which is taken up by the suffering of illness," the meaning of the text is that the back pain and so forth constitute the illness.
This "dusty body" clarifies that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his relics remain in the world, being identical to dust and soil.
Other instances can be understood by taking this one as an example for all. Since impermanence is thus, how could any body endure?
"This excellent body" refers to a body endowed with the thirty-two marks and so forth. Alternatively, it may be said that "excellent body" is contrasted with "non-excellent body," which is evil.
As for "being able to be this or that," this concerns only the distinction between true and provisional, which possess right and wrong.

"Being the body without hindrance" refers to the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and the transformation-body (saṃbhogakāya). "Being the body all day long yet not being the body" is because it is detached from the three periods of time.
"Not being the body all day long yet being the body" is because it accords with sentient beings.

Although it is not eternally abiding, it is not subject to momentary extinction; this demonstrates that returning to nirvana is impermanent, yet differs from the arising and ceasing of the mundane world.
For now, I shall record this, though it shall be refuted later.
Regarding the remaining two sets of fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) that can be understood:

according to the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation) of the Great Master Tiantai, while the number of propositions here is slightly different, the remaining propositions should be stated as follows:
the third proposition is "both existent and non-existent," and so on. This is explained in detail in that text. It is simply existence; it is not merely...

This is not something for a reader; it should be practiced within *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight), at which point one will begin to correspond with this [teaching]. This meaning is not yet fully detailed.
Regarding "not departing from the ineffable": this refers to resolving the ineffable by means of the four single propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
"Being non-existent yet existent" means, according to the interpretation of our school, that this "existence" is not an existence external to non-existence.
By opening up this "non-body," it is precisely the eternal body, the Dharma-body, and so forth. This is like the passage in the *Lotus Sūtra*:
"That which you practice is the bodhisattva path," because the hired laborer is in fact the son of the elder.
