Furthermore, regarding the elimination of the characteristic of "one": anything outside of the single characteristic is termed "two," and all such things are not the body;
they are not called the Dharma-body.
Since even the Dharma-body does not exist [in a substantial sense], how could there be the other two? Therefore, it is said that they are "eliminated."

Regarding the fact that the "one hundred negations" (śata-apavāda) also differ in terms of being shallow or deep: this is because the first three teachings are shallow, while the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrti’s *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*) is deep.

Furthermore, regarding the "thoroughly possessing the ten [wholesome paths]" (*daśakuśala*): each of these ten wholesome paths takes the nine others as its means (*upāya*), such that the ten wholesome paths thus comprise one hundred.
Regarding the "fivefold purity," this refers to the fivefold [purity] of the Hīnayāna.

As for the statement that "the pure body is entirely possessed of existence," it means that the *piṭaka* bodhisattvas possess bodies of affliction within the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
Therefore, they are said to have the retribution of existence and so forth; thus, they are rebuked in the *Mahā-śāstra*.
That which kills when eaten is the poison of impermanence; it can [only] permanently sustain the life of wisdom.
One who practices with a mind of attainment is one who practices the six perfections as a bodhisattva while harboring a mind of grasping.
Regarding the statement that "the nature of merit is empty," it is empty because it is free from the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*).

As for the Buddha-body of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭhasādhāraṇa-yāna*) being free from the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*), this refers to practicing the ten wholesome paths and thereby abandoning the hundred evils; it differs from the former [Distinct Teaching] only in terms of skillfulness and clumsiness.

Furthermore, it is not that the hundred evils enter the hundred blessings; rather, in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the hundred evils of the three preceding teachings are opened up to enter the perfect blessings.
This act of opening them is what is meant by "non-[entry].
As for the distinction between superiority and inferiority before and after, it is because evil is abandoned sequentially through emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way.
Regarding "differentiation and obstruction": this refers to the fact that the bodies have not yet attained mutual fusion, such that one body is not identical to the three bodies.

As for the intent of other sutras—that which explains the Buddha’s dharmakāya separately outside of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—this is for the sake of the Separate Teaching (*prthaktva-naya*), because the paths of the doctrinal teachings differ.
Regarding "not knowing what is erroneous": this asks in which teaching it is erroneous.

That which one drills into and admires becomes ever more difficult to fathom; now, explaining this according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), I fear that even so, one will still fail to empathize with the realm of the Buddhas, for the more one drills into it, the harder it becomes, and the more one looks up to it, the more difficult it remains.
"That which is the mundane is the true" refers to the three truths; it is the same within the truth of the ultimate.
"Entering the middle from the extremes" means that both the extremes of emptiness and the provisional enter the Middle Way, such that the names of 'extremes' no longer apply.
That which is simultaneously emerging, entering, and abiding in the middle means that when all is empty, there is not a single provisional or middle element that is not empty.
That which is simultaneously entering, emerging, and abiding in the middle means that when all is provisional, there is not a single empty or middle element that is not provisional.
"Simultaneously abiding, simultaneously entering, and simultaneously emerging" means that within all things there is no provisional emptiness that does not abide therein.
It is three while being one; it is one while being three; it is neither three nor one, yet it is three and one, and so forth—this is what is called "subtle and wondrous.
This is Master Zhangan’s interpretation of the meaning of this passage from the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* concerning the "hundred negations," which fully traverses the various teachings.

Regarding each and every dharma, he further provides three successive expositions. This is the spontaneous freedom of integration; how could there be various interpretations that fall into partiality?
He demonstrates the breaking down of the body, the body of dust and soil.
Regarding those who eat meat for the sake of hunting and so forth, this refers to the period before the three types of purity were established; the details are as explained in the subsequent text.
As for the sūtra’s mention of a "body of peace and happiness," this does not refer to a body that has been emaciated or deprived of food.
Regarding the phrase "Teng raises doubts by questioning the records": this refers to Teng elevating the fruit of the *dharmakāya* and questioning its cause.
As for "taking a similar cause," this refers solely to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and its resultant flow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because of protecting the Dharma, one attains the indestructible Dharma; through the attainment of the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*, one obtains the fruit of the indestructible Dharma.
Regarding the fundamental intent behind their actions: it was originally for the sake of protecting the Dharma.
Although such persons have received the five precepts, they violate the literal form while preserving the underlying principle; thus, they are said to be "not receiving" [the precepts].
Their reversal of formal deportment and so forth are all for the purpose of guarding and protecting pure bhikṣus.
The Sūtra states that those who are "pure" are those who possess the complete precepts at the time of the Great Nirvāṇa.
Regarding the "monk of unknown conduct" and the "powerless layperson," these refer to a powerless layperson and a monk of unknown conduct;
neither of them succeeds in protecting the True Dharma.

Regarding the second phrase, "each being incapable": as previously stated, this is because they lack power and are without names, formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth; thus it is said, "it is still the same.
As for "what was formerly right is now wrong" and so forth: at that time, one's hands should have maintained the precepts (*śīla*) and not held weapons; this constitutes what is now wrong.
"Those who now do not uphold the precepts while claiming to protect the Dharma, yet carry swords, staves, and the like—therefore it is said that they are not [true practitioners] today.
Regarding the statement "to discard principle and preserve phenomena is difficult," Kāśyapa’s intention was as follows:

being apart from protection and dwelling alone in empty seclusion is the phenomenon (*dharma*), whereas protection is the principle (*tattva*). The phenomenon is itself the true bhikṣu. "If there are those below... refers to the True Dharma.
One should know that these are indeed difficult questions.

To the answer, "Abandoning the phenomenon (事) while preserving the principle (理)": the Buddha’s response takes as the phenomenon the names of the ninefold scriptures (*navāṅga-dharma*) of the Hīnayāna—characterized by few desires and contentment—and is able to roar the lion's roar to extensively expound the wondrous Dharma;
this refers to the ninefold scriptures of the Mahāyāna as the principle. As for the "lion's roar": it is [the roar] of...

This is called the "Definitive Exposition," which is able to explain the Buddha-nature of sentient beings. Regarding the ninefold division of the Mahāyāna, there is no section on parables or discussions;
regarding the ninefold division of the Hīnayāna, there is no section on extensive inquiries or records.
The Sūtra states: "One who thus breaks the precepts" is the answer given to the previously mentioned bhikṣu dwelling in solitude;
although they are called "observers of the precepts," because they do not protect the Dharma, they are termed "those who break the precepts."
"Free from anger" means that this Pure Land is devoid of the various delusions of greed, hatred, and ignorance.
The one who was the first bhikṣu in his previous life is like Śāriputra and others; the one who was the second in his later life is Maudgalyāyana.
Therefore, they became his two disciples on the left and right sides. They are also called the Generals Who Turn the Dharma Wheel.
...and so forth.
As for taking both together as proof, it means taking the superior [aspect] of both.
The analogy of "painting on stone" refers to Kāśyapa perceiving the Buddha’s permanent body (nitya-kāya) as being like a painting on stone, steadfast and never fading away. If...
The impermanent body is like water drawn upon a surface that vanishes as soon as it is made.
To cite both cause and effect together: as the sutra states, taking the protection and upholding of the True Dharma as the cause, one obtains immeasurable retribution as the result.
Furthermore, those who protect the Dharma are not persons without precepts; this refers specifically to bhikṣus.
When the Sūtra states that one must not carry a royal parasol, an oil flask, or similar items, it is for the sake of avoiding derision and humiliation.

If someone were to offer such things, the king would assume that the bhikṣu craves these objects. As for the question of how one can transform others while maintaining the precepts oneself—the intended meaning is as follows:
To travel with those who carry swords and staves is to be without precepts; if one maintains the precepts, one should not travel [in such company].
Therefore, there is this question.

Regarding "encountering powerful conditions" in the Vinaya: both Sūtra and Vinaya state that for one’s own practice, it is necessary to rely on those who possess external influence as well as internal understanding.
Only then can one protect the Dharma.
Herein, the "five dharmas of spiritual understanding" refers to the clear comprehension of divine wisdom.
"Teaching and transforming according to the times" simply means expounding the sutras.
Regarding the phrase "one must not select [the recipient]," this means that transformation occurs whenever there is a sentient being with the capacity [to be saved].
As for the passage beginning "indiscriminately guiding and pouring down" (and so forth), this refers to not knowing the capacities of beings.
This is because, for example, two disciples of Śāriputra both committed the error of failing to accord with their respective capacities.
Regarding those who have not yet committed the preparatory offense (*prayoga-pāpattika*), one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya*, but has not yet committed the fundamental offense (*mūla-āpatti*).
For example, when it was said to Śrīgupta, "Are you a sage that you do such a thing?"— or as when Śrīgupta revealed his origins to the Great Being (Mahāsattva),
and while the Great Being was fishing in the Chicken Pond, Śrīgupta said, "Are you the one destined to succeed [the Buddha] in the future?"
"How could he be here? he asked. When [the deity] spoke, saying, "The head is adorned with a celestial crown that illuminates it," [Zhi] immediately saw the blazing radiance.
The Great Being (Mahāsattva) thereupon took refuge in his heart; thus it is said, "I realized only that he was a sage himself."
The five names are as follows: first, *śīla*, which means to prevent [transgressions]; second, *vinaya*, which means to extinguish evil;
third, *mokṣa*, which is translated here as "liberation"; fourth, *svādhyāya*, which refers to reciting from memory what was previously memorized from the text;
and fifth, *vinaya*, which refers to that which can realize and measure the limits of gravity [of offenses]; thus it is called by the single character "vinaya."
"One who must master one *piṭaka*" means that among the three—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—one who understands even one is capable of being a teacher.
"One who wishes to cross over" refers to crossing over birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Because he now wishes to violate the precepts and return to secular life, it is called "crossing over."
Section Six: Explaining the Merits of the Names and Terms.

Regarding the combination of the eight "goodnesses" at Kaishan Monastery: the superior, middling, and inferior [levels] are combined into one goodness; when added to the preceding seven goodnesses, they constitute eight.

Now, regarding the explanation of the seven types of goodness through seven similes: these correspond sequentially to the process of the eight rivers entering the ocean, up until the point where they are endowed with the eight flavors;
this too constitutes the perfection of goodness.
"Those who have eternally severed longing possess this supreme flavor; it is like having eaten milk-rice, after which nothing more is required.

'Skillfully taming the distracted mind' refers to the sublime practice of the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya) and the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa), for through these one is able to cultivate meditative concentration (samādhi); thus it is called 'skillful taming.
If one does not cultivate concentration, one is a sentient being with an empty and distracted mind, and this is not the concentration of this Mahāyāna."
First, regarding "the teacher of all Buddhas": the principle of the eternally abiding secret treasury is the teacher of the Buddhas.
Second, regarding "the gate for Bodhisattvas": a gate is that which enables passage; it refers to the teaching of the Great Nirvāṇa cultivated by all Bodhisattvas.
From cause to fruit, realizing the principle of the three virtues is called the True Dharma; it is like a great physician.
Regarding "blocking the four evil destinies of sentient beings": upon hearing this name, those who have deep faith in its merit cannot be defiled by evil, and thus it is said they are "blocked."
This text derives its name from the Dharma it upholds; that is to say, it refers to the merit of its title.

Regarding the mutual citation of one side [of each]: for those who cite the treatise, this refers to the Dharma; by citing the Dharma, one knows there is a person [who upholds it], and by citing the person, one necessarily possesses the Dharma.
Therefore, they are said to be "mutual."
Regarding "neither this nor that, nor between them": saṃsāra is the near shore and nirvāṇa is the far shore, while the arousal of the bodhicitta is the middle reliance.
Since one now contemplates that saṃsāra is itself nirvāṇa, it is said to be "neither this nor that, nor between them."
Regarding "one question and three answers": the question concerns the "other shore" (pāra), which constitutes the one. The "three answers" refer to the three [aspects] within this and that [shore].

As for those who have ascended to the stage of nature (dharmatā-bhūmi), the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-yāna) do not fall [into the realms] by their very nature; why would they need to rely on hearing the sutras?
"To act as a distant condition" refers to the intention regarding another time; it does not mean being free from [suffering] at that very moment.
"Names and non-names, etc. refers to entering the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
"Transcending the flow of existence" (*bhava-srotas*): "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the three realms of existence, and "flow" (*srotas*) refers to the four flows.

To believe in this is what it means to "receive" [the teaching]. As stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*, when a person who first rejoices in others' merit has deep faith in the principle of truth and accords with the mind of *nirvāṇa* through the understanding of the three virtues, this is called "receiving. When these thoughts continue in succession from moment to moment, it is called "upholding.
The five grades and six faculties can be attained through compassion; how could it be that one achieves this merely by hearing the sūtra?
The Sūtra states, "as well as those of the nature of Māra. This refers to names that do not change.
Defilements and other māras disturb and confuse the practitioner, agitating them in various ways, as explained at length in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Regarding the phrase "the ten thousand virtues as the beginning," the intention is to refute others by asking: how can the ten thousand virtues within the fruit be considered the beginning?

The scripture states that "words of superior, middling, and inferior" refers to the first category of excellence in expression (*vyañjana-kuśala*). "Meaning" refers to excellence in meaning (*artha-kuśala*). "Text" refers to excellence in phrasing (*vyañjana-kuśala*).

"Pure and complete" refers to singular excellence. "Purity" refers to excellence in conduct (*caryā-kuśala*). "Brahma-conduct" refers to excellence in kindness (*maitrī-kuśala*). "Fulfillment" [refers to excellence in realization].
The "foot" (pada) signifies the possession of goodness.

Therefore, those who provide mutual explanations state that because it is eternal, it is great; and because it is great, it is eternal. "Greatness" and "eternality" are one essence with different names.
"Milk is its source" means that milk is one; raw and cooked [milk] are two; curd and whey are two; thus they constitute the five flavors.
*Private Notes on the Commentary to the Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Private Notes on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.
Commentary on the Seventh Chapter, "The Four Marks.
Regarding the phrase in the sūtra, "by means of the four marks," it is as stated in the subsequent text: first, self-correction; second, [correction of] others; third, ...
They are able to provide answers in accordance with questions. Fourth, they are skilled in understanding the meaning of causes and conditions (and so forth).
As for "revealing and analyzing," it is as stated in the preceding text: "I pray that the Buddha will reveal the subtle and secret [teachings]," and so on.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning is briefly not fully revealed": this answers the preceding discussion on cause and effect. It simply clarifies that by cultivating the causes for long life, those who protect the Dharma obtain the causal fruit of longevity;
thus, it is said to be "contained" therein.
"There are no [beings] without liberation" means that the two vehicles do not possess liberation without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
"Kāśyapa requests that [the Buddha] open [the teaching]" refers to opening up the [distinction between] permanence and impermanence.

"This is the skillful means (*upāya*) for the two functions of *nirvāṇa*" means that by opening up the skillful means of the present and the past, one reveals the ultimate reality; therefore, it is said:
It is neither eternal nor impermanent.
That which was previously called "the three points of impermanence" refers to the eternity of the vertical and horizontal [dimensions].
This is precisely the mental faculty (*manas*) upon wisdom that is capable of objective cognition; it is a mental factor (*caitta*).
Furthermore, one who cannot be said to possess "false permanence" must be treated with the medicine of impermanence; only now can it be said that they possess both.
That which possesses both is the permanence of impermanence.
The river does not wind or curve, but flows straight like a taut cord directly into the western sea, and so forth.
"Together forming a single path" refers to their traveling as a pair.
These four phrases all subvert correct reasoning; for they use three to subvert one, and use one to subvert three, each clinging to their own [view].
This is the same. Therefore, I cite the *Śāstra* to establish this and fulfill the intent of the four *siddhārtha*s (fourfold purposes). The first four lines represent the worldly (*loka*) intention.

As for the statement that "all four lines are gates of skillful means," it means that by entering through these four gates, one attains the vision of principle; this is precisely the production of wholesome roots.
When a wise minister is able to provide an explanation for that which was not understood, it constitutes an antidote.
Furthermore, as these four lines are all correct principles, one may enter through any of the four gates to see the king; there is nothing that is not the principle of the three virtues.
This principle is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding the phrase "Are both not skillful means?": this is intended to refute others. Now, these four gates are all skillful means;
because they are such gates, if one can perceive the principle, they are all reality. Because they universally constitute these gates, if one can perceive the principle, all four gates are [reality].

Regarding the term "penetrating the secret": this refers to the fact that [the teachings] have not yet been disclosed. The four propositions mutually serve as antidotes—such as impermanence as the antidote to permanence, and permanence as the antidote to impermanence—and these four propositions are themselves the principle (*li*).
Whether it be impermanence, permanence, both impermanence and permanence, or neither permanence nor impermanence, all of these are the Dharmakāya.
To expound in this manner means that within a single phrase, various phrases are distinguished, yet all those phrases are in fact a single phrase;
thus it is called "expounding the secret.

As for the current four phrases which encompass both ordinary beings and sages: they begin with the principle itself—the names and practices of ordinary beings—and proceed through contemplative cultivation.
Up to the ultimate Sage, all possess these four propositions.
For instance, when Nirvana is divided into four aspects, it is the One that is discussed as Four.
As for the extensive exposition throughout the entire work, from the beginning to the end, there is nothing that is not an explanation.
To reach the place where there is no reaching is called "opening"; this is opening without opening, the meaning of which is like "reaching.
To constantly have nothing proclaimed is called "speaking"; this is speaking without speaking, the meaning of which is like "speaking. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"If the Tathāgata never speaks the Dharma, that is true 'much hearing' (bahuśruta). This is precisely its meaning.

Regarding the judgment based on the majority: although there are instances where these [attributes] are mutually lateral, here we follow the majority and the primary [meaning], and thus speak of them as the "three mysteries.
As for "not seeking the signless": the sign of the signless is called the true mark (dharmatā); what more, then, is there to be sought?

As for "there is not even nirvana": since even a single characteristic does not exist, yet the four characteristics are not lacking, this is because they are spoken of through provisional names and characteristics within that which is devoid of names and characteristics; hence it is said they are "not lacking."
"To open the four [aspects] as the conventional truth" means that "conventional" refers to differentiation.
"Non-self as self" refers to the true self of the Middle Way.
The phrase "for example, as in the *Prajñāpāramitā*" and so forth is like the previous [explanation] that the one characteristic is identical to the four characteristics, and so on.
Furthermore, regarding "the secrecy of the body" (*kāyaguhyaka*): "furthermore" (*jian*) means that the Way is integrated, as it pervades speech, body, and mind.

If one distinguishes them, "furthermore" refers to speech encompassing the body. The same applies to transforming others. Since there is already the transformation of others, this constitutes one's own practice (*svacaryā*).
For now, we shall follow the majority.
As for the statement that "the body and mind are likewise," this is because they both possess the other two [factors]; it is simply said here according to what is most prevalent.
Regarding "the exposition of the fourfold discrimination": this means to open up [the teaching] so that the single *nirvāṇa* is not perceived as having four distinct characteristics.
As for the phrase "if a Buddha, if a Tathāgata," Śākyamuni manifests himself as being identical to all Buddhas; therefore, it is said "if a Buddha, if a Tathāgata."
Regarding the term "Tathāgata": if one accords with suchness (*tathatā*) through wisdom and thereby attains the fruit, this is "coming" in the sense of self-correction.
If one comes by means of the path of reality to achieve perfect enlightenment and subsequently manifests traces in response to sentient beings, this is "coming" in the sense of correcting others.
"The one who sees is the one with correct wisdom" means seeing within a single moment of mind by means of the five eyes.
"All causes and conditions" refers to using wisdom to take the realm of true reality as its object; because of this accord through wisdom, the teaching of the One Vehicle is proclaimed.
Since the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is able to realize this principle, it is called "self-rectification."
Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata and the Buddha do not differ in meaning: "Buddha" has the sense of awakening (*buddha*), while "Tathāgata" refers to the object.
Since wisdom can accord with its object, they are not different.

"Because the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is not a cause, it is not self. Here, "self" refers to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); "other" refers to the ālayavijñāna; and "common" refers to their conjunction.
"It is not without cause" means that the ālayavijñāna is the dharma-nature, and the dharma-nature is the ālayavijñāna; therefore, it is neither self nor other.

Because they have thoroughly realized the true nature (*dharmatā*), they are "seers. Since they realize that the true nature is free from the four modes of existence (*caturvidha-svabhāva*), it is ultimately empty and quiescent;
thus, they see the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*).

To illustrate the profound by means of the shallow, consider for instance a bhikṣu who observes a fire in the world; this serves as an analogy to establish the object of contemplation, let alone what the Buddha has taught.
Is it not the profound sūtras of the twelve divisions?
That which arises has no source from which it arises; seeking fire through the four propositions, it cannot be found—this is the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

That which ceases has nowhere to go—this is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). Since neither nature nor characteristics exist, the entire mind is fire; this mind is the mind [of fire].
Furthermore, when one has no mind and seeks fire but cannot find it, this is precisely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); it does not arise from conditions.

"Embracing fire to burn one's body while vowing never to hold false views" means that because one has previously investigated the mass of fire and found it does not arise from conditions, one’s wisdom accords with principle, just like embracing fire.
Seeing this true mark, one realizes the oneness of the Triple Gem and does not give rise to false views.
Regarding the phrase "one who vows not to speak falsely even if a sharp blade cuts the tongue": this is because of wisdom. Therefore, it is called a "sharp blade.
The harmonious union of object and wisdom is termed "not speaking falsely."
As for the phrase "furthermore, as for the Buddhas," this uses the small to illustrate the great and the shallow to illustrate the profound.

Regarding the statement that "different explanations are given based on conditions," this answers the intent of the previous objection. It means that one should not apply the same logic to claim that the Three Jewels are merely a single entity;
rather, while they are fundamentally one, they are now explained as four because, for the sake of transforming others, they cannot be treated as one.

"Causing the production of roots of goodness" means causing the production of the goodness of principles such as permanence and so forth. These four [explanations] according to the *siddhi* method correspond to the text itself;
no other schools possess this intended meaning.

One may only hold ghee in the mouth. Ghee is a metaphor for the praise of the characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas). Whether one is weak or strong, eating it is in both cases improper;
one has not yet attained the benefit of the antidote that gives rise to wholesome states.
"From the subtle to the manifest" refers to the progression from the stage of joy (*pramuditā*) up to the entry into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
"Compassion is the root of all that is wholesome" means that unconditioned compassion (*apratyaya-maitrī*) is the foundation of all dharmas;
therefore, the Sūtra asks, "What is the root of all dharmas? and one should reply, "It is compassion."
The infant is a metaphor for one who has newly given rise to initial faith; in the teachings of the Tripitaka, the beginner's mind has not yet attained [realization of] impermanence and so forth.
"Praising with joy" means that they rejoice in understanding the characteristics of phenomena; this is the world of mutual rejoicing.
"To further increase their illnesses" means to increase the maladies of greed, pride, and so forth.
"Fearing they might meet an untimely death" refers to the fear that their eternal life-span might be cut short.
"Delighting in idleness and hindering the Way" means obstructing the path of the world.
Furthermore, for those who have produced wholesome roots, impermanence and permanence serve as their remedy.
That even hard food may be digested is a metaphor for the benefit of attaining the true teaching.
That they are capable of being refined through friction is due to being tempered and corrected by the Mahāyāna; thus they obtain the benefit of being forged in opposition.

Regarding the necessity of applying the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold intentions) to this scriptural passage, this is based on an exegesis of the sūtra itself; it is not intended as a conceptual construction established through other textual meanings.
The sūtra states that those who have "regard and concern" do so by the power of compassion, fearing that faith might fail to arise.
Regarding the phrase in the Sūtra, “*duō hán ér sū*”: the character *hán* (with the phonetic *hú gàn*) is written with the jade radical (*yù*) as *hán* in the *Zìlín*;
various other texts write it with the mouth radical (*kǒu*) as *tóng* or *gǔ*. The *Liángzhuàn* states: “*Bèiwáng hán* refers to providing someone with what they may hold in their mouth;
it is also said that what one eats from within the mouth is called *hán*, while feeding the mouth with the mouth is called *hán*.”
Regarding the fourth point, the quantity of the requested Dharma: the four [aspects] are many, while joy is few.
As for the scripture’s statement that "it increases one's lifespan," it first increases the impermanent life and subsequently increases the eternal life of wisdom.
Regarding the four previous interpretations, each addressed the specific matters of the teaching but had not yet explained how they accord with the profound principle.

As for the critique that they are inadequate: the former teachings on permanence were themselves inadequate, as they necessitated the teaching of impermanence; the present teaching on permanence serves precisely to remedy those former views.
The Sūtra states that [the world] was not fully provided for because the capacities of beings were insufficient and the [teaching’s] potential had not yet been fully realized.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "Those who have already perfected their merit, upon hearing the teaching of impermanence, find their roots of goodness gradually ripening;
this is also the manifestation of the body of samādhi within the Vaipulya [sūtras], such as the majestic and magnificent majesty of the Tathāgata’s merits."
Regarding the statement that there is a distinct meaning in the commentary "and so forth," this refers to the supramundane samādhis, the mundane samādhis of ordinary beings,

and the samādhis shared by both ordinary beings and sages. It continues until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reveals the previous flavors and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* manifests the secret samādhis while still retaining provisional ones.
The Sūtra states that "afflictions serve as fuel. This means that the constant delusions of ordinary beings serve as the fuel, while the impermanent wisdom of the Two Vehicles serves as the fire;
together they produce the food of the present Nirvāṇa of the Three Virtues.

Regarding the initial statement that the three *siddhis* are themselves "evil sons": for now, we consider them "evil" because, from the perspective of those who have not yet realized the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*), they still involve the breaking of the illness of impermanence.
However, if one discusses the five flavors and the two types of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), there is a subtle entry [into the truth] within them.
The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is not termed "evil.

This is that which both the Small and Great Vehicles commonly regard as the four *siddhāntas*: the Deer Park represents the two [vehicles] of the Small; the "butter" represents the Small and Great in contrast to one another.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reveals and clarifies [the truth], which is identical to the introductory exposition of the present sutra; furthermore, it is constantly applied in the final age because birth is taken as the differentiation of the impermanent.
Thus, using the permanent to treat the impermanent, that which is neither permanent nor impermanent constitutes the primary meaning.

If one discusses [the teachings] and knows that they all take the permanence [of phenomena] as the basis for attaining the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, these are merely judged as the three *siddhāntas*.

Regarding "knowing his house": he takes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as his house. Because he contemplates this lustful body of the five aggregates as being permanent, it is said that "there is a Buddha."
The Buddha raised this question of "no method" (*wufang*). "Method" refers to a fixed rule; he did not rely on a fixed rule to provisionally pose this question as a means to end the eating of meat.

If one were to rely on fixed rules regarding the use of wealth for giving, up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), then in this very moment, giving without anything given would itself be true giving.
Even unto the Prajñāpāramitā, it reveals constant wisdom to the ignorant; for to realize that delusion and confusion are themselves liberation is [the true gift].
That there is no loss to oneself while accomplishing great giving has two aspects: first, it reveals the equality of the mind of giving; second, it reveals the name of that virtue.
Furthermore, because wealth is not diminished, it is called "great."
Furthermore, regarding those who rejoice in merit (*anumodana*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "It is like those who buy and sell incense, and those who merely look on;
all three people equally perceive the fragrance.

As for one who sees suffering and arrives [to help], they are called a "great donor" (*mahādāyaka*). This is because their merit in bestowing life is vast, and thus they are "great" by virtue of the abundance of their merit.
The Sūtra says: "Those who hear the voice of the Śrāvakas. To ask about sounds and hear that "I have realized it" is called "hearing"; for my voice to reach them is called "asking.
The Sūtra says: "One who well understands my intent. My teaching that one may eat meat is a provisional (upāya) teaching; the Mahāyāna true teaching is as follows: [omitted].

All meat is prohibited. Your current command to cease [eating meat] deeply accords with the Buddha’s mind; therefore, the preceding passage serves as the definitive conclusion regarding the prohibition of meat.
Third, regarding "the turning back of one's retinue," the Precept Sūtra states: "All sentient beings have been my parents."
Since there is nothing that does not arise from these [elements], one should not consume them.
Fourth, regarding the identity with the four great elements and the five aggregates: furthermore, the Precept Sūtra states, "All earth and water were my former bodies;
all fire and wind are my original essence," and so forth.
Regarding "impurity of semen and blood": all sentient beings are alike in being formed from the union of the semen and blood of their parents;
hence it is called impure.
Regarding "contrary to the Bodhisattva’s path of transformation": the Bodhisattva acts as the cause for a pure land for all sentient beings, taking compassion as...
Fundamentally, if one eats their flesh, it contravenes the mind of compassion.
As for why eating meat constitutes many minor offenses: it is because for every single morsel of meat eaten, one must repay the debt with five hundred morsels.
The former kings were Prince Śūcintita, Prince Sudhārin, and others.
As for the fruits, vegetables, and so forth, which were all portions of others' lives, these were portions intended for the sustenance of their bodies.
Because he gave away what was his own portion, it is called "one's own portion" (*jīvitabhāga*).
The Sūtra asks: "Why does the Tathāgata not permit the eating of meat? The objection is: "Why was it previously permitted, yet now is forbidden?
One explanation states: "The Buddha is one of great compassion; since all beings shall eventually attain Buddhahood, one ought not to eat meat."

The first stage (*bhūmi*) is that of Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*). If one takes the position of the stage of skillful means (*upāya*), then since the nature-stage (*gotrabhūmi*) of the first stage has not yet attained the meaning of Great Compassion, it is something that ought to be attained.
It must be said that for one who acts as "for my sake," food cannot be consumed.
Regarding the serpent that resembles a dragon: because the dragon has performed a service for humanity, it is not to be eaten.

If one speaks according to the words of others, this refers to the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna as being excellent. If one speaks from one’s own perspective, this refers to the sudden prohibitions of the Mahāyāna.
Today, non-glutinous grain and the like are considered excellent.
Those who greedily consume wealth are called *tāo* (饕); those who greedily consume food are called *tiè* (餮). To starve oneself is said to be a failure to reach [the goal].
Regarding "opening three and prohibiting ten": first, it opens the three kinds of purity and prohibits the ten kinds of meat from being eaten.

Although there are those who currently eat meat, this is a provisional demonstration of the Hinayana teachings for the sake of sentient beings; because it captures the Buddha’s true intent, it is said that one does not eat [meat].
"Being separated from sentient beings" means, as stated in the *Śīla-sūtra*, that all sentient beings see [the practitioner] and depart;
thus, one cannot transform them, which constitutes being "separated.

Regarding the statement that "all are teachings of provisional names and causes and conditions," if we take this in its general sense, even the secular scriptures of the world likewise employ benevolence.

The five constant virtues—benevolence, propriety, wisdom, and so forth—serve as causes and conditions. The teachings of external paths take spontaneity (ziran) as their principle and do not follow causes and conditions;
Buddhist teaching takes causes and conditions as its fundamental tenet. Therefore, it is said that "all are equal" [in this regard].

First, regarding the "conditions for arising": this refers to the advancement and withdrawal of the robe and bowl. Next, clarifying the "essence of the precepts": this refers to the attainment of the precepts.
Finally, the "extensive exposition of characteristics": this refers to the explanation of the phenomenal aspects.
Regarding the judgment that "it is explained below," the causal origins are fully detailed in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation).
This refers to Queen Mallikā, who feigned the King’s command not to kill the kitchen attendants and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "the precepts are the constant joy of the Mahāyāna" and so forth: the precepts are the foundation. Because the precepts exist, the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity can endure;
therefore, they are described as profound and subtle.
*Vinaya* (mokṣa) is called "liberation" (*vimukti*); it is also termed "individual liberation" (*prātimokṣa*), as well as "attainment of liberation through preservation," and so forth.
*Vinaya* is called "extinction" (*nirodha*), for it can extinguish the transgressions of body and speech.
Regarding "reciting with the mouth": Upāli recited [the Vinaya] eighty times during a single summer retreat.
Furthermore, regarding "falling into growth": it refers to the growth of offenses from the subtle to the manifest.
The ten wholesome deeds are likened to the Sudden Teaching, which refers to the initial preaching of the Avataṃsaka doctrine.

They are likened to the Gradual Teaching, which means opening up the Sudden to produce the Gradual; that is, without departing from the site of enlightenment (Vaiśālī), one transforms beings at the Deer Park.
Regarding the meaning of "opening and closing": "opening" refers to the sudden teaching emerging from the gradual, while "closing" refers to the gradual returning to the sudden, and so forth.

If it is said that because they are neither one nor four, they can be described as "one and four," then it should also be said that because they are both one and four, they can be described as "four and one."
"Proving what is correct for oneself" refers to the realization of *nirvāṇa*.
"Extensively elaborating based on others" refers to the questions and answers concerning *nirvāṇa*.
That the *dharmakāya* is the specific while *nirvāṇa* is the general means that the four faculties share a single characteristic.
Regarding "Nirvana as the specific and the secret treasury as the general": since Nirvana is itself the four [aspects], it is said that the secret treasury is the general.
Alternatively, when it serves as the general, it refers to the single name "Nirvana."
The phrase "at times it is distinguished" refers to the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
As for those who raise counter-arguments, such as the sūtra stating that "space is non-existent," since the four names do not differ and there is no falsehood therein.
The four characteristics of *nirvāṇa* are likewise also real and substantial. There is an answer [to this]: the answer is that *nirvāṇa* is one.
There is a comprehensive [explanation]: *nirvāṇa* is the general name for the four characteristics.
Regarding "neither basis nor correctness": when the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom is extinguished, what discussion can there be of basis and correctness?
Now, as for that which serves as the teacher’s Dharma in Nirvana, it takes the essence of the three virtues as its teacher.
Now, regarding the statement that there is a Tathāgata within *nirvāṇa*: it refers to the eternal abiding of the *dharmakāya*.
First, clarifying the extinction of evil is the cause; second, clarifying the extinction of existence (*bhava*)—where "existence" is the effect—is as follows:
"extinguishing all existences" refers to the passage in the sutras concerning the mire of various existences, which means the universal extinction of the twenty-five places of birth.
All that can be sought according to the Buddha’s intention is as follows: the Buddha’s intention proceeds from the small to the great; therefore, he cites the past to raise a challenge.

One should not allow things to be confused under a common name such that what is eternal is made out to be impermanent. You [the opponent] recall that although the name "Nirvana" is the same, you take it to be eternal, whereas [I] take it to be the same as impermanent.
Regarding the difference between what is abandoned and what is attained compared to the past: that which is abandoned according to the present teaching is itself nothing other than attainment.
This is because "attaining eternal bliss" and so forth refers to the three delusions, which are in fact the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

Regarding the statement that there is "sublime existence" within *nirvāṇa*: it refers to transcending the twenty-five forms of existence (*bhava*) and attaining the sublime existence of the twenty-five *samādhis*.
As for what is called "reverence," it is the sublime dharma; to take the Dharma as one's teacher and to be able to show reverence to others is precisely this.
The Sangha is the complete integration of these three bodies. As for the text,
although there appear to be two sections that seem to constitute three difficulties, they are designated as "seemingly" so because the first difficulty concerns afflictions and existence,
while the subsequent passage concerning karma— beginning with "one does not know where it goes"— contains elements of both, hence it is called "seeming."
It is because the movement of karma means that karma reaches its destination.
That which cannot reach such a destination lacks the corresponding fruit of a body.
Therefore, that which "has existence" refers to having a body in the place of future rebirth.
"Attaining the wondrous existence" refers to attaining the wondrous existence of the twenty-five samādhis of the eternally abiding Dharma-body.
"Iron is the ordinary person" means that, just as iron that was red-hot returns to black,
so too the afflictions of an ordinary person may be extinguished, yet the afflictions arise again, just as the iron becomes red once more.
Furthermore, regarding "the impermanence of ordinary beings": in relation to the Dharma-body of the Middle Way of the First Abode, this is termed the impermanence of ordinary beings.

As for "not being the same as the two extremes": externalist ordinary beings represent the extreme of existence, while the ordinary beings of the Two Vehicles represent the extreme of non-existence. As it is said:
Coming, they are at the periphery while being different within; having ceased, they arise again. There is nothing capable of producing the wondrous existence of the Middle Way.
As for ordinary beings who, after extinguishing delusions, still undergo further rebirth, the sutra refers here specifically to two types of ordinary beings.
Regarding the statement that "the object perishes before and the name arises after": the object is like the substance of a jar; once it is broken, a name arises, such as "broken jar" and so forth.
The *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata is also like this: once [the defilements] are destroyed, a name arises. This is not the same as the annihilation of ashes.
This is not the same as your question regarding [the Buddha] being born again after having perished.
The Sūtra cannot say that the Holy King has passed away; it is like the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where he actually exists yet speaks of his death and so forth.

The Sūtra says, "Wandering among the flowers of awakening. This is like a tree that bears fruit, which immediately brings peace and happiness. The Tathāgata is likewise: he possesses the flowers of awakening.
These flowers signify purity; peace and happiness signify permanence and bliss; and his sovereign play signifies the self (*ātman*).
Therefore, it is said that there are four virtues.
Second, regarding the extensive opening of the secret of the body: the Tathāgata manifests bodies of the nine realms, which are termed "secret" because they were previously unopened;
now, all are opened. Thus it is said, "He produces various bodies," and so forth; these are merely the differences among the nine realms. Now, he causes them to...
Because all equally attain Great Nirvana, it is said that they are "opened.
As for the claim that one thing covers another while another opens it: "covering" simply means being concealed, and "opening" simply means being revealed.

For example, when the Dharma-body is hidden and Prajñā is manifest, or when the Dharma-body is manifest and Liberation is hidden, each is respectively concealed or revealed; thus, the three mysteries are distinct.
"To conceal what was previously disclosed and to disclose what was previously concealed" refers to concealing what was discussed in the past and disclosing what is discussed now;
since there is no other distinction, their essence is simply "concealment" (zhi).
Regarding those who do not understand: their lack of understanding is simply because the Dharmakāya is shrouded; therefore, they do not understand.

As for the question "What else could be understood?", this is intended to censure [the notion that] even if one were to approach Prajñā and Vimukti through the Dharmakāya, one would still be unable to understand them.
Regarding his clarification that "the immense and the minute are mutually compatible," he cites the following analogy to explain it, such as Mount Sumeru entering a mustard seed and so forth.
"The arts of the sages" refers to matters that are shallow and mundane.
That which is not [produced by] causes and conditions is entirely inconceivable. It is not that there is a response when there is no stimulus, nor that there is a stimulus when there is no response;
it is the causal condition of the Great Matter. Therefore, it is said that "emptiness, the provisional, and the middle" are the single mind's discourse on causes and conditions.
"Immeasurable and not admitting even a single speck of dust": since "dust" (*rajas*) is itself the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is said that it does not admit [anything else].
"Extending and abbreviating the past and present": "extending and abbreviating" refers to *kalpas*, while "past and present" refers to time.

"That which remains even in a state of dazed confusion" is an illustration of the profound by means of the shallow; if even the dream-events of the mundane world are thus, how much more so the inconceivable ultimate reality?
The scripture’s statement, "You should not say," encompasses the three subsequent points.

The Sūtra says, "I only wish that the Tathāgata would explain its causes and conditions," which is a request to explain the causes and conditions for the birth of Rāhula and the causes and conditions for crossing over afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Sūtra says, "The Buddha told [him]," and so forth, which restates the objection and refutes it as a whole; therefore, it says, "It should not be so."
The Sūtra says, "One who can establish the Great Purpose. What is the Great Purpose?
That I have now fathered Rāhula, thereby manifesting the cause through the fruit and abiding in Great Nirvāṇa—this is called the Great Purpose.

Regarding "the first, abiding in faith; the second, abiding in truth": this refers to the initial arousal of the bodhicitta and entry into the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). "Truth" (*satya*) refers to the stage of realization (*adhigama*).
Although it is not [itself] cause and effect, it is the essence of *nirvāṇa*; yet, as a bodhisattva, one can constantly contemplate *nirvāṇa* while practicing the path.
Regarding "result and cause": by virtue of the nature of the true cause, principle inherently possesses both cause and result.
As for why the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states that a bodhisattva cannot [perceive it], this is to refute the first of the aforementioned teachers.
Regarding the practice of various modes of conduct: this refers to the five practices and ten merits.
As for the direct example of Mount Sumeru entering a mustard seed, the detailed explanation is as found in the "Inconceivable" chapter of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

Since both Mount Sumeru and the mustard seed are the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and since even the worlds of the ten directions are entirely the Dharma-realm, a single atom possesses the ten [merits].
How much more so, then, regarding the function of inconceivable liberation!
As the sutra says, "like a potter's wheel," this refers to all worlds being like a single lump of clay placed upon the wheel.
To say that he "transcends the six realms" indicates that he serves as the teacher of devas and humans; hence, it is called "transcending.
To speak in full detail, he also transcends the four noble ones to serve as the ultimate teacher.
Regarding "because of awakening to the unawakened": one awakens to one's own afflictions and is further able to awaken others to their afflictions; this interpretation is superior.
Regarding "capable of producing all things": it means being capable of generating all manner of wholesome virtues.
As for the statement that autumn is the "land of death," it means that autumn can cause the myriad things to wither and decay; this is a metaphor for the extinction of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, regarding the fact that sentient beings perceive and experience things differently, this is explained through the progression and regression [of their faculties]; thus, even within the state of birth, there is the significance of the four fruits of spiritual attainment.

The Sūtra states: "Kāśyapa, by means of causes and conditions... This concludes the third section. It explains that a Bodhisattva abiding in the Great Nirvāṇa is able to manifest causes and conditions.

To raise a difficulty regarding the subsequent meaning based on the preceding intent, one cites the previous objection raised by the Buddha, stating: "It is just as when a fire is extinguished, there is nothing at all."

Regarding the passage beginning with "All [lamps]," etc.: the current statement that "the lamp is extinguished" merely takes up the commonality of extinction as a point of contention. Following this objection, it demonstrates the seed capable of producing [the result].
As for raising this objection: because the Buddha brought up the lamp-vessel, and since the vessel is impermanent, how can it be the Dharma-body?
Regarding the Mahāyāna *anāgāmin* who does not undergo birth in the two extremes: the *anāgāmin* of the first dwelling abides in the Middle Way and thus has no birth in the two extremes.
[End of] Explanation of the Chapter on the Four Marks, Part Two.
Regarding Xinghuang’s statement that "the secret of the person is not yet exhausted," the meaning is that the "Chapter on the Four Marks" has not been fully expounded.
Is it not the case that the "secret of the mouth" refers to the words of the Tathāgata? Since "words" (yan) mean "to speak" (shuo), it is called the "mouth" (kou).

Regarding "he reveals the Buddha’s secret": the Bodhisattva takes others as his objective. From the time he attained the Way, he has universally revealed the four preceding flavors, all of which are the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and so forth.
"Seeing a small portion of the Buddha-nature" refers to the stage of the first dwelling (prathamabhūmi); it is called "small" because [the realization] is limited.
Furthermore, regarding the opening of three functions within each of the four propositions—namely, the four propositions of "others," "opening," "Buddha," and so forth—[this refers to the same].
Regarding "opening what was not opened" as previously analyzed: the essence of nirvāṇa is neither revealed nor concealed;
however, for the sake of sentient beings, it manifests various appearances extensively, as explained in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.

Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*’s rejection of the Hinayana: this is explained at length in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) in sections such as "Destroying the Three to Reveal the One" and "Harmonizing the Three to Reveal the One.

"Rejection" (*chi*) is a specific term for "abandonment" (*fei*). Ancient commentaries were incorrect in judging that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is definitive while [the *Lotus Sūtra*] is non-definitive; both equally reject the Hinayana.
How can it be that while one is enlightened, another is not?

This is because of the distinction between the manifest and the secret. For example, at the *Avataṃsaka* assembly, those who heard together perceived differently: while the followers of the Two Vehicles secretly heard the Lesser Teachings (*hīnayāna*), eighty thousand devas at the Deer Park immediately awakened to the Great Way (*mahāyāna*).
Regarding these two passages: the former passage concerning the secret of the body (*kāyaguhyaka*) and this present passage concerning the secret of the mind (*manoguhyaka*) constitute the two texts.
Since it is improper to definitively judge one as superior to the other, they are described as being "both."
Therefore, this "non-existence" does not mean that the principle of the secret treasury is not admitted.
When the Sūtra says, "there is only secret speech," "speech" refers to the teaching.
For example, regarding the phrase "like a master of illusions," "master" means a sovereign or controller; it refers to the one who creates the illusion.

Regarding the presence of both opening and concealing, this is discussed in terms of the five meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). What was previously unseen is termed "concealed"; therefore, it is now opened.
As for "accumulated gold being the reverse," it means that by reversing [the process], one accords with the natural order.
The "beginner" (ādikarmika) is one who is moderately wealthy; this refers to the stage of the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*).
The "one who has attained the fruit" (*phalaprāpta*) is one who is greatly wealthy; this refers to the ultimate fruit (*niṣṭhā-phala*).
To speak of them as "indebted" (*ṛṇin*) is like a person who, although they owe another wealth, does not take it back even when wishing to return it; they are still called "indebted. As it is said:

The coming [of the teaching] is likewise so: the treasury of all dharmas constantly desires to bestow itself upon sentient beings, yet sentient beings do not accept it; in meaning, this is like being burdened by a debt.

As the Sūtra says, "fearing that one will not quickly achieve success," this refers to those who initially lack the great capacity [for the teaching], as in the case of the three-week period in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
"Contemplating such matters as these at midday (and so forth).
That which is free from erroneous teachings is entirely the true Dharma of worldly words."
Regarding the initial "narrative praise": it is praised and then recounted; hence the words "Excellent," and so forth.

As for "the permanent and the impermanent being the common ground": one first contemplates impermanence as an illusory transformation; those of sharp faculties then receive this through the understanding of permanence.
"Always distinct" means that the initial mind knows the permanent as being for the sake of the Middle Way; thus, one practices in successive stages.

Regarding "one should apply the four intentions," this refers to employing the present four teachings to distinguish the inclusive and transitional meanings of various sutras, as well as to reveal the perfect and permanent.
Regarding the statement that "not sowing seeds means there is no secret condition":
although they grow from the same earth and are moistened by the same rain, they do not—unlike the three types of grasses and two types of trees in the *Lotus Sūtra*—attain growth.
"That which is difficult to change even now" refers to that which does not alter until death, because the mind's grasping is so firm.
As for the statement "the Buddha’s wisdom is fluid," this merely describes its nature of impermanence and constant transition.

The Buddha’s answer regarding the three meanings is as follows: first, there is no accumulation; second, there is the accumulation of non-accumulation; third, it clarifies that within accumulation there is no non-accumulation.
As for "accumulation," although it explains accumulation, the underlying intent lies in non-accumulation.
The accumulation that is non-accumulation is the Tathāgata’s perfection of the wealth of Dharma, which is the unconditioned Middle Way.
The non-accumulation of what has been accumulated refers to the śrāvakas’ cultivation of emptiness, such as not storing the eight kinds of impure things.
The Sūtra says: "If there is one who possesses craving, they are conditioned; such is the Saṃgha of Śrāvakas. If there is no craving, this is the unconditioned;
such is the practice of the Tathāgata."
The Sūtra states that "traces difficult to trace" refers to the unconditioned path of the Tathāgata;
"traces easy to trace" refers to the conditioned Śrāvaka Saṃgha.
The Sūtra says: "Though one departs, there is no one who arrives"—this refers to the Śrāvaka. "There is one who has a place of arrival"—this refers to the Tathāgata.
"Permanently abiding without accumulation is purity"—this means being free from the defilements of the two extremes. "Contentment is bliss"—this means that the Two Vehicles are not yet content.
It is suffering.
This is the absence of accumulation; it is the absence of the accumulation of the path and so forth.
That both the path and cessation are characterized by permanence and bliss means that both cause and fruit are fully endowed.
"The afflictions and entanglements are all eliminated" means that the three delusions and the two deaths are entirely removed.
"The object and wisdom are in accord" means that wisdom accords with the object; this is called "conformity to wisdom."
Regarding the accomplishment of essence and function: the *dharmakāya* is the essence, while *prajñā* and liberation are the function.
It is also the fulfillment of both self and others: the *dharmakāya* is the self, while *prajñā* and liberation are the other.
Regarding "the principles being roughly complete": the three [aspects] such as the Dharma-body each possess all three; this is what is meant by "completeness.

Regarding "its nature being vast and extensive": it is not only that the Dharma-body at the stage of fruition is vast and extensive, but the nature of the six identities (*liu ji*) is likewise none other than extensiveness.
For while the nature itself is neither vast nor extensive, it nonetheless possesses vastness and extensiveness.
That which is "great" without depending on the "small" is a greatness that is neither small nor great;

it is the inconceivable greatness that transcends all dependence. Because its nature is vast and expansive, that very nature is inherently transcendent—not by excluding the small and the great, but by being named "transcendent" precisely because it does so.
"An immeasurable lifespan is the vertical metaphor" means that because it is a long-lasting life, it is called "vertical.
"Valuing the True Dharma" refers to abiding in the Middle Way.
"One person possesses all eight" means that within each individual virtue, all eight are fully present.
To say that the general term can encompass the specific ones: the name "Nirvana" subsumes both liberation (*vimukti*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
To explain the general through the specific: Nirvana is explained by means of being free from afflictions (*āsrava*) and liberated.
As for what cannot be confused: this reverses the general definition.
The Sūtra says, "to extract the poisoned arrow," which refers to the three delusions; "to cause them to leave suffering" refers to leaving behind the two types of death.
"Wondrous Bliss" refers to the *amṛta* (the finest essence).

"The Good Physician" refers to the Buddha. "Attaining peace and bliss" means realizing *nirvāṇa*. This is merely a reciprocal manifestation: because one is oneself free from afflictions (*gaṇḍa*), one is able to treat others;
when the afflictions of others are exhausted, one's own are made to be exhausted as well. If one's own [afflictions] are not yet exhausted, how could one transform others? Therefore...
The Sūtra says: "One who is ill cannot save themselves, yet they can listen to those who are ill.
Those whose body and mind do not suffer are the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas; for them, body and mind are non-dual.
"Being without fear" means being free from the five fears.
"Constantly being without hunger or thirst" means being fully provided with the food of the three virtues.
"Having no affairs of humans or devas" means having no affairs such as the three sufferings and eight sufferings of the world.
As for the burden of defiled attachment, it cannot be burdened by the two extremes.

To "reject the past and manifest the present" means to reject the past, wherein the three virtues were neither horizontally nor vertically complete, and to manifest the present, wherein the one virtue is fully endowed with the three virtues.
The Sūtra asks, "What is called nirvāṇa? This question intends to raise the general topic, while the answer distinguishes the specific locus of liberation.
Regarding the statement that the Buddha-fruit possesses form (*rūpa*): it is not yet known what kind of form this is. Sublime Wisdom (*prajñā*) clearly perceives principle through wisdom;
this is like the eye perceiving form—though it is not itself a visual organ, it is said to possess form.
Regarding "this formless form": it should manifest as form. Regarding "the essence of liberation": this refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Regarding "for the sake of two conditions, etc.": first, its fundamental nature is not form; second, it is taught as form according to the capacities of sentient beings.
All of these must involve the four gates and the three truths—emptiness and non-emptiness—and so forth; this is termed the "inconceivable."
The Master said, "There is no need to differentiate between cause and effect. His intention was that cause and effect are attained simultaneously.
However, because [the interlocutor] has not yet understood this, the Master now refutes him by saying, "It is not so," and so forth.
Regarding "expounding" (*yanchang*): "expound" (*yan*) means to open up and elaborate.

As for the statement that the number of "heads" (*toushou*) is eight, four, five, or so on: starting from the initial name "Distant Removal" (*yuanyili*), if one follows the sequence in the text, those who have attained liberation are termed "heads.
It would not be appropriate to say there are four or five; it should simply be stated as eight.
Fourteen in total.
If the large and small are counted together, there are ninety-seven or ninety-eight; the "large" refers to the head or leader, while the "small" refers to the retinue.
In the text, this is what is meant by "liberation. In the text, there are thirteen members of the retinue in total, which, when combined with the aforementioned head, [totals]... (as stated).
Ninety-seven. It is incorrect to say "eight.

Regarding the statement "extremely subtle," this refers to the textual explanation of the number of afflictions (*kleśa*) as a metaphor for liberation (*vimokṣa*). Within the synthesis, the name "liberation" lacks a fixed standard.
For now, we shall provisionally rely on the perfect hundred as the numerical square.

The Great Master once spent a summer retreat at Lingshi (Spirit Rock), where he expounded upon these "One Hundred Verses on Liberation. This site is located to the northwest of Huangyan County in Taizhou;
it was formerly known as the Gandha (Amṛta) Monastery and contains the Gandha Well. In the past, an Arhat drank this water while practicing his path.
He encountered the rebellion of Sun Xizi, and a band of rebels gathered there to take a bell and boil meat. At that moment, a large square stone [emerged] from...
Descending over the mountain, the bandits were dispersed. For this reason, it was subsequently renamed Lingshi Temple (Spirit Rock Temple); the rock remains there to this day.

As for the phrase "those who have already satisfied themselves through prior study," this refers to the words of the commentator Zhanran; it is regrettable that they were not recorded [in the original text].
Regarding "each and every phrase being complete both horizontally and vertically": a single phrase universally encompassing all phrases is "horizontal";
each of those phrases penetrating deeply into one another is "vertical. Non-duality is itself vastness; it is itself being free from wounds; it is arriving at the place of liberation.
A single phrase thus possesses the meanings of the aforementioned three; these meanings are the three virtues (*triguṇa*); the three virtues are the true self (*ātman*). The true...
"I am the secret treasury. Because one is three, and three are one, it is said that the three points are mutually identical and complete without deficiency.
How could words ever reach this? The commentator deeply laments that the essence of inconceivable liberation transcends the scope of speech.
This cannot be accomplished through one's own power. Since it has not been written [in full], I shall simply divide its text here.
The Sūtra states: "True liberation is called 'the state of being far removed'.

To explain this liberation, I shall now take the single phrase as interpreted by the Great Master as the foundation, adorning it with ten phrases. Hereafter, the lower will explain the upper; first, "being far removed" is as follows:
Fundamentally, this is fully explained according to the four teachings in terms of the three delusions, the two deaths, and the three meanings such as being free from affliction and blemish.
This "separation" refers to being separated from the delusions of the two deaths of the previous three teachings. Because of this separation, it is called "non-arising";

because of this separation, it is called "emptiness and non-existence"; because of this separation, it is called "unconditioned"; and because of this separation, it is called "freedom from illness. By means of...
Because of detachment, the sores and wounds of the outflows (*āsrava*) are forever absent. Because of detachment, there is no contention.
Because of detachment, it is called tranquility. Because of detachment, it is called security. Because of detachment, there is no equal companion.
Because of detachment, there is no sorrow. In the absence of sorrow, there are no sores; in the absence of sores—
This is precisely what is meant by "vast and extensive. Because it is vast and extensive, one reaches the state of liberation; this "state" serves as the basis of reliance.

A single phrase is thus, while all subsequent phrases follow in reverse order, each taking its predecessor as its head. All are adorned with the ten [qualities], continuing even unto a hundred phrases, which turn back upon one another to provide mutual explanation;
hence it is called the "myriad dharma-gates."

Regarding the extensive explanation of the "places of liberation": first, one personally arrives at the place of true reality; second, through self-discipline, one enables others to attain it as well.
The Sūtra says: "It is like a door-sill" (the character *kǔn* is a variant of *kùn*). The *Book of Rites* (*Lǐjì*) states: "External words do not enter the *kùn*. Zheng Xuan commented:
"*Kùn* refers to the threshold of a door."

That which can wound the Dharma-body and damage the life-force of wisdom—as explained by the ancients—all fails to accord with the present text’s exposition of the essence of liberation as eternally abiding; therefore, it is said to "damage" it.
"Those who sever the majority through other causes" refers to those prior to perfect enlightenment (*sambodhi*).
"Nirvāṇa within the principle" means that the three paths are the three virtues; it is called "within" because they are internal.
The "self within the principle" is precisely the true self of the causal Buddha-nature (*hetu-buddhadhātu*).
That which is later called "one body" refers to the identity of name with different meanings.
What is stated here as "not so" means that from beginning to end, they are entirely one body.
First, because the essence is wondrous, it corresponds to three; that is, within a single essence there are three wondrous functions.
Second, because the names and meanings are to be distinguished, it corresponds to three; the name is one, while the meanings are three, namely, the distinction between the Three Jewels.
Regarding "neither wondrous nor precious": because its essence is not wondrous, it is not one; because it is not precious, it cannot be called three.
Since the three are identical with the one essence, it is called "wondrous."
"These are indeed the wondrous jewels" means that the three names and the single essence are one.
Now, regarding the refutation of the separate teaching of the three as being one: this refutes the three distinct characteristics so that they become the single essence of the present.
Since the essence is itself the three, there is no contradiction.

The Sūtra states: "Now, as for nirvāṇa, it is the relinquishing of both body and wisdom. Regarding this, the explanations of the three preceding masters are as follows; the third master’s interpretation accords with this text.

As for the question, "Who experiences peace and bliss? Kāśyapa adheres to the view that in the past, at the time of nirvāṇa, both body and wisdom perish; therefore, he asks, "Who experiences it? The Buddha [replies].
It is answered by the Great: Nirvana is without sensation, and thus it is called "Great Bliss.
Regarding "vomiting because of affliction": this refers to the internal afflictions of views, discursive thought, and ignorance.
If ignorance is vomited out, one will no longer undergo further rebirth, and thus attains peace and bliss.
Whether one uses empty space as a metaphor for the Buddha’s body or does not, it is because the essence of the Dharma-body is identical to empty space;
thus, "not using" it would mean it is not a metaphor.

Whether one uses clouds and thunder as metaphors for the Buddha’s body, they refer to the response-body (nirmāṇakāya); whether one does not use them, they are simply not metaphors. In all cases, [the choice] is taken according to...
Because it is only a partial [truth], I have cited the analogy of the snowy mountains and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "none can be definitively explained," I have cited two metaphors to demonstrate that when the Tathāgata speaks, he does not do so with fixed certainty;
for if it were fixed, it would not be the ultimate reality. Why, then, do you challenge me by asserting these two distinct modes of explanation?

If it is said that there is no offense when one actually commits an offense, then in terms of the single essence (*ekatva*) there is no offense, while in terms of distinct essences (*pṛthaktva*) the offense of parricide (*ānantarya*) is established.
Whether [the offense] is determinate or indeterminate can be understood by analogy with this principle.
Chapter Eight: Explaining the Four Reliances.
If one relies solely on the Dharma, it means relying on the Dharma for one's own practice.
That one also attains the Dharma is because people can propagate the Dharma.
"Those who have attained are human beings" means that these people have attained the vast and great Dharma; they may also rely upon it as the Dharma for their own practice.
Furthermore, those "people of old who were mixed with falsehood" were Māras manifesting in the likeness of Arhats.

Now, regarding the mixing of the Great and Small Vehicles and the principle of relying on the person rather than the teaching: although the teaching may be common to both vehicles, one need only rely on those who are Bodhisattvas.
This is because the teaching is not universal; for those of the Two Vehicles possess only the teachings pertaining to the realm within [saṃsāra]. Thus, they abandon birth...
"Seeking nirvana after death," thus it is said that "one proceeds toward it.

As for the current clarification that "the person immediately upholds the Dharma without abandoning it," this refers to a bodhisattva manifesting in the form of one who has attained the four fruits of a śrāvaka.
Without abandoning birth and death, one becomes a refuge for sentient beings by relying on this Dharma of *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the application of the four *siddhāntas*:

the previous question and answer were different, which corresponds to the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint). The present answer—that those who have attained the Dharma are [the ones to rely upon]—is the *janana-kuśala-siddhānta* (standpoint that engenders goodness).

The distinction between the true and the false is the *pratikāra-siddhānta* (standpoint of remediation). And the fact that the Dharma is both pervasive and non-pervasive is the meaning of the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate standpoint).

Regarding those who appear after the Buddha's passing: these are the Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances. Since they must necessarily appear after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if one were to create images of them, there would be a fear of confusing them with the teachings of Māra; therefore, they may not be made into images of the Buddha.

People say that those who have attained the four fruits of the path are true fields of merit; because Arhats are worthy of offerings from the world, sentient beings place great faith in and accept them.
However, the forms of Bodhisattvas have no fixed standard and their dharmas do not follow constant rules; thus, they may manifest as those of the four fruits.
Generally speaking, all such manifestations are made by Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas, who can display the images of the nine realms, such as Avalokiteśvara with his wondrous voice and others.
There are thirty-three bodies and nineteen modes of teaching the Dharma; these shall be discussed separately for the sake of convenience regarding the meaning of the four fruits.
As for those who are Tathāgatas as Tathāgatas: when the Buddha was in the world, the Tathāgata himself was a Tathāgata.
When the Tathāgata is the one who relies upon the four refuges, he may be an ancient Buddha who, assisting the current Buddha in his transformative work, serves as the four refuges.

When the four refuges are the Tathāgata, it may be that his original state was humble while his manifested traces were lofty, or his original state was lofty while his manifested traces were humble; in all such cases, they mutually propagate the teaching.
When combined, it is still the Buddha who constitutes the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*). The meaning of the four phases of the four reliances is identical;

whether they are expanded or condensed is a matter of convenience. Only the Buddha alone is that which can be relied upon. As in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he is therefore said to be "returned to" (*huan*).
The initial instruction to rely on the Dharma and the subsequent instruction to rely on the person constitute the former teaching, which was "rely on the Dharma, not on the person.
The present teaching is to rely on the person and, furthermore, to rely on the Dharma.

Regarding the statement that "in the *Dilun* [school], the stage prior to the thirty minds is the rank of disciple," this intends to take the ten stages of faithful mind (*śraddhā-citta*) as the disciples.
That "the thirty minds are the rank of master" refers precisely to the first stage of reliance (*prathamāśraya*).
"From the first stage up to those who occupy the rank of teacher": from the first stage to Equal Enlightenment constitutes the fourth stage of reliance;
therefore, it is said "all.
