Regarding "continuing as humans and devas": those at the stage of semblance have not yet emerged from the triple world; for the time being, they remain among humans and devas.

Furthermore, when the sutra says "if they are in the three miserable destinies," this refers to those who have not yet destroyed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*).
Since one leaves the three miserable destinies upon reaching the stage of semblance, it is said here that they are "humans and devas."
The Sūtra says: "That which is spoken by the True Buddha is actually the response-body and transformation-body, not the True Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma.
This wondrous scripture is spoken without speaking; thus it is called the True Buddha.
Regarding "perfuming and averting [the obstacles to] wisdom born of reflection": because of internal perfuming, the wisdom born of reflection arises.
Regarding "anointing the eyes as a simile for wisdom born of cultivation": because the eyes are purified, the eye of wisdom is opened.
"Seeing" is analogous to the reader; "seeing" belongs to form (*rūpa*), and form is the written text.
"Smelling" is analogous to the reciter; because one can personally reach it, it is as if the recitation resides within the mind.
The commentary explains that "goat's horn" refers to the commonality of being subject to destruction.
Regarding the "essential path to bodhi," at the very outset of generating the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta), one must necessarily sever evil and thereby naturally give rise to goodness.
Those who act as eyes for future generations are those who establish the paths by which consciousness may extinguish evil and give rise to good.
For one who studies the Mahāyāna, even though they possess only the physical eye, it is said to be called the Buddha-eye and so forth.

"Ten each for the inverse and the direct" refers to the ten states of mind in both the inverse and direct orders. "Direct" means proceeding from the subtle to the coarse, from ignorance (*avidyā*) down to the icchantika.

"Inverse" means proceeding from the coarse to the subtle, from the icchantika up to ignorance. "Repentance" (*chan*) is named for cultivating what has come; "regret" (*hui*) is named for reforming evil.
Repentance is named for cultivating merit; regret is named for mending transgressions. This is explained in detail in the fourth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation).
This is a broad clarification.
Repentance and protection constitute its two periods: repentance pertains to the past, while protection pertains to the present.
As for the "limit of birth and death" being the past, it begins where there was no beginning; ignorance serves as that limit.

"Reaching the place where there is no reaching" refers to designating the end by means of that which has no end; this constitutes the stage of attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) from the first dwelling upward.
As the Sūtra says, "The nature of all Buddhas is such": they are all able to cause sentient beings to give rise to the bodhicitta. [This applies even to] those of no-faith (*icchantika*).
Lack of faith remains as before; however, giving gifts ultimately causes them to resolve their minds [toward awakening].
As for "not destroying one's retinue," this is entirely a cause for long life.
The Sūtra says, "It is like fire covered by ash": the ash of ignorance covers the present causes and effects of transcending the world. It does not...
This refers to seeing the future.

It clarifies that evil does not receive its retribution immediately, just as milk does not instantly become curd. Evil is discussed in terms of the future, while curd is discussed in terms of the present;
therefore, it is said that retribution is not immediate.

Regarding those who skillfully explain the stage of similarity in external transformation: it refers to how a Bodhisattva, at the initial stage, can cause a single sublime voice to pervade the trichiliocosm, such that all Buddhas turn toward them to preach the Dharma, and so forth.
"One who does not conceal the teaching" means that what they say accords with principle and their words correspond to their practice.
"A lotus growing in the mud" means that the mire of afflictions can give rise to the flower of wisdom.
The "asañja disease" refers to the foul leprosy.
The confession of present [faults] is due to their being directly perceived; the confession of past [faults] is due to their long duration.
Regarding "seeking principle as the permeation": since principle is internal, "dwelling" refers to the internal.
Regarding "this being the abode where transgressions reside": this clarifies that both the primary and secondary retributions are received, taking them as one's home.
"Compassion (maitrī-karuṇā) is the home of the sages," as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding "great compassion as the chamber" and so forth;
this refers to non-referential compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*), which is able to universally cover all sentient beings. "The robe must also be removed" means that one should always be liberated;
even if the teachings of permanence or impermanence arise, they likewise vanish, thereby manifesting the Middle Way and right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).

Regarding those who repeatedly fall ill: if one discusses permanence and impermanence, this applies to both the present and the past; however, if one discusses falling ill, it refers exclusively to the past.
Therefore, the preceding text treats them with eight methods.
The passage in the sutra beginning with "Having awakened from this" also expresses the meaning of the inconceivable response and transformation (*nenggan yingying*) of this very sutra.

Regarding the phrase in the sutra, "there is a great fruit of retribution": it refers to the attainment of the partial fruit of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), characterized by permanence and bliss, through the arousal of the bodhicitta;
thus, it is termed "great."
"First, 'relying on the teaching to produce understanding' means relying on the teaching of permanence to give rise to an understanding of the principle.
'The medicine and the illness differ' means that the Tathāgata, knowing the appropriate time, can employ medicines such as permanence and impermanence to treat illnesses such as impermanence;
therefore, it is said that he is 'skillfully proficient in understanding.'"
"Once the deluded mind is resolved" means that understanding arises from within delusion.
"Fulfilling the ten stages" refers to fulfillment because understanding has reached its ultimate limit.
"The two vehicles are like dry [wood]" means they have severed all pervasive delusions. "Ordinary beings are like moist [wood]" means they possess greed, anger, craving, and views.
The drum smeared with lacquer is a metaphor for the former teacher. The teaching can express the principle, and the principle can destroy evil; thus it is called "death.

When one encounters the time and hears [the teaching], the capacity of the listener and the stimulus of the teaching meet like a magnet attracting iron; hence it is said that there is no intentional desire to hear.
The former teaching was like that of the night because [the practitioners] had not yet shattered ignorance and had not yet seen the Buddha-nature.

As for being able to untie the bonds of others: in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it is stated that there is no such possibility as one who is themselves bound being able to untie the bonds of others;
therefore, one must first untie them oneself and so forth.

Regarding "the former refers to the stage of cause": if one discusses it from the time the name 'arousing the mind' (bodhicitta) first arose, or from the stage of 'liberation from bondage and the true aspect' (mucimukti-bhūmi) upwards, this is the stage of the true cause.

It is designated as such because [the Buddha] acts as the Great Shipmaster at the ultimate stage, and because he embodies both the self-practice of cause and effect and the capacity for transforming others through skillful means.
The aforementioned "the power of the Dharmakāya Sugata" refers precisely to the hidden response (*mingying*).

That sentient beings are able to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment is likewise a hidden capacity and a hidden response, as extensively detailed in the sixteen phrases of the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), and so forth.

Now, regarding this "responsive body" (nirmāṇakāya) and "responsive power": it is because sentient beings possess the capacity to evoke the Tathāgata, who manifests from the realm of the *dharmakāya*.
As the Sūtra says, "those who give rise to pure faith obtain the wind of the teaching of nirvāṇa. Here, "wind" is synonymous with faith, and the "king" is the teaching itself.
"Lord, one who possesses faith can cross the great ocean.

Regarding the phrase "should come to each place," he comes to extinguish evil and manifests the bodies of the nine realms; he departs to give benefit to sentient beings by generating goodness within them.
Yet, the essence of the Tathāgata truly has no coming or going; therefore, it is said to be eternally abiding.

Regarding the statement that "the flowers and fruits, whether long or short, all follow the will of the devas": this refers to the different manifestations of the three grades of superiority and inferiority according to the capacities of those who perceive them.
As for the point that "one essence is mostly discussed in terms of the person of fruition" (*phala-pudgala*): this is explained from the perspective of the ultimate *dharmakāya*.

Since fruition must arise from a cause—just as the "Original Practice of the Bodhisattva Path" described in the *Nidāna-parivarta* of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes its cause—it is said to be "mostly" so.
The Sangha consists of those who rely on others, for they practice in dependence upon the Buddha.
As for the "four non-eternals," these are simply the four [marks] of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

Regarding the fact that a single instance of impermanence encompasses four meanings: these refer to permanence, impermanence, both permanence and impermanence, and neither permanence nor impermanence;
they are also the meanings of the four gates of emptiness.
The phrase "the meaning of which is set forth below" refers to the intent of the Four Teachings (*catvāra upadeśāḥ*).

That which accords with the *Fourfold Meaning of the Teachings* is as follows: the Buddha’s teaching on arising and ceasing is the Tripitaka Teaching (*piṭaka-vinaya-śāsana*); that which is non-arising and non-ceasing is the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-upadeśa*);

and that which is both arising and non-ceasing is the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-upadeśa*). Within the Distinct Teaching, there is still arising and ceasing prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), while from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) onward, there is no arising.
"Extinction" refers to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), which is neither arising-and-extinguishing nor non-arising-and-non-extinguishing.
Regarding the three "swords" and four "pāramitās," there are different ancient translations; there are three names with one reality, where the first two names and the latter two names differ.
First, regarding the explanation of the majesty and virtue of the sutra, namely the decline of the Dharma: it is because of the decline of the Saṃgha that the Dharma comes to decline;
for the Dharma is propagated by means of people.
To obtain excellent disciples—those who are like younger brothers or sons, who transmit the Tathāgata’s teachings as the Buddha himself practiced them—is what is meant by [the term].
"Excellent.
As for 'it amounts to eight *hu* and one *dou*': one *hu* is one *shi*, so this means eight *shi* and one *dou*. This is because it has been increased four times."
Regarding the seven phrases of the combined parables: the cowherd woman adding water four times constitutes four parables; the fifth parable represents the student who receives the teaching;

the sixth parable represents the one who propagates the sutra; and the seventh parable represents the person who hears the Dharma, who is even superior to those of the Hinayana, and is thus said to be "a thousandfold" better.
Regarding the subsequent analogy of the person who propagates the Dharma and the analogy of the cowherd woman who propagates the sutra, what is the distinction between them? Answer:
The analogy of the cowherd woman illustrates adding to the translation, while the analogy of the propagator of the Dharma illustrates seeking profit.
The wife is likened to the constant realm because the realm is able to give rise to understanding.
The other forms of knowledge and views are likened to guests; that which is beyond the single reality is termed "the provisional."
Regarding the "efficacy of skillful means," this is spoken for those bound as ordinary beings.

As for the "intelligent one who can apply it through the conjunction of conditions," the object of application refers to the Buddha, who speaks only of the Truth. "Milk" refers to that which can be applied according to the capacity of the recipient.
The two truths are not the same.

Regarding the phrase "adhering to the latter" in the Sūtra, the character *zhu* (pronounced *zhù* with the second tone) means "place," according to Zheng Xuan; in the *Guǎngyá*, it means "to supplement."
The reading "yìlì" (亦立) is also recorded with the phonetic transcription "zhīlüèfǎn" (知略反), which is not used in the present [text].
Regarding the "four propositions": first, a man who does not know that Buddha-nature is precisely womanhood;
second, one who knows that Buddha-nature is precisely the Great Man (puruṣa); third, a woman who, if she knows that Buddha-nature is precisely manhood; fourth...
Not knowing the Buddha-nature is what is called being a woman. In the sutras, men and women each obtain but a single phrase.
When the sutra says, "I do not conform to worldly dharmas," these worldly dharmas are in fact the supramundane dharma of nirvana.

Regarding "disappearance": in the final dharma age (*mofa*), as the [teachings] gradually diminish, false views increasingly proliferate, and the Buddha-dharma is on the verge of extinction; hence it is called "disappearance.

"Vehicles being like the absence of nature, etc.
means that while there are distinctions among the three vehicles, the one vehicle is itself without distinction.
"Already identical with principle" means that this present distinction is itself without distinction; it is identical with the principle of the one vehicle.
Those of middling faculties who attain awakening through the "Questions of Kāśyapa" are those who attain awakening within the thirty-four questions mentioned in the preceding text.

As for Mañjuśrī further raising doubts, it is as the sutra says, "there is still a mind of doubt," and so forth. In the preceding text, the Tathāgata has already completed his explanation of the eternal body and the Dharma-body;
now, because the doubts are raised once more, it is said that "there is still [doubt]."
The Sūtra states that there is "no distinction whatsoever between the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

This means that it is difficult to conceive how the Tathāgata, who has now attained permanence, could be the same as the world, which is entirely impermanent; what difference would there be between this [Tathāgata] and the three vehicles, which are likewise impermanent?
Regarding the scriptural statement that "there is both difference and no difference," the Buddha’s intended meaning is as follows: that which was impermanent in the past constitutes difference;
that which is heard as permanent today constitutes non-difference. Difference is itself non-difference, and non-difference is itself difference. It is neither difference nor non-difference.
It is impossible for there to be dharmas existing throughout the three periods of time. If there were difference, then dharmas would exist throughout the three periods of time.
This is impossible.
That this single verse appears four times is because it constitutes the ultimate core of this sutra and the final destination of its exegesis.
Since antiquity, it has been known as the "Four Pillars of Nirvana. If even one of them were incorrect, the chamber of Nirvana would collapse. This verse originally existed... [now].

Regarding "that which is neither originally existent nor presently existent": this simply means that which was originally existent is presently existent, and that which was originally non-existent is presently non-existent. What does it mean for something to be "originally existent and presently non-existent"?

It refers to the case where afflictions were originally present but are now absent, and nirvāṇa was originally absent but is now present. If one claims there is a discrepancy in the dharmas existing across the three periods of time, such a position is untenable.
If there is no discrepancy, yet there is a discrepancy, then such a position is tenable; this is precisely what constitutes differentiation. Thus, cause and effect are not [merely] causes.
They are not the fruit; all cases are to be understood by this analogy.

Furthermore, for those with the three grades of faculties: those with superior faculties [attain] this grade; those with middling faculties [attain] the next two lower grades; and those with inferior faculties [attain] up to the fourth grade.
As for "now non-existent," it means that because it is eternal now, there is no impermanence.
As for "now existent," it refers to the existence of the eternal *vajra*-like final mind.
That which Cunda doubted was not related to the meaning of the verse; rather, it was to refute the notion of past eternity and to demonstrate that one attains eternity now—eternity.

This is precisely impermanence. It is exactly at this point that the doubt arises. The intent of the verse fundamentally clarifies the opening toward permanence. "Originally impermanent" (the first half-verse) refers to what originally existed;

"now there is no impermanence, which is permanence" (the second half-verse) refers to what was originally non-existent but now exists. That these differences are in fact no difference is precisely in accord with the intent of the verse.
Furthermore, the statement that "the first half is no different from the former" is explained as before, following the previous commentary on the *Vajracitta* (Diamond Mind).
As for the remark that "people of the Three Vehicles enter together," this reflects the intent of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).

Regarding the statement by the followers of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that "the eternal is not something newly acquired," etc.: this refers to their reckoning that the *ālayavijñāna* possesses a pure and translucent consciousness;
this consciousness contains and stores all phenomena (*dharma*).
"Furthermore, that which is manifested and then returns to concealment is identical to Mañjuśrī; the intent of the objection is that after attaining permanence, it once again becomes impermanent.
Furthermore, that which remains concealed and does not manifest is because impermanence and permanence do not coincide; thus, it is still subsumed within the three periods of time."
Regarding the phrase "the Tripiṭaka Master says," this refers to the commentary of Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
The expression "is the same as what the local people [already] had" means that what was previously hidden is now made manifest, being identical to what was already present.
Regarding "delusion ceases and the Way remains": afflictions have a beginning, which is termed the cessation of delusion; Nirvana has no end, which is termed the persistence of the Way.
As for "formerly one became three, and now these three are but one": the three are the three of this single family, within the One Buddha.
The threefold classification is explained according to the vehicle, like fingers spread apart by a stick.
When they are one, it is as when the fingers are grasped to form a fist.
That which is "now non-existent" is the "now" of that former time.
Thus, that which was originally non-existent but now exists is the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) of today.
That which is present and yet past is that which existed originally but is now non-existent.
That which is present and yet future is that which was originally non-existent but now exists.
Regarding the statement "as for the ultimate discussion of Buddha-nature," it refers to the current version [of the text]. It is impossible for dharmas to exist across the three periods of time;
this serves to explain the first half [of the verse], and is thus called the "current version."
Regarding "the impermanent is permanent": impermanence is itself permanence, and permanence is itself impermanence; [it is] neither permanent nor impermanent, and so forth.
That there could be dharmas existing throughout the three periods of time is impossible.

Furthermore, as for the statement that "original existence is simply existence," this means that original existence is simply present existence; why? Because where there is difference, there is no difference.

As for the statement that "present non-existence is simply non-existence," this means that present non-existence is simply original non-existence; why? Because the present absence of the Three Vehicles is precisely the original absence of the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "originally it was not existent and now it is not non-existent," "not existent" does not mean existence, and "not non-existent" does not mean non-existence.
There is none. For it is impossible for dharmas to exist throughout the three periods of time [without being interconnected].

Thus, as they revolve and turn, they cannot be separated from one another; this is because each and every phrase is based upon the Three Truths, wherein the single truth is all-pervasive and penetrating, such that their differences are mutually identical.
Regarding the phrase "that which is impermanent is itself eternal," this has already been answered above; Mañjuśrī repeats it here, hence the words "it is also.
As for the metaphor "clouds dissipating and ice melting," the interpretation of our school differs from that of others; it is like ten thousand li of vast ice that cannot [otherwise] pass.
On a day of constant spring, things naturally melt away;
the same is true for the awakening of wisdom. This simply means that object and wisdom are non-dual: one wisdom is three wisdoms, and three wisdoms are one wisdom.
This is what is called awakening.

To say that it both exists and does not exist is the teaching for humans: it means that there both exists the excellence of the deeds of the Two Vehicles performed in the past, and there does not exist the excellence of the principle of the Bodhisattvas realized today.
The statement that "dharmas exist throughout the three periods of time" up to "the ultimate truth" means they are neither existent nor non-existent; this reveals the Middle Way.
Now, this single *siddhānta* (teaching) fully possesses the four *siddhāntas*; such a perfect explanation is sovereign.
Within a single phrase, there is the worldly sense capable of producing goodness, destroying evil, and entering into principle; the remaining three *siddhāntas* follow this same pattern.

Regarding "the original existence is the phrase of existence and the gate of existence": the phrase of existence refers to the Dharma, while the gate of existence refers to the teaching. The same applies to non-existence and so forth.

As for the statement that there is still a distinction between Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas: they are called "distinct" because they have not yet awakened to the One Vehicle; now that they have awakened to the One Vehicle, there is no distinction.
Regarding the first three phrases, which state that what is negated is neither the nature of existence nor the nature of non-existence:

the intended meaning is that "what originally existed now no longer exists" does not negate existence itself, and "what originally did not exist now exists" does not negate non-existence. This is precisely the state of being neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, it is called a "conclusion.
As for the phrase "this existence can be made non-existent," it refers to making the existence of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) non-existent.
"That which cannot be made to exist" refers to the wondrous existence of nirvana.
"That this existence is not existence, and thus is not [mere] existence," means that it does not render the existence of the former Three Vehicles into non-existence.
Regarding the statement "this non-existence is not non-existent, therefore it is not non-existent": today there is no longer the non-existence of the three vehicles, nor the existence of nirvāṇa.
That which is thus "not of the present" refers to the root of afflictions from the past; it is not the root of the present nirvāṇa.

That which is the "present without a fundamental basis" is as follows: what was formerly the fundamental basis for the household of afflictions (*kleśa*) is precisely the fundamental basis for the homelessness of *nirvāṇa* today.
This present is not the fundamental basis; it is the "present without a fundamental basis. This present is the present-day *nirvāṇa* of homelessness.
This present [state] is not the same as the present state of those who formerly possessed a household.
The Sūtra says, "To benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
If all sentient beings are able to hear this teaching of non-differentiation, it can cause all sentient beings to attain nirvāṇa; therefore, it is called "peace and happiness" (an-lo).
The phrase "immediately becoming startled and astonished" is like a guardian who, having once given rise to doubt, is able to know the color of the milk because of his faith.
The karmic retribution of sentient beings is precisely the retribution of the same true cause, which causes the milk to be of a single color.

As for the statement in the Sūtra, "because they equally exhaust outflows," this means that both [the Bodhisattvas and the Śrāvakas] equally attain the outflow-free Nirvāṇa of the rational nature (*dharmatā*).

As for the question, "When did they ever enter [enlightenment]? it is because the Two Vehicles have realized the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding and unchanging nature; therefore, it is said that they have not entered [the ultimate state].
Since they truly share the same single nirvana as the Tathāgata, how could there be anyone who, having advanced three hundred paces on the path, fails to reach the place of treasure?
It is only for those who are indolent that two nirvanas are taught.
The Sūtra states that "Nirvāṇa is called a 'wholesome existence' (kuśalabhava). This refers to the nature of original existence, which is designated as "wholesome.
The Nirvāṇa of the two vehicles is not called a "wholesome existence."
Yet in reality this is not so; for it was not the case that before the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he caused those of the two vehicles to enter parinirvāṇa.
The statement in the *Prajñāpāramitā* that "I shall cause all to enter nirvana without remainder" refers precisely to this meaning.
Regarding the dual reception of the two meanings: in the past, the three vehicles were termed "differences.
Now, in the teaching of the One Vehicle, difference is itself non-difference, as they are identical in the single Buddha-nature; hence it is called "dual reception."
The Sūtra asks: "What are the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all sentient beings? Nature refers to the internal; characteristics refer to the external.
When these are grasped, one can distinguish the nature of sentient beings from the nature of the Three Vehicles. As for their characteristics, are they the same or different?
They establish distinctions within that which is without distinction. The answer is: their nature is the same, but their characteristics are different, due to their admixture.
This is because of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

As for the scriptural statement that [the body] "cannot be cut or destroyed," this is explained as in the previous passage regarding the protection of the True Dharma and the observance of the precept against killing;
the attainment of the fruit of longevity and the adamantine body (*vajra-kāya*) is precisely its meaning.

"Those whose mouths become insipid are those born blind; they cannot perceive flavors, just as those who do not see colors [cannot perceive them]. This is because the Three Jewels pertain to form (*rūpa*).
Those who do not recognize their hands and feet do not recognize the three realities within the single body."
Regarding the seventeenth chapter, "The Questions of the Great Assembly":

that which constitutes the object of the questions posed by the great assembly refers to each member of the assembly taking the transformation Buddha who received their offerings as their respective object.
Regarding the intent of this chapter: according to Master Guan’s interpretation, the title "The Questions of the Great Assembly" refers simply to Kāśyapa’s inquiry.
As for the manifestation of the characteristics of *nirvāṇa* shown here, the Buddha employs the emission of light to urge the offering as a symbolic expression of that state.
The answer that clarifies the question refers to the questions posed by the great assembly and the Tathāgata’s response thereto;

furthermore, the question concerning those who are close to the Unsurpassed Way refers to the "transcendent answer," as this passage follows after the section on those with no further [remaining] questions.
Regarding the three instances where humans and devas obstructed [the offering]: this refers to the refusal to allow Cunda alone to receive the offering.
As for what the sutra says—that "various vessels were filled and complete"—how could Cunda’s eight *sheng* of polished rice have been sufficient to do so?
It was entirely through the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata that they were said to be "complete."
The Sūtra says, "The devas of great majesty" refers to the devas of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The Sūtra says, "Cease now, Cunda; do not let him offer [the meal]" refers to these very devas. This means that they thought the Buddha would accept Cunda’s offering alone and then enter *nirvāṇa*, rather than accepting the offerings of humans and devas.
They did not know that the Tathāgata was specifically receiving Cunda’s offering for this very purpose.
Both humans and devas owe this entirely to Cunda.
As for the scripture’s statement that it is "just like the Western Land of Peace and Bliss," it means that the Tathāgata, by lending his majestic power,
causes that land to be pure.

The scripture states, "At that time, the bhikṣus," which refers to the assembly that does not receive offerings; because they are all able to produce wholesome roots in sentient beings, they receive the offerings of humans and devas.
The scripture further states, "The food they consume is also without distinction," meaning it is neither coarse nor non-coarse, and neither subtle nor non-subtle.
All of this is the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata.
As the Sūtra says, "The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus": when the capacity [of beings] arises, it manifests; when the capacity declines, it withdraws. All of this is for your sake.
There is no need for sorrow.

As for those who have already passed through immeasurable kalpas, it is as stated in the "Life Span" chapter of the Lotus Sūtra: [the Buddha] constantly dwells on Vulture Peak and in other various abodes.
As for the scripture’s statement that "all shall attain peace and happiness": because I have long since realized nirvana, I now cause you, the great assembly, to all likewise attain nirvana;
therefore, it is called "peace and happiness."
Regarding these two birds being able to dwell together: this refers to matters that are inherently contradictory, yet are made to appear harmonious, such as "I shall enter nirvāṇa.

Now, since they are contradictory, how could they allow me to enter nirvāṇa? Therefore, all of these are provisional designations; they are provisionally established so that they may accord with the Tathāgata.
Yet, even while not entering nirvāṇa, he regards all sentient beings just as he does Rāhula and others—thus are the various pairs discussed below.
[The Buddha] said: "For example, the Tathāgata does not truly enter nirvāṇa. Why, then, do you request that the Tathāgata not enter nirvāṇa?

As for the statement 'the Dharma is identical to the person,' this refers simply to the true reality in which the person and the Dharma are one body, fully endowed with the three truths within the center."

This is the truth (*satya*). It must not be understood through the perspective of partial truth (*pratisaṃvid-satya*). This is explained at length in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) within the exposition on the sevenfold two truths (*dvisatya*).
Those who violate and harm the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)—with the exception of the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*)—those of the preceding three teachings are still termed *caṇḍālas*. If one...

One who has perfected the Bodhicitta is called an Arhat. Why? Because the person who is on the path to Arhatship is identical to the one who has perfected it, for the latter will certainly be attained later.
As the Sūtra says, "A single speck of dust is a Buddha"—these are all provisional expressions. If Cunda were to crush his rice into dust-like particles as an offering...
Even the Buddha cannot encompass it all. Why? Because the mind’s comprehension is entirely through the majestic assistance of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, which causes these matters to manifest.
As for the "exposition of secret questions," this refers to that which is obscured by concealment; it is not the secret of the Mahāyāna. This is because...
Because it conceals the remainder within the remainderless, it is called "esoteric" (*mi*).
It is not a level path that reveals the principle; rather, its winding expressions that adapt to the capacities of beings while concealing the ultimate principle are termed "esoteric."
The sūtra states, "all sūtras," which refers comprehensively to both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna; all are termed "sūtras" (契經).
The "small" refers to those with remainder (sa-upadhiśeṣa), while the "great" refers to those without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa); hence, it says "all."

Regarding the phrase "attaining proximity to the Unsurpassed Way while simultaneously answering two questions," this refers to the final question. Now, following the sequence of the text, it is answered by skipping ahead;
hence, it is said to be "simultaneous" (兼).

Regarding the meaning of the three interpretations of "taking the intent" (*yì*): although these individuals are transgressors, there is a sense in which they possess qualities worth adopting; thus, it is called "intent.
As for how breaking the precepts and stinginess can be praised: "breaking" refers to the three types of sick persons, while "stinginess" refers to those who uphold the precepts.

The scripture states that those who have broken the precepts are "those who have attained penetration" (tong). These three types of sick persons are excluded because they are *icchantikas* who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment;
thus, they are distinguished by this qualification.
The Sūtra states, "Those who remain in other [categories]" refers to the three types of illness as they apply generally to the fourfold assembly and others.
As for the phrase "yet they are heading toward [it]," this takes up the aspect of verbal slander;
since your mind has not yet reached its limit, it represents the initial stage of an icchantika, which is why it is called "the path of heading toward."
The scripture states that there is no Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha; this refers to the denial of cause and effect and the lack of faith in the Triple Gem.

Regarding the scriptural question, "What is the meaning of 'breaking the precepts'?", Cunda raises this inquiry because he observes those who break the precepts all claim to be heading toward the path of an icchantika. Therefore, he asks further.
Regarding the "six sublime medicines," one must rely on these six, as well as the ten minds of direct and reverse order, according to the *Vaipulya* repentance rituals.
Fifth, "penetrating the characteristics of offenses" means realizing that the nature of offenses has neither internal nor external existence;
emptiness itself is the repentance of non-arising, such as the practice of sitting upright and contemplating the true marks of reality. This is called the "Great Repentance."
The scripture states that those who can be rescued and delivered possess this meaning: it is the eternally abiding Buddha-nature.
The scripture further states, "It is like the rising of the sun," which refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*’s description of its ability to shatter the darkness of ignorance.

Regarding the statement that "generating the aspiration for enlightenment and reaching an understanding of offenses can likewise be brought into accord with this": first, because one has not yet discarded the Dharma robes, one is able to generate the aspiration;

and because one still understands the characteristics of offenses, one is able to receive, uphold, recite, and chant [the scriptures]. This is also the same as the practice of contemplating the mind while reciting the sutras.
"One should be complete as before" means that it is like the six kinds of intentions for extinguishing transgressions mentioned previously.
Regarding "citing what is right and citing what is wrong," the text itself contrasts making offerings and obtaining merit as being "right," and obtaining no merit as being "wrong."

The woman is a metaphor for a bodhisattva of shallow practice; this refers to those who, through the initial mind of the three preceding teachings, are able to give rise to perfect understanding (yuanjie), and are thus called "women.
"Traveling far to another land" means that birth-and-death (saṃsāra) is one's own country, while nirvāṇa is the other land.
"The celestial temple is like this sutra" means that by relying on this teaching of perfect understanding and eternal abiding, one realizes the principle of innate nature (*t'ien-jan*).

Regarding the phrase "the various views of annihilationism and eternalism are like the Ganges," this wording is still incomplete; it should rather state that "the Ganges is like annihilationism, eternalism, and so forth."
Regarding those whose nature is inherently corrupt and evil: they give rise to thoughts of breaking the precepts and are unable to produce understanding; this is called "inherent nature.
Regarding those who obtain the fruit of retribution and are born in heaven: they obtain a partial fruit and are born in the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "You should not now speak in such a manner," there are two intended meanings.
First, since I have already excluded the icchantikas in various places, why should I need to ask again whether those who can resolve their minds and repent will still attain the fruit?
[The answer is that] giving to such persons does not yield merit, because they are certain never to repent.

That an icchantika can become a Buddha is also called slandering the Buddha. First, because the sutras do not state it; second, because I have excluded them [from the category of those who can attain Buddhahood];
third, because they are icchantikas. Therefore, it is said that this constitutes slander.
To claim that one does not become a Buddha is also called slandering the Buddha; this refers to the Buddha’s teaching that icchantikas possess buddha-nature.

As for the scripture’s statement that "all [beings] are [endowed with it] to a small degree," this is an incomplete (sāvaśeṣa) teaching. It was spoken in relation to non-Buddhists and is not yet a complete (niravaśeṣa) exposition.
Regarding "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Vaipulya): "Vaipu" refers to the Dharma; "lya" means extensive.
Because the Dharma is extensive, that which is the convergence of all dharmas is the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the "ninety-five types": are the first ninety-three both name and substance [of heterodox views], while the latter two—the Vātsīputrīya, Abhidharma, Sūtra, and so forth—are the correct substance?
As for the "ninety-six" in the *Avataṃsaka*, this is because the Great [Vehicle] looks toward the Small;
it generally includes the Two Vehicles, yet also excludes them as being heterodox. Therefore, it says "ninety-six."

Regarding the statement that "greed is like a mother to the subsidiary afflictions": because it acts as the root and stem, it is able to produce and nourish them; therefore, they are said to be "co-existent" (*sahabhū*).

As for the phrase "except for those that assist the Path, this is the meaning of 'without remainder'" (*anavaśeṣa*): this means that both "with remainder" (*sāvaśeṣa*) and "without remainder" exist at every stage (*parvan*), and furthermore—
"Without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*) is the ultimate simplification that distinguishes it from "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*).

Regarding the attainment of the fruit of the ten thousand practices through the cultivation of the causes of the ten thousand practices, one must further distinguish this according to the teachings and explain it as a definitive truth.
That there is no dharma that is not exhausted means that the perfect dharma (*pariniṣpanna-dharma*) is the truth.

That it is neither cause nor fruit is the statement of the correct principle. The present intention is not so; within both the Great and Small [Vehicles], there are both the "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and the "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
Furthermore, the inquiry regarding merit is divided into two parts according to the text: first the question, then the answer. Regarding the first line, which indicates the request:
the first half and the second half constitute the request.

As the Sūtra says, "He paused for a short while. When the devas and humans saw the Buddha accept their offerings, they did not dare to request that he remain in the world for a long time; hence [the text].
This means "minor.
Regarding the two lines explaining the request for the two who have left the household life to be cited, etc.: Ānanda and Kāśyapa are the transmitters of the Dharma;
as these two possess great merit, they requested the Buddha to remain. King Ajātaśatru is a sovereign king; therefore, he too had to request his remaining.
Regarding the citation from the six-fascicle *Contemplation of the Tathāgata’s Two Feet* which states that one knows for oneself whether [the body] is permanent or impermanent:
this indicates that Kāśyapa was able to comprehend the meaning of permanence and impermanence; Ānanda is mentioned as well because both individuals were capable of such comprehension.
Regarding those who produced the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is fully detailed in the *Zhiguan ji* (Commentary on Stopping and Contemplation).
As for the scripture’s statement that one should "make offerings with various things," this refers to repaying the kindness of hearing the Dharma and symbolizes the transition from cause to fruit.
The scripture states that "receiving a prediction" (vyākaraṇa) refers to a general prediction, without specifying the duration of the kalpa or the land, the proximity of the time,
or the name of the Buddha.
The scripture states that "such True Dharma" is the eternal Buddha-nature, the secret treasury of the single essence.

Regarding the present occasion when the Buddha acts for the sake of Subhadra: since his spiritual capacity (*indriya*) is not yet mature, he further explains the meaning of the five practices, the ten virtues, and the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) to bring him to maturity;
only then does he employ the methods of subduing and gathering (*saṃgraha-vinaya*) according to the nature of good and evil.
Private Notes on the Tiantai Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Six (Part Two, End).
