Private Notes on the Tiantai Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Seven (Third Edition).
Compiled by the Tiantai śramaṇa Xingman.
Commentary on the Eighteenth Chapter, "Manifesting Illness," Part Two of the Second Cycle.
Regarding the "Second Cycle": taking the preceding section from the conclusion of the questions and answers as the first cycle, this now constitutes the second.
Regarding the latter part of Emperor Wu of Liang’s [objections], the excessive rambling of the monk Shi has been refuted as before.

As for the opening response concerning being "free from all ailments," since the previous questions have already been answered, it is shown that the Tathāgata has long been free from the causes of illness;
he manifests this illness now only for the sake of sentient beings.
"What prevents further explanation? means that although three types of sick children were previously mentioned, what prevents them from being explained again now?
This serves as a response to the preceding text.
"Looking toward the future as the primary" refers to birth within the five elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*).
Regarding "the first stage of illness and so forth up to the fifth, the infant," the noble Brahmā is the cause and celestial conduct is the fruit. [The remainder of the text concerning illness...]
As for the statement that "civilization is free from illness," it is as explained in the following passage concerning the threefold inference regarding the Tathāgata;
there, having departed from the causes of illness, he extensively expounds upon the characteristics of being free from illness through his preaching of the Dharma.
"Eliminating all sufferings at once" means that there is no mention of the cause of illness in the text.

As for the specific mention of "four parts," these belong to the afflictions of discursive thought (*vitarka*). If they are associated with sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*) are likewise included within this category.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "He taught Mahākāśyapa, the Elephant King among Men," and so forth: this was requested by the youth Kāśyapa;
thus, he is designated by his honorific title "Mahā" (Great) to distinguish him. This Kāśyapa and his peers have already received their predictions of enlightenment in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Alternatively, it may serve as a subsequent indication that these Śrāvakas had not yet entered the Mahāyāna, and thus it was appropriate for them to request [the teaching] through skillful means. Or, it may be based on the names used in the past.

This also embodies the fourfold intent (*catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu*): first, the diversity of disciples corresponds to the worldly intent; second, the invitation to the Mahāyāna corresponds to the ultimate intent;

third, the non-retrogression of the three teachings and the perfection of the production of wholesome roots correspond to the purposeful intent; and fourth, the subduing of evil persons corresponds to the remedial intent.

The single pride (*māna*) is divided into two: the single [pride] is simply *māna*, which is further divided into the lesser and the middling—the two types of pride consisting of the superior and the middling. Regarding the "pride of pride" (*mānātimāna*):
it is to consider oneself equal to those who are superior, and to consider oneself superior to those who are one's equals.
Regarding "the equal-middle, the superior-superior, and the middle-superior": this means that the equal-middle refers to the superior, and the superior-middle refers to the equal.
As for the cause of attachment to "mine," it is pride resulting from attachment to the self.
Regarding the statement that karma leading to the four destinies definitively obstructs the first fruit (*phala*), this is a definitive explanation made from the perspective of the Hīnayāna.
From the perspective of the Mahāyāna, however, such karma does not obstruct bodhi.
Regarding "explaining the cause within the fruit": these grave evils are all produced by karma; therefore, it is said that the cause is explained.
Regarding "all are the fruits of prior karma": because one performed actions in previous lives, this present karma returns to repay the future fruit, which is termed "retribution" (*vipāka*).
For example, having habitually practiced excessive desire in the past, one now experiences the body of a sparrow and so forth—this is precisely what constitutes retribution.
Regarding the statement that "the prose is brief first and the verse is detailed later," this is because the brevity and detail correspond within the text.
The verses are divided into three sections—namely, the formal request, the explanation, and the conclusion—and are therefore termed "detailed."

Generally, when the name Gautama is used, there is a distinction to be made. For instance, as stated in the Vinaya, the "Lesser Gautama" (Kṣudra-Gautama) refers to the "burnt seed" of cow-dung sugarcane;
this is the same as how he is addressed by non-Buddhists. This [name] is derived from the original clan of the Great Gautama (Mahā-Gautama).
Therefore, this is not pride.
As the Sūtra says: "Only the various Bodhisattvas, and even those skilled archers... The intended meaning is as follows:
Mañjuśrī and the other great Bodhisattvas had already heard [the teaching on] permanence previously; however, because there were later Śrāvakas of dull faculties, they requested it again.
That light issuing from the body manifests the Dharma-body; this means arising from the True [Dharmakāya] to manifest the Responsive [Nirmāṇakāya].
The manifestation of the lotus flower symbolizes the cause, and the manifestation of the transformation Buddha symbolizes the fruit. From cause to fruit, all is for the sake of sentient beings;
thus it is said that "the flower can contain the fruit," and so forth. How could it be that the Tathāgata has an illness that enables him to manifest such a thing?
Regarding "the body being perfumed by great compassion": because compassion can extract suffering, it is called the "body"; because loving-kindness can bestow happiness, it is called the "mind.

As for the transformation Buddhas who benefit beings within each flower, their physical and environmental bodies (the *niṣyanda* and *adhiṣṭhāna-kāya*) vary in various ways in terms of size and characteristics.
The Sūtra states: "All sentient beings who pass through this light shall obtain both hidden and manifest benefits.
The Sūtra further states: "At that time, all devas, nāgas, and so forth... [and] "those who merely use flowers and incense for offering.
This indicates that after midday, it is unnecessary to present food; therefore, one uses only flowers and incense. Thus, it is said: "First offer, then request."
The Sūtra says: "How can you suddenly abandon your original vow? This is because the Tathāgata has long practiced his great vows;
why, then, do you now abandon us and enter into nirvāṇa? Thus they entreat him.

The examples of the worldly devas (*laukika-deva*), the celestial-born devas (*jāti-deva*), the pure devas (*śuddha-deva*), and so forth up to the devas of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-deva*) are given because they differ according to their respective teachings.
As for the phrase "all heterodox winds" in the sutra, it means that one is not shaken by the various heterodox views of either the internal or external extremes.
To be free from external adverse conditions refers to various māras and non-Buddhists;
internal adverse causes refer to the eight winds, both strong and weak.
To attain internal virtuous causes refers to subtle and wondrous wisdom.
Regarding those with external favorable conditions: they have already made offerings in the past.
As for the twelve matters of esoteric terminology (*saṃdhābhāṣya*): "not ill" or "free from illness" is an esoteric term.
Among these, the three types of patients who differ from the previous three are those who cannot be cured; this is based on [the fact that] the former three... cannot be treated.
Regarding the phrase "because of generating the resolve": the first three types of sick persons refer to those who have generated the resolve.

This is the meaning of "giving" and "taking away. "Taking away" refers to the fact that they were previously unable to receive and uphold [the precepts] and so forth; "giving" refers to permitting them to act as instructors for the sake of admonishing and guiding others.
Regarding "those who have not yet been cured" and "those who have not yet opened," these refer to what later opens up as the five kinds of illnesses.
Regarding "those who have been cured" and the opening out of "fear up to the six matters," this refers to the person who is a Bodhisattva;
whether for their own practice or for transforming others, they encompass the remaining four [matters], and thus it is called the "six matters."
Writing this down constitutes five types of Dharma-preachers; together with the six matters mentioned previously, they total thirty.
Regarding the "intermediate" category, there are further five types of sick persons: those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) who dwell in a state that is neither cured nor incurable.
Regarding those added later: by including the four fruits, the pratyekabuddhas, and the previous thirty, there are thirty-five.
Adding further the three types of persons who are incurable, they constitute a total of thirty-eight kinds.
These practitioners who carry their "illnesses" include those of the four fruits and others whose ignorance has not yet been eliminated; this is what is termed "illness."

That "a Bodhisattva in the causal stage should also be understood by this analogy" means that even for a person of perfect capacity (*yuanren*) at the initial stage of the semblance-position (*xiwei*), it is termed a "sickness. One must interpret this as follows:

the eighty thousand [teachings] and so forth are all based on the provisional teachings (*quanjiao*), such as the hearing of the Dharma, faith, and so on, which are likened to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Chapter Nineteen: Explaining the Chapter on the Noble Practices.

Regarding the previously mentioned brief and extensive expositions on the fruit of *nirvāṇa*: the "brief" refers to the clarification of the five fruits of eternal abiding within the *Cunda-parivarta*.
The sections on "Decay and Sighing" and "Clarifying the Superiority" explain the fruits of the three types of cultivation, such as the new *īśvara* and others.

Subsequently, the thirty-four questions of Kāśyapa Bodhisattva provide a detailed response concerning the causes and conditions for longevity, culminating in the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly," which extensively clarifies the fruits.

Regarding the "Ten Virtues Assembling Merit to Encourage Practice through Causes," these all describe the resultant merits of the Tathāgata, such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*).
This is like the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which integrates the primary and secondary realms so harmoniously that one yearns for the fruit while practicing the causes.
What is meant by "inferior"? This refers to the primary position of our own school.
As for what was previously explained regarding the fruit of perfect culmination, all of that concerns the fruit of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature.
How could the fruit of perfection ever permanently follow upon gradual causes? Therefore, it is not accepted here.
One should not say it is "the practice of the Buddha," for the Buddha is the ultimate fruit.
One should not say it is "the cultivation of a bodhisattva," for a bodhisattva is one who is still on the path of cause.
Furthermore, the reason why the present refutation of the five practices is not a complete cause is that they are sequential and distinct causes;
the reason why the ten virtues are not the ultimate fruit is that they are fruits of partial realization.
The noble practice is that which opens the path of the dharma of emptiness. The dharma of the five practices is the path of ultimate emptiness.
Because the path is the cause, it is called the "dharma-path."
That which is the ultimate principle (*paramārtha*) is the realization of the principle of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

"Neither coming nor going" means that because coming lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is empty; and because there is nowhere to which one goes, this is the emptiness of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
This is the Tathāgata’s esoteric teaching: he speaks of "no illness" in response to illness. No illness is itself emptiness;
these five elements of the path are called emptiness. Why, then, do you say that the five elements are existent?
To now hear and know [this] is itself "having something to obtain.

To explain extensively the giving of the Great Parinirvāṇa means that, beginning from the *Cunda-sūtra* and continuing until the end when the great assembly receives the offerings, every instance of giving in response to questions throughout this interval is none other than the eternally abiding Buddha-nature; therefore, it is called "concluded" (*jing*).
Those who practice this method do so precisely by manifesting the sequential within the non-sequential; thus it is called a "method.
It is that which is practiced by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and because it is the practice of the sages, it is termed the "Noble Practice" (ārya-caryā).

Regarding the general designation "noble practice" (*ārya-caryā*), its specific meaning has not yet been clarified. The term "general" (*sāmānya*) encompasses [all], whereas the "specific" (*viśeṣa*) does not encompass the general.
"Noble" (*ārya*) refers to the general, while "practice" (*caryā*) possesses specific distinctions; therefore, we shall now further discuss the sequential and non-sequential aspects thereof.
"Those in the mundane world do not know the Truth" refers to the inconceivable mundane realm that emerges through the Ten Practices.
"The mundane world does not know the Middle Way" means that those prior to the [Ten] Grounds have not yet perfected the single practice as all practices, nor the all-encompassing wisdom.
Practice is that which is observed; wisdom is that which observes. Because wisdom accords with practice, it is called "all-encompassing."

"Brahmā means purity" refers to taking the ultimate limit of purity as the basis; being able to give rise to compassion and respond to the six realms of existence is why it is said that he "enters into existence.
This is not like ordinary dust; rather, he is like a lotus flower which, though situated in the mud, is not defiled by it.
"Existence" here refers to the twenty-five places of birth. This explains his functional capacity in terms of transforming others.
Regarding the establishment of names through the analogy of an infant’s walking: as in the subsequent passages, there are analogies such as the gradual infant, the wooden ox, and the yellow medicine;
the "perfect infant" refers to that which neither comes nor goes, and does not perform acts of great or small [magnitude], all of which are based upon metaphors.
Regarding the establishment of names based on that which is to be remedied: this refers to the one type of bodhisattva in relation to the five kinds of illnesses, such as non-deviation and deviation.

Regarding the establishment of names based on the person of perfect fulfillment: "The initial resolve and the ultimate end are not two; from the very beginning, one contemplates nirvana while practicing the path."

"Not abiding" refers to the practitioner. It is called "not abiding" with reference to the cause of practice; since, once cause and effect are fulfilled, one is subsequently able to transform others and lead them to practice, it is said that one causes others not to abide [in samsara].
Regarding the statement that "having the same illness as others is merely a secondary branch": the Tathāgata is free from illness and thus shares this state with sentient beings;
therefore, it is not the fundamental essence. Now, taking a single practice as the root and five practices as the branches—while the root is universal, the branches are distinct.
Regarding that which has nirvāṇa as its object: in terms of principle, one discusses cultivation; furthermore, one transforms others by means of this central principle.
Since this is fundamentally based on compassion, it is called the "Brahma-faring" (brahmacarya).

To advance spontaneously by means of principle is called the "Vehicle of the Celestial" (tianxing); this is the Vehicle of Realization (*zhengsheng*). Within this school, its name and meaning are also termed the "Vehicle of Practice" (*xingsheng*) and the "Vehicle of Teaching" (*jiaosheng*).
Upon attaining the principle of the First Abode (*dizhu*), one advances through that principle to the Second Abode; this is what is meant by "advancing."
"To abandon the root and follow the branches" means that rejecting others while taking up the practice of illness as the root actually turns it into a branch.
"One who can act out illness" is like saying one has an illness when there is no illness.

Regarding the sequence of the five practices from shallow to deep: among the noble practices (*ārya-caryā*), the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla-ārya-caryā*) occupies the first position and is thus established as shallow.
The practice of illness (*vyādhi-caryā*) refers to the functional application on the level of the Tathāgata’s fruition; therefore, it appropriately belongs at the end.
Regarding the discussion of "one practice" (*ekācāra*) and so forth: this refers to non-sequential practice, wherein one brings all five practices into a single practice.
Since we are speaking here from the beginning, it is said that "the practice of illness is complete within the five practices."

Regarding the distinction between the general and the specific: if one uses the specific to judge the general, the practice of devas is considered general because it accords with principle, while the other four are specific.
Conversely, if one uses the general to judge the specific, it is not that the five practices do not exist within the specific.
That it "cannot be taken as absolute" means that within each individual practice, both the general and the specific are fully present.
Regarding "the superior being able to bind the inferior": non-sequential practices can bind the five practices so that they all return to a single practice;
this is called "binding. To be able to open up a single practice such that it is precisely the five practices is called "scattering."

Regarding the inability of what is below to roll up or extend toward what is above: among the successive practices, the practice of precepts (*śīla*) occupies the first position; it cannot achieve mastery over the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

As for why three are taught and not two: the "two" refers to the two types of illness—the celestial and the human. If one takes the present illness as primary, it constitutes [the basis for this teaching].
It speaks of four [stages] rather than one. Now, following the sequence of the five elements, it says "speaks of three" only.

I privately maintain that "that which is within the *Saṃpuṣpita* (Flower Ornament)" refers to the *Avataṃsaka*, which extensively clarifies the stages of the initial practice and dwelling; therefore, he points to it for further investigation.

"Not exceeding a single principle" means that within the Universal Worthy Gate of that sutra, from the first stage upward, the causes and effects, the environments and beings, and their mutual interpenetration are all fused and realized as the natural principle.
Since this principle already encompasses all, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.
Regarding "the conduct of the devas" (*deva-caryā*): this is spoken in terms of progressing toward the true cause. It is called "conduct" (*caryā*) because conduct is itself the principle (*tattva*);
therefore, it is named "the conduct of the devas."
Those who practice for the sake of the heavens are so named because, from their initial aspiration, they fundamentally seek the Principle; thus, they are called "heavens.

As for "pointing distantly to the heavens," this refers to the fruit of initial awakening (shijue), which is termed "distant" in that sense. Furthermore, according to the gradual approach of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), it is also termed "distant" with respect to that which has not yet been realized.
Regarding the general and the specific: the "heavenly course" (*devatā-caryā*) is termed general, while the remaining four courses are specific.
Although these would naturally manifest after the Path, only three courses are mentioned; this is because the heavenly and illness courses are already self-evident.
Next, regarding "those who do not yet exist," this refers to the two types of Brahma-children. As for the principle of the object of focus, it means to cultivate with single-minded devotion.

Regarding "curing them so that they are healed and so forth," this precisely refers to the aforementioned five types of sick children; it is the exhortation to practice *nirvāṇa* when they have fallen into the states of illness.
Because the Tathāgata’s own practice is identical to that of others: the bodhisattva relies upon the perfect cause, which is the cause for the state of fruition; therefore, he is named "Tathāgata."
Regarding "the cause is itself the fruit": the Mahāyāna is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; the fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true reality of all phenomena;
thus, cause and fruit are non-dual. Regarding "not exhorting":
this is the practice of the Tathāgata, which differs from the practices of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*); therefore, there is no need for exhortation.
Answer: Although they take the same object, nirvāṇa, the practices established differ for two reasons: first, because one cultivates gradual practice with a mind directed toward nirvāṇa;
second, because through complete cultivation, the initial resolve and the ultimate goal are not distinct. Thus, there is a difference between the partial and the perfect.

Regarding the "double explanation of the five practices" (pañca-vṛtta): within the noble practices (ārya-caryā), after the explanation of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, each concludes with a summary of both sequential and non-sequential practices; therefore, it is called a "double explanation."

If one follows the Śrāvakas, they are like those who attend to the sick. In the *Mahā-śāstra*, the Tathāgata is the Great Physician, the scriptural teachings are the medicinal prescriptions, and the Śrāvakas are like the caregivers.

As for the statement "following the Śrāvakas," it may refer to cases where the Mahāyāna was added to the teachings of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, or to instances after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances assumed the form of Śrāvakas to expound the Mahāyāna.
This refers to those who are curable, for they encounter both persons and the Dharma in their entirety.
As the Sūtra says, regarding those who "engage in great strife," Māra is the one who provokes strife; therefore, it is called "strife. As for the Bodhisattva, in reality...
There is no dispute. Within the parables, [the offenses] proceed from the four grave transgressions (*catur-guru-dharma*); these are precisely the offenses of the five categories (*pañca-varga*).
In the Mahāyāna, the categories and clusters are not divided; they are simply explained in combination.
The Sūtra states, "I shall cause you to attain peace and enter Nirvāṇa. This refers to the pleasures of the five desires being called Nirvāṇa;
it is not the Tathāgata’s true Nirvāṇa.

Second, regarding the possession of both phenomena (vastu) and principle (li): "phenomena" refers to the precepts of phenomena (*vastu-śīla*). Because Mahāyāna precepts encompass both phenomena and relate to principle, they are called "phenomena and principle.

Regarding the preceding and subsequent retinues: *sthūlātyaya* constitutes the preliminary preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*), while the second category and the four lower categories generally constitute the retinue.
This refers to the subsequent skillful means.
"Guarding the mental ground" refers to impure meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*).

Regarding the "precept concomitant with the Path" (*mārga-sahagata-śīla*), the discourse on the Path states that those from the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) upward, who possess the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*), are able to be endowed with this precept.
Regarding "taking the heavy nature as the foundation": if this heavy nature is destroyed, the rest may not be complete.

The character for *gēng* (革*茸) in "patched robe" (*gēngyī*) is explained in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "patching. According to the commentary, it refers to an ornament made of *mò* (wool). Alternatively, it is written as *sàn* (散-ㄆ+毛), which means the hanging wool fibers of *kūbèi* (cotton).

Regarding the character *jīng* (經) in [序-予+(這-言+(庚-(序-予))))]: the character *jīng* (經) is pronounced as *zǐyè* (姊葉反). According to the glosses of characters (*zìgù*), *jīng* is now written as *jiē* (接), meaning the "seed" (*zǐ*) of a tree.
The pronunciation *dì* (蒂) is not the intended meaning here.
The "City of the Eightfold Path" (Aṣṭāṅgamārgapura) is a game of strategy. In the western regions, for this military game, two players each employ twenty jade elephants.
In this land [of China], there are also painted boards used as the path.
Regarding the wish to be equal with others: in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is asked whether a bodhisattva should give to others the cause or the fruit.
If one gives the cause—the practice of a bodhisattva—then the essential [of that practice] would be deficient; if one gives the fruit, one's own practice would be fulfilled.

"Redirecting the fruit to others" means that for one who has reached the ultimate depth, the moment they first give rise to the mind of upholding the precepts and penetrate the depth of the true nature (*dharmatā*),

this is precisely the fulfillment of the ultimate perfection of benefiting oneself and others— the very depth of the other shore. "Fruits to be summoned as retribution" refers to the fruits to be experienced in future births.
Regarding "neither near nor far" now: "near" refers to the human and celestial realms; "far" refers to the ultimate partial realization of the first bhūmi.
"True understanding of the first bhūmi" refers to the wondrous understanding of *tathatā* (suchness).
"Those who realize the Way together" refers to those who equally attain the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding the third point, "according to the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*": this means that the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* correlates the ten *pāramitās* with the ten stages;
since the present subject is precept (*śīla*), it corresponds to the second stage.
"Entering into principle is called 'abiding'" refers to the practitioner following the gradual path realizing the principle of the True Truth (*satyadharma*).

"'Practice takes mastery as its meaning'" means that when emerging into the conventional world to transform sentient beings, one encounters various dharmic conditions; therefore, it is called "mastery."
The stage of fearlessness (*abhaya-bhūmi*) is the state of being free from the five fears.
The meaning of the text is not singular; it clarifies both the sequential and non-sequential [aspects].
Being eternal, it is immovable; that is, the essence of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is not moved by the two extremes.
Because it is blissful, one does not fall. The bliss of nirvāṇa does not lead to falling into the four realms of existence.
Therefore, I do not regress; because of this mastery, I am unlike those of the Lesser Vehicle who undergo regression.
"Pure and thus undispersed" means that one cannot be destroyed by the eight winds of the world.
Now, taking the ordinary perspective, worldly phenomena are naturally different from the Great Sūtra.
Regarding the "one who raises both the partial and the perfect," these refer to the Buddha and the Bodhisattva.

As for the character *xiǎo* (曉) in the phrase "the sūtra brain-expert" (*nǎo xiǎo*), according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is read as *gǔmù* (古木反), meaning the big toe; however, this is likely not what is intended here. According to the sense, it should be pronounced *jiě* (解, hù mài 反), meaning that the brain is "unraveled" or explained.
This is consistent with the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* (*Wúshàngyī jīng*), which explains the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata, specifically the second mark: the cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*).
This explains it.
Regarding the phrase "one who has not yet attained this stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*)," the text states that after performing this contemplation, one has therefore "not yet attained" it.
As for the reference here to the "sixteen special excellences" (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*) and so forth, it means they are mutually related and integrated within the entry [into the stages].
Since it is not fundamental, this contemplative wisdom is not cultivated by means of the tainted (*sāsrava*) minds of the four dhyānas;
rather, it is entirely untainted (*anāsrava*) and enters into the first stage (*bhūmi*) and beyond.
"Opening the storehouse of the body" is like opening a worldly granary to clearly see its contents, such as the five grains.
"Not giving rise to attachment to flavors" means this is not the same as the fundamental [afflictions].
This resembles the realization of the nine perceptions; it is called "resembling" because it excludes the three desires, and thus this passage remains somewhat mixed.
Regarding the statement that "enduring greed, desire, hunger, and thirst is the patience of dharmas," this refers to insentient objects.
Since mosquitoes, gadflies, and other such beings are sentient objects, it is called "patience toward living beings."
Second, regarding the explanation of perfect concentration (*pariniṣpanna-samādhi*): the very place where there is transgression is itself upholding.
Since one has attained mastery over both upholding and violating, one attains mastery within transgression by clearly perceiving upholding;
thus, precepts are concentration, and transgression is upholding—these precepts are themselves concentration.
The Sūtra asks: "Is there any cause and condition by which one may break [the precepts]? The intent is that because there are occasions of great benefit, one may indeed break them;

thus he asks. The Sūtra records the Buddha’s reply: "There are causes and conditions by which one may break the precepts. This refers to cases where one perceives the capacity of others and is moved by the four *siddhāntas*.
One may also break the precepts due to their causal conditions.
A sutra states: "If there is a bodhisattva who knows through breaking the precepts," the single word "knows" precisely refers to a bodhisattva who perceives the opportune moment (*jī*).

Regarding the scripture’s statement, "I would rather fall into hell for an eon," etc.: this refers to one who cultivates with the mind of *nirvāṇa* up to the stage prior to the first *bhūmi*, before having yet shattered ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) still persists, one undergoes this retribution.

Regarding the phrase "the matter is contrary while the principle is compliant": the matter is contrary because he violates the precepts; the principle is compliant because he perceives the opportune moment (*jī*). For the sake of protecting the Dharma, the Sūtra states that "one who cuts off his life-force" refers to that king who, perceiving the opportune moment, violates the precepts and gives rise to the intention to kill; that Brahmin then immediately falls into hell. When all sentient beings reach hell, they all give rise to three thoughts. First: [The remainder of the passage follows: "...that the king has committed such a grave offense for my sake; second, that I have not yet repented of my own transgressions; third, that I have not yet cultivated roots of goodness. Because they give rise to these three thoughts, their suffering is slightly alleviated. Furthermore, when they emerge from hell, they are born among animals. Having been born as animals, they are then born as hungry ghosts. Having been born as hungry ghosts, they are then born as humans. Having been born as humans, they encounter a Buddha and attain the fruit of Arhatship. This is called the power of the Bodhisattva’s vow. It is like a person who, having fallen into a pit of fire, is rescued by another who extinguishes the fire and provides clothing and food; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having committed a crime and been sentenced to death, is released by the king due to a pardon; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having been struck by a poisoned arrow, is cured by a physician who extracts the arrow and applies medicine; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great famine, is saved by another who provides food and drink; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great flood, is saved by another who provides a boat; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great fire, is saved by another who provides water; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great thief, is saved by another who provides protection; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great illness, is cured by a physician who prescribes medicine; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great enemy, is saved by another who provides protection; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great wind, is saved by another who provides shelter; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great rain, is saved by another who provides a roof; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great darkness, is saved by another who provides a lamp; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great mountain, is saved by another who provides a path; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great river, is saved by another who provides a bridge; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great abyss, is saved by another who provides a ladder; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great precipice, is saved by another who provides a handhold; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great net, is saved by another who provides a knife; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great snare, is saved by another who provides a cutter; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great fetter, is saved by another who provides a key; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great chain, is saved by another who provides a hammer; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. It is also like a person who, having encountered a great lock, is saved by another who provides a tool; because of this kindness, the person develops a heart of gratitude and subsequently attains the Way. First, he knows that [the king] slanders the Mahāyāna; second, he knows that he will be killed by the king; third, he knows that he is currently undergoing this suffering. Upon realizing this, he immediately resolves his mind [on awakening].
By the power of this mindfulness, the Dharma Drum of Ambrosia arises. As it is said: "That which the Tathāgata has traversed over a hundred kalpas... and so forth.
Regarding his claim that this refers to the meaning of "opening and closing": as for the terminology of opening and closing, one has not yet understood what is meant by "opening.
As for "closing," to which teaching are the Four Noble Truths reduced? Ultimately, within emptiness, there are no truths at all; how could there be any further designation of "truth"?
Regarding the statement "opening four into sixteen," this refers to the following passage: "knowing the cessation of suffering," "knowing the path to the cessation of suffering," and so forth;
taking each of the [four] truths as the primary focus, they mutually constitute sixteen aspects.
As for the difference in names and meanings, it refers to the distinct meanings of arising-and-ceasing versus non-arising.
As for their being entirely different in relation to conditions, it refers to the four conditions being distinct according to the capacities of the four teachings.
There is much of significance here: the fourfold Four Noble Truths differ; each single Truth is further divided into sixteen aspects; each single Truth again possesses four gates;
and within these four sets of four, there are sixteen gates, each gate comprising the four *paryāyas* (universal principles), which is what is meant by their being "different."

Regarding the statement "now, for the time being, corresponding to the Tripiṭaka and so forth," this refers to the correspondence with the objects [of cognition] according to their sequential order; the intention is not to follow the non-sequential [classification].
Thus, it is said "for the time being" (yīwǎng) because there are four sets of the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding "successive accomplishment" (*kramasiddhi*): this refers to the cultivation of the mind of Great Nirvāṇa, proceeding from the stage of "breaking down" (*pratipakṣa*) into the essence, such as the contemplation of emptiness during the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Regarding "mutual accomplishment of object and wisdom" (*ālambana-jñāna-saṃsiddhi*): there is indeed a sense in which it exists, yet it is not known what specific object and wisdom are mutually accomplished; therefore, [the previous explanation] was not quite appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "neither objects nor wisdom," etc.: the first two truths are objects but not wisdom; the latter two truths are both objects and wisdom.

The two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and with outflows (*sāsrava*). The truth of the path (*mārga*) is conditioned and without outflows (*anāsrava*). The truth of cessation (*nirodha*) is unconditioned and without outflows.
This is because the two truths of suffering and origin are worldly cause and effect, whereas the two truths of the path and cessation are supramundane cause and effect.
There are pairs.
Regarding the fact that the meaning of the Four Truths is manifold: it is as previously stated, that they pertain to many places within the five flavors of the four teachings.
That "all are the objects of contemplation for Bodhisattvas" means that they are what is contemplated by the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding the combined discussion of subject and object: non-action is the subject that contemplates, while the preceding three are the objects contemplated;
non-action is the subject that opens, while the preceding three are the objects opened. Thus, there are four kinds of the Four Noble Truths.
That "the body is the root of suffering" means that the three types of suffering, the eight types of suffering, and so forth, all exist because of the body.
As for the first approach, it is based on the bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka; as for the second approach, both involve cultivating successive practices with the mind of the Great Nirvāṇa.
This is because those of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) initially enter from the sequence of arising and ceasing; thus, this [first approach] is also a preliminary one.
Regarding "suffering as the manifest aspect": this refers to the manifestation of the three types of suffering.

Regarding "the aspect of transformation because the causal aspect is subtle and secret": the subtlety of the names of good and evil is what is meant by "secret"; it is through the transformation of the cause that one is able to proceed toward the fruit.
Regarding the phrase "seeing the manifest to know the subtle, and from the subtle reaching the manifest": seeing the effect and thereby knowing the cause is called the "manifest";
proceeding from the cause to the effect is called the "subtle. This is the same principle as that of water droplets gradually filling a large vessel.
Regarding the transformation of the two minds: the transition from the causal mind to the resultant mind constitutes the "two minds.
As for the term "accumulation" (*saṃcita*), it refers to the uninterrupted succession from one birth-and-death to another birth-and-death; this is what is meant by "uninterrupted."

Regarding the establishment of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*): "establishment" (*vyavasthāpana*) refers to the formulation of names and the formulation of principles; that is, it means determining cause and effect based on dharmas, hence it is called "establishment.

As for the statement that they are "expounded as two" in terms of meaning: although the essence of cause and effect is one, they are spoken of as two from the perspective of their realization; therefore, it is said they are "expounded as two" in terms of meaning.
Regarding the growth of the six parts: first, it refers to the divisions of the body; second, it refers to the two hands, the two feet, and the head. Hence, they are called "six.
Regarding the growth of years and illnesses: both years and illnesses are forms of growth.
The Sūtra states that "aging moment by moment" refers to the differentiation of each kṣaṇa.

As for "miscellaneous illnesses" and "guest illnesses," these encompass the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). For example, when a person suffering from a fever suddenly develops a cold ailment, this is not something originally present;
it is called "guest" because it is adventitious. Furthermore, it is called "miscellaneous" because it is unstable.
The Sūtra states: "Those with mental illness. In various texts, afflictions (*kleśa*) are considered mental illnesses; however, that is not the case here. Why?
Even grasping at extremes (*antagrāha*) is called an illness, as it all arises from the mind. For example, a person's grief and sorrow are also illnesses.
First, regarding the mutual distinction between the two causes from the past: for instance, one may practice giving while also killing;
thus, there is merit yet a short lifespan. Or again, one may observe the precepts while being stingy and parsimonious; thus, there is a long life yet the exhaustion of merit.
The Sūtra states that death is a great suffering. There are four types of suffering all of which are termed "death," and for this reason it is called a "great suffering.

As for the statement that the "intense flourishing of the five aggregates" is its specific essence: this is because the eight [sufferings], such as birth and so forth, are all violent and intense. If one were to provide a general name for them:
This refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Because they induce the preceding seven [stages], they are said to be "comprehensive.

As for the statement that the five aggregates of the stage of preparation (*prayoga*) are not the essence of suffering: those who possess the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) are called persons of the stage of preparation.
Furthermore, regarding the selection of one specific suffering: as the sutra states, "excluding the suffering of old age," for old age is not necessarily [present in all cases].
This is because Buddhas and devas are entirely exempt from it.
The analogy of the woman to a "born fruit" means that birth itself is the fruit; thus it is called a "born fruit. It is also termed the "fruit of an evil household."
Regarding the observation of the initial arising of birth: at the moment one first receives a body, one takes up residence within the house of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The "host" is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva who performs the investigation; by means of the wisdom of observation, he discerns the reality or unreality of birth.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra concerning "making offerings" and so forth: because the Bodhisattva protects this body and causes it to proceed toward Bodhi, it is called "prostration.
As for the phrase "where fruits grow, there is much splendor": whether one is poor or wealthy, wherever one dwells, one has already [established] oneself.
Joy; the distinction between noble and base can be known therein, for it is called "glory.
As for those whose golden hearts have already returned, they no longer undergo birth and death; thus, true non-arising becomes their place of rest.
Regarding the third, the Bodhisattva’s Joyful Celebration: it is called "joy" because one accords with the objective realm through wisdom and thoroughly comprehends birth and death.

As for "the realm of birth examining and yielding to the ordinary mind," the meaning is that while ordinary beings know that birth must inevitably entail death, they are unwilling to relinquish both together due to a lack of wisdom.
Generally, when the mind responds to objects, it corresponds with the objects arising at the initial moment of entering the body; thus, the Sūtra says, "causing them to dwell in my house.

As for those who are like young children, whose understanding and practice are shallow and weak—referring to the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka who have not yet severed their afflictions—they are called "young."

Regarding "fruit within dung": one whose body has not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) is like being within dung; for now, taking those born in the heavens as representative while including humans as well, it is called "fruit.
As for "the wise person," this refers generally to Bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) and have transcended desire.
Regarding "reproaching with the mind": why do you not seek unsurpassed bodhi, yet instead take up the fruits of humans and devas?
As the Sūtra says, "desiring to wash them clean, one discards them," the Bodhisattva, being reproached, practices the contemplation of impurity and abandons the states of humans and devas.
That which first receives [the practitioner] is the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.

Second is the contemplation of old age; within the sutra there are twelve repetitions, each with both a simile and its application, because the afflictions of old age are so numerous that it is therefore explained repeatedly.
The fourth, the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Suffering of Death*, explains death through ten successive stages (*daśa-paryāya*), as the metaphors employed differ.
Those who have not yet completely escaped death include everyone from the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) downward, for they still possess at least one grade of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Regarding the initial statement that the Buddha is called a bodhisattva, the intended meaning is: "If even a Buddha is still designated as a sentient being, how much more so would he not be designated as a bodhisattva?
This does not accord with the sutra; for the sutra states only that a bodhisattva abiding in Great Nirvana is not called a Buddha. It should be understood accordingly.
That which cannot even give rise to birth-and-death is because birth-and-death is entirely *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is not birth-and-death.
That which cannot injure the vast, towering diamond refers to "vast" as a great stone and "towering" as the appearance of height;

this is a metaphor for the person of the Perfect Teaching Bodhisattva, who possesses the substance of the three virtues that are lofty and expansive, and is not shattered or dispersed by the three preceding teachings.
Vajra: That which is destroyed by the rain of Dharma becomes upright and sharp.
If one were to separate these into twenty phrases, there are only ten phrases when pointed out according to the text; they are divided into twenty through detailed classification.
The Sūtra says: "In a place of peril and difficulty where there are no provisions," yet there are places that are not difficult and where provisions exist;
as previously stated, this applies to all except for Bodhisattvas who dwell in Great Nirvāṇa.
There are those whose destination is far distant and who have no companions; there are also those whose destination, though distant, has companions and so forth.
There are those who travel day and night without knowing their limit; there are also those who travel at times and have a limit.
Regarding "profound and dark, without the light of a lamp": there are places that are profound yet possess the light of a lamp.
The subsequent phrases should all be understood by following the explanations provided in the text.
"There must be a place from which they come" means that after death, one is reborn to receive retribution within the six realms; hence it is called "the place from which they come.
"The path is inexhaustible" means that after being born, one dies again, and after dying, one is born again; hence it is called "inexhaustible."
Death is the ultimate limit for those who follow the Way; once the precipice of life has been exhausted, there is no place to avoid it.
This is not because of foul colors; at the moment of initial death, the eyes and ears remain perfectly intact, with no further change.
Regarding "the cessation of life within the intermediate state": this refers to the cessation within this present body.

"That which arises from the separation of conditions is itself the suffering of change" means that what arises from conditions refers precisely to the beloved objects of both the primary self and its environment.
Regarding the difficulty of departing from one's own mind: because craving arises from the mind, it is called a "difficulty.

As for the statement that "Māndhātṛ was one who ought to have been born," if one interprets the text according to its underlying principle, this refers to my own person; thus, I am the one who ought to be king.

Regarding the term "mao-wei" (hair-tail): the character *mao* (pronounced *mo gāo*) refers to the hair of a horse. According to the *Liji* (Book of Rites), when a Great Officer resides in the capital, he rides a *mao-ma* (hair-horse).
The *Shuowen Jiezi* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) states that *mao* means hair; it refers specifically to the finest hair among the coat.

Liu Xiaobiao lived in seclusion on Mount Jinhua, where he composed the *Shanqi zhi* (Record of Mountain Dwelling) in seven chapters; though he did not emerge from his retreat, his influence was not limited.
Among the eminent and talented men of the sea, it was said that his literary style was expansive and his virtue profound as he served in office.

Regarding the phrase "each being esteemed by their respective [circumstances]," the intended meaning is that since there is a distinction between having a son and not having a son, one simply takes what is most highly esteemed as the "Precious Woman" (ratnastri).

As for the scripture stating "only those who can blink," the character *shùn* (瞬) is identical to *kuàng* (矌) [with the phonetic reading *dùrùn*]; it is also written as *xiù* (眴), while the *Shuowen Jiezi* uses *shùn* (瞬).
The phrase "cloud-eyes" refers to frequent blinking. The *Lüshi Chunqiu* states that ten thousand generations view [time] as a single instant.
The *Zhuangzi* states that one may gaze all day without blinking.
For one who "comprehends with the mind and is pressed by the environment": if the mind does not comprehend it, how can there be peace? If it is empty, then there is no suffering.

Regarding the discrepancy between the past and the present: this raises an objection from the perspective of the past against the present by asserting that there is only suffering and no pleasure. The Buddha’s intended meaning in his response was that, in reality, the past was indeed suffering;
it was spoken according to the inclinations of others, who falsely imagined it to be pleasure. This is no different from the present.
The phrase "now fully enumerating the six sense organs, etc. probes the meaning of the subsequent passage.

Regarding the "mysterious resolution of the five difficulties": the Tathāgata simply states that to perversely give rise to the perception of pleasure within suffering is itself the mysterious resolution.
Why? Because in the past, following the intentions of others, suffering and pleasure were considered distinct; now, they are all suffering.

The Buddha’s intention was that what is considered "light" constitutes the lowest grade of suffering; among the three types of suffering, that which contains a slight degree of pleasure is regarded as light in comparison to [the other] sufferings.
Kāśyapa’s objection intends to take the heavy sufferings of the three miserable realms as the "lowest," and further divides suffering into three grades;
thus, he says it is a "mistaken calculation. Furthermore, this objection is raised because ordinary people of the final age might give rise to such erroneous conceptions.
Next, regarding the "reversal" objection (*viparyāsa-ākṣepa*): it is called a "reversal" because one anticipates that pleasure will give rise to suffering.

Regarding the objection based on actual facts (*vastu-ākṣepa*): suppose a person is struck with a thousand blows; if even one blow has passed and the others have not yet been endured, would pleasure arise? The Buddha replied, "For the time being, yes.
However, his statement that this is "pleasure while not yet subdued" does not reflect his true intention. Why? If one were to receive a thousand...
If one receives a single blow of the staff and is released, one may consider it a point of liberation; one can only find joy therein. If one were not released, how could there be joy?

Regarding the phrases "one [instance of] threefold instruction" and "two [instances of] threefold suffering instruction," "instruction" refers to the two teachings of the present and the past, while "three sufferings" refers to the names of the three types of suffering.
This is because it applies to both the present and the past.
Regarding the marking of the three types of sensation (*vedanā*), the single dot is used to indicate their correspondence to the three types of suffering (*duḥkha*); thus, it is called a "single dot.

As for the statement that these two types of suffering do not require the pressure of external objects: because the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) is subtle, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) lacks an external object; it is merely afflicted by the absence [of permanence].
That which is constantly subject to decay and transformation is called "decay. Because it is not the same as heavy suffering, there is no oppression by suffering.
To restate the question in order to seek an answer clarifies that those of the previous lives—such as the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—joyfully sought an answer.
"Furthermore, 'adorned with its phrasing'—'adorned' means decorated—as in the passage from the Sūtra concerning the World-Honored One:
'In the immeasurable [realms], up to having already departed from falsehood,' and so forth."
The root of bodhi is so called because the root can produce; as a cause, it is itself a condition, for the cause brings about production.
The phrase "even unto having the cause of production," as used in older translations, means that worldly phenomena first come into existence.
The revealing cause of the Buddha-fruit nurtures the singular, true wisdom of bodhi; it is able to reveal the objective realm and thus accomplishes the fruit of the Dharmakāya.

Now, regarding what is called "having causes and conditions," this refers to the causes and conditions of the four *siddhāntas*, which can also be described as "productive causes" (*janakahetu*), because they serve as the causes for the [attainment of] the *pariniṣpanna* and *parikalpita*.
Later, when it is explained that they act as conditions for suffering, it is because suffering arises due to prior pleasure; thus, it is designated as a "condition."

In the "Chapter on Explaining the Noble Practices," regarding the causes and conditions of the aggregates (*skandha*), it refers to the six causes and four conditions as the causal conditions for their accumulation.
As for "originally being afflictions" (*kleśa*), it means that by virtue of the afflictions, they are able to moisten karma.

Regarding "ignorance has no sphere of activity; it practices equality and is equal to the world": this means that one realizes the essence of ignorance is itself the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and therefore it has no sphere of activity.
"Practicing equality in the world" means that the cultivation of ignorance circulates throughout the six realms of existence.
This is called "equanimity.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the twelve links of dependent origination are neither arising nor ceasing: to realize that these twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the Buddha-nature is what is meant by "neither arising nor ceasing."
"Accomplishing what is cherished" means being able to bring about this cherishing with respect to the resultant body.
"That which is required is what is cherished" refers to "what belongs to me" (*mamakāra*); that is, one first gives rise to cherishing toward both the primary body and its environment.
In all cases, the fruit is mentioned first because there is past karma; thus, in this present life, one practices the conditions for karma.
As for the causes and conditions of afflictions, they arise from the habituation of their causes, thereby giving rise to the latencies of affliction.

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says "discriminating and calculating," etc.: this refers to the various views held by ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) who, through their false wisdom, calculate the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*), such as the sixty-two [views] and so forth.
Because these views differ from one another, they are called "immeasurable."
If one expects that understanding constitutes what is called "truth" (*satya*), then because the Bodhisattva understands the conventional, it receives the name "truth.
Furthermore, if it conforms to worldly sentiment, it is termed "conventional"; for, in transforming sentient beings according to their capacities, it is again called "conventional."
Regarding the citation of the four sūtras first: as it says in the sūtra, "In other sūtras, for the sake of all sentient beings, karma is taught as the causal condition;
or pride and so forth are taught. These constitute the four sūtras. "Other sūtras" refers to the various Hīnayāna sūtras, such as the Āgamas.

Regarding the "four stations of consciousness" (*catasraḥ vijñānasthitayaḥ*): this refers to the four aggregates, such as feeling (*vedanā*), abiding within form (*rūpa*). Therefore, it is called the "five flourishing aggregates" (*pañca upādānaskandhāḥ*).
As for the scriptural statement, "not [the cause] nor not the cause": while various afflictions (*kleśa*) are not *not* causes, they alone are capable of directly nourishing the fruit.
Therefore, it is due to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Regarding the statement that the two vehicles have not yet severed their residual habits (*vāsanā*)—like one who has returned property but not exhausted it—it means they have not yet severed the specific delusions (*viśeṣa-kleśa*), which is termed "not yet exhausted.

Third, as for the analytical distinction: following the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*), the four truths of non-arising (*anutpāda*) are considered in relation to the Separate (*vyavasthita*) and Perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) [vehicles] therein.
Therefore, it is contrasted with arising and ceasing; thus, it is called "discernment" (*liaojian*).
"Forgetting what preceded" refers to forgetting birth-and-death, which means forgetting suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*).

"Forgetting what follows" means forgetting *nirvāṇa*, which refers to forgetting the Path and Cessation. This is because within the Four Truths of Non-arising (*anutpāda*), one is able to forget both the preceding and the subsequent.

"Thereby causing the second, third, and fourth turns to all be manifest" means that the [truths of] the Immeasurable (*apramāṇa*) and the Unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) are identical to the texts concerning arising and ceasing.
The following analysis can all be understood later. Why is this so?
Having raised the fourfold Four Truths as a point of inquiry, why is there no explanation of the text on the Four Truths itself, but rather an analytical investigation now?

My intention is simply this: that within the worldly truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), these are themselves non-arising (*anutpāda*)—namely, the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*). Why? Because [cessation] is...
The principle is the same; therefore, there is no need to wait for what follows. The latter two truths are self-contained in their textual structure, which is why it says "all are revealed.

Regarding "in emptiness there is no arising": this means there is no arising of suffering (*duḥkha*) or its accumulation (*samudaya*). This is because the Path (*mārga*) is non-dual, being both the capacity to understand and the object understood.

Regarding the clarification that both extremes are non-arising: the worldly causes and effects are non-arising as "having limits," while the supramundane causes and effects are non-arising as "being limitless.
Therefore, it is called "non-arising."
As for that which is immeasurable in its intent: briefly stated, it is the Four Noble Truths; extensively, it is the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.

Through the four gates of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising, and the fourfold application of each, there are distinctions from form and mind up to the knowledge of all modes. All of these are non-arising.
Regarding the reduction to four chapters based on the four truths of the simple [version]: it refers only to the four chapters on the arising-and-ceasing truths of suffering and its origin;
subsequently, the four chapters on the unarisen four truths are explained.
As for the "Newly Established Edition" (Xindingben), it was edited and finalized by Master Xie and is known as the "Southern Edition" (Nanben).
As for that which bestows and that which takes away: "bestowing" refers to having conventional truth but lacking ultimate reality;
"the two vehicles" refers to those who possess a small measure of wisdom, namely, supramundane, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
The phrase "unable to contemplate suffering and so forth" serves to distinguish [the Śrāvakas] from Bodhisattvas.
This is because those of the Two Vehicles cannot contemplate cessation as a Truth (*satya*), since they have already realized the principle of cessation.
Third, the extensive explanation of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) interprets the cessation of birth and the path to its cessation.
That is to say, "the gateway of abandonment" refers to it in terms of that which abandons; "the gateway of detachment" refers to the interpretation in terms of that which is abandoned.
Regarding the statement that "the Bodhisattva is endowed with four matters, such as wisdom and virtue" (and so forth): "virtue" refers to the four virtues.
Alternatively, it may refer to the five virtues; this consists of the fifth phrase, "I am eternally [the refuge] for the two," added to the preceding four to form five.

Now, regarding the provisional establishment of the four virtues: as the sutra states, that which is called "permanent" (*nitya*) refers to the permanence of unconditioned cessation through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is precisely the principle of the truth of tranquil extinction (*śānta-satya*).
That which attains the experience of bliss is the *nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna.
It is called "purity" because it seeks the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
It is called "self" because, by means of the non-arising of the twenty-five existences, one immediately attains the self of mastery (*vaśitā-ātman*).
The Sūtra says: "To see coarse and subtle things. The coarse refers to worldly cause and effect; the subtle refers to supramundane cause and effect.

Regarding "illuminating things such as the permanent and the impermanent": the permanent refers to what ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) conceptualize, while the impermanent refers to the reality of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
Regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned: that which is worldly is conditioned, while that which transcends the world is unconditioned. Regarding sentient beings and non-sentient beings:
the primary retribution is sentient beings, whereas the environmental retribution is not sentient beings.
Regarding "things and non-things": the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) of the world are called "things. Because they cannot be perceived [in their ultimate nature], they are "non-things.
Suffering and pleasure, self and non-self, the mundane and the supramundane—these can all be known.
"Pure and impure," up to "real and unreal," are all explained in terms of the mundane and the supramundane.
Regarding "vehicles and non-vehicles": vehicles such as those of humans and devas are non-vehicles, while supramundane vehicles and the like are indeed vehicles.
To know that there is no knower means that the worldly realm is devoid of wisdom; the supramundane is itself wisdom.
That "substance (dravya) is not substance" refers to the primary truth of the non-Buddhist outsiders; that it is "not substance" is the correct tenet.
Regarding "seeking" and "not seeking": the externalist calculation relies on cessation as non-seeking; this is the correct calculation.
Regarding "view" and "non-view": the worldly gate is non-view, while the supramundane is right view.
Regarding "form" and "non-form": that which is worldly is called form; that which is supramundane is non-form.
Regarding "the path" and "non-path": that which is worldly is not the path; that which is supramundane is called the path.
Regarding "understanding and non-understanding": worldly states are non-understanding, while those that transcend the world are called understanding.
"In the end, there is but one path" refers to the untainted path that penetrates both the mundane and the supramundane.
Regarding "from faith up to giving": faith is the foundation, for it is the primary condition for entering the Path. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"One enters by means of faith."

First, regarding "using the present to challenge the past": this means using the Eightfold Noble Path of the present to challenge the fact that the various sūtras of the past contain differing explanations.
When a sūtra says, "Long since free from error," the intent of the challenge is as follows: I also know that the Tathāgata is without error;
however, for the sake of sentient beings, I pose this question so that the present and the past may be made consistent. Thus, the Tathāgata challenges and grants permission to all of them.
The Sūtra says, "By these causes and conditions. This refers to why the fourteen kinds of causes and conditions previously mentioned differ from one another.
It is because they converge that their principle is the same; this is because the various sūtras mentioned above all share the same name, "Eightfold Noble Path" (Aṣṭāṅgika-mārga).
Regarding the name of the water "Pāriśabdika," it may be that this sound is used as a conventional designation for this water.
As for the sutra’s statement, "in a single dharma-characteristic," it refers solely to the single dharma of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
The Sūtra says, "yet it does not depart from gold. This is like the Eightfold Noble Path, where the single application [of the path] differs according to its function.
Kaishan’s claim that this refers to whether the inclusion of dharmas is exhaustive or not is ignorant of which dharma is considered exhaustive and which teaching is considered non-exhaustive;
it is merely words without any supporting evidence. One may understand this by correlating it with the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding the reference to past events mentioned previously, it is uncertain which sūtra this refers to; however, I now maintain that the *Āgamas* already contain immeasurable such meanings.
As for the statement that the specific characteristics were not explained therein, this refers to the establishment of the defining marks (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena.
"Collecting by means of names" refers to the immeasurable Four Noble Truths.
"The categories being different" refers to the differentiation of the immeasurable Four Truths.
When the Sūtra says, "I [taught] in that sūtra," it points to past sūtras such as the Āgamas.
The five aggregates (skandhas) of ordinary beings and sages refer to the distinctions among the ten realms, namely the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of sages.

Regarding "each and every aggregate" and so forth, this refers to the three thousand worlds, the hundred realms, the thousand suchnesses (tathatā), and so on; therefore, they are said to be immeasurable.
Regarding each individual body-dharma: the body is the ten realms, and the dharmas are the ten suchnesses.
Each liberation further possesses the immeasurable, as in the previous hundred phrases; each is explained in turn to serve as its retinue and so forth.
Regarding the identity and difference of names: if they share the same name, "Four Noble Truths," then they are fully encompassed. If they differ, they are immeasurable and inexhaustible.
This is like the single term "great earth" being used for immeasurable things; the great earth is indeed one, yet there are truly immeasurable Four Noble Truths and Ten Realms that are distinct.
For example, just as the single great earth can produce various things such as ears and so forth—this is precisely the meaning.
Regarding the "four persons who judge the middle": this refers to the two vehicles, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, as categorized by person (*pudgala*) within the sūtras.

As for the statement that "the Bodhisattva’s *skandha* covers both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa," this means that while they conceal their own [defilements] to benefit sentient beings, it is not the same sense of "covering" as mere obscuration.
Those who are unable to reach the place of treasure halt at the transformed city for three hundred yojanas;
those of the two vehicles who are attached to the subtle pleasures realize the limited true nirvana.
That the Bodhisattva’s aggregates are both [existent and non-existent] means that they are able to attain nirvāṇa while simultaneously illuminating the entry into saṃsāra.
That the Buddha’s aggregates are neither [existent nor non-existent] means that entering the Middle Way is to be the center precisely through the extremes.
Next, regarding "knowing that entry constitutes the gate": "entry" refers to mutual penetration; "gate" refers to that through which one comes and goes.
For example, the eye can enter into forms, and forms come to enter the eye; this is called "entry," and it is also termed the "wheel-gate."
"Even unto the mind it is thus" refers to entering the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The "gate of tranquility" (*śāntimukha*) is the fruit of *sarvajñā* (all-knowing wisdom); the "gate of equality" (*samatāmukha*) is the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm).
The gate of non-suffering is the gate of *nirvāṇa*.
The gate that is both pleasure and suffering is to regard one’s own practice as pleasure and the transformation of others as suffering.

Furthermore, regarding "knowing the nature of the divisions of the realms" (*dhātu*): "realms" refers to distinctions; "nature" refers to that which is not divided or altered—namely, the differences among the eighteen realms.

Furthermore, regarding those who cannot hear sounds: for the sake of brevity, it is based on one sense organ being fully present; strictly speaking, one should say they "smell odors," "perceive tangibles," and so forth.
As for those who can see forms, hear sounds, and so on, this is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the ten ways in which the six sense organs are mutually interchangeable.
Furthermore,
"corrupting wholesome concentration" refers to corrupting the ten wholesome paths of action, the four dhyānas, the eight liberations,
and so forth. "Corrupting causes and fruits" refers to being able to destroy the causes and fruits of the mundane world.
Regarding "destroying existence and destroying non-existence": this refers to being able to destroy the non-existence of the two vehicles' nirvana within the twenty-five existences.

Regarding "the Buddha's form destroys the aforementioned various destructions": the forms of the nine realms are all capable of being destroyed as they are identical to the single Buddha-nature. Regarding "the forms of the six paths destroy bliss, which can destroy nirvana":
[this refers to the fact that] the forms of the six paths destroy the bliss that is capable of destroying nirvana.
Regarding the phrase "the initial realization of the outflow-free (anāsrava) [state], etc.," this refers to the fact that even up to the Pratyekabuddhas, all are outflow-free.

Furthermore, the Sakṛdāgāmin realizes the exhaustion of the three grades of afflictions in the desire realm; the Anāgāmin [realizes] the nine grades; and the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] represent the total exhaustion of the three realms.
Regarding "awakening and non-awakening, etc.": awakening is the Buddha Jewel; non-awakening is the Dharma; that which is neither awakening nor non-awakening is the Sangha.
These are fully present as a single essence.
Those who drink bitterness and eat poison find that all six realms are impermanent.
These subsequent aggregates (*skandhas*) serve as the conditions for producing a future body.

This "unequaled form" refers to the Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*), who possess only a single grade of ignorance; because they have no [remaining] equal [to them], [they are called unequaled].
...and so forth. Therefore, it is called "unequaled with the unequaled" (*asamasama*).
This "liberation of form" (*rūpa-vimokṣa*) is precisely true liberation (*bhūtā vimukti*).

Regarding "having already transcended yet being born again," this refers to the eight grades of the ninth level of the non-perception realm (*asaṃjñi-āyatana*), which are abandoned through the cultivation of the outflow-tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) by non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
The ground [of rebirth] leads back to falling into the three miserable realms (*trāya*). "Ashes severed, not arising" refers to the entry into extinction with the ash-body (*kṣāra-kāya*).
Those who abandon goodness for evil destinies fall into the four evil realms;
those who abandon evil for goodness proceed toward the human and heavenly realms.

"There is neither departure nor arrival" means that because the Path is itself the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there is no destination to which one can go. How, then, could there be a "path" or a "non-path"?
"Because all dharmas are themselves the Buddha-way" refers to what the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* says: "To walk upon non-paths and yet penetrate the Buddha-way."
"The Path. This constitutes the Dharma-gate of Non-duality, and so forth.

Regarding the statement "the movement of views and the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment," these four phrases are categorized according to the teachings: the first is the Arising-and-Ceasing (shengmie);

the second is the Unarisen (wusheng); the third is the Immeasurable (wuliang); and the fourth is the Unconditioned (wu zuo). Because the factors of enlightenment (daopin) differ accordingly, the commentary states "and so forth. It should also be understood in this way.
Furthermore, this refers to the principle of entering the non-conceptual and inconceivable through the convergence of the gates.
Regarding the direct knowledge of the Three Dharma Seals: as the sutras state, impermanence, non-self, and the quiescence of nirvana are called the Three Dharma Seals in the Hīnayāna;
however, in the Mahāyāna, taking the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) as the seal constitutes the Single Dharma Seal.
Regarding what worldly people refer to as the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*), ancient masters in general have only clarified the meaning of the two truths (*dvaya-satya*).
How could there be immeasurable characteristics within the ultimate truth according to our own school? They fail to understand this through calculation;
how much less so regarding the sixteen gates of the fourfold-fourfold [analysis] and so forth? Therefore, it is said to be "boundless."
Regarding the "Four Truths and Sixteen Truths": in the Hīnayāna, one merely clarifies that within each of the Four Truths there are four aspects (ākāra), which together are called the sixteen.

The "four continuities" are simply the conventional designation of continuity (prajñapti-saṃtati). The "arising from six causes" is simply the conventional designation of causal formation (prajñapti-hetusaṃbhūta).
Regarding the five matters of principle: "matter" (shi) refers to the conventional (sāṃvṛti), while "principle" (li) refers to the ultimate (paramārtha).

Regarding the six degrees of kinship: the conventional is distant, while the ultimate is intimate. The primary meaning (paramārtha) is without fault, as it transcends both the conventional and the ultimate.
Regarding "because it is not false or deceptive": both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) are real.
