There are those who examine according to worldly sentiment, up to those who examine with the discernment of wisdom and sentiment. The present intent is that, following sentiment, there is the conventional;
following wisdom, there is the ultimate; and following self and other, there is the ultimate and the conventional. All are called "truths" (*satya*), which differs from the views of others.
"寧當一體者" (Níng dāng yītǐ zhě) means "it would rather be a single entity," which is a refutation. Who, moreover, within the various schools, asserts that there is no intermediate essence?
As for the point that the two truths differ in their opening and closing, our school’s correct interpretation contains seven layers of distinct two-truth formulations.
Regarding the passage, "Is it not that the Tathāgata speaks falsely? the intended meaning is: since the Tathāgata does not speak falsely, how can the two truths be differentiated?

As for the phrase, "All [passages] appearing in the sūtras mutually manifest their texts," this refers to such statements as "the conventional does not exist within the ultimate" and "the ultimate does not exist within the conventional," concerning the ultimate and the conventional.
The identity of the two [truths] is precisely the intended meaning here. Therefore, it is said that "the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is identical to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding the phrase "it returns to being a single truth": this was already questioned previously; now it is raised again as a further objection, which is why the word "returns" (*huan*) is used.

Regarding the statement that "the two truths are taught by means of skillful expedient (upāya-kauśalya) as a condition": if one were to discuss the ultimate reality, it is as you have asked—there is only a single truth.
Since even a single truth does not exist [independently], how could there be two? It is for the sake of conforming to worldly convention and common usage that we speak of two truths.

It is like a person under the influence of intoxication who speaks of a "revolving day. Just as when the ultimate truth is transformed into the conventional, there are two names, if one is not intoxicated, it is simply the single ultimate truth, and there is no further characteristic of transformation.

One master says that although there are seven kinds, they are unified as one; this master’s intention is that while there are seven kinds, they constitute only the single Truth of Reality (*ekasatyatā*).

As for the phrase "may be spoken differently according to conditions," this [passage] now refutes [the claim] as to what specific conditions are used to speak of the differences between various teachings.
As for the first master’s statement that the seven types are each distinct, his refutation is also the same as before.

Regarding the point that although the names differ, their meaning can be reconciled: in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra), the seven layers have names different from those in this sūtra;
those seven layers are established based on the opening and closing of the four teachings, wherein the provisional is opened to reveal the real, returning all to the One Vehicle.

Regarding the meaning: these are merely seven [truths] spoken according to conventional sentiment; from the perspective of ultimate wisdom, there is only one true reality (*satya*). Therefore, it is said that "their meaning can be reconciled.
Third, "single conventional and compound true" refers to the truth within the integration of the provisional and the real in the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*); hence it is called "compound.

Fourth, "single conventional and single middle" refers to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*) connecting with the Distinct. Fifth, "compound conventional and single middle" refers to the Distinct Teaching connecting with the Perfect.

Because it is merely the Middle. Sixth, the "double conventional and double middle" refers to the Perfect [Teaching] connecting with the Separate. Seventh, this is the actual substance of the Perfect Teaching;

these seven layers of the Perfect connecting with the Separate are evident from the text. As for the "single conventional and single middle," its name is clearly indicated [elsewhere], yet it differs from the *Xuanyan wen*;
at present, I cannot fathom its intent.
"The Buddha's intention is difficult to know; for now, let us set forth the view of a single master. These are the words of the commentator’s humility.
"I shall now provisionally rely upon the seven kinds [of causes] established by the Great Master."

Regarding "grasping at the aggregates is called birth": the aggregates (*skandha*) are substantial dharmas (*dravyadharma*), whereas "name" (*nāman*) is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*). This refers to the fact that there are various names for a particular individual or master.

Regarding "the aggregates and that which is apart from the aggregates," etc.: this explains that while suffering exists, there is no [inherent] suffering, and thus there is the True Truth (*satyadharma*).
"Conforming with the characteristics of phenomena" means that because form is emptiness, emptiness is form; thus, it is said they are conforming.

One must not say that suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Suffering and its origin are themselves the true path, and cessation is itself the Middle Way;
since this now contains both the True and the Middle, it is called "repeatedly true."
Regarding the mutual presentation of the Dharma and the analogy: the analogy precedes the Dharma. These five dharmas are all like *nirvāṇa*;
therefore, both the Dharma and the analogy are empty, being equally mere conventional designations.

Regarding "the mind being free from inversion": it should be stated in full that the eight inversions refer specifically to the Middle Way; for what is "as-it-is" (yathābhūta) is precisely the perfect Middle.
As for the clarification concerning "conditioned arising," "non-arising," and so forth: because the various [teachings] such as the Tripitaka are all equally illusory existences.
"Pointing to the one ultimate reality" refers to the inconceivable middle.
"That is, by means of the two beginnings" refers to the initial burning and cutting of the body into two parts. "The two endings" can be understood as death and disintegration.
The "compound conventional" is as previously described. There are those who assert that the true and the conventional are both termed "conventional," and so forth;
these still constitute the two truths of the single conventional and the compound true. This refers to the same meaning as the aforementioned "perfectly interfused" stage.
Regarding why it is not at all surprising that this treatise explains seven kinds [of truths]: others merely provide an interpretation of two truths;
how could that be surprising?

The third section clarifies the single ultimate truth (*ekasatyam*); this is the teaching of the finest cream (*amṛta*), identical in flavor to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and in essence with the true reality (*dharmatā*).
There is no difference. Once the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has fully opened [the truth] such that all dharmas are known to be identical to the Single Reality (*eka-tattva*), it is concluded.

Now, because there are those who have not yet entered into this reality, the previous section clarified the two truths in seven layers, while opening up six layers to explain the single truth of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*). The first three baskets (*piṭaka*) concern arising and ceasing;
now it is explained that the single reality is itself the ultimate truth.
Regarding the statement "raising four and raising two," this serves as an introduction.

To consolidate four into two makes the meaning more convenient; first, convenience of the scripture (*sūtra-vaśa*), and second, convenience of the meaning (*artha-vaśa*). These three and two are merely differences in expansion and contraction; their underlying meaning is not distinct.
Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) constitute the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*) are the ultimate (*paramārtha*). If one were to consolidate...

It is divided into three [truths]. Within the "True" (zhen), the First Noble Truth (paramārtha-satya) is further distinguished; thus it is said that "a little is not convenient. As for its meaning being pervasive, it is therefore said to be "a little.

Regarding "removing delusion to reveal the ālayavijñāna": this is because within the ālayavijñāna there are seeds of the three parts—defiled, pure, and neutral—and thus the intention is to remove [delusion].
The "one part of defiled seeds" reveals the pure portion.
Regarding the "Master Zhongjia," the name of the ancient master who propagated the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* is not specified.

As for "Xinghuang [Senglang] rejecting them all," this refers to his general repudiation of the aforementioned masters; he refuted that which is relied upon—the fruition of Buddhahood—and that which it relies upon—the single [nature].
It is indeed so.
To speak of the "middle" in contrast to the "extremes" is to refute those who treat the middle as a mere provisional construct.
To speak of the "real" in dependence upon the "false" is precisely the meaning of relative dependence; how could it be the reality that transcends all dependence?

If one were to explain this differently according to various conditions, our school’s intention permits the teachings of Xinghuang because he expounds upon the One True Truth; therefore, we do not refute him.
The Sūtra says, "without inversion," which refers to the four inversions, the eight inversions, and so forth. Because the mind is not inverted, it is termed "real.
The "four" refers to persons, as the Sūtra names it the Mahāyāna, which refers to the person who is able to ride [the vehicle]. Text.
This is because it is that which the Great Being Samantabhadra mounts.
Sixth, regarding the cause: as the sutra says, "the single path of purity" is the meaning of cause. Because one proceeds from cause to fruit, it is called "purity."

Regarding Xinghuang’s naming of the first section as the "Chapter on the Reality of Cessation" (*shimie zhangmen*): the intent is that afflictions (*kleśa*) are taken as "reality," and that which can sever them is "cessation.

As for taking the principle (*li*) as the reality of cessation, the meaning of "principle" is too general; if one does not know [the specific nature of] cessation, what teaching provides the actual realization of what kind of principle?
Furthermore, "non-duality is reality" means that because object and wisdom are non-dual, suffering itself is the truth; thus it is termed "reality.
To exclude the two phrases and use only "reality" as the truth means that there would then be suffering and there would be truth, but they would not be reality. One simply takes what exists...
In reality, a single phrase constitutes the Truth (*satya*), for "reality" (*sat*) is its meaning.
As the Sūtra says, "That which is neither suffering nor truth is reality. If both the preceding and the subsequent are equally real, what is the distinction?

It is because the former refers to the existence of suffering, whereas the present refers to the absence of suffering; by negating all three previous [categories], it is precisely this that constitutes the present reality.

Regarding the statement that "the latter three truths are also thus": the three truths of origination and so forth are all defined by way of "neither [existence nor non-existence]. The Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature is likewise.
As for the statement that it is "explicitly named Tathāgata and implicitly named Buddha-nature," the Tathāgata is "explicit" because he is the fruit, whereas Buddha-nature exists in the cause.
Therefore, it is hidden. If discussed in full detail, the Buddha-nature also encompasses both cause and effect.
As for why space is said to be non-dual in terms of manifestation and concealment: the essence of space does not pertain to cause and effect; hence, it is called non-dual.
Regarding the subsequent explanation that "the truths are all as in the text": this refers to this very single Truth of Reality (*ekasatyam*).
In the previous passage on the Four Truths, everything following [the first] was designated as "real" (*satya*); hence the word "subsequent" (*krama*).
Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that suffering is without suffering: this applies the name of "truth" (satya) to the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao).
However, if we speak from the perspective of the two vehicles of the Tripitaka Teaching (zangjiao), even by way of negation, it still cannot be called a truth.
Those who have not yet exhausted the reality of principle have not attained the Middle Way, and therefore lack true reality.
When the Sūtra states that the Tathāgata is neither conditioned nor outflowing, it should likewise be understood by analogy that empty space and Buddha-nature are neither conditioned nor outflowing;
it is simply that the text is abbreviated.
Regarding "viewing both advancement and retreat": if one does not regard inversion as real during advancement, then the inclusion of phenomena is incomplete;
therefore, it is called an error. When the Sūtra states that "all inversions are not called real," the objection means:

if inversions are not real, why did the preceding text state that they are fully subsumed within the Four Noble Truths? The response means: because they are all subsumed within the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya), they are not real.
Regarding the two things that can be perceived: as stated in the sutra, this is because the two things—the sentient beings and the followers of the Two Vehicles—are different in their falsity.
"The primordial darkness gives rise to cognition" means that the primordial darkness is the cause, while the five great elements and so forth are the effect.
Regarding "the primary truth and the dependent truth": the primary is the cause; the dependent is the fruit. A sutra states:
"Within the Buddha-dharma there is nothing to be contested; the Tathāgata is real. Outside of the reality of the Buddha-dharma, there is nothing else that is real.
Since various things are taught as being real outside [of it], yet they are not the true Buddha-dharma, [the latter alone] is without such [contradiction].
Eighth, regarding [the argument] based on physical form: as in the sutras, jars, garments, vehicles, and so forth, all proceed from the subtle to the manifest.
A jar arises from clay; a garment from thread; a vehicle from wood. All of these are existent. If they were impermanent, they should not increase moment by moment.
Regarding the characteristics of the great earth: because they are fully accomplished, all things are eternal. If they were impermanent, there would necessarily be interruption.
Third, regarding the reliance on pure vessels: the vessels of humans, devas, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Dharma-body are pure.
Eighth, regarding the basis of companions: because there is a self, one knows there are companions. If it were impermanent, who would know of these companions?
As the preceding sutra states, "like a person carrying a heavy burden," if it were impermanent, its activity would not endure; therefore, we know it is [the self].
"Permanence.

Regarding the phrase "The view of a permanent self is the primary root of all attachments" in the latter part of the *Śrāvakabhūmi* (or *Śaṅxing pin*), it means that all non-Buddhist doctrines take the notion of a permanent self as their foundation; now, however, its... [text fragment ends]
Because it is constantly delighted in purity and departs by itself, it is called "abbreviated.

As for this calculation arising in opposition to the mental object (dharmadhātu) and the mind: when the sense organ and its object encounter one another and transition into the stage of the mind, this is precisely birth from conditions.
This refers to establishing what is correct by contrasting it with what is incorrect. It establishes that the Buddha’s non-arising is correct, extensively refuting the errors of the non-Buddhists.
Because it negates their views of annihilationism and eternalism, it states that [the Buddha] "comes and goes" and so forth, yet is not subsumed within the three periods of time.

The old interpretation that "the Buddha-nature of the future fruit" is therefore neither arising nor ceasing is incorrect, for the explicit text of the sutra does not refer to the future and so forth.
How, then, can it be called the "future fruit"?
If one perceives this principle, it is the principle of the Three Jewels as a single essence.
The Sūtra says: "It is not produced by causes, nor is it produced without cause. Some reckon it as spontaneous;

some reckon it as annihilation or permanence, or as a creator-lord—hence the term "creator. Some reckon it as colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white—hence the term "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Some reckon it as arising from atoms, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), or parents; [it is] neither named nor nameless—thus they reckon.
The heterodox views always take that which exists as "named existence" (*nāma*), while they reckon things such as annihilation as "named non-existence" (*anāma*).
Regarding the phrase "neither form, neither long, nor short": it may be that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are taken as the self;

thus, being neither form, nor long, but possessing only the designation of a "divine self" (*ātman*), it is called "not short. Furthermore, some reckon the self as pervading the entire body and call it "long," while others reckon it to be like the size of a thumb.
This is termed "short.
The Sūtra says, "Later, one sees something similar. That which externalists calculate as a continuous succession of before and after is termed "permanent";
yet they fail to realize that the difference in time is itself impermanence. This error is no small matter; to choose the minor while overlooking the major is a grave mistake.
Furthermore,
as for the icchantika’s belief in "action" and lack of belief in "non-action": the icchantika believes in impure (sāsrava) wholesome deeds,
which they designate as "action," but they do not believe in the Mahāyāna’s pure (anāsrava) non-action.

As for what kind of non-action (*avijñapti*) is being realized: whether small or great, if one follows the practice of the noble precepts as previously described, one cultivates the fivefold pure precepts with the mind of Great Parinirvāṇa;
thereby, one encompasses both the small and great precepts, which is precisely what is meant here by the "intention of non-action."
However, this passage clarifies only the four great elements and the five colors. This means that the two types—mind and form—are treated as the five colors.
Form consists of the four great elements, while mind is non-manifest form (avijñapti-rūpa); therefore, they are said to be five.
The eleven types of matter explained below consist of the five sense organs, the five objects, and unmanifest form (*avijñapti*).

The statement that they "appear reciprocally on one side rather than being restricted to a single location" means that while the five sense organs mentioned here are not without their corresponding objects,
the objects mentioned in the subsequent passage are likewise not without their corresponding organs and unmanifest form.

The Sūtra states that "the visual consciousness is distinct [from the others]. This means that the eye itself corresponds with visible forms, and so on, up to the mind corresponding with mental phenomena (*dharma*).
Since one faculty cannot possess the functions of all the faculties simultaneously, they are said to be "distinct. If these were permanent, there could be no such distinction;
therefore, it is said that they are impermanent.
Furthermore, regarding the differences in appearance and disappearance: among the previous eight [sections], four remain here while the other four texts differ from those before.
The phrase "not refuting" applies to the four texts beginning with "based on causes" (*hetu*). The character "not refuting" (*bùpò*) extends through the subsequent sections beginning with "Mǐnshēng."
The Sūtra states that whatever one recites or chants should not increase.
If it were eternal, one should not say that it proceeds from one Āgama to another. "Āgama" means "incomparable Dharma. Since there is increase, it is therefore impermanent.
First, regarding "the prior birth being before and the subsequent birth being after": as the Sūtra says, "its meaning has already been revealed" refers to that which is prior;
"it shall again be for you" refers to that which is subsequent.

Regarding the eighth point, "the difference between destruction and conjunction": when this aggregate (skandha) ceases and that aggregate arises, it is called "conjunction. This refers to the cessation of the intermediate state (antarābhava).
This is because these aggregates arise again.
As for "privately obtaining this statement," it refers merely to names such as "permanence" and "bliss.
Regarding "that which has already been answered in the seventh fascicle," this refers to the answer given in the "Chapter on the Four Perversions" within the seventh sutra.
Regarding the "notes" (*ji*): perhaps there were separate chapters or notes that are no longer extant.
As for the statement "suffering and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure are likewise," this means that within the three types of sensation (*vedanā*), there is no self (*ātman*) whatsoever.

The Sūtra states, "those who grasp but a small portion within the Buddha-dharma. This refers to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who also contemplate the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as being with outflows (*sāsrava*) and sever afflictions;
hence, it is called "small.
"Destroying the preceding discriminating mind" means destroying the minds that discriminate among the four truths, the two truths, or the one truth, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the practice of wisdom is destroyed" and so forth: my intention here is not to accept the interpretation of others, as it involves successive contradictions.
Since the practice of wisdom is situated at the very end, if the preceding stages have not been destroyed, how could the subsequent one be affected?
Regarding the statement that "if the five elements are destroyed, there is nothing to be cultivated": the Sage and the Brahma-Heaven are the cause, while the heavenly realms are the fruit.
Since the cause has been destroyed, how could the fruit remain? Therefore, they do not exist.

It should be understood that this passage clarifies the practice of the Perfect and Complete Wisdom practitioner. Regarding the seventh of the seven Two Truths mentioned in the preceding text, as well as the Perfect and the Single Real Truth:

if one discusses their sequential order, they belong to the stage prior to the ten stages (bhūmi) in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*), specifically the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

To cultivate this passage within the subsequent mind constitutes the Perfect Stage of the First Abode (*prathama-vihāra*). According to the intent of the scriptural text, its sequence is discussed in terms of the stage prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*).

This refers to ascending sequentially to the first stage, the First Abode (*prathama-vihāra*). Furthermore, the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) presents seven layers of the two truths (*satyadvaya*) and applies them here to interpret this sutra, which differs slightly from that approach.
That text takes the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*) as its basis and opens up the preceding six layers to unify them into a single perfect reality.

Here, however, we discuss the sequential [teaching], interpreting the seven layers without yet addressing their unification prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). When it comes to the non-sequential [teaching], it refers to the very beginning of the first stage, the First Abode.
This is why. As for "initially initiating," it refers to initiating the preceding conditions so that the Tathāgata would speak; thus, Mañjuśrī serves as the starting point for the request.

Regarding the phrase "Now, furthermore, he turns [to explain] the single, ultimate truth": "now" (fāng) means "should" (dāng); "furthermore" (gèng) refers to what has already been explained previously.

The "single" [truth] is entrusted to Mañjuśrī to lament those who have not yet attained realization. Those who have not yet attained realization are the assembly of fifty-two bodhisattvas; that is to say, regarding the Tathāgata...
He has come to enter parinirvāṇa; therefore it is said, "How can nirvāṇa be non-nirvāṇa?
Second, the text challenges Mañjuśrī as one who has not yet attained realization, as the sūtra says: "The Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging, and does not enter parinirvāṇa;
why do you say that the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa?"
The phrase "traversing all seven matters" refers to taking cause and effect as those matters.
As for "vertical integration," this is designated as "vertical" solely in reference to the ultimate, profound penetration realized by the Tathāgata.

Since the preceding text has already shown that phenomena are identical to principle, it causes the horizontal to enter the vertical and the vertical to enter the horizontal; thus, the horizontal and vertical are non-dual, constituting the exclusive realm of the Buddha.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "one does not repeat because the differences have already been clarified," this is distinguished by contrasting the present with the past. Since it was never previously turned [in the past], how can one say it is repeated?

For example, if one has traveled from the house of the Wang family to the house of the Zhang family, and then returns again to the house of the Wang family to travel there once more—this is what is meant here.

This means that what I previously taught as the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) has now been transformed into the teaching of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna); therefore, it is said that there is no "renewal" (or "change").
As for why it is said there is no renewal because they are identical: the turning of the Wheel of Dharma in the past is precisely the turning of it now; there is no difference between them.
Since difference itself is non-difference, why speak of "renewal"?
The difference regarding the four virtues is explained in terms of practice; there are those that are middling and those that are superior.
The difference regarding the pervasiveness of the eight sounds lies in their horizontal and vertical distinctions as they pervade the ten directions.

The Sūtra states that those of inferior capacity are *icchantikas*. This refers to those among humans and devas who possess mundane goodness but lack the karmic affinity for the Three Vehicles to inspire the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
Regarding the phrase "beginning well and ending well": only the sages can truly be said to have both a beginning and an end.
Regarding the statement that the former Buddha concluded the *zongtong* (the transmission of the essence): this refers to the Tathāgata’s address to Kāśyapa on behalf of Mañjuśrī;
it is the later lineage of Kāśyapa. The Tathāgata’s separate conclusion pertains exclusively to the various practices of all Buddhas; therefore, it is called "separate."
Regarding the Tathāgata’s opening of the knots: "opening" means revealing. It refers to the practices cultivated by the five types of sick persons as well as by bodhisattvas and others.
As for the fact that those of the two vehicles possess the principle of cultivation, it is because their noble conduct of precepts is discussed according to a sequential order; thus it is so named.
This refers to cultivation.

As for the "Bodhisattva of Crude Expedient Means," although such a Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka has not yet severed the afflictions, they are nonetheless categorized as being in the stage of "sickness-practice" (vyādhi-caryā),
just like those of the Two Vehicles.
"All have been cured" means that Bodhisattvas who hear this sutra and give rise to perfect faith and understanding reach the first stage (Prathamabhūmi);
hence it is said they are "cured.
"Entering this Dharma-gate" refers to the perfect practice of the Tathāgata.
Regarding this sequence of knots: it consists of five successive stages.
From the first stage to the sixth stage constitutes the first ground; from the seventh stage to the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā) constitutes the second ground.

Regarding "those with sharp and swift penetration of the Way": "penetration" refers to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and "Way" refers to the path of transformation. From the seventh stage onward, one is able to exercise the transformative functions of supernormal powers.
Regarding "those with dull penetration of the Way":

this refers to the difficulty in understanding the preceding text according to our own school's interpretation; following the passage on precepts and meditative concentration, it does not allow for such immovability.
Since it is already established that the names of the two stages are thus, and they are both fruits of the same stage, why should they not also extend as far as the profound Cloud of Dharma?
Therefore, it is said that the two stages extend to the Cloud of Dharma. These two stages consist solely of the two [stages] beginning with the Immovable (Acalā).

Now, to clarify that these constitute a single stage: although there are three different names—such as Immovable, Fearless, and so forth—the application of each name according to its respective context is identical in realizing the first bhūmi.
"Should not be opened again" refers to a repeated censure of past scholars; it means that the two stages should not be opened, thereby further establishing the fruit of wisdom (*prajñā-phala*).
As for this text being consistent with the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, it means that the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* is also called the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*.
Regarding those whose names differ slightly: this sutra speaks of "fearlessness toward greed and anger," whereas that [other] text names it "the absence of fear regarding livelihood.
As for the first, "fear regarding livelihood," it refers to the worldly requisites used to sustain the body; now, one realizes the Dharma-body.
Therefore, there is no lack of livelihood.

Second, regarding the absence of fear of death: it is said that as long as one possesses a body in this world, there is death and so forth. Now, since one has already departed from these two types of death, there is no fear of death.

Third, regarding the absence of fear of the evil realms: having realized the first stage (*bhūmi*), one will certainly not enter the sufferings of the three miserable paths; therefore, it is called "fearlessness.
Fourth, regarding the absence of fear of ill repute: a Bodhisattva of the first stage never slanders the Vaipulya sutras nor commits the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*).
Therefore, there is no fear of ill repute.
Fifth, regarding the absence of fear concerning lack of great majesty and virtue: before realizing the first bhūmi, one lacks understanding regarding others, which is termed "fear.
Once the dharmakāya is attained, one is able to subdue both internal and external [obstacles], and thus possesses sovereign fearlessness within the great assembly.

Regarding "the absence of fear of death is permanence": if these five fears are discussed in their proper sequence, they constitute the departure from the limited, segmented [death] within the realms.
Now, this first stage is precisely the name for the four virtues—permanence and so forth—which consist of departing from both the internal and external deaths of the realms.
Regarding the phrase "the various kings of samādhis" and so forth: samādhi is a single [state], yet it is designated as "various" according to its different ways of destroying delusions.
Although there are these various names, they are all one and the same king of samādhis.

Regarding the comprehensive inclusion of all samādhis: the aforementioned successive four truths, the sevenfold two truths, and so forth, are all subsumed within this primary, perfect samādhi of ultimate truth.

Regarding the statement that the light of the sun and the light of the moon serve as the benefit for humanity: the sun is able to cause the hundred things to grow and bring joy to people, which is the generation of wholesome roots (*kuśala-mūla*).

The moon is able to provide coolness, which is the samādhi of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); it accomplishes the samādhi of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the samādhi of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), all of which are capable of generating the principle of wholesome roots.
Regarding the statement that "non-retrogression, joy, and so forth" constitute the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*):

because animals are subject to retrogression, the attainment of this non-retrogressive samādhi now destroys the retrogression of thoughts, the retrogression of [afflictions as numerous as] the sands of the Ganges, and the retrogression of ignorance; therefore, it is called "non-retrogression.
Furthermore, the ability of joy to eliminate suffering is itself a counteractive measure.
First, regarding the explanation of all existing faults and afflictions: in general discourse, the three delusions are discussed; in specific discourse, the four destinies are the most grave.
Second, regarding the merit of the fundamental dharma: this refers to that which is realized as the foundation, and is thus termed the "fundamental dharma."
Regarding the third, "the accomplishment of the practice of the three fetters": this refers to realizing the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and being able to enter the first bhūmi.

Regarding the fourth, "compassion destroying existence": this refers to giving rise to the four great vows from the first bhūmi onward, teaching and transforming sentient beings across hundreds of buddha-worlds by uprooting their suffering and bestowing happiness upon them.
Regarding "other realms of rebirth," the sutra provisionally cites the single realm of the hells as an illustration for all realms; this is a general statement within the specific.
As for "concluding by comparing the lower to the high": while the virtues of the lower stages are thus illustrated, the height of the Buddha-fruit stage is truly ineffable.
Regarding the question, "The merits of these bodhisattvas are all equal," the intent of the inquiry is:

since both the Buddha and the bodhisattvas have equally realized the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), why is there still inequality with those below? This current interpretation differs from that of other commentators.

Regarding the question, "How can there be any fixed determination of horizontal and vertical?"—the intention of the ancients was that "horizontal" refers to equality, while "vertical" refers to the presence of degrees of depth.
If this were so, it would again result in a lack of fixed determination; how, then, could one speak of equality? Now, if we discuss equality, within the horizontal there is the vertical.

The vertical and the middle are established; the non-duality of the horizontal and the vertical is called "equality. This does not mean there is no distinction between high and low. For example, in a great carriage, the height and breadth are non-dual;
this is its equality. To travel in the four directions is its horizontality; to proceed directly to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is its verticality.
The non-duality of the horizontal and the vertical is the very body of the carriage; it possesses the name "Great Carriage. Thus one contemplates it.
They ride the Great Vehicle, even unto the ultimate Great Vehicle; hence it is said that there are "high and low.
That the Mother can give birth to children means that true wisdom acts as the mother capable of producing the true sons of the Buddha—namely, the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect [Teaching].
The Sūtra says, "As you have said," and my intention is likewise: the teaching that takes the Dharma as the teacher is precisely what is meant by the phrase "the Dharma is thus.

Kaishan claims that regarding the analogy of the teachings of the five periods, although there are names for these five periods, they are worlds apart from our present school's position. Furthermore...
The *Bian zhongshicheng* (Discrimination of the Initial Formation) establishes five periods beginning with the Deer Park; this is refuted in detail below.

Regarding the citation of the "Ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*) chapter of the *Śāstra*, the intention of the ancients was to cite it as proof that the *Prajñāpāramitā* culminates in *nirvāṇa*, which is the ultimate.
According to the present school’s usage, however, this is merely the limit [of the previous teachings]. Those of dull faculties have not yet entered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Alternatively, there may be those who later realize the small fruits [of the path], and it is further taught that through the refinement of Prajñā, they arrive at Nirvāṇa.
As for hearing about the "permanent," what does this have to do with the sequence of the five periods?
If that were so, the previous objections would be briefly refuted.
Regarding the twelve divisions of the Hīnayāna Piṭaka, they establish five periods as four collections (*piṭaka*).
As for the *sūtra* being the *kṣudraka-piṭaka*, it is called "miscellaneous" because the *sūtra* category encompasses both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the latter two [categories] as being based on principle (*li*): the intention is that "principle" refers to the Buddha-treasury (*buddhagarbha*).

As for the statement that "Prajñāpāramitā attains the fruit of Nirvāṇa," since cause and effect are phenomena (*dharma*), how could they be called "principle"? Therefore, these are not employed [in this context].
"One who studies these twelve [treatises] will understand the sūtras" means that one grasps the *Xingxiu Cidijing Lun* (Treatise on the Stages of Practice) regarding the five periods.
"The Vaipulya [sūtras] give rise to the Prajñā[pāramitā]" intends to say that wisdom arises from the teachings.
Regarding "from the many to the few" and so forth: this refers to the twelve divisions of the canon as the "many," and the single phrase on *nirvāṇa*—the Buddha-nature—as the "few.
However, one does not realize that *nirvāṇa* is the single flavor of the finest cream (*amṛta*), which contains all flavors; therefore, *nirvāṇa* is vast.
The arguments are all incorrect; this is a general refutation of various interpretations.

How could it be that only the "Lesser" [school] is at fault? First, the Kai-she school’s claim that the Lesser [Avataṃsaka] is not the initial teaching has already been refuted, as we now take the Avataṃsaka itself to be the initial teaching;
therefore, they are not accepted.
As for the question, "Do other sūtras not also have prose sections?"—the name *sūtra* applies universally to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Other sūtras likewise contain prose;
why should it be addressed to the *Prajñāpāramitā* alone?

Furthermore, regarding your contradiction of the sequence of the five periods: you previously established your own system of the five periods of the sūtras, wherein you designated the *Prajñāpāramitā* as the second period.
How can it then be reached as the fourth period in the *Nirvāṇa*? Thus, your earlier and later statements are mutually contradictory.
As for the lamentation regarding other sutras: those are the preliminary teachings on the principle of cause and effect; these were spoken by way of concession and are not the present sutra.
As for what is not praised in the text: if one follows the sequence of liberation, it is not the teaching of this text; the King of the Treasury and his followers merely lament in vain.
That which is not subject to praise, you say is "supreme"; this is precisely what is meant by "extensive. How can you say it is "concise"?
If it were concise, it would not be fit for praise. Since it is now praised, it must therefore be extensive.
Regarding the phrase "unaware that one has missed the true teaching by a mere inch": the eternal Buddha-nature in this present sutra constitutes its true teaching.
The interpretations of various masters have all lost its essence within this very teaching; yet, as the literal text still appears in their expositions, it is said to be "a mere inch" away.
"The story of 'learning to walk from Handan and gaining nothing from either' is an account found in the *Zhuangzi*.
There was a person who went to the region of Handan to learn how the people there walked; he returned crawling on all fours, having lost both ways of moving.

When the ancients categorized the teachings, those who studied the doctrines of the five periods of the Buddha's teaching likewise lost both the preceding and the succeeding stages, gaining nothing from either."
Those who exhaust the profound and reach the ultimate subtlety enter the perfect from the gradual. The profound depth and vastness of the principle of perfection is called "exhausting the profound";
that which encompasses everything within the essence of *amṛta* (clarified butter) is called "subtle."
One who attains the Dharma of *amṛta* (the supreme essence) and becomes a person of *amṛta* is a perfected Bodhisattva.
As for the various dharmas in the interim, from milk to clarified butter (*ghṛta*), all four stages of flavor successively become *amṛta*; therefore, they are called "dharmas.
"Dharma" refers here to the teaching, while "flavor" refers to the temporal sequence; both ultimately converge in the eternal and unchanging.

If one looks toward a single period (*ikki*), the former was based on the sequence of the five periods of the *Sūtra of Praise*, whereas the present is based on the Tathāgata’s pedagogical methods throughout his entire life;
hence, it is called a "single period."
"When beings were unable to endure the Great [Teaching], he then preached the Small": "Beings" refers to those with the karmic capacities of beings.

When the śrāvakas sat in the assembly as if deaf and mute, the Buddha did not depart from the site of enlightenment (the *śīta-vana*) to convert them at the Deer Park (*mṛgadāva*). As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"He immediately cast off his jeweled necklaces and put on tattered, soiled garments," and so forth.

Regarding the "refutation of the small" (*xiaozhe*) and the "partial disparagement" (*piantan*), as well as the "admiration of the great" (*dantao*) and the "praise of the perfect" (*yuanbao*): we now employ the eight characters of the ancients.
The ancients said, "Refuting the *śrāvakas* and praising the bodhisattvas"—yet this principle was not exhaustive. Now it is said: "Refuting the small" refers to the five classes of *śrāvakas*;

"disparaging the partial" refers to the eight thousand bodhisattvas; and "admiring the great" refers to none other than Mañjuśrī, who alone was able to inquire after the illness, acting in accordance with the Buddha’s sacred intent.
"Praising Yuan" means that the layman Vimalakīrti feigned illness at the Āmra grove (and so forth).

Regarding "the three people hearing together," it means that those of the Three Vehicles sit together upon the bed of liberation; the bodhisattvas of sharp faculties attain entry into the One Reality.

Furthermore, for those who abide in skillful means and have not yet realized the lesser fruits—specifically, the period after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and before the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*—the *Prajñāpāramitā* was still taught.
Therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna path—the term "yāna" meaning "vehicle"—is [the vehicle].

Below the passage concerning the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, it cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which refers to eight thousand śrāvakas who received their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

This is likened to "harvesting in autumn and storing in winter," and so forth. This sūtra also describes this as the "teaching of gathering what was left behind" (*kuṇḍika-śāsana*), upholding the Vinaya while expounding the permanence [of the Buddha-nature].

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the broad inclusion of the precepts is as explained in the text," this is fully detailed in the preceding passage. All the various precepts, both great and small, and the bodhisattva vows are completely fulfilled therein;

there is nothing not fully possessed that corresponds to the stages of bodhisattva practice in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. This is because the beginning [of this text] corresponds to the beginning [of that sūtra].
Therefore, it is said that they do not contradict one another.
Regarding the phrase "for this reason": the merits of the aforementioned five flavors are all inconceivable.

"One who grasps the purport" refers to grasping the previous teaching that the five flavors of the Dharma are identical to the single period of the *tīrtha* (the ultimate essence) of *mākṣika* (ghee).
Second, regarding those who, out of compassion for others, wish to give rise to the great vow: as the sutra says, "He secretly reflects. To reflect is to deliberate within the mind;
to contemplate is to think. Because this has not yet been manifested outwardly, it is called "secretly."
The Sūtra states: "If there are sentient beings who are greedily attached to wealth and goods, this is precisely the practice of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Wealth and goods constitute *dāna* (giving).
Next, if they are those of noble status, this constitutes *priyavāditā* (kind speech). Thereafter, one should gradually employ the Great Nirvāṇa, which constitutes *arthacaryā* (beneficial conduct)."
As for "practice": if one has a fondness [for the Dharma] and even goes there in person, this is "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*).

As the Sūtra says, "searching everywhere for Mahāyāna scriptures," this refers to the fact that because there are latent conditions from past lives, the Mahāyāna awakens within one in a hidden manner;
thus it is called "searching."

The scripture speaks of "the regulation of the Way" (*daojian*). Regarding the character *jian* (pronounced *jiǎn*), according to the *Cāngjié piān*, it means "laws and measures. It also implies "to restrain" or "to encompass.
This refers to the passage in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* stating, "If one enters the correct position (*samyaktva-niyāma*) of the śrāvaka," and so forth.
Next, regarding the three combined trials: first, he will test his wisdom with half a verse, combining them like burning;
second, he will manifest a terrifying form, combining them like beating; third, he will demand his body, combining them like grinding. If one can endure these trials, it is known that he is genuine.
If the mind is firm and stable, it rests as if in emptiness.
Regarding "the abiding dharma not being manifest," this means that because the abiding dharma is considered permanent, its meaning of impermanence cannot be manifested; therefore, it is omitted.
Regarding the teaching that speaks only of one side, impermanence: if one perceives impermanence and thereby knows that permanence exists, this constitutes wisdom.
It is as when the "Noble Practice of Precepts" is taught, one immediately knows that concentration and wisdom exist, and so forth, up to the single reality and non-sequential [teachings].
Therefore, the meaning of the partial text explained previously is identical to this.
The reply states: "As for those who say this is the abiding of the impermanent, this abiding is not a permanent abiding; it is indeed impermanent.
Regarding 'the permanence of non-abiding' (and so forth), the intended answer is as you have described: there is also the permanence of the Mahāyāna, which is precisely non-abiding."
The text states: "Regarding the meaning of emptiness as explained, it refers to such things as the sūtras' opening of the path of the dharma of emptiness and so forth.
As for the phrase "taking the path as the standard," this means that the essence of *nirvāṇa* answers questions without fixed direction; it accords with whatever you may say.
It may be said that the Way is simply this. Regarding what is analogous and what is not: if one does not answer such a question, it is incorrect.

What is truly intended by "removing birth and removing extinction" is to remove the birth of ordinary beings and to remove the extinction of the Two Vehicles; therefore, it is called "quiescent extinction" (nirvāṇa).

Chapter Twenty: Explanation of the "Brahmacarya" Chapter.

When various masters claim that the four minds constitute the essence of the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*), they implicitly refute why the seven wholesome factors (*saptakuśala*) are not so considered.
As for the statement that "the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are the path to the Brahma-heavens," the "four minds" refers to the four contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds within the desire realm.
"Brahma" means purity; "heaven" refers to the causal path of the four dhyānas, which is the principle of the True Truth (*satyadharma*). This explains the principle of the Four Noble Truths.
This is called "turning the wheel of Dharma" and constitutes the ultimate heaven (*paramārtha-deva*).

Regarding the statement that the four minds are the twelve-gate dhyāna, which is concentration (*samādhi*): because these four minds can give rise to concentration, the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) constitute the twelve gates.
"Knowledge is wisdom" means that "knowledge" refers to *jñāna* (wisdom). Since all seven types of goodness can employ wisdom, it is said they are "complete.

"Brahman" refers to transforming others, while "sagehood" (*āryatva*) refers to one's own practice. This is a preliminary discussion of the preceding sages' writings in terms of their lateral and vertical dimensions.

All [these] give rise to transformative functions upon the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*); these are still transformations for the sake of others. Looking at present compassion, they are provisionally called "self-cultivation," whereas here they are called "transforming others.
Since they are spoken of from the perspective of their cause, they also include self-cultivation.
Regarding the "accomplishment of the characteristics of the precepts": this refers to the accomplishment of wisdom through the preceding two [precepts].

"Noble" (ārya) means that which is practiced by noble ones; this is stated according to the realization [of the fruit], for even ordinary persons tread the path of the noble ones and practice the pure way.

Furthermore, regarding the Master’s statement that cause and effect constitute the essence (*tattva*) of the holy life (*brahmacarya*): in our view, how can cause and effect—which are merely phenomena—be designated as an "essence"?

As for the phrase "not the Great Nirvāṇa," the intent is to refute others; for this [holy life] consists of mundane, outflow-tainted goodness (*sāsrava-kuśala*), so how could it be the Great [Nirvāṇa]?
Regarding the essence of *nirvāṇa*: that which takes the three categories as its essence refers to the three of precept, concentration, and wisdom.
As for "not transcending the two vehicles," it means that although the two vehicles also cultivate these three categories, they cannot constitute the essence of this present sutra.

Regarding those who still maintain the existence of cause and effect: since we have now refuted that the essence of nirvāṇa is neither cause nor effect, how could it further take cause and effect as its essence while being capable of producing them?

"Who is this practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārin*)?"—this refers to the various masters' explanations as to whether this is the holy life of the two vehicles, or the holy life of a bodhisattva who cultivates the emptiness of partiality; thus it asks, "Who?"
Regarding "the purity of purity": although those of the Two Vehicles are called "pure" when compared to ordinary beings, their purity is not yet pervasive throughout the essence of nirvana.
To purify that purity so that it becomes pervasive is ultimate emptiness; therefore, it is called "the purity of purity."
Regarding "purifying the impure": the phenomena of the world are themselves impure; because I am able to purify them, it is called "purifying the impure.
Regarding "neither pure nor impure": this is the essence of the Middle Way, which is neither pure nor impure.
What is called "supernatural power" (abhijñā) refers to inconceivable resonance and response— responding without being prompted and responding without being sought,
and so forth, as explained extensively in the subsequent text.
"Neither cause nor fruit" means neither pure nor impure.
"Neither self nor other" means that the inconceivable conventional is impure yet capable of being purified.
"Neither defiled nor pure" means that the ultimate essence is capable of purifying all things, which are themselves inherently pure. Thus, it is the purity of purity itself.
If these three types of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) were such, they would be the loving-kindness of the three successive truths and of the two vehicles;

therefore, they are not "wondrous" (*miaoyan*) and so forth. That which is one yet three is this non-successive loving-kindness, called the inconceivable, perfect, and wondrous loving-kindness. Therefore, below...
The text contains thirteen points that praise the inconceivable.
Regarding the initial inquiry: as in the sutra, it consists of the two characters "how" (云何) found below the words "Good son" (善男子).
Regarding the first three [superknowledges] being both for oneself and others: this means that when one masters the dharma and its meaning for others, it is simultaneously for oneself.
Regarding the latter two being for others: because there is a multitude of people, one thereby knows their status as superior or inferior; thus, they are said to be "for others."
This means that while the primary focus is transforming others, it also includes one's own practice. The four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) take compassion (*karuṇā*) as their foundation;

thus, it is not that self-practice is absent. If the "Chapter on Noble Practice" (*Ārya-caryā-varga*) primarily concerns self-practice with the transformation of others as secondary—since one is able to employ transformative means upon reaching the stages (*bhūmi*)—then here too, we discuss what is primary and secondary in relation to that.

Regarding the explanation of the five meanings: both those with translations and those without possess these five meanings, as explained extensively in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra).
As for "sūtra" (*qi jing*), it means that which accords with principle and accords with the capacities of sentient beings.

The *Shènglùn* (Treatise on the Establishment) states: "Regarding *geya*, which are verses that restate the *sūtra*: this refers to those *sūtras* outside of the eleven divisions [of the canon] that are restated in verse.
These are cases where the Buddha spoke of matters concerning offerings or other specific circumstances (*nidāna*), and were later versified;
hence they are called 'distinct' (*bīé*)."
Regarding "a phrase consisting of a number [of syllables]," it means four syllables constitute a phrase. It is also called a "verse" (gāthā), which refers to a verse that summarizes the prose.
Kaishan says that "equal phrases" (tulyapada) refers to verses that are equalized as equal phrases.

Guangzhai says that "repeated verses" (geya) refers to those who recite in verse; this is explained according to the capacities of those who are dull and those who are sharp. For those of dull capacity, the Four Truths are explained in full.
For those of sharp capacity, they are explained again later on. Passages such as "not seeing the four true truths" in the sutra are instances where the names of the Four Truths are abbreviated.
Regarding verses in prose (gāthā): as explained in the treatises, a verse consists of thirty-two syllables according to the sūtras;
alternatively, it may consist of three, five, or more syllables that capture the essential meaning of the subject matter discussed.
The treatise states that the *Arthaviniścaya-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Explanation of Meaning) is precisely what is taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Regarding the bestowal of predictions for the six destinies and the three vehicles: the six destinies constitute the general prediction (*sāmānya-vyākaraṇa*), while the three vehicles constitute the specific prediction (*viśeṣa-vyākaraṇa*).
As the sūtra provides specific predictions, [the treatise] explains them by correlating the specific with the general, as in the case of Maitreya and others.
One explanation states that "unequal lines" (visama-pada) refers to being unequal to the prose (gadya). It is likewise the case for verses (śloka);
those which have distinct lines are called "unequal."
"Except for those verses that are applied to prose" means: setting aside the characteristics described in the prose, there are subsequently verses;
thus they are said to be "applied. When there is something distinct to be expressed, it is called a "solitary verse" (gūqǐ).
Regarding this verse from the *Dharmapada*, it is as explained at length in the *Dharmapada-sūtra*.

Now, as for the fact that the *Jātaka* (Birth Stories) and the *Itivṛttaka* (Past Deeds) are not distinct: it is simply that within the *Itivṛttaka* there are "births" (*jāti*), and within "births" there are "deeds" (*vṛtta*).
Combining "deeds" with "birth" constitutes the ninth [category]; combining "birth" with "deeds" constitutes the eighth. This is because of such statements as these. Now...
Because they are explained according to their opening [teachings], they are divided into eight or nine categories.
The *Śāstra* states that "extensive" (*vaipulya*) refers to the twelve divisions of the Hīnayāna, while "vast and extensive" (*vaipulya*) refers to the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna.

If discussed separately, the twelve divisions within the Hīnayāna consist only of nine and lack the three categories such as the *Vaipulya*, *Upadeśa*, and so forth; whereas the twelve divisions within the Mahāyāna do not [lack these].
The three conditions are metaphors for phenomena.
"Unprecedented" refers to rare events that do not exist in the world.

Regarding the meaning of emptiness and equality in the twelve divisions of the scriptures: the "scriptures" are the written words, termed the "expressive," while the "meaning" is that which is expressed.
"Exposition" refers to the meaning of the Middle Way; hence it is called "equality.
"Explaining immeasurable meanings" refers to inconceivable conventionality. "Ultimate purity" refers to inconceivable emptiness.
Regarding the sense that "the momentum is all-pervasive": this means that the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*) are identical within a single principle.

Most of the remaining phrases pertain to one's own practice (*sva-caryā*). While one's own practice is not devoid of transformative activity for others, for the time being, among the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), the transformation of others is primary, while the others are predominant [in their own practice].
The Sūtra states that "one who knows contentment" does not mean that merely possessing the four requisites constitutes contentment;
rather, regarding all sentient beings within the ten dharma realms, one must know [the measure] in both their staying still and their advancing.
As it is said of Zengzi: "I daily examine myself three times," and as the *Analects* states: "I daily examine my own person three times. "Examine" (*sheng*) means to inspect.
This refers to my examining my own transgressions three times throughout my life; this is synonymous with the meaning of "self-knowledge" (*zizhi*).
Regarding the expedient path of the Two Vehicles: it is a stage of semblance-understanding where true cultivation has not yet occurred.
In this manner, as each successive stage alternates between superior and inferior, that which is characterized by faith is superior, while that which lacks faith is inferior;
this extends even to the Bodhisattvas of the ten realms being considered inferior, and so forth.
Regarding those among the noble ones, sages, and devas: in the first three teachings, the stage of skillful means is called "noble" (賢), while the fruits of the three vehicles are termed "sage" (聖).
The goodness of the Perfect Teaching (圓教) is the most supreme and honored among these.
It is one category within the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Among the three categories, the category of wisdom (*prajñā*) is explained first; therefore, it is called "one.

As for the statement that "because the mind of self has a single characteristic, it is called 'equal'": although there are many objects, the mind universally takes them as its object, and thus it is called "equal.
The objects are termed "immeasurable," yet the mind itself is termed "single" because it possesses a single characteristic.
Regarding the phrase "the object is also called 'equal'": it is equal to the mind.
Regarding "the mind is also immeasurable": it is equal to the object. Thus, because the mind is equal and the object is equal, they are termed "one characteristic."
Regarding the subsequent clarification of the fruit of the mind: the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are precisely what is intended by the correct explanation in this chapter.
As for the difficulty of making [the mind] one: the capacity to take the three objects as its focus is, in fact, a single mind.
"To have but a single meaning" refers to that which is capable of being the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
If one knows that sentient beings must know the Tathāgata and so forth, it is because sentient beings are themselves the knowledge of suffering,
while the Tathāgata is the knowledge of bliss.
As for from what the five aggregates arise: they arise from the things required by conventional designations (*prajñapti*).
As for "even up to taking the Buddha as the superior object": this means that when one takes the Buddha as the superior [object], and possesses the two aforementioned objects, there are then three.
First, regarding the refutation of the attachment to a fixed set of four: the four that I now speak of are also not four. Why? Because their objects of perception differ.
For what reason do you insist on the difficulty of establishing them as exactly four?

Next, in response to the objection regarding the absence of four [categories]: if even the name "four" does not exist, why do you object to the fixed numbers of three, two, one, and so forth, given that the tenets held differ?
Regarding the lack of fixed breadth or brevity: it is as when the Buddha taught the twelve links of dependent origination; he sometimes spoke of them as one or two, and sometimes as...
"Four up to eleven," etc.
Second, explaining the reversal of the ordinary and the indeterminate: for example, the four foundations of mindfulness and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the constant dharmas;
yet the Tathāgata reverses them, stating that purity is impurity and permanence is impermanence, and so forth—this is called the reversal of the ordinary.
The Sūtra says that when one speaks of "one cause and condition," it refers to the twelve [links] being combined into a single cause; they are all equally conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The Sūtra says that "two kinds of causes and conditions and their fruits" means that past ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) serve as the cause for the present.
This constitutes the fruit; it is fully subsumed within the three periods of time.
Regarding the *Nagarasūtra* mentioned in the scripture—some call it the *Dicheng jing*, others the *Daobai cheng jing*.

As for the statement in the scripture that "it speaks of non-entities as entities": the defilements of the world are not actually entities, yet they are spoken of as such; [they are described as] blue, yellow, red, and so forth.
That which is called "white" is designated as a thing; to be able to penetrate this thing is precisely to realize it is not a thing.
When the sutra says, "To speak of the unreal as real," those of the Mahayana call this "arousing the real," yet they conversely describe it as being real.
Regarding "the real is said to be unreal": for the two vehicles, that which is real is conversely said to be unreal.
Regarding "that which is not an object is said to be an object": when wisdom has not yet arisen, it is termed "not an object"; at the time when wisdom exists, it is termed an "object.
Because the object and wisdom are unified, the object is said to be "not an object."
The Sūtra states: "That which is described as form is not form. That which is not form is the mind; the entire mind is form.
Because form and mind are united, it is said that what is not form is described as form.

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "claiming what is not the Path to be the Path," those of the Two Vehicles designate it as the Path; because their path is not ultimate, the [Buddha] describes that path as not being the Path.
"The retributions obtained are different" refers to the places where they shall be born upon completion [of their practice].

Regarding "attaining universal purity through loving-kindness (*maitrī*)," this refers to the fourth dhyāna heaven. Furthermore, according to the old *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the four [immeasurable] minds extend into the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*);
however, according to the new translations, these four minds exist only within the four dhyānas. These have been matched in sequence accordingly; there are omissions in the text.

Some say that the "receptacle" (bhājana) is the objective field (viṣaya). Since the function of a receptacle is to contain things, and an objective field possesses the sense of containing the mind, and since there are already four [elements] as objective fields, how can there be only three?
This is also not the case. That is to say, this "true and semblance" refers to the true and semblance [stages] of the Mahāyāna; or else, does it refer to the semblance stage of the Hīnayāna?
If it were the Hīnayāna, what would it have to do with the true stage of the Mahāyāna?
The Sūtra states: "The Buddha said there are [beings]. The answer is: there are Bodhisattvas who dwell in Great Nirvāṇa; it does not refer to those with Great Compassion and so forth.

As for "not yet having attained the three grades of happiness among neutral persons," this refers to these three enemies attaining the three successive grades of happiness, while they have not yet attained the three grades among neutral persons or the three grades among friends.
Only later do they attain the three grades among neutral persons and the three grades among friends; therefore, it says "combined."
Regarding "equal" and so forth: since these are enemies, one should provide them with much happiness;
this includes calculating all enemies together with those of the three grades of self and the neutral relatives—namely, the twenty-seven grades of happiness resulting from the three times three.
Furthermore, regarding the direct engagement with the three types of happiness, the previous explanations of "foolishness" do not exceed these two interpretations.
As for the brief mention of four stages of entering contemplation: the first stage consists of one's close relatives; the third stage consists of enemies;
and neutral persons are not discussed, which is why it is called "brief."
The Sūtra states, "Because it is difficult to accomplish," because this refers to the cultivation of the mental application of sequential compassion (*anupūrva-maitrī-manasikāra*).
Therefore, it is said that it is difficult and not the same as the contemplation of perfect compassion (*pariniṣpanna-maitrī*), which is the ultimate uprooting and bestowing [of benefit].
Regarding the perfection of compassion through the eradication of delusions: one contemplates that afflictions are none other than the true mark (dharmatā) and thus perceives no fault in them.
As the Sūtra says, "Compassion like a flash of lightning" refers to a compassion that is momentarily attained but then lost; it is not yet ultimate compassion.
As for not perceiving faults: since there is no further distinction between the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings, what fault could there possibly be?
If one discusses contrariety and compliance, from the afflictions of an ordinary person up to the single grade remaining before Equal Enlightenment, these are still occasions where faults arise.
Now, because one observes all equally with the three types of universal compassion, one does not perceive anger.
The Sūtra speaks of the "Bodhisattva of the First Abode. Previously, it proclaimed the "First Ground" (bhūmi), and subsequently it explains the "First Abode" (vihāra).

Unless one is of the Perfect Teaching (yuan) or the Distinct Teaching (bie), where the paths of realization are identical, how could one otherwise explain this scriptural passage? This is because the "ground" (bhūmi) serves as the basis of support.
The Sūtra says: "Except for that which is unbeneficial. Any compassion, even as small as a single hair's breadth, is beneficial;
this is because it excludes those who do not cultivate it.
The Sūtra says: "If one does not perceive my dharma-characteristics within one's own body," dharma-characteristics are simply what belongs to the self (*ātmiya*). Since there is no self...
"Mine" means that there is no self-body.

The Sūtra says that one who is fully endowed with the six pāramitās is one who possesses the *anabhisamskāra-pāramitā* (the perfection of non-action). Since each single pāramitā contains all six, it is said that "generosity is perfected to its ultimate limit.
The dharma-realm is itself the pāramitā of giving (*dāna*). Being fully endowed with the precepts is the ultimate Mahāyāna precept. [This applies to] meditative concentration (*samādhi*)...
This is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. "Wisdom" refers to the three wisdoms within a single mind, and so forth.
Regarding "the two within equanimity": having seen that sentient beings have attained ultimate bliss, one feels joy throughout the entire dharma-realm. Joy is itself equanimity;
since equanimity is also pervasive, when the mind of equanimity is pervasive, it can bring about great joy. Therefore, it is said there are "two."
Regarding the threefold basis of the intrinsic characteristic: it takes the immeasurable qualities of the world as the basis for generating the resolve [for enlightenment].
Because one directs the mind toward Bodhi and does not cultivate a compassion directed toward Brahmā or other such realms, it is called the "basis."
"This is a provisional designation" means that it strips away the aspect of reality, as sentient beings have not yet attained happiness.
When the Sūtra says, "truly bestowing happiness," this is a concessive statement made by those sentient beings to raise an objection:
"For what reason do sentient beings still experience suffering and fail to experience happiness?"

Regarding the third rebuttal of objections: fearing that the Buddha’s statement might be merely figurative and that he had not actually attained bliss, [the author] cites the Tathāgata’s own attainment of benefit to refute this.
If it were merely a conceptual construction, how could there be a karmic retribution?
The Sūtra says, "Those who are without fear. This is a praise of you, for as a person of inferior station, you are able to ward off the difficulties facing the stage of fruition of a Tathāgata.

The Sūtra says, "If [one practices] even toward a single sentient being. The Buddha’s intention is that if one can attain such loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward even a single sentient being, how much more so [toward many].
I pervade all and bestow ultimate happiness upon all sentient beings; is this not great compassion?
The Sūtra says, "This is called the noble lineage. Compassion is the lineage of the Buddhas; because it can bring about freedom from suffering, it is termed "noble."
Therefore, it is called "planting" [seeds].

The Sūtra says: "It does not equal even one-sixteenth part of practicing a single act of loving-kindness. This means that if one can give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward even a single sentient being, the merit is already vast;

how much more so when one universally directs the three types of loving-kindness with a single mind toward all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, fully possessing even one-sixteenth part [of such merit]?
This is sufficient.

The Sūtra states that "truth" (*satya*) refers to ultimate reality. "Truth" here denotes the principle of reality; based on this principle, compassion arises. This compassion is able to universally take all things as its object, unlike the sequential types of compassion.
"However, it enables those who see [him]": the intention of this master is that the Buddha manifests himself whenever sentient beings are fit to see him.
"One master says" refers to the tradition inherited by our own school; alternatively, it may mean that he is called "one master" as a distinct title.
If one says that all phenomena possess the nature of peace and bliss, how could they be separated from tiles, stones, and sentient beings?
They are also sentient beings.

As for the claim that this meaning is difficult to believe, it refers to those who have not yet realized the non-duality of the dependent and the primary [receptacle world and its inhabitants], and thus say that the three bodies pervade all while remaining separate from insentient things.
Therefore, it is difficult to practice.

As for the phrase "this is eternally revolving": "eternal" means non-eternal. Why? If the two—the environment and its inhabitants (the *niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*)—of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are non-dual, this is called eternal;
the false delusions of sentient beings are not eternal. How would soil and sand differ from the seven treasures?
It is merely according to what one perceives.
If the Buddha-nature is identical to all phenomena, how could it be separated from the sentient and the insentient?
As the Sūtra says, "One who can sever anger and the notion of a sentient being" refers to one who is able, by means of a single mind, to relinquish [all things] throughout the Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, both "self" and "what belongs to self" are ultimately empty.
As for the phrase "merit, tranquility, bliss, and so forth," merit refers to the four dhyānas; because they can subdue the afflictions, they are termed "bliss."
That the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) are precisely *prajñā* refers to the *prajñā* of the three wisdoms within a single mind.

That they are truly the root of goodness means that they serve as the foundation for both the Mahāyāna and the Three Vehicles; by virtue of their unconditioned and immeasurable essence, they are the *dharmadhātu* which universally encompasses all phenomena.

The Sūtra says, "By means of the causes and conditions of giving": with a single mind and the three types of compassion, one gives throughout the entire Dharma-realm to cause beings to attain the bliss of Nirvāṇa.
The Sūtra says, "One must certainly dedicate [the merit]": as the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states, it is like a hot pan; there is no one who comes before it who does not [suffer].

It causes them to burn away. It is the same with the bodhisattva’s production of the mind of awakening: every single hair’s breadth of merit cultivated for the sake of those to be transformed must be dedicated so that they may attain bodhi.
This dedication is also like holding a torch: it can both illuminate oneself and illuminate others. Dedication is just like this.

Regarding the phrase "serving as the basis for the eight matters below": in the subsequent text, one is able to generate vows for each individual matter such that both principle and practice are fully complete.
Because this is not the severance of a bodhisattva, and because giving can eliminate the faults of the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, it is said: "it acts as such a severance."
It is equal [to this].
The Sūtra says, "One constantly practices giving without interruption. This refers to the constant bestowal of all things through objectless compassion (*apraṇihitā maitrī*);
therefore, it is said that there is no giving.

The Sūtra states that one who does not fully possess the *dāna-pāramitā* lacks completeness. The preceding five perfections (*pāramitās*) constitute the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), while the subsequent *prajñā* is termed the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*).
If one grasps at signs and does not incline toward Bodhi, one cannot function as either a conditional or a revealing cause;
because this fails to support the manifestation of the true Dharma-body, it is said to be incomplete.
The arrow is a metaphor for the arising of stinginess. This means that when a person is exhorted to give, it is called "arising"; if there were no such conditions, stinginess would not arise at all.

It is also like the discrimination regarding giving: one does not give to those who are dear, yet is able to give to those who are disliked, and so on, discriminating between much and little. Therefore, it is said:
It is also like bamboo and willow.
As the Sūtra says, "seeing the seed grow large until it can sustain itself" refers to those from the first *vihāra* (stage) upward;
this is what is meant by "growing large."

The Sūtra says, "One who makes such vows as these. Although these practices and vows do not equal the extensiveness found in the *Avataṃsaka*, in the *Avataṃsaka* each individual matter and principle constitutes a vow;
whereas this single vow gives rise to immeasurable Dharma-gates within a single matter, all of which are based upon the four immeasurables.
Thus, both matter and principle are fully complete.
Regarding "each side being four inches": the robes worn by the Tathāgata are each four inches away from the body on all four sides;
therefore, it is said to be one chi and six cun.
This "precept for those without precepts" is precisely the ultimate precept of the Mahāyāna. To transgress this precept is to deviate from the Middle Way.
Because it is empty, it is said to be "non-existent.
As for the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s statement, "precepts like space," this precept is found among the ten precepts of that scripture.
"Precepts with nothing to rely upon" refers to the precepts of the Middle Way, which do not rely on the two extremes.
The Sūtra says, "One who sits in the station of the four dhyānas": the Śūraṅgama Samādhi serves as the basis, and thus it is called a "station.

The Sūtra says, "One who kindles the lamp of the Mahāyāna and leaves behind the oil-lamp of the two vehicles": the character for "lamp" (dìng, pronounced *tìjiàn* in the fanqie notation) is sometimes written as *diàn* or *sù*.
This refers to an object adorned with various jewels; furthermore, it is said that what has a stand is called a "lamp" (*dēng*), while what lacks a stand is called a "lamp" (*dìng*).
