"If sentient beings have not yet seen the Bodhisattva, how can they see him? How can they understand him? Since they have not understood him, this is equivalent to not seeing him;
and since they do not see him, they do not hear him. How then can you say that they hear what was previously unheard?"
The Sūtra asks, "From whom did the Tathāgata hear [the Dharma] in the past? Since there was hearing, there must have been a teacher;
therefore, it asks "from whom.
The Sūtra then says, "[It was] from the Āgamas, etc.," which conversely implies there was no teacher. If there was no teacher, why does it further say that he "heard" it?
It is not heard of.
That which is subtle and invisible refers to things such as the color of atoms (*paramāṇu*) or the forms of spirits and ghosts; therefore, they cannot be seen.
Regarding the case of seeing only one side of a pillar: it is like when a person stands facing east or west beside a pillar, and thus does not see [the other sides].
Sound is also like this: if it is loud, it is not heard from afar; if it is faint, it cannot be heard even when near.
When the Sūtra says, "Having been heard, the sound ceases," the term "heard" refers to that which can be expressed through the meaning of syllables.
A single syllable does not constitute being heard, because by the time the subsequent syllable is uttered, the preceding syllable has already ceased. Therefore, it is asked: how can it be heard?
This constitutes the "praising and answering. First there is praise, followed by the answer. As the sutra says: "Skillfully knowing that all dharmas are like illusions," and so forth;
how could there be any fixed certainty in such things as "not hearing what has been heard"?
From "not seeing blue yet seeing blue" and so forth, up to "an auspicious sign," all are signs of indeterminacy. That which does not come yet comes manifests the Middle Way;
that which is unheard yet heard is the mark of Nirvana. Therefore, it is called an "auspicious sign."

Regarding the fact that these three answers cause the three faculties to be suddenly clarified: first, the response of praise is explained; following this, there are two further responses, hence the mention of "three.

As for the "distinctive answer," it refers to the inquiry concerning the light of lapis lazuli and so forth, which simultaneously answers what was previously heard; therefore, it is called "distinctive."
Furthermore, as for this "light-body," it takes the light of the Middle Way as its essence.
As for this "light-function," it refers to the seeing of blue where there is no blue, and so forth; this answers the previous inquiry of the King of Virtue regarding hearing what has not been heard.
This refers to the function of attaining equal benefit.
First, regarding the manifestation that all phenomena are ineffable: this light is the fundamental essence of principle.
Therefore, the four bodhisattvas successively remained silent, like Vimalakīrti’s silence; all of these manifest the inconceivable.

Second, clarifying the fundamental through provisional words: while the preceding [section] on the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is expressed through non-discourse, this [section] on conventional language (saṃvṛti-śabda) is expressed through words.
The Sūtra states:
"That which is light is precisely the one who recollects the Buddha. This is the single essence of the Triple Gem; therefore, it is said to be eternally abiding.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that there are also causes and conditions; these are precisely the causes and conditions of inconceivable resonance and response.
The essence of Nirvāṇa is an inexpressible treasure, yet for the sake of sentient beings, it can also be expressed.
"Destroying this and establishing that" means to universally destroy and universally establish.

Regarding "that bodhisattva is a Buddha," the Master's intention is as follows: Mañjuśrī and others are all ancient Buddhas who manifest as bodhisattvas to assist the Buddhas in their transformative activities;
therefore, it is said that they possess light. Alternatively, it is said that a bodhisattva at the first stage (prathamabhūmi) partially realizes the Dharmakāya.
There is also the basis of the constant radiance.

That which is not identical to the Buddha-way refers to the four *siddhāntas*. The distinction between this land and that land is the *loka-saṃvṛti* (worldly) perspective. Merely giving rise to correct goodness here is for the sake of others;
eliminating the evils of this land is the *prātipakṣika* (remedial). Causing one to see their nature and attain the Way is the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth).
Regarding this Buddha’s mention of that bodhisattva: it is as the sutra says, "In this great assembly, there was this radiance," and so forth. Question:
This radiance is precisely what is being mentioned.

The same applies to Kāśyapa: it means that he too was met with teachings suited to those of a permanentist disposition, so as to generate roots of goodness in him and lead him into the ultimate truth;
it does not mean that the application of remedies to support the Vinaya was not appropriate for him.
Regarding the phrase "the aforementioned discussion with the Buddha," this refers to Cunda’s discourse with Mañjuśrī in the presence of the Buddha.
As for the phrase "the Dharma does not deviate," it means that Cunda’s formal argument concerning unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas establishes the doctrine of permanence (*nityatā*).
"Coming because there is going and coming" refers to coming from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"Coming because there is no going and coming" refers to coming from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The Sūtra states: "If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were permanent, there would be no going or coming in principle; if they were impermanent, they would arise and perish moment by moment."
Nor is there any coming or going.
Regarding the latter eight points: first, concerning sentient beings, there is indeed coming and going; second, concerning pride; third, concerning grasping and attachment.

Fourth, it concerns the *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata; fifth, it concerns the realization of the nature (*dharmatā*); sixth, it concerns the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*);
seventh, it concerns the four virtues of the *śrāvaka*; and eighth, it concerns the four virtues of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, this answers those of noble status who hear what was not heard: it means that the fundamental (the source) is itself non-hearing, yet within its traces there is hearing;
the trace is itself the fundamental, and thus non-hearing; non-hearing is itself the fundamental and the trace, which is the identity of identities—non-coming yet coming.

For the benefit of future generations, it is thus: the trace is itself the fundamental, and thus originally non-coming; the fundamental is itself the trace, so that non-coming is coming. This is the nature of delusion and enlightenment.
It is for this reason that it is so.
As for the passage in the Sūtra stating, "Having received permission and being further admonished," this is the explanatory commentary (*śāstrakāra*) on the meaning of the admonitory text;
it remains within the context of the subsequent answer.
The question regarding the "extensive" by the King of One Virtue refers to the three pairs mentioned above, such as "seizing" and "releasing.
The question regarding the "realized" by the King of Two Virtues refers to "hearing what is not heard," wherein "not hearing" is the realization.
Regarding Ryūkō’s question on cultivation: since it is said that one asks about what has not been heard, hearing it is itself cultivation. Ryūkō is in the "original" (hon);
"original" refers to his native land. He asks about the meaning of that Buddha’s "hearing what was not heard," and so forth.
Regarding the fact that the assembly’s questions concerning Vipaśyin and the others were omitted, there are two reasons for this brevity:

first, within this [assembly], the great multitude had already heard the conclusion of King Guṇa’s questioning and the subsequent emission of light; second, as for the great multitude who followed the light to arrive, they too had already finished hearing it.
Therefore, it is merely heard in brief.

As for "the celestial practice spontaneously increasing in clarity": after first attaining the stage of abiding, one enters the stream of the Dharma in every thought-moment; hence, it increases in clarity.

Regarding the phrase "resembling the six perfections": how could one fathom the profound and subtle nature of the Buddha-dharma? For now, I shall merely explain it by way of analogy through the lens of the six perfections.
This refers to diligence, as permitted [by the teaching], such as in the sutra: "If you now wish to exhaustively master such a Mahāyāna," and so forth; this is precisely diligence.
This is progression.
The Sūtra states that the "Ocean of Great Nirvāṇa" refers to the essence of nirvāṇa, which is profound and subsequently vast, and is thus metaphorically likened to an ocean.
The Mahāyāna is the person who rides [the vehicle]; from cause to fruition, this is termed "Great Nirvāṇa."
The Sūtra says: "It happens that I am now able to explain it well. This does not mean that he was not skilled in explanation prior to this;

rather, it means that until now, the conditions for his audience had not yet converged and the time had not yet arrived. Now, however, the conditions have converged and the time for teaching has arrived;
therefore, this is called "explaining well."
The Sūtra says: "As for all the nets of doubt you now possess. This refers to the period prior to this sūtra, when both the provisional and the real were doubted regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Although these doubts had been dispelled, there remained that which was not yet fully understood. I shall now extract the poison of attachment to the literal text and eliminate the doubts concerning the provisional teachings.

The Sūtra says, "You have not yet clearly understood the Buddha-nature. This means that although one has partially realized it at the first stage (*bhūmi*), one has not yet fully understood the ultimate nature.
The Sūtra says, "You now wish to cross the great river of birth and death. This refers to crossing the river of the two types of death. I...
He is able to act as the ultimate captain of the ship.
As the Sūtra says: "If you conceive of me as your father or mother, you are a child of the true cause; our natures are interconnected just like those of parents.
Furthermore, because we have formed karmic connections at various points along the way, I am to you a condition-cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). Therefore, regarding you...
This is to give rise to the heart of an infant. The Sūtra says:
"If one encounters me, there are many who are able to bestow through wisdom. This Dharma is truly like a treasury of gold;
it is as if I, as a father, have this to bestow upon you, and thus it is called "able to bestow. Regarding "many," it is as stated in the Lotus Sūtra: "I, by means of..."
He bestowed upon his sons countless great chariots made of the seven treasures; since the sons were not one and the chariots were likewise immeasurable, it is said that they were "many.
Furthermore, because of the ocean of the Great Nirvāṇa, one is able to sever the net of doubt. Because doubt is severed, one perceives the Buddha-nature.
Because the nature is perceived, one is able to cross the river of the two deaths and attain one's original parents. Because of this attainment...
The parents act as great shipmasters; by having parents who can show them the True Dharma, they obtain the great, substantial vehicle.
Because they have obtained the great vehicle, they travel through the four directions, proceeding from cause to fruit until reaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
If they do not obtain the vehicle, they remain wherever they happen to be.
Regarding "the broad Buddha-nature," this refers to the three kinds of Buddha-nature.

As for "awakening to and understanding even a single phrase or half-phrase to see the Buddha-nature," this means that the two conditions—the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) and the contributory cause (*nirvedhika-hetu*)—jointly support the fundamental cause (*dhātu-hetu*);
therefore, it is said that one "sees the nature. As for the "three phrases," why are they not raised? They refer to the three phrases beginning with "not hearing the not-hearing" and so forth.

"Never having heard, yet hearing" refers to the *vijñapti-hetu* (revealing cause). This is explained again by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the three causes and the five kinds of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Since "not hearing" pertains to the merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), it is called the revealing cause.

Regarding the statement that "hearing and not hearing are the conditional causes (*pratyaya-hetu*)," this refers to the cultivation of merit. Because of hearing, it serves as a condition; together with the fundamental cause (*mūla-hetu*), they mutually support one another, such that "not hearing" and "not not hearing" are likewise [conditional causes].
That which is heard as the nature of the objective sphere refers to the evil five aggregates of birth and death.
Furthermore, regarding its nature as a cause, the nature of the objective sphere encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome.

Regarding "hearing and non-hearing being the cause of the causal nature": taking hearing as the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) and non-hearing as the actualizing cause (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*), it is therefore called the "causal nature of causes.
One should likewise speak of the "nature of effects" and the "nature of the effects of effects," and so forth. Non-hearing is the nature of the effect;
non-hearing is the effect, and non-hearing is the nature of the effect.
Regarding examples such as "coming and not coming," "arising and not arising," and "reaching and not reaching," whether they are attained or unattained, all are based on hearing and not hearing;
this is because these four propositions are explained in relation to the three causes and the five kinds of Buddha-nature.

Regarding the statement "acting as a boatman," this refers to the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). If one cannot endure the two extremes of adversity and favor, how can one become a guide to omniscience?
As a boatman, one transforms others and ferries them across the river of the two types of death.

Regarding this in terms of the perfection of dhyāna, it refers to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. It manifests in various ways as a sovereign and as a guide, regarding all sentient beings as if they were one's own infants.

Regarding the statement that "Wisdom-bestowing" refers to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) within the context of the six perfections as being "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*): it means the fulfillment of the *dāna-pāramitā* through the six perfections being free from volitional effort.

As for the instruction to "listen attentively so as not to be like a covered vessel" and so forth, this is an admonition concerning the three types of wisdom—those arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-mayī*, *cintā-mayī*, and *bhāvanā-mayī* prajñā*).

If one does not listen attentively, it is like a covered vessel; the water of the Dharma cannot remain within it. If one hears but does not reflect, it is like a leaking vessel; the water will not stay.
It abides. Just as a defiled vessel cannot be used for consumption, hearing and reflection without cultivation are likewise unfit for use; therefore, one tests them.
This is because it has been explained at length in the aforementioned citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The Sūtra states, "First deliver oneself. This is explained by the Four Great Vows: if one lacks these four vows, one cannot transform others;
if one gives rise to arrogance, one will fall back into the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, this is used as a warning.
If one were to treat them as separate entities, one would be unable to revere the Teacher. Now, based on their single essence, we take the Dharma as the Teacher;
this Teacher is the embodiment of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

Regarding the practice of the ten dharmas that constitute the ultimate sincerity, there are three stages within the initial concealment (*paryavasthāna*); next, within the outflows (*āsrava*), there are the latter two defilements (*kleśa*).
Within this, there are five; thus, they are called the "ten dharmas.
As for the "ancient exegesis of the South," this refers to the period of the Qi and Liang dynasties of the Southern Dynasties, when this sutra was widely propagated.
The final two sets of four propositions are metaphorical explanations; that is, the four propositions concerning reaching and not reaching, arising and not arising, and so forth.

However, the present intention concerns the teaching of the Dharma as such. Now, what is called a "metaphor" is used to provide an illustration for the Dharma. How could one take the Dharma itself to illustrate the Dharma?
Therefore, these are not employed here.
The first four phrases concern the aspect of teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*); that is to say, "not hearing" and "hearing" constitute the teaching.
The next two concern the aspect of realization (*adhigama-lakṣaṇa*). This explanation is still brief; it should be stated as "practice and realization.
What does not arrive and what arrives refers to practice. What is not born and what is born refers to realization. These correspond respectively to the triad of teaching, practice, and realization.
"To accommodate those of the three faculties" means that this interpretation is the same as the intention of our own school.

Regarding the phrase "those who have seen and heard" in the sutra, it simply refers to the *tattva* (Ultimate Truth); however, what is true within which teaching? This refers to the principle of the Middle Way;
therefore, it says, "not heard, not heard."
"Comprehending that which should return to the True" means hearing this and not questioning the return to the True.
"Hearing and seeing that which corresponds to the traces" means hearing and seeing the constant responding to sentient beings.
"If one is able to cultivate the Path, then that which was heard becomes unheard. This means that the entanglements of birth and death are what is "heard";
to be able to sever birth and death is to be "unheard.
"That which is constantly hearing" refers to the fact that the birth and death of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is constant.
"Non-arising arising is nirvāṇa: beginningless yet having a beginning. This means that non-arising is beginningless, while arising is the beginning;
therefore, it is said to "have a beginning.
"Arising non-arising is nirvāṇa: endless yet having an end. This means that non-arising is endless, while arising is the end.
It concludes; thus it is said, "and concludes.

Next, regarding birth and death, it is said that "non-birth is birth," which means that which begins where there is no beginning. Ignorance (*avidyā*) has no beginning and is entirely the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
this is called "non-birth. Yet, returning to the nature of phenomena, ignorance arises; therefore, it is said, "and begins. There is no [beginning].
"Ending with the end": this can be understood by referring to the commentary.

"There is nothing that is not encompassed and penetrated": from the Avīci Hell at the beginning up to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment at the end, all possess the fourfold categories such as "not hearing yet hearing.
Taking their true cause (zhengyin), they all possess the sense of being capable of arising; this is not [limited to] the Buddha-nature alone.

"How can one obtain the outflow [teachings] as if they were the teaching, practice, and realization? This is a general refutation of the various masters who speak in terms of dharmas, parables, and so forth.
"Not only do their 'squares' not accord with the 'circle'"—here, "square" (fang) refers to the dharma. Each of the various masters establishes a single dharma;
thus, while their squares are fixed, they still manage to reach an understanding. However, this present school’s principle is the inconceivable, perfect truth of the three truths.
Furthermore, regarding those who slaughter and maim the body, as previously explained through the categories of teaching, realization, dharma, and analogy,
they all wound the true essence of the eternal Middle Way of Nirvana.
Furthermore, another master explains the four propositions based on a single truth; this is an interpretation that refers exclusively to the ultimate (paramārtha).
To say it is "even more remote" means that the principle is increasingly distant from the meaning, and because it does not encompass the conventional (saṃvṛti), it is termed "remote.
Moreover, since the Tathāgata always teaches the Dharma by relying upon the two truths, it is described as being "remote."
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the complications of the two truths become even more numerous": this refers to your reliance on the two truths according to the teachings;
now, by interpreting the two truths through seven layers based on the sūtras, it is said that they have become even more numerous.

Furthermore, regarding the three phrases beginning with "the production of production" (*jātijāti*), as previously explained when interpreting "hearing hearing" (*śravaṇa-śravaṇa*) through the lens of *jātijāti*, these are merely discussed in terms of the beginningless and endless nature of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
It is not that the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*) itself is currently ineffable; therefore, it is called "profound."

How much more so regarding the establishment of mutual non-existence: as in the previous case of nirvāṇa being absent within saṃsāra, and saṃsāra being absent within nirvāṇa, one would not be able to judge the presence or absence of beginning and end based on the principle of "hearing what was unheard" regarding whether there is a beginning and end or no beginning and end.
"Merely the partial intent of the Hīnayāna" means that one has only attained the *pariniṣpanna-satya* (partial truth) nirvāṇa of the Tripiṭaka teachings;
since one has not yet attained the principle of "the middle being emptiness," it is called "partial."
Furthermore, these ten matters refer to the ten merits.

As for the simultaneous inquiry regarding realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), King of Virtue [Ratnaśrī] attained hearing from realization; therefore, it is said that he "heard what was not heard," and so forth.

Luminous Radiance [Prabhāsa] entered realization through cultivation; therefore, it is said that he "realized what had not been heard," and so forth. Since the meaning of realization is identical in both cases, they inquire about realization together.
"Thousand paths and ten thousand tracks" means that the merits of the ten matters are like the thousand paths, for they all converge at a single realization, which is like the ten thousand tracks.

"The pampas grass flying in the wilds and the duckweed drifting beyond the seas" refers to how the aforementioned masters each departed according to their own interpretations, their principles exceeding [the mark].
"Far-reaching and spreading like flying tufts of *páng* grass that never cease" refers to the wilds; it simply explains them as being on two sides.
"Metaphorically likened to duckweed drifting through the currents of birth and death," therefore it says "the sea is far."

"Those whose intent is to practice universally" refers to those who understand both the sequential practices prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and the people who realize the small fruit of eternal abiding.
"The path of cultivation suddenly ceases and there is nothing further to be attained" means that from the stage prior to the *bhūmis*, one realizes the single-moment aspect of the first stage.
It should be called "sudden" (*hu*). Because one realizes the Dharma-body, it is said that there is nothing that can be possessed.
Regarding the realization of the arising of delusion and its cessation: delusion is precisely hearing, and cessation is precisely not hearing; therefore, it is called "hearing and not hearing."

It is named "The Hearer of Hearers. The upper character "Hearer" (wen) signifies constant illumination; the lower character "Hearer" signifies responding according to the triggering of conditions. Therefore, it is called "constant. The first phrase clarifies the wisdom of realization:

it means that non-arising arising is precisely all dharmas; because they do not arise, Prajñā arises. Thus, it is said: [the first phrase] clarifies the wisdom of realization. This refers to the fact that non-arising arising is precisely all dharmas, and because they do not arise, Prajñā arises. Therefore—
This refers to wisdom.
The second phrase clarifies the realization of principle; "principle" means non-arising, and non-arising is termed Great Nirvana.
The third clarifies the realization of abandonment; this refers to arising and non-arising, wherein non-arising is itself abandonment.
The fourth [point] clarifies the evidence for the "response" (應). This refers to "the arising of arising," because arising itself is the response.

The reason all four phrases are called "evidence" (證) is that they transform the previous four—such as "hearing what was not heard"—thereby citing the Buddha’s own interpretation along with other commentaries to serve as clear proof.
Regarding "if it concerns phenomena, principle, wisdom, or abandonment, whether for oneself or others": phenomena refers to the activity of transforming others;
principle refers to the fruit of one's own practice, which is nirvana; and the pair of wisdom and abandonment constitutes the function of that fruition.

Regarding the first realization, based on the first merit, there are four propositions concerning non-arising and so forth; because the causes and effects of both self-cultivation and the transformation of others are fully complete therein, it is said to be "without deficiency."
"Exhausting the ocean of nirvana" means that the three virtues encompass all things.
"Resolving the doubts of the two people" refers to the question of whether there are six or one rays of light from the Virtuous King; this [doubt] is spontaneously dispelled with a sudden clarity.

Furthermore, "hearing what has not been heard" refers to one who realizes the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*). Since the preceding explanation of the noble practices was all based on the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is said that "one hears what has not been heard.

"Hearing what has not been heard" refers to one who realizes the Brahma-practice (*brahma-caryā*). "Brahma" refers to compassion in terms of phenomena; thus, it is called "hearing. This likewise refers to realizing the first stage.
Therefore, it is said that "he does not hear. This demonstrates that the practice of the Celestial (Tianxing) is, in terms of principle (*li*), "not hearing"; "not hearing" is easy to understand.

To demonstrate the practice of the Infant (Ying'er), it is said that he "hears what is heard," meaning that he gives rise to function (*yong*) from within the principle. Thus, it is called "hearing what is heard."
Regarding the statement that "hearing and hearing is the realm of realization," this realm differs slightly from the preceding one.
The former was discussed in terms of the cause (*hetu*), whereas this is discussed in terms of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), because it is the object of contemplation.
Furthermore, "hearing what has not been heard" refers to the realization of perfect purity (*pariśuddhi*). This is in terms of the realization of the three types of *nirvāṇa*;
because one is able to overcome all [obstacles] from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, it is called "perfect.

As for "not hearing what has been heard," "hearing what has not been heard," and so forth, these all pertain to the application of transforming others; therefore, they are called "expedient means" (*upāya*).

If one attains this meaning—that is, if one attains the four propositions of "hearing what is not heard" and so forth according to our own school—then with respect to the meaning of realization, it universally applies to both the discourse on self-cultivation and the discourse on transforming others;
therefore, it is said that "it should be expanded. Why is this called the "meaning of non-difference"? It explains the identity [of the teachings].

This means that [the teaching] is identical in realizing the single principle along with the four propositions of "hearing what is not heard" and so forth; therefore, it is said that "this and that are not different."
This is indeed remarkable.

Regarding the verses on "originally existing but now non-existent" and "the Śvetaśaila [Snowy Mountain] cutting off his own flesh," the two verses concerning the Snowy Mountain and the cutting of the flesh differ in their sequence.
As stated in the subsequent text, "The Tathāgata realizes nirvana," this refers to the verse on cutting the flesh, whereas the [verse concerning] the Emperor... [is different].
This interpretation remains consistent with the current school’s preservation of functional utility.
Regarding the statement that "the non-arising of arising is the original existence": it is called "non-arising" because there was originally no affliction;
it is called "arising" because there is now nirvana.
"Non-arising is the original state; that which is now absent" means that originally there was no nirvana and now there are no afflictions; therefore, it is called non-arising.
"Arising and non-arising are the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena" means that arising is itself the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and non-arising is their impermanence.
"Non-arising arising is this dharma of arising and ceasing" refers to the cessation of afflictions and the arising of wisdom.
"Arising arising is the cessation of arising and ceasing" means that both types of arising—namely, those of knowledge (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*)—are incapable of further arising;
thus it is said, "arising and ceasing have already ceased. This is stated according to conventional discourse.
That which is "non-arising arising" is the Tathāgata’s realization of nirvāṇa. Non-arising is nirvāṇa; arising is the Tathāgata’s attainment.
That "birth-and-death" is "arising arising" refers to the birth-and-death of others through his power of transformation; thus it is called "arising arising."
"Non-arising arising" refers to those who practice all wholesome virtues. Because these wholesome virtues are the "wholesome of cessation," they are said to be "non-arising.
To "practice" them refers to the "wholesome of cultivation.

As for the phrase "if one realizes non-hearing and so forth," this refers to those of superior faculties who have already entered the stages; for such individuals, there is no need for further investigation. It does not apply to others.
Because those of middling and inferior capacities have not yet fully understood [the process of] "birth after birth" and so forth, I shall now investigate it further.
Regarding "entrusting oneself to the holy embryo": this refers to the initial descent from Tuṣita, wherein the Sage manifests his entry; hence it is called the "holy embryo."

Regarding the cultivation of skillful means (*upāya*): the contemplative practice of the five stages is called "skillful means. When one penetrates through the stage of semblance (*sādṛśyāvasthā*), it is termed "abiding" because [the afflictions] do not arise.
Since this is the initial entrustment to the noble womb and the first dwelling upon emerging from the womb, it is called "hearing."
Furthermore, although nirvāṇa is beginningless, it is spoken of as having a beginning because its initial realization is like a beginning.
Likewise, although saṃsāra is endless, it is called "ending" because birth has been exhausted.
Regarding his statement that there are "six stages of abiding" (*ṣaḍ-vihāra*), this refers to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, also known as the *Bhūmi-vastu-śāstra*.

The four stages prior to the [first] ground constitute four abidings, while those from the attainment of the ground upward constitute two abidings; thus, it is said there are six abidings, which is identical in meaning to the present intent.
Regarding the fact that "not yet" and "no longer" each follow the convenience of their respective meanings: internally, with respect to the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are termed the "root";
externally, with respect to the seeds (*bīja*) and so forth, they are termed the "branch. Therefore, it is said that [the terms] are used according to what is convenient.
Regarding "among the three and four": this refers to the three types of fourfold propositions, such as "not having heard, hearing," and so forth;
however, it specifically challenges the second fourfold proposition and the fourth fourfold proposition, which is the "arising from arising" proposition.

Regarding the "extensive explanation of the various phrases": this refers to the remaining three phrases and the two sets of four phrases, all of which are pervaded by "arising from arising" (*jātijāti*) throughout.
If it were intended as "arising for the sake of permanence," then every single phrase should state "arising from arising."
If birth were permanent, it would mean that it is truly permanent.
If birth were impermanent, then because the characteristic of birth perishes, that which is produced should be permanent.
This intention means that while the out-flowing (sāsrava) is the produced and birth is the producer, since birth is impermanent, that which is produced must be permanent.

Regarding "in relation to oneself and both self and others": in relation to that which can produce itself, whether it be with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), as well as both self and others, none of these can be definitively stated.
These six propositions are all based on principle, because they pertain to what is realized through realization; therefore, it is said that they cannot be spoken of.
Therefore, regarding the statement that "non-arising is non-arising and is ineffable": first, the term "non-arising" cannot produce anything else;
second, the term "non-arising" does not apply to the untainted (anāsrava). Both are ineffable.
The objection regarding "original existence" arises because it possesses the nature of being unarisen.
The objection regarding "original non-existence" arises because empty space cannot give rise to anything.
As for the statement that it "can also be spoken of because there are causes and conditions," this refers to the inconceivable causes and conditions of response and resonance.
As for the contradiction between phenomena: arising contradicts non-arising, and non-arising contradicts arising; therefore, it cannot be described.
If arising were impermanent, then arising would give rise to further arising. Since impermanence is cessation, once there has been cessation, there is arising again;
hence it is called "arising of arising."
Furthermore, regarding "that which is extinguished," it refers to being extinguished by the characteristic of extinction (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding "the entire substance is extinguished," this is because both the agent of extinction and the object of extinction are non-arising.

Regarding "arising does not arise of itself; it fundamentally takes birth-and-death [as its basis]," it is said that arising does not arise of itself because it proceeds from afflictions (*kleśa*). [The text continues: afflictions...
Because it takes up birth and causes the extinction of birth-and-death, it is called "non-arising.
This "birth" is itself permanence; this true permanence of nirvana is not the same as the self-nature permanence of the out-flowing (sāsrava) dharmas.
The Sūtra states, "Because it is attained through the cultivation of the path. This concludes the two types of non-arising: first, that Nirvāṇa is fundamentally non-arisen from the beginning;
second, that it is non-arisen because it is attained through the cultivation of the path. This also refers to the non-arising of both wisdom and abandonment.
Regarding that which has not yet arisen but already exists: since even arising itself lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how much more so the unarisen? Therefore, it cannot be said [to exist].
Furthermore, regarding the fact that there is something obtainable: because arising occurs through conventional causes and conditions, it is not the case that there is no arising;
thus, it cannot be said [that it does not exist].

Regarding the statement that "the first ten serve as the causal conditions for arising": these ten causes constitute the objective realm of those to be converted (*vineya*) and the locus where the potential for birth (*janman-kāraṇa*) arises.
The last two branches are excluded because they have not yet arisen in the future. Specifically, past ignorance (*avidyā*) moistens formative action (*saṃskāra*), thereby establishing karma.
This essence of karma may be categorized according to four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). If it is the functional capacity for arising and ceasing, it acts as the cause for further arising.
The same applies to the explanations of non-arising (*anutpāda*), the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*); these can be understood by analogy.
Regarding the slightly more extensive explanation of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, that section concerns the gate of non-arising contemplation.

The Great Master first explains the Buddha’s sutras and subsequently provides his own interpretation of the sutras’ meaning in accordance with the scriptures; therefore, it is described as "extensive."
Regarding "all accord with the gate of nirvana and non-arising": now, based on the four gates, all are non-arising;
therefore, none of the four propositions can be spoken.
Regarding "not understanding the concentration of emptiness": because this concentration of emptiness pertains to ultimate principle, it is said that they do not understand it.

Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on a single proposition: previously, concerning the four propositions regarding "arising from arising" (*jātijāti*) as asked by Rāhula, the question was raised as to what it means for something to arise, since the name "arising" is the same [for both].
The Tathāgata refuted this with six propositions, stating that all are inexpressible.
Now, concerning the single proposition "non-arising from arising," it likewise possesses four propositions; one must not treat it as "arising from arising."
It is taught that even the non-arising of non-arising cannot be expressed; the same applies to the latter three phrases as well.

Why should one explain them only in terms of one, two, or three? It is not possible to treat "arising," "non-arising," "both arising and non-arising," and "neither arising nor non-arising" as a single phrase alone;
rather, each single phrase inherently constitutes four phrases. Therefore, it is said that they are "inexpressible."
If one knows that the Tathāgata never preaches the Dharma, this is called being "much-heard.

Even if one fully expounds the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it does not constitute being "much-heard" if, among those twelve divisions, one has not heard the Vaipulya sūtras, nor even the teaching on "not hearing what is heard," and so forth.
These various phrases are not yet "much learning" (bahuśruta). What is true much learning? It is the eternal, for it contains all principles within its silence;

therefore, it cannot be described. Within a single thought-moment, it is fully endowed with the three thousand [realms]. It cannot be definitively explained as emptiness, the provisional, or the middle.
It is also called "much learning" (*bahuśruta*).
While it may superficially appear that this meaning is not absent, when examined thoroughly, the meanings established are identical.

As for the distinction between the singular and plural, or the separate application to delusions and their resolution, such explanations offered here in contrast to others are not definitive standards; therefore, they are merely apparent.
This refers to the general and specific afflictions, as well as their general and specific resolutions; these are to be applied according to the four logical permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
"The non-arising of arising" refers to the specific [affliction] or the single [factor]; it is designated as "single" in reference to the ignorance that is deluded regarding the principle (*tattva*).

"Arising and arising" refers to the pervasive delusions that are "double," meaning they possess both the pervasive and specific aspects of the views, afflictions, and ignorance pertaining to both the internal and external realms;
thus, they are termed "double.
"Arising and non-arising" refers to the pervasive liberations that are "single," which is to say that the twenty-five existences within the internal realm do not arise; this is termed [the single].
This is for the sake of explanation.

Regarding "non-arising and non-arising," this is a detailed explanation of the term "repeated" (*fu*). First, it refers to the non-arising of [afflictions] through views and thoughts; second, it refers to the non-arising of ignorance.
Because it possesses both types of non-arising, it is called "repeated."
Regarding the fact that these single and manifold delusions and their liberations are all ineffable: delusion is the three paths (*trivartman*), and liberation is the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Now, because one contemplates the three paths as being identical to the three virtues, they are ineffable. Furthermore, in terms of conceptual deliberation (*cintya*):

universal delusions (*sāmānya-kleśa*) are the delusions of conceptual deliberation within the realm (*dhātu*), while specific delusions (*viśeṣa-kleśa*) are the inconceivable delusions beyond the realm. Universal liberation (*sāmānya-vimukti*) is the conceptual deliberation within the realm...
Explanation: "Separate explanation" refers specifically to the inconceivable explanation outside the realms (*dhātu*).

Therefore, the phrase "arising" concludes the conceptualization (*cintya*) and non-conceptualization (*acintya*) of afflictions (*kleśa*), while the phrase "non-arising" concludes the conceptualization and non-conceptualization of explanations. One cannot definitively state them as either conceptual or non-conceptual;
thus, they are both inexpressible.
The Sūtra says: "Good son, as for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), their arising is also permanent. This means: if they are based on permanence, why are they impermanent?

It is because they are transformed by the four characteristics (*catvāri lakṣaṇāni*). Why is this so? Because abiding (*sthiti*) abides in arising (*utpāda*). As the Sūtra says: "Because abiding is impermanent, arising is also impermanent."
The Sūtra states that "even abiding is impermanent. Abiding ought to be permanent; it is only arising that is distinct from coming-into-being and abiding.
As the Sūtra says, because there is the arising of arising, abiding is also impermanent.
The Sūtra states that "alteration is also impermanent. This means that because the phenomena of arising and abiding undergo alteration, they are themselves impermanent.
The Sūtra states that "destruction is impermanent. This refers to the fact that what was originally termed "non-destruction" is now termed "destruction";

this very process of arising is impermanence and is also called cessation (*nirodha*). "Cessation" refers to total extinction, while "destruction" refers to disintegration, such as when an object is ruined. It is also said:
"Guài" (怪). When one applies effort, it is called "guài"; when one has finished applying it, it is called "huài" (壞, dǐng lèi fǎn).
As for its divisions, the four marks are called "constant" (cháng), which is termed "division" (fēn); because arising itself is constant, it is called "intrinsic nature" (zìxìng).
Just as worldly people each designate a period of five hundred years and so forth as "constant," yet it undergoes coming and going and change—
this refers to both the "constant" and the "impermanent" among the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena.

Regarding "that which originally existed but is now non-existent is further impermanent": because that which originally existed has now undergone destruction and gives rise to cessation and decay, it is called impermanent.
Regarding "the principle of original existence": this means that the nature capable of arising is as yet insufficient; therefore, it is said that it is only now [arising].
This is still [an answer] to the sixth point.
To respond comprehensively: "That which is originally non-existent" refers to the state prior to arising as described in the sutra.

This is precisely "non-arising," which is not the same as empty space. Empty space lacks the nature of arising by definition and thus cannot undergo arising; this is because the present objection concerns that which has not yet arisen.
To answer both points simultaneously means that [the cause] possesses the two capacities of producing others and producing itself.
That each has its own nature means, for example, that fire has the nature of heat and the eye has the nature of seeing. Both must encounter conditions:
fire requires a person and a rope as its conditions; the eye requires form and the discernment of consciousness as its conditions. Thus, it becomes visible and perceivable.

"Arising" (utpāda) is the meaning of "refuting intrinsic nature" (svabhāva). The intention was first, within the context of the six difficulties, to refute its self-nature, other-nature, common-nature, and causeless-nature;
thus, the four attachments are concluded. However, an analogy is now adduced to establish that it possesses the capacity for arising.
This is what is meant by "there is no error. As previously stated, while the six [positions] refuted earlier cannot be explained, the causal conditions established later can indeed be explained.

If one becomes attached to any of these propositions, there is a fault. Now that the faults of the four natures—both self-originated and other-originated—have been refuted, it is said that there is no error.
First, the narrator describes the signs. As for the passage stating that [the assembly] leaped into the void, this symbolizes that the realization of the Dharmakāya is unattached, just like space.
When the Sūtra says, "The Tathāgata earnestly instructs and exhorts," it refers to what was previously explained: hearing what is not heard, being born where there is no birth, and so forth.
The sixfold explanation extensively analyzes the refutations and proofs of the treatise; hence it is said to be "earnest.

When the Sūtra says, "One first attains awakening and understands what was not heard before," this refers precisely to the non-hearing of what is not heard, and the hearing of what is not heard, and so forth.
Regarding the "gate of attaining liberation" (*mukha-prativedha*): it refers to the principle that "non-arising arising" and so forth are all the reality of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Therefore, it is called the gate of attaining liberation. This means being able to penetrate from cause to fruit and realize the stage of the first dwelling (*prathama-bhūmi*); because one partially attains this, it is termed "liberation."
This is solely because there are those who have not yet understood the four lines beginning with "Not arriving at arrival. This refers to those of middling capacity who still do not understand.
When the Sūtra says, "I have now already understood and severed the net of all doubts," it is called "already understood" because one has seen the Buddha-nature;

thus, the net of doubts is entirely removed. It is as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, where the Bodhisattvas, upon hearing [the teaching], had their nets of doubt regarding the complete Dharma entirely removed.

Next, regarding those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), they are collectively categorized according to the three different types of faculties discussed in the treatises. Here, "those of sharp faculties" refers specifically to those of superior faculties (*adhimātra-indriya*).

As for these two being mutually complementary: because this cultivation of the Pure Land is identical to the inquiry of Abhayamati, it causes one to cultivate the Pure Land; that Bodhi... [text truncated]
Because Bodhisattva Sa (Śāriputra) likewise heard [the Dharma] in this land, he was able to know the benefits of that land.
Regarding the fact that there may be superiority or inferiority among the bodhisattvas of various lands, the *Siddhārthasamuccaya-sūtra* states:

"The bodhisattvas of all other pure lands who maintain pure precepts for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas do not equal those in this land who, from morning until the mealtime, possess no mind of anger or obstruction. This refers to the present.
The land is superior. Furthermore, it is as when the bodhisattvas of the World of Fragrant Accumulation each attain the Samādhi of the Treasury of Virtue beneath their respective fragrant trees;

thus, the pure land is superior. If one enters the truly pure land, it is superior, just as in the World of Fragrance, where each [bodhisattva] attains the Way by smelling the fragrance beneath their fragrant tree.
If one enters the expedient defiled land, it is as in the World of Fragrance [where others do so].
Regarding the phrase "all bodhisattvas," it is called "superior" because it refers to the practice of both [calm abiding and insight] in tandem.

Furthermore, it simultaneously answers the subsequent question: if one can practice these two virtues of calm abiding and insight, one will immediately attain sharp faculties within that perfection and realize Great Nirvana;
thus, it is said to concurrently answer the second question.
The first ten practices constitute the goodness of cessation (*śamatha*). These correspond to the ten non-virtues; the cessation of evil is itself virtue.

In the sutra, these are correlated respectively with the three actions of body, four of speech, and three of mind. The subsequent eleven practices are judged to clarify the goodness of cultivation (*bhāvanā*);
regarding the four perfections of giving, patience, ethical discipline, and diligence, they may be understood as they appear in the sutra.

Regarding the passage on seeing others obtain benefit: this refers first to the cessation of greed, followed by the cessation of anger—as in the sutra’s statement that one does not afflict sentient beings—and thirdly, the cessation of delusion.
These are the three [poisons] and so forth.
As for the phrase "the general and the particular are not different": the "general" refers to the bodhicitta, which seeks the Buddha-way above and transforms sentient beings.
The four great vows are called the "general" [vows]. The "particular" refers to the various different practices within this chapter;
since each and every one of these is fully endowed with the four great vows, they do not differ from them.

Regarding the phrase "for those who have already understood the superior and middle [capacities] but have not yet awakened": those of superior capacity have already attained awakening through hearing what was previously unheard, and thus they are fearless;
they inquire further about the practice of the Pure Land. Those of middle capacity have already understood, and now act as the basis for those of inferior capacity.

King Devasena further inquires whether [the goal] is reached or not, so that those of inferior capacity may attain awakening. Because this request universally benefits all three capacities, he makes this petition.
Regarding the "three kinds and six kinds": this refers to the different ways of affirming and negating within the questions concerning the three pairs and six pairs;
hence it is called "three and six kinds.
As for the Buddha’s teaching of the six similes, as stated in the subsequent text: "One who well understands all phenomena to be like a magical illusion, a mirage, and a *gandharva* city..."
Regarding the passage beginning with "Bālakṣema and others" and ending with "the answer concerning the auspicious light": this does not mean that one sees blue as blue and so forth.
As for the points that appear intermittently before and after: previously, the section on the "non-arrival at arrival" was placed before the "arising of non-arising";
now it is explained later, which is why it is called a "question. In reality, there is no shallowness or depth in the Dharma.
Answer: Regarding "conditioned by the simple and the compound": this refers to ordinary beings of inferior capacity who remain within the cycle of birth and death;
if they are able to cultivate the path and reach nirvana, it is merely "simple. The former [case] concerns those of superior capacity and is termed "non-arising non-arising";
the latter concerns wisdom and abandonment as "non-arising non-arising. Therefore, it is called "compound."

Regarding the statement that "not reaching" and "reaching" are mentioned alternately with respect to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*): the former was discussed in terms of the arising of wisdom, while this is discussed in terms of not reaching birth-and-death.
The intention is as follows: since wisdom exists even within the realm of birth-and-death and is still able to observe it, one speaks of "not reaching" birth-and-death;
yet, because the realm where wisdom resides also contains birth-and-death, which is that which is to be severed, one speaks of "reaching" it. Thus, they are mentioned alternately.

Regarding the statement that "reaching" (*prāpti*) and "not reaching" (*aprāpti*), and so forth, are also mentioned interchangeably: the former, "arising" (*utpāda*) and "non-arising" (*anutpāda*), refers to the absence of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
This treatise, however, discusses "reaching" birth-and-death. As a sutra states, even within the present, it is called "reaching. Thus, "having birth-and-death" is itself "non-birth-and-death";
therefore, they are said to be mentioned interchangeably.
The Sūtra states: "Anāgāmin is called 'the one who has reached the ultimate' because of the causes and conditions of their afflictions.

This means that because their afflictions are not yet exhausted, they remain identical to ordinary beings who have not yet escaped the twenty-five states of existence; therefore, they are called "the one who has reached the ultimate."
Regarding the distinctions between others' teachings, practices, and realizations in terms of their depth and shallowness: "not hearing what has been heard" refers to the teaching;
"the non-arising of what has arisen" refers to practice; and "reaching or not reaching" and so forth refer to realization. Thus, they are said to be distinct.

As for the reason why it is appropriate to provide three explanations: this is because the capacities of the three grades of practitioners—superior, middling, and inferior—differ in what they require to hear;
therefore, three explanations are given.
Furthermore, within the third question, four sections are established because the four types of hearing can be discerned therein. From "impermanence" onwards...
Because names exist, impermanence constitutes the four chapters.
As for "not" directly forming seven questions: this includes the preceding three questions to make seven.
Regarding the abbreviated questions: as the sutra says, "How can it further be said to be permanent, blissful, self, and pure? This question follows from the preceding answer-text.
This refers to "permanence," "pleasure," and so forth. Since it was already stated that they were not heard [in the state of birth], how could they be heard now?
This includes the other four as well; that is, these four questions all constitute challenges regarding impermanence.
Now, by citing five causes, one further distinguishes the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) as being identical to the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*); therefore, externally there is impermanence.

Regarding the statement "resembling the four conditions and three causes": there are both similarities and differences between these and the six causes and four conditions of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*;
thus they are called "resembling. Furthermore, their respective enumerations do not correspond.
That "good and evil naturally resemble one another" means that they correspond with the mind and resemble a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
However, regarding the absence of an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), this is the same as the case of the equal and immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Regarding the statement that "the preceding six perfections are the inquiry into the cause," this refers to the fact that the Buddha previously answered that giving is the cause of nirvana;
because it is the external cause for Great Nirvana, this inquiry arises.
The Sūtra states: "From not hearing of giving, down to not seeing Great Nirvāṇa.

This refers to the person of perfect cultivation who, from the stages of name, contemplative practice, and semblance onward, remains entirely unattached, practicing with a mind free of marks (animitta).
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "From knowing and seeing the Dharma-realm, one understands reality. This is the stage of a Bodhisattva at the first dwelling (prathama-bhūmi).
Furthermore,
the Sūtra says: "Those who hear only the names of the twelve divisions of the scriptures but do not hear their meaning" refers to those of the Two Vehicles who,
at first, merely hear the name of *nirvāṇa* but do not grasp the meaning of the Buddha-nature of the three virtues.
"Because non-arising is itself non-arising, it is profound" means that because it is the ultimate depth, it is termed "abysmal" (*sui*).
While the preceding provisional teachings discuss only its depth (*shen*) but do not speak of its abysmal nature, this sutra is both deep and abysmal; nothing can follow after it.
This is also that which is both existent and non-existent. In the preliminary provisional teachings, it is non-existent yet existent; in this sutra, it is existent yet non-existent.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, for it is fully endowed with the three truths, as can be understood by analogy with the principle of being both empty and not empty.
○ Commentary on the "Chapter on King De-wang," Part Two:

Regarding the statement that "Buddha-nature does not sustain [one]," the underlying intent is difficult to grasp. If one possesses Buddha-nature, it would logically follow that one could not commit evil and fall into hell;
yet now, since they have indeed fallen, it follows that they lack Buddha-nature. Thus, Buddha-nature would be powerless.
What is meant by "furthermore, there is no permanence, bliss, self, or purity"? It is that the Buddha-nature possesses these four virtues, and all sentient beings possess them in their entirety.
Why, then, is it said that there is "permanence, self, bliss, and purity"? This refers to the case of an icchantika who, having severed the Buddha-nature, how could they initiate cultivation?
At that time, one further attains permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Now, the intention is merely to sever mundane goodness; the Buddha-nature is not severed.
For this reason, one shall indeed attain it.

If the Buddha lacked the four virtues, he would be identical to ordinary beings. As for the icchantika also lacking the principle of attaining Buddhahood, it is because of [the obscuration of] the Buddha-nature.
Since they are indeterminate icchantikas, they will likewise not resolve their minds toward enlightenment in the future.

Regarding the difficulty of causing all people to turn [from their ways]: this refers to those who have not yet attained [realization] being made to attain it, and those who have attained it being made to regress.

If one discusses the Buddha’s regression and his manifestation of entering the three miserable realms, there may appear to be such a principle; however, he certainly does not commit the five heinous crimes as an ordinary person.
First, regarding the praise of present virtues: this is for the purpose of causing the bodhisattvas who have currently resolved their minds to further increase in merit.
The Sūtra states: "Among all the worlds, whether devas or humans, there is none at all capable of inquiring about it.
This Buddha-nature is a supramundane and most profound dharma; it is not something that can be inquired about by mundane devas or humans.
One who is called an icchantika because they have severed their fundamental grasping refers to one in whom [the roots] have been severed and then regenerated.
Since it is not certain that [the roots] exist, one cannot prevent the arising of present wholesome states.
If it were not definitely existent, it would not yet possess the four virtues.

Now, as for the statement that "the nature is not yet attained" and that this also dispels the fourth question: the previous question held that one who has not severed their Buddha-nature is not called an icchantika;

the present answer holds that although the nature is not severed, one is still called an icchantika. Why? Because [an icchantika] has already severed what they ought to have attained—namely, the wholesome.
Regarding the statement that "evil persons are not fixed": as it says in the sutra, they were originally unable to attain bodhi;
now, because they are able to attain bodhi, they are called "not fixed."
Regarding "form" (rūpa) and the "characteristics of form": "characteristics" refers to such qualities as blue, yellow, red, white, long, and short; "form" refers to that which is visible.
Within the state of non-fixity, there are nevertheless fixed characteristics; for all dharmas are entirely indeterminate, and the Tathāgata does not...
Concentration is itself concentration; therefore, it is said that "it exists.
Regarding the path of skillful means, this refers to provisional teachings concerning the manifestation of traces, such as entering into nirvana, which are termed "indeterminate."
Regarding the phrase "clothing the body": "clothing" (chǔn) means to reach or to approach; it also means "near. These two [aspects] are imperishable.
The "original ground" is a metaphor for the Dharma-body, while "being outside" is a metaphor for impermanence. Since impermanence is itself permanence, these two are imperishable.
Or it is a definitive definition. This means that the Dharma-body is inherently the Dharma-body, and the Respondent (the Pratyupanna-kāya) is inherently the Respondent;
they do not merge into one another, and thus it is called "definitive.
Now, when it is explained that the ghost is non-ghost and yet also non-non-ghost, this is interpreted according to the mutual identity of the Three Truths.
This very phrase "not a ghost" is fully endowed with the three truths. Why? "Ghost" is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
"not a ghost" is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); and "neither a ghost nor not a ghost" is the middle way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). These three truths are that which performs the negation.
The Sūtra states that for the sake of the elder Ghoṣila, the Tathāgata manifested a body three feet tall.

This means that when the elder’s spiritual faculties had matured and the Tathāgata wished to deliver him, he manifested the body of a son to make him realize that this body does not belong to himself, yet through it one can attain the fruit of the Path.
Regarding the statement "neither outflow (āsrava) nor non-outflow is the twelfth chapter": this refers to the twelve textual passages based on the preceding series of "neither-nor" formulations.
The current explanation corresponds to the sixteenth section-gate; therefore, it is said to be the final explanation.
Regarding the statement that the first two are the substance of the outflows (*āsrava*): the two delusions of views and thought-entanglement constitute the substance of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the latter five being the conditions for the outflows: external conditions assist internal afflictions so that they become outflows.
This is as stated in the Vinaya, such as the passage concerning how a foolish person opens the gates of all outflows.
"One should possess ten fetters. This means that at the stage of suffering (the lower realm), all [fetters] are present.

As for the statement that "doubt and views are mutually related," it is because the doubting mind fails to comprehend, and subsequently gives rise to the grasping of views; thus, they are said to be "mutually connected."
First, those who conceive of a true self within the conventional self engage in horizontal conceptualization of a self.
This suffering is the most pervasive, meaning it extends to both ordinary beings and sages.
That these cannot be considered as one refers to the differences between the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering.
The oil is a metaphor for the precepts; the precepts take form and mind as their substance, just as oil is contained within a vessel.
The drawing of a sword from behind is a metaphor for impermanence, meaning that [the precepts] do not abide for even a single moment.
Regarding the statement "called 'detachment' (vairāgya) from the perspective of the path of cultivation," this means it is identical to the explanation of the term provided by the commentators.
As for the phrase "that which is born again and again does not fall," this explains away an objection.

Regarding the phrase "merely attaining slight benefit," this refers provisionally to the seeds of the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), and thus speaks of only seven kalpas; whereas the previous [passage] referred to the revealing cause (*jñāna-hetu*). Therefore...
It is said that this arises from birth.
Some have critiqued it, saying it is very much like a "door-socket" [a triviality], meaning it is identical to the fruits of worldly pleasure experienced by ordinary worldlings.
However, this single phrase can also be understood from two perspectives. First, it signifies the complete fulfillment of the Three Jewels in one body.
Why? Because "reaching the ultimate destination" refers to seeking the Buddha; "the Teacher of the Buddha" refers to the Dharma; and "the person who is able to seek" refers to the Sangha.
Furthermore, "constantly attaining immeasurable bliss" refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); because one penetrates this suffering, it is entirely the Dharmakāya. Therefore...
This refers to bliss.

Regarding "permanently severing the lower," which signifies the virtue of liberation: because one is able to sever the two types of death and depart from the bodies of the nine realms, it is called "permanent."

Regarding "listening with a sincere mind to the virtue of prajñā": because one possesses wisdom, one is able to listen with sincerity; therefore, it is called *prajñā*, which corresponds to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding the necessity of explaining each point individually: this refers to the subsequent citation of various texts for clarification.
The statement that both person and dharma are eternal means that the ordinary person attains the eternal Dharma, and both master and disciple are eternal;
this is also its intended meaning.
If there is no self, who is it that hears? Who is said to be the sovereign master? If there were no true self, there would likewise be no sovereign master; hence the question, "Who?
Now, the reason the commentary does not provide further explanation [as indicated by the ellipsis] is that this is a brief response: the Tathāgata has realized nirvāṇa, which is non-arising.
Non-arising. To eternally sever birth and death is itself the arising of non-arising. If one can listen with a sincere heart, then there is the non-arising of arising.
All phenomena do not arise, yet Prajñā arises; therefore, one constantly attains immeasurable bliss. This is because the application of this "arising of arising" is inexhaustible.
Regarding the phrase "the characters are slightly added and must be well-discriminated": this takes the latter half [of the verse] to explain the former half.
Since they are mutually absent within it, it is called "intermingled" (*jiaojia*).
When Nirvana is sometimes spoken of as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), this is precisely the meaning of the text in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
If one can listen with a sincere mind, this is precisely the world. This means that when the subject and object are not of one mind, there is the differentiation of the five aggregates;
therefore, it is said that "I" and "non-I" are [identical].
"Each person for themselves" means that within each of the four *siddhāntas*, one attains the ultimate joy of generating wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*).
When the treatise states that "a single dharma is divided into two types of teaching," this is also evidence of the intent to provide remedies according to the individual.
Within these remedies, there is likewise the intent to generate wholesome roots.

If that which is not produced by causes and conditions constitutes the meaning of "nature," it refers to the essence of nirvāṇa, which is free from the four types of nature because it is neither self-produced,
other-produced, co-produced, nor uncaused.
If there is a provisional self, it is called a "provisional self" because it exists provisionally based on a name.

Regarding "the cause of causes": among the twelve links of dependent origination, afflictions serve as the cause; since one is able to observe that these afflictions are themselves causes, it is called "the cause of causes."
Regarding the phrase "merely contemplating": "merely" (liao) means "briefly. The intent is that it is described briefly, with no further elaboration of words.
Because the ten meanings explain what is profound, it is termed "Great. This indicates that its principle is immeasurable; how could it be the same as other interpretations?

The "old interpretation" which states that this merely concerns the difference between shallow and deep [merit] (and so forth) means the following: In the preceding passage on the holy life (*brahmacarya*), when a woman offered actual food to a sick monk, the object of his perception was inferior;
therefore, he experienced suffering and pain. This verse, however, refers to the Tathāgata’s stage of practice (*bodhisattvabhūmi*), where he made offerings to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Consequently, the object of his perception was superior, such that he did not experience suffering; furthermore, the merit was profound. Thus, it is said to be "shallow" [in comparison].
This is profound.
Regarding the phrase "respectfully encountering those who have broken [the gates]," a Daoist text states: "Double doors are secured with bolts to await violent guests.
This refers to those such as watchmen who strike the hours and chant their watchwords.
This refers to wicked elephants, wicked horses, and various wicked beasts.

For instance, even the physical birth-body (*janma-kāya*) of a Bodhisattva on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as described in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* cannot avoid the perils of tigers, wolves, and lions; therefore, the Buddha taught ten *dhāraṇīs* to protect them.
Since that sūtra contains the meaning of transcending [the stages] and ascending to the ten stages within a single lifetime, it is called the "birth-body."
"Awakening is sensation" refers to the three types of sensation.
Regarding the "threefold mental activity of wrong thought" in the *Śrīguṇarājaparivarta*,
it is said that although the other four types of mind do not fail to produce outflows (*āsrava*), they are designated as such because their mental activity is subtle.
This refers to mindfulness. It is capable of producing all outflows (*āsrava*).
When the Sūtra says "committing various evils," it means giving rise to the ten paths of unwholesome action (*daśa-akuśala-karmapatha*).
When the Sūtra says "tending toward the good realms," this refers to the Bodhisattva who fears birth and death and is able to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Furthermore, the first six [lines] illustrate the conditions for the Path; that is to say, they serve as powerful conditions for cultivating the Path. One contemplates the four great elements, the five aggregates, and so forth, regarding them as an empty village.
This is intended for those of the final age, who cultivate the contemplation of phenomena starting from the level of ordinary beings, all while maintaining the mind of *nirvāṇa*.
Cultivating the two birds flying together, one is able to know the principle of the permanent and the impermanent; therefore, it is called "conditioning" (*pratyaya*).
Next, the single analogy refers to the practitioner of the path: by relying upon the forty-seven categories of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one attains them;
taking these as the cause, one is able to proceed toward the fruit. Therefore, it is called "reaching the shore."
That ignorance can ensnare sentient beings means that ignorance acts as the king. The four great elements are likened to four snakes.
Regarding the varying degrees of gravity within the precepts: for instance, violating the first precept is grave, while the remaining three are light;
the four pārājika offenses are grave, while those below them are light, and so forth.
If one attains true understanding, this is the stage of the first abode (*prathamā-bhūmi*).

Regarding the character "xiāng" (瓨) in the phrase "jīng xiāng qì" (經瓨器): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it resembles a jar (*yíng*) with a long neck that holds ten *shēng*. (The character is pronounced with the second tone, as in "jiāng.")
To settle the mind within the realm of emptiness is to employ the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).

Here, it is said that one "flees" because one is initially subduing the afflictions; since the roots of goodness are weak while the afflictions are powerful, this is metaphorically described as fleeing.

"To loathe birth-and-death as one who looks back" does not mean that the objective realm itself is originally birth-and-death and thus turns back; rather, it means turning back because of fear, and having turned back, looking back again.
"Hiding the sword" refers to hiding the sword of right wisdom; because one speaks of a false self, it is said that one covers over non-self. There is no... [text continues].
"I" is precisely the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*).

The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are that upon which consciousness (*vijñāna*) relies and dwells; they take the pure four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) as the basis for consciousness to rest upon.

The "six thieves" are a metaphor for the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); the six objects themselves are not thieves, but by leading the six internal faculties, the six objects gain entry, and thus they are so named.
Regarding its being a thief:

the scripture says "returns and departs" because one fears being defiled by the six sense objects; thus, one immediately cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, which is why it is said that it "departs."
"Those who can plunder the wealth of goodness" refers to both mundane and supramundane wealth of goodness.

As for the passage in the Sūtra stating "encountering a river on the road," it is because of the abundance of delusions that one constantly remains within birth and death (*saṃsāra*); now, while practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, one is obstructed by birth and death, and thus it is said that one "encounters" it.

The phrase "moving hands and feet is an analogy for the function of the Way" means that precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth are precisely the functional power (*vṛtti*) of cultivating contemplation;
thus they are termed "function.

As the Sūtra says, "There is no raft," the character for "raft" (筏) is pronounced with the second tone (符目反). This refers to the passage in the *Analects*: "Mencius rode upon a cask and floated across the sea. (Note: The text here mentions Ma Rong, likely as a source or commentator on this usage.)
It is said that a *fú* (桴) is a raft made by lashing together bamboo and wood. The large ones are called *fà* (筏), while the small ones are called *fú*. The pronunciation of *fú* is *fǎnyú* (返于反);

in the region south of the Yangtze River, it is called *tàn* (潬, pronounced *wénjiā* 文佳反). In the canonical text, the character is written with the radical "wood" and the phonetic "wǒ" (我), which is not the standard form.

Regarding "the raft cannot be relied upon": while practicing the factors of enlightenment on the Path, one has not yet reached the other shore and remains in the middle of the stream, fearing that one may not cross over.
The two hands are a metaphor for the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate; taking conventional truth as provisional wisdom and ultimate truth as ultimate wisdom. That is to say—
This refers to the provisional and the real within the single, perfect essence.
However, as for the first three minds, because form and so forth are coarse, they are not yet able to give rise to defiled activity;
yet because the mind is subtle, attachment arises in every thought-moment, which is termed "craving."
Regarding the statement that upon advancing one sees nothing at all, this refers to the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
As for the claim that the six faculties (*ṣadindriya*) are also called the six emotions (*ṣadkleśa*), etc., this is merely a general discussion for the time being.

If one follows the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the faculties are defined by their capacity to produce [cognition], the emotions by their tendency toward defiled attachment, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) by its function of discernment; thus, they are not the same.
The Sūtra states that "those who travel along the road" is a metaphor for practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, proceeding from cause to fruit, and reaching the other shore.
"Giving rise to three kinds of dharmas" refers to the dharmas consisting of four matters, five matters, six matters, and so forth.
That which is called the "four subtle elements" (catvāraḥ paramāṇavaḥ) is so named by way of their capacity to produce [coarse matter].
As for the statement that "that which is produced is coarse, and is therefore called the four great elements" (mahābhūtāni), this term should apply to the coarse objects that are produced.

Regarding the statement that "each of the four great elements possesses four [attributes], yet none is complete with all four": for instance, the wind element lacks color and possesses only two attributes, such as tangibility;
furthermore, they are categorized as having four, three, or two [attributes] based on their relative strength or weakness.
Regarding the "five matters" being sufficient for the single object-field of sound: the first four subtle elements constitute these five matters.
As for the opening of these two rivers, it refers precisely to the mutual connection between the two rivers of affliction and birth-and-death.
