The Sūtra states that one praises and speaks of the wholesome paths but does not speak of the unwholesome paths. "Path" (mārga) carries the meaning of "cause"; thus, it refers exclusively to the teaching of wholesome causes and not to unwholesome causes.
As for the meaning of "enumeration" (saṃkhyā), this refers to the doctrines of the Saṃkhya school and the Sarvāstivāda.

Now, seeing the Buddha’s power awakens those who previously cultivated meditative concentration means that those who once practiced this concentration in the past awaken their latent habits upon seeing the Buddha;
thus it is said they "attain birth."

Since they did not yet recognize the students' capacities, they taught the two disciples practices such as counting the breaths and the contemplation of impurity; both instances involved the error of failing to match the teaching to the capacity.
When the Tathāgata recognized their capacities, they immediately attained arhatship.

Regarding the phrase "the washerman who loathes filth," this refers to the treatise’s instruction to first practice the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and subsequently cultivate the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and so forth.
As for the statement that the former four concern the literal text while the latter four concern the underlying principle:

the "text" refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), which, being common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, constitute the meaning of "extensive learning" (*bahuśruta*). The "principle" refers to the profound Mahāyāna cultivation of the principle of silent quiescence.
As for the essential meaning, it refers to the meaning that elucidates principle.
To value this principle as "much learning" means that if one knows the Tathāgata never preaches the Dharma, yet considers this to be much learning,
it is because principle encompasses the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
The Sūtra states that "to be able to endure what is difficult to endure" refers to the object of endurance, which is the Great Nirvāṇa.

The Sūtra further states that "to be able to give what is difficult to give" means that while wives and children are the external body and one's head and eyes are the internal body, to be able to practice giving by regarding the internal and external—the person and their environment—as non-dual constitutes the Great Nirvāṇa; this is what is called "difficult."
"Because of having cultivated the samādhi of emptiness" refers to ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the initial mention of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), it is as the sūtra says: "Because of their similar continuity, the dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are empty by their very nature.

Ordinary persons erroneously reckon form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates to be permanent; this is called 'similarity. They reckon that within a single lifetime there is a moment-to-moment arising [of a self]."
Cessation is called "continuity. Because one does not know emptiness, it is said that [the continuity] is lost.

The Sūtra says: "A Bodhisattva who is endowed with five things" refers to being endowed with the five aggregates (*skandhas*), and being able to realize that the nature of these phenomena is fundamentally empty and quiescent.
As for the statement in the Sūtra, "One should know that such a person is not a śramaṇa," etc., this refers to one who is actually a denizen of hell;
speaking figuratively, they are said to be a member of Māra’s retinue.
One should know that "original emptiness" (prakṛti-śūnyatā) is that which possesses [this nature]. If there were no emptiness, even cultivation could not be attained;

therefore, it is called "original emptiness. As for citing internal phenomena as an analogy: birth, abiding, and cessation—cessation itself returns to cease of its own accord; thus, they are called "internal."
If there were nothing visible, one should not speak of a "seer. To speak of seeing would be a perversion.

It is simply to extinguish that which is conceptually grasped: sentient beings conceptually grasp all things as non-empty; now, by extinguishing that conceptualized view, it is said that "the non-empty is made empty."

Regarding "one should know that they act as conditions": for the sake of sentient beings, it is said that conditioned phenomena exist for the noble ones; therefore, it is said that unconditioned phenomena are indeterminate in their conditions and are entirely empty.

As for the current clarification that "it is not so," this means that the path-factors of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-mārga-aṅga*) are able to encompass the six perfections, just as described in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā-mārga*.
The details regarding the categories [of beings] are explained extensively in the main text.

As for the scripture’s statement, "Those who do not believe will transmigrate through birth and death," this refers to those in the four fruits of the śrāvaka path, the pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas at the stage of skillful means (*upāyabhūmi*) who do not cultivate the Mahāparinirvāṇa;
because they still possess birth and death outside the realm (*dhātu*), it is said that they "transmigrate."
Regarding "being no different from beginning to end": taking up the initial merit, it is already complete in what follows; likewise, what follows is also complete with the initial merit.
Therefore, it is said to be "no different.

As for the interpretation that this [view] greatly errs, as previously refuted, regarding merit in terms of realization (*pratyakṣa*), from the very beginning, all are based upon the permanence of *nirvāṇa*.
If "abiding" constitutes the essence [of the fruit], how could it be said that the essence is only fully realized at the very end, the tenth stage? Therefore, this is called a great error.
As for the "five kinds of salt" mentioned in the Sūtra, it refers to the differences among them, such as black salt, red salt, green salt, white salt, and so forth.
Private Notes on the Commentary to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Ten;
Private Notes on the Commentary to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Scroll Eleven.
Chapter: Explaining the "Lion’s Roar" (*Siṃhanāda*).
"It is not exclusively so" means that others might think that although the Emperor alone is capable of hearing [the teaching], it is not that he lacks this intention;
now, because of the question, there is an ability to answer. Since these two meanings mutually establish one another, it is said that "it is not exclusively so."
"Having completed three years, one is able to roar" means that just as a lion cub becomes a lion king, so too does a Bodhisattva preach the Dharma in a manner similar to the Buddha;
therefore, it is called "roaring. The character for "roar" (哮) is pronounced with the *xiao* (孝) sound.
One who can roar the immeasurable lion's roar is one who can expound all dharma-gates—whether partial or complete, sudden or gradual.
Regarding the twofold simultaneous clarification: this means that both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas each possess these two meanings, and their teachings are without distinction. Why did the ancients...?
"Solitary" refers to those capable of questioning;
"extensive" refers to those capable of encompassing the concise, for the extensive textual exposition of the sūtra is able to encompass the concise title.
"Roaring" applies to both locations, as both Buddhas and bodhisattvas are named by their ability to both question and answer.

Furthermore, regarding the character "師" (shi) with the radical "阜" (earth/mound) and the suffix "匝" (za): this is a "compound ideograph" (會意字) among the Six Scripts. It signifies that the task is completed and is thus named "師" (shi).
This means that both one's own practice and the transformation of others have all been fulfilled. The character "阜" is pronounced "yi" (according to the phonetic tradition).

Furthermore, regarding the character for "master" (師, *shī*), it is explained as "leading" (*shuài*) an army. The character "leading" (*shuài*, pronounced *zú* according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*) refers to a handkerchief;
thus, it signifies the one who leads by transformation. Five *lǚ* (units) constitute a *shī* (army); *shī* therefore refers to the multitude. *Lǚ* is the name for a military division.

Regarding the phrase "there are generally six stages" (and so forth), this refers to the stages of the Six Identities (*liù jí*). All sentient beings are, from the very beginning, lions in their fundamental nature (*lǐ xìng*);
from the stage of Name (*míng zì*) up to the stage of Partial Truth and the Ultimate Stage (*jiūjìng wèi*), they are like lion kings.
This is the definitive teaching on the Buddha-nature (*foxing*).

Regarding "the secrecy of speech penetrates the six, which is the world": this means penetrating both oneself and others. Since the teacher is the sixth and is distinct [from the other five], it is called the "worldly" (loka) mode of teaching.

"Singlefoldly concerning the child" refers to that which proceeds from the human state; this is because the Bodhisattva is able to inquire about Buddha-nature and is able to generate goodness for both self and others.
"Singlefoldly concerning the roar" refers to that which proceeds from the application of remedies; "roar" means definitively proclaiming Buddha-nature, which is able to shatter what lies before it.
This is because the *Bianjiao* (Exposition of the Teachings) does not provide a definitive explanation.
Regarding the "Master alone," from the perspective of the primary truth (*paramārtha*), the Buddha-dharma is the Master; that is, the Buddha-nature and the Middle Way.
Therefore, it is called the primary truth.

Therefore, regarding the title which possesses manifold meanings: it briefly refutes others who discuss only the capacity to inquire, whereas our own school [discusses] both master and disciple as each possessing six meanings and four distinct *siddhi* (purposes).
Thus, there is no dharma-gate, whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, that is not fully encompassed.
"If one enters into realization, there is no teaching. This is intended to refute others;

it means that since this is the Bodhisattva questioning the Buddha-nature at the very moment it should be explained, how could there be any verbal expression? Therefore, it is said that "there is no teaching."
Regarding the question "Who is it that asks about the nature of peace and bliss?": since the previous question by Kāśyapa has already been answered, there is no need to answer it again here.
As for the various divergent explanations, these are the questions of Siṃhanāda and the answers of the Tathāgata; thus, the meaning of the "divergent" refers to the interlocutors.
They are not related; therefore, it is said that "none are employed.
When the previous chapters all refer to *nirvāṇa*, this refers to the first three chapters.
As for the statement that "nirvāṇa is simply Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and Buddha-nature is simply nirvāṇa": Buddha-nature is spoken of in terms of the cause, while nirvāṇa is [the result].
If the fruit can indeed proceed from cause to fruit, it is because its nature permeates both cause and fruit.

As for "subsuming the particular within the general": the term "Buddha-nature" is a specific designation, yet here we speak according to the general sense; therefore, it is said to have the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "one shall penetrate the Middle by means of the Buddha-nature": this refers to the sequential arising of the four phrases. The Buddha-nature is the foundation;

from this foundation, practice arises, whereby one attains the Middle Way. "Middle" (zhong) is the name, while "character" (zi) is the phonetic reading. "Penetrate" (tongda) means to thoroughly understand.
Regarding "being bound because of non-recognition": not seeing the Buddha-nature is called non-recognition; seeing the Buddha-nature is called liberation.
This liberation arises from cultivation.

The Sūtra states: "All the great assemblies, O sons of good family. This is the Tathāgata’s universal proclamation that the capacity for inquiry regarding all dharmas resides in the Bodhisattva Siṃha.
The mention of "vehicles" and "non-vehicles" refers to the *nidāna* (the cause of realization). Within the Sūtra, all dharmas are explained in sequential order; it is as if there were something real.
There is no reality; one simply takes up reality. There is no vehicle and there is no non-vehicle; one simply takes up the vehicle. A vehicle is that which enables one to go from here to there;
it is precisely the revealing cause.

Regarding the statement that "the myriad virtues and the One Vehicle all belong to the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*)," the myriad virtues are the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*); how then can they be called the revealing cause?

Now it is clarified that they reveal through the contributing cause; the contributing cause is able to assist the revealing cause. If one speaks from the perspective of the virtues themselves, they constitute the contributing cause;
for all phenomena must be assisted by the revealing cause in order to realize the Correct [Dharma].

Regarding "the nature of existence and the nature of non-existence," these refer to the nature of the fruit and the nature of the fruit-of-fruits; in the present context, both are taken as having bodhi as the nature of the fruit, and nirvāṇa as the fruit-of-fruits.

Regarding the citation of the nature of the true cause (*zhengyin-xing*): from the Avīci Hell at its beginning up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) at its end, all are called sentient beings, and all possess the nature of the true cause.

Regarding the citation of the nature of the objective realm (*jingjie-xing*), "existence" refers to the twenty-five realms of existence. "Non-existence" and so forth, up to "the existence of the True," refer to the nature of the objective realm. "Existence" is precisely the twenty-five realms of existence.
As for "abiding": that which is real is the goodness of the True Truth (*satyadharma*). Good and evil five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) constitute its objective nature (*viṣayabhāva*).
Furthermore, regarding "the object giving rise to wisdom": this means that wisdom takes the object as its condition (*ālambana*), and the object triggers wisdom; this is termed "arising.
Thus, the object of contemplation is the "objective sphere" (*viṣaya*).
Regarding "karma is not the afflictions themselves, but that which is wholesome or unwholesome": this means that karma is called "karma" because it is moistened by the afflictions.
When this moistened karma brings about retribution, it is therefore called "karmic fruit."
The first two phrases clarify the supramundane cause and effect, as in the sūtra’s mention of "having a cause" and "being without a cause.
The latter three phrases clarify the mundane cause and effect, namely the three phrases concerning "that which is conditioned," "that which is unconditioned," and so forth.

"The existence of a Buddha is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This means that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is identical to the five turbidities; thus, it is called the conventional truth.
"The non-existence of a Buddha is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This means that there is only a name, and since the name is itself empty, it is called the ultimate truth.

Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "Next, based on the Three Jewels" down to "for what reason is it called Buddha-nature," this properly constitutes the inquiry into the meaning of Buddha-nature.
Here, however, we extract the subsequent text to explain and establish the nature of all phenomena.
The Buddha has eighteen articles of exhortation for bodhisattvas. These are: the Three Jewels as three; the Four Noble Truths as four;
the Truth of Reality as one; the Four Virtues as four; the Five Buddha-natures as five; and Cause and Effect as one. Thus, they are called the eighteen articles.
Regarding the raising of six types of questions concerning identity and difference: this briefly refutes the interpretations of others.

It is not seen that the meaning of these six types [of questions] in this text corresponds to the previous sixfold classification. Here, the questions posed regarding the intended meaning of the Buddha-nature are termed "identity," while the distinctions among the six types are termed "difference."
Therefore, as for the Buddha’s separate exhortations followed by a general inquiry: the Buddha enumerates six kinds, eighteen distinct categories, which he calls "separate";

his exclusive questioning regarding the meaning of *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) is called "general. Since the general contains the particular, it is said that [the interlocutor] has deeply grasped the Buddha’s intent.

"Exhorting and encouraging" refers to the passage in the sutra stating, "The entire assembly was unable to come forward and ask; only you are able to ask. This is a term used for pressing and urging [the questioner].
"Causing the assembly to obtain benefit" refers to the benefits of the four *siddhāntas* (the fourfold teachings) arising from the nature of wholesome insight.
It also serves as a means for verifying characters; that is to say, the three karmas are reverent and cautious, making "verification" (jian) paramount.
Next, regarding the formal utterance of words: as in the sutra, the three characters "addressed the Buddha" (baifo yan) are intended by the compiler of the scripture to introduce the meaning;
they are merely borrowed here to form a complete sentence and thus belong to the following text.
First, regarding the exhortation to make offerings: because this possesses merit from the past and the present, one makes a definitive proclamation (*niścaya-vyāhāra*) amidst the great assembly;
therefore, it is offered as an exhortation.
As the Sūtra says: "Now, those who wish to roar the lion’s roar before me"—the lion’s roar is defined as a definitive proclamation. That is to say:
This is because this samādhi is able to inquire into the meaning of buddha-nature.
As for the scripture’s statement, "like a royal teacher," it is because what is taught is similar to that of a king and the Buddha.
That the body is the six perfections means that it is the fulfillment of non-action; this is the Dharma-body.
That the teeth are wisdom means they are the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

Regarding "the ground is itself ethical discipline" (*śīla*): the Mahāyāna of true reality takes this as its foundation. Because one's precepts are pure, one realizes this samādhi, which is stable and immovable;
thus it is called a "ground. A ground is that which serves as a support and is capable of giving rise to all phenomena.

Regarding "the cave is the state of meditative concentration": the various *śūraṅgama-samādhis* constitute that which provides stability. To settle the mind within this state is like being physically situated in empty space.
As for the "analogy of the three practices," these refer to the three types of conduct [of the deities] such as the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) gods and the Brahmā heavens.
The emergence from the cave at dawn is a precise metaphor for the moment when spiritual capacity meets its stimulus.
The complete alignment of the eleven matters follows the sequence beginning with "for the sake of sentient beings"; this can be understood by referring back to the preceding text.
Regarding the combination where the initial minor sequence is not in order: the analogy for the second, the *saṃbhogakāya*, is combined with the first phrase concerning the *dharmakāya*.
Furthermore, the eleven matters are combined as the first, prior to the early morning.
The Sūtra says, "Furthermore, they are unable to utter the lion’s roar. This means that those of the Two Vehicles were unable to utter the lion’s roar prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

To say that one brings forth a later person to question them regarding an earlier teaching refers to those who possess both the Dharma and the person. One should also further state: "Bringing forth..."
To question later people regarding the former Dharma is precisely the Dharma of persons. It is not that the meaning is merely of the Dharma while persons are separate.
When one first asks about the principle of Buddha-nature, one is asking about the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings.

Next, regarding the inquiry into the meaning of the *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) as the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*): this refers to attaining the Buddha-nature through the factors of enlightenment.
Finally, regarding the inquiry into the ultimate Buddha-nature: this is a designation for the fruition-nature attained upon reaching suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding "abbreviated in the middle": as the sutra states, from "up to being able to know the ten abodes" and so forth, all that lies between is omitted because sentient beings do not see it, nor is it clearly perceived what specific dharmas they abide in; therefore, it is called "abbreviated."
Regarding the Prajñā of Mantras: because it pertains to the aspect of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it belongs to merit (*puṇya*).
Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā: because it pertains to the aspect of wisdom (*prajñā*), it belongs to emptiness-wisdom (*śūnyatā-prajñā*).

Furthermore, taking the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) as wisdom and the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) as merit, the practice of the five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*) consists of outflowing phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); therefore, they are called "merit."
The fruit is itself untainted; therefore, it is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
As for those in this land whose merit surpasses their wisdom, this means their merit is strong while their wisdom is inferior. Because of their merit, they have things to practice;
because their wisdom is inferior, they do not cultivate the mind to perceive the principle.
"Those who aspire to wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the stage of fruition.
That "the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes and the Buddhas are alike in being possessors of wisdom" means that ancient masters designated the *bhūmis* (stages) as "abodes" (*zhù*);
the "ground" (*dì*) is that which is relied upon, while the "abode" (*zhù*) is that which relies. This refers to the ten stages of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiào*).

The phrase "the same applies to the remaining examples" means that both the general and specific teachings must also be approached through the process of advancing and retreating. Regarding the two interpretations, there are those that involve being "received" [by a higher teaching], because there are those who attain it now.

As for the statement that "the distinctions are not fixed," this refers to the three teachings mentioned above; one must distinguish them according to the differing suitability of conditions, as they cannot be fixed.
This is the essential point.

That you and I each possess the two kinds of adornment means not only that you are able to ask and also able to answer, but also that I am now able to answer and likewise able to ask; therefore, it is said that we each possess them.

Regarding the apparent reference to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): it still poses questions and answers that individually correspond to the aforementioned interpretations of others; therefore, it does not provide a definitive judgment.

As for the statement that "the question and answer are not the Two Adornments," the intent is as follows: such questions and answers are all based on verbal expression; they are the dharmas of ordinary beings and are not Nirvana.
If [the Bodhisattva] were already fully endowed with wisdom, he would not need to ask, and the Tathāgata would not need to answer.

Furthermore, there is not even a single kind or two kinds; that is to say, one refers to the questioner and the second refers to the respondent. Therefore, it is said to be "one kind, two kinds," and so forth.
It is not that one or two exist within one or two; it does not involve forming a fixed attachment to one or two.
Rather, it is the state of being "one or two" wherein there is neither one nor two, because it is both simultaneously absent and simultaneously manifest.

This also refers to "speaking about the ineffable. As in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, where each of the bodhisattvas speaks of entering the gate of non-duality, yet when Vimalakīrti remains silent, he uses this silence to realize speech through non-speaking.
Regarding the preceding difficult point (as elaborated at length): the Bodhisattva is contrasted with the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and *nirvāṇa* is contrasted with birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Because it is precisely through *nirvāṇa* that one is able to fulfill the two kinds of adornment (*dvividha-saṃbhāra*), it is said that [the Bodhisattva] is "joined with" the ordinary person.

Regarding the statement that "these one or two are not the characteristics of ordinary beings," this is explained correctly in the text below. That is to say, these are the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles;
because they have not yet eliminated the duality of ignorance and birth-and-death, they are the characteristics of ordinary beings.

First, regarding "those for whom this very statement is precisely required": it means that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvāṇa, and nirvāṇa is itself birth-and-death; therefore, it is called "this statement.

Regarding "the absence of the two faults of 'one' or 'two' means they are not ordinary beings": it refers to the Bodhisattvas’ ability to know that the two types of nirvāṇa of the two vehicles [of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas] do not exist.
Second, both take the Middle Way as their object; therefore, neither of the two faults applies.

When the Buddha answers with the Perfect Teaching by means of simultaneous illumination, the Lion’s Roar raises an objection based on "illumination while being quiescent" (i.e., the absence of the three), whereas the Buddha provides an answer based on "quiescence while illuminating," which possesses the two adornments.
Therefore, "the simultaneous negation of both one and two" refers to the questioner;
"the simultaneous illumination of both one and two" refers to the respondent.

That "Buddha-nature is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth" means that the causal factors—the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—are themselves the principle of the emptiness of the ultimate truth.

Thus, "identical with the three yet identical with the one, and identical with the one yet identical with the three" means that because Buddha-nature is empty, it is identical with the three yet identical with the one;

because it is wisdom, it is identical with the one yet identical with the three. This is because both are based upon the Middle Way; it is neither three nor one, for it illuminates both simultaneously.
The three are one.
What is valued is that the realization of the meaning cannot be fully exhausted in words; it cannot be fixed as one, nor can it be fixed as three. Why?
Because the One Truth is itself the Three Truths, it cannot be fixed as one. Because the Three Truths are themselves the One Truth, it cannot be fixed as three. It is not...
Because the three are not one, the path of language is cut off; yet because they are three and one, they cannot be fully described.
Regarding "revealing the 'is' by means of the 'is-not': this means that by negating the two extremes, it reveals the "is"—namely, the non-emptiness of the four virtues.

Regarding the phrase "because it follows [ordinary] sentiment," the intended meaning is that while a Bodhisattva is able to see it, here, in contrast to the Buddha who perceives from the perspective of wisdom (*jñāna*), it is said to be "unseeable.
As for using what follows to verify what precedes—namely, that the former refers to the vision of the Middle Way—it is as stated in the Sūtra: there are three ways of seeing the Middle Way.
"Species" refers to the literal text itself.

As for "experiencing suffering as a result of suffering," this means that the various non-Buddhists who practice such useless ascetic disciplines as the dog-precepts and so forth will experience the fruit of suffering as their retribution.
Those who are inferior in terms of transforming others cannot transform others because they are submerged in emptiness.
Those who practice the path of fixed suffering and pleasure refer to those who attain the bliss of nirvana by practicing asceticism.
That which contradicts the aforementioned names refers to that which is contrary to the Middle Way of Buddha-nature mentioned above. Ordinary beings falsely and arbitrarily speculate;

those of the Two Vehicles cling to partial emptiness; and Bodhisattvas cling to existence. Therefore, it is said that they lack the meaning of perfect pervasiveness. The Middle Way of Buddha-nature is what is termed "pervasive."
"Meaning" (*yi*) refers to the "reason why" (*suǒyǐ*). This is asking what the reason is for *buddhadhātu*.
Now, to say it is "perfect" (*yuán*) and "pervasive" (*biàn*) is precisely that reason; this is called the meaning of *buddhadhātu*.
The Sūtra speaks of "seeds of the Middle Way," which differ from what others conceive—the newly perfumed seeds within the eighth consciousness.
Now, according to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, the prayers of afflictions serve as the seeds of the Tathāgata; the three paths serve as the seeds of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
These are precisely the fundamental causal seeds possessed by sentient beings.
"Nature is the perfect Dharma" means that "Dharma" refers to the Nirvāṇa of the Three Virtues; it is designated as "Dharma.
Furthermore, "all Buddhas are perfect persons" because the term "Buddha-nature" applies universally to all Buddhas; therefore, they are called "perfect persons.
"Enlightenment (bodhi) is the perfect fruit" means that enlightenment is nature, and nature is capable of producing the fruit, the fruit of fruits, and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "one knows this fruit arises from causes and conditions": enlightenment and nirvana are accomplished through two causes—namely, the object and wisdom.
Therefore, it is said that they arise from causes and conditions.

The Middle Way is that which is neither cause nor cause-cause, and neither fruit nor fruit-fruit; this is the essence of the True Cause, for it is entirely the Middle Way and does not fall within the categories of cause or fruit.
"Because all are based on the Buddha-nature as their seed" means that it can produce the two causes and two fruits, causing them to manifest.
As for these two causes and two fruits being "also seeds," the three causes are the seeds of the three paths, and the three paths are the three virtues;
therefore, it is said that they can manifest the Middle Way.
"Mutually serving as seeds for one another" means that the three causes are the seeds for the three paths, and the three paths are likewise the seeds for the three causes;
all are conditioned by the Middle Way and thus receive their names through mutual dependence.

Question: Since the Buddha-nature consists of four kinds of seeds—namely, the causal nature (*hetu-bhāva*), the cause-of-cause nature (*hetu-hetu-bhāva*), the resultant nature (*phala-bhāva*), and the result-of-result nature (*phala-phala-bhāva*)—these constitute the four.
Answer: This is merely an abbreviated presentation and represents both the secondary and the primary aspects. To speak fully, all of them are seeds of the four natures.
Briefly stated, it is correct to say that the seed-nature of the fruit of bodhi is primary, while the other three are secondary.
Furthermore, the seed of the Middle Way is primary, as the others are likewise secondary.
For example, a bitter melon (*trapusa*) is not itself a fever-inducer; yet taking its textual meaning as a condition is an "auxiliary" (*pārśva*) factor.
This is just as, for instance, while the primary cause is the direct condition, that which is understood [as secondary] is the auxiliary.
Regarding these four, among the "Eight Negations" of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, "neither ascending nor descending" means that "not ascending" is "not departing" and "not descending" is "not coming.
The remaining two can be understood as "non-arising and non-ceasing.
Since their intent is to counteract [the views of] birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as well as annihilationism and eternalism, they are called the "eight."
That which is neither above nor below within the essence of all Buddhas is the ability to penetrate this inversion; thus, being neither above nor below is precisely the Middle Way.
Regarding that which is between these two: the five links, beginning with consciousness, situated between the past and the present, constitute the path of suffering. To penetrate this suffering—
The Way is entirely the Dharmakāya; therefore, it is said that one does not perceive birth-and-death and so forth—this is precisely the Middle Way.
As for your question regarding its meaning, "its meaning is such as this," it is as explained in the four previous interpretations: it is the meaning of Buddha-nature.
As for the scriptural passage stating, "Why? Because it is the supreme," this Middle Way is distinct: it does not fall below the level of Brahmā, nor does it take up the heights of the Two Vehicles;
because it does not cling to the two extremes, it is called the "Middle. It is called the "supreme" precisely because it is the Middle.
Regarding "seeing according to reality": this refers to taking the principle of ultimate emptiness as the primary meaning.

As for the scriptural passage concerning "the original limit of birth and death" (*saṃsāra-pūrvakoṭi*): it means that beginningless ignorance is called the "origin," while the fruit of suffering adjacent to the future is called the "limit."
Regarding "two causes flanking one fruit, with the one fruit situated in the center": ignorance (*avidyā*) is the past cause, and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are the present causes;

these are called the "two causes. Consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth constitute the "one fruit. Because this fruit is situated between them, it is called the "Middle Way.
Since Buddha-nature is entirely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is termed the "wondrous middle."
Regarding the phrase "in this treatise," it briefly refutes the interpretations of others.
Now, in providing an easy explanation, I intend to show that the three paths are themselves the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

Therefore, as for the statement "there is no birth-and-death" or "destroying birth-and-death," birth-and-death in its entirety is *nirvāṇa*; these [expressions] merely refute [the notion of birth-and-death] from the perspective of the non-dual doctrine.
The Sūtra says, "For example, like a poor person. This refers to those caught in the cycle of birth and death within the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Because they do not yet possess the Dharma-treasure of Nirvāṇa with its three virtues, they are called "poor."

Regarding the clarification of "this" in the middle [section]: it is not said that the Bodhisattva is like the sūtras—neither impermanent nor eternal—but rather that this is called the Middle Way and so forth;
therefore, it says "this.

When the Bodhisattva contemplates the object and gives rise to wisdom, they profoundly accord with this object. The object is able to give rise to wisdom; the non-duality of object and wisdom is called [the Middle Way].
Because it is the synthesis [of the two], it is called the Middle Way.
One must not take the cause of the causal realm as the cause of wisdom; the twelve links of dependent origination are the cause of wisdom.
It cannot be a "heavy cause" (paccayuppanna-paccaya), because it is a single cause. One cannot take the fruit of the fruit-division as a "fruit-of-the-fruit" (phala-phala);

that is, enlightenment (*bodhi*), being the fruit, cannot be the heavy fruit of *nirvāṇa*, because it is a single fruit. However, one can take the fruit of the cause-division as a "cause-of-the-cause" (hetu-hetu);
for instance, the wisdom of contemplation (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) is the fruit within the twelve links of dependent origination, and thus it can serve as a heavy cause. It is so obtained.
Regarding the fruit of the fruit of the fruit: Nirvāṇa is the fruit of Bodhi; its attainment constitutes the "heavy fruit.
Neither a single cause nor a single fruit can be considered a heavy cause, because they belong to the category of causes and fruits that do not constitute a heavy fruit.
"Contemplating wisdom from cause to cause" refers to contemplating the causes in successive moments.
"Nirvana from fruit to fruit" refers to proceeding from the fruit of bodhi to the fruit of nirvana.
This is not so, for it is not identical with the dharma.
That which does not proceed from cause to cause is merely a single cause taken as an object; it cannot constitute contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
Regarding "not proceeding from fruit to fruit": this refers merely to a single fruit that is not identical to *nirvāṇa*.
As for "proceeding from fruit to what," it is like the single cause and single fruit in the analogy; both employ two phrases, yet a repeated cause is not permitted.
Therefore, it differs slightly from the fruit within the [actual] Dharma.

Regarding the second example, "the fruit is also thus": the essence of the bodhisattva is itself the fruit, yet it further serves as the fruit for the wisdom of contemplation; thus, the fruit of the family is also called the "fruit of the fruit.
Nirvana is itself the fruit, yet it further serves as the fruit for the family of bodhi. Therefore, it is so named.

Regarding the statement that "this is the cause and not the fruit, which is the nature of the objective realm," this is because Kaishan clarifies the five Buddha-natures by establishing four logical propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
As for "this is the cause, namely the revealing cause (*jñānahetu*)," it is now treated as the third proposition, being identical to the cause and fruit of *bodhi*.
The nature of conditions consists of two aspects, namely the condition as such (*pratyaya*) and the condition as understanding (*pariniṣpatti*); these are designated as "two.
These two are cause and effect: that is to say, the condition as such is the cause, and the condition as understanding is the effect.

"To unify the two into one" means to unify the fruit into the cause; it refers simply to the twelve links of dependent origination acting as the causal condition. Therefore, it is said that "unifying the conditions constitutes the primary.
As for "the primary has no further enumeration," if even the primary is beyond number, how much more so the three or the twelve vows?
The Sūtra states that "its meaning is extremely profound," which refers to the principle of the three truths, wherein object and wisdom are merged in an inconceivable manner.

The Sūtra states that "one attains the fruit and retribution despite being neither eternal nor annihilated": because the twelve links of dependent origination do not abide throughout the three periods of time, this is called "non-eternal";
yet because they revolve without end, it is called "non-annihilation. The causes experienced across the three periods are termed "fruit and retribution. Now...
Contemplation is precisely the fruition of the Middle Way. The Sūtra says:
"There is no deliberative cognition that exists through combination. That which arises from ignorance and craving is called "combination.
The absence of deliberative cognition means it does not arise; existence through combination means it does not perish. This non-arising and non-perishing is called the Middle.
This is the Way.
The Sūtra says that those who practice together with the twelve links of dependent origination are ordinary persons who are constantly turned by the twelve links.
In meaning, this is like being carried along through the three periods of time without choice, as if following a whirling firebrand; therefore, there is neither beginning nor end.

Regarding the mutual manifestation of disappearance: the Tathāgata perceives the beginning as disappearing and the end as appearing; the Ten Abodes perceive the end as disappearing and the beginning as appearing.
This is termed "mutual" because, taking only a small portion of it, each perceives both the beginning and the end.
As for the statement that "in the beginning it was profound and obscure, therefore it is said that it cannot be seen": this means that from time immemorial, delusion has arisen within the Truth;
this is designated as the "beginning," and thus it is described as being "profound and obscure."
Regarding the "Tenth Abode, Chapter on Destroying the Root Ignorance": the Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) stage severs only the final single grade, which is designated as the "root.
As for "the fruit to be realized," it refers to the non-arising of the fruit of suffering associated with the transformation of support (nirmāṇa-vaiparītya).

Regarding the statement that "the non-existence of intrinsic nature is easy": the meaning is that those in the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are able to penetrate the subtle nature [of reality], wherein ignorance is entirely non-existent;
this is called cultivation, and is therefore described as "easy."
"Arising from causes and conditions" means that at the time of delusion regarding the Truth, the arising of delusion within the Truth is its beginning;
therefore, it is called "difficult.
[The author] privately comments: the subsequent passage explains what is severed at the first stage of abiding; thus, it says "seeing the beginning."
"Those at the first dwelling whose wisdom is shallow see only the end and the beginning" refers to the end of ignorance and the initial arising of wisdom;
this is precisely the conclusion of the afflictions.
"Lacking the wisdom that treats the fundamental category" refers to the very commencement of the first grade of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Because it has not yet been severed, it is said that one does not see. Furthermore, the end of the preceding afflictions constitutes "seeing," while the beginning of the subsequent reversal of delusion constitutes "not yet seeing.
As the Sūtra says, "it is like beating a ball": this refers to the twelve links of dependent origination revolving through birth and death, which is metaphorically likened to a ball.
It refers to the unceasing coming and going.
The Sūtra states, "This is the one who sees the Dharma. This is because the Dharma is the single essence of the Triple Gem, which is named Buddha-nature.
The Sūtra further states, "All Buddhas take this as their nature," meaning that all Buddhas contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.
This is because the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the Buddha-nature.
This principle may be applied by analogy to the previous statement that those who practice fixed austerity, fixed pleasure, and so forth, all do not see [the truth].

In the preceding text, those who practice fixed austerity refer to ordinary worldlings; those who practice fixed pleasure refer to Bodhisattvas who have emerged from the provisional; and those who practice both suffering and pleasure refer to...

This refers to those of the Two Vehicles and others; they do not perceive [the reality] within the practice of bliss. This is because, from their perspective, they have emerged into the provisional (niryāṇa-vyavahāra), and thus it is said that they do not see it.
Furthermore, this is because they have not yet shattered ignorance (avidyā), and therefore their realization is not clear and distinct.
This refers to the meaning of the "separate transition to the [Shared] Teaching. In the Shared Teaching, one exhausts the afflictions of views and thought across nine stages;
because those of inferior capacity enter the first stage of the Separate Teaching from there, it is so called.
The nature of the cause of bondage is the nature of the object (*ālambana*).
The nature of the cause of the cause of bondage is the nature of the revealing cause (*parijñā-hetu*).
This ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is not the same as the ultimate emptiness among the eighteen kinds of emptiness. Why? Because that [latter] refers to...
That which is empty is emptiness; this refers to the essence of that which performs the emptying, which is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
This concluding statement is most subtle: it means that all sentient beings are entirely the primary emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), which is itself bodhi and nirvāṇa.
At first glance, these appear to be a single question; that is, the first question is without distinction. However, the second question asks for what purpose one cultivates the path.
According to the Buddha’s response, these constitute two questions; thus, it is said they "appear" to be one.
Regarding the necessity of adornment because its function is not yet fully perfected: sentient beings are the cause and the Buddhas are the fruit.
Since the function of the fruit does not yet exist, one must cultivate the thirty-two marks to constitute the two types of adornment.
It is like those blind men touching an elephant; they do not grasp its true form.

If one perceives this meaning, although there is no differentiation within the causal state, one relies on the path of cultivation to be undifferentiated, for then differentiation has no manifest function.
Regarding "that which is not a question": as the Sūtra says, this meaning is not so; that is to say, one should not pose such a question.
Why? Because cause and effect are distinct, and because non-differentiation is itself differentiation.

Regarding the difference established by conditions: the Buddha is already an accomplished sentient being, whereas [the Bodhisattva] is different because he is at the initial stage of cultivating contemplative wisdom based on causes.
Regarding the insufficiency of functional activity: it is because the function of transforming others through the thirty-two marks has not yet been perfected.
It is not meant that these are entirely non-existent; rather, they are fully present within the principle (*li*).

When the Sūtra states that all sentient beings do not yet truly possess the thirty-two marks and so forth, its intention is to say that the rational nature (*li-xing*) of sentient beings inherently possesses the body of a Tathāgata with its thirty-two marks;
if one practices, one will immediately attain it while sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
Therefore, it is said that "it does not yet exist.

When the Sūtra speaks of "there being three kinds," it fully enumerates the existence across the three periods of time. This refers precisely to what is stated in the verse: "originally existing" and "now existing.
As for "the future attainment of Bodhi," this is "future existence."
The Sūtra states: "All sentient beings currently possess afflictions, and so forth.

If this refers to the lines in the verse stating "now non-existent" and "originally non-existent," then "now non-existent" refers to present afflictions, while "originally non-existent" refers to past afflictions.
Regarding the phrase "having long since attained Buddhahood," this does not mean that it is called "long since" in reference to the time of original attainment as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Rather, it is called "long" in reference to the aspect of having severed the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"To bind all together as existence" means that the first half [of the verse] is collectively considered as existence.
Furthermore, "that which is originally existent is now non-existent" is a re-explanation of the first half.
"To discuss non-existence without departing from existence" means that the existence of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself the non-existence of *nirvāṇa*. This is...
"It was originally non-existent and now exists.
To say that existence is not discussed apart from non-existence means that nirvana was originally non-existent and now exists.
"This one phrase is without differentiation" means that because it is neither existent nor non-existent, there is no differentiation.
Regarding the existence of two roots and two branches: this refers to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, as each has its own root and its own branches.
As for the two rivers facing one another and mutually constituting beginning and end: the river of saṃsāra is taken as the end, and the river of nirvāṇa is taken as the beginning.
Taking nirvana as the end and birth-and-death as the beginning; taking the beginning of nirvana and the beginning of birth-and-death as both the root;
and taking the end of birth-and-death and the end of nirvana as both the branches.
"Taking the root and not the branch" refers to the root of nirvāṇa, not the branch of saṃsāra.
"The branch is not the root" refers to the branch of saṃsāra, not the root of nirvāṇa.
"Neither root nor branch" means that it is the root of birth and death, not the branch of nirvana.

"Neither root nor branch" refers to the simultaneous negation of both nirvana and birth and death, thereby manifesting the Middle Way Buddha-nature, which is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
That the mind is not identical to the Buddha-nature refers to the present bodhicitta being the Buddha-nature as a result.
That the mind is not identical to the Buddha-nature means that the resultant Buddha-mind cannot be the causal nature.

He said that the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) consists of the myriad virtues (sahasra-kuśala). The myriad virtues are the conditions; even a single snap of the fingers or a joining of the palms is encompassed by these myriad virtues.
Thus, they should be understood as being identical to the Buddha-nature and the Middle Way, which constitute the One Vehicle.
Regarding the fact that the six perfections and the One Vehicle have no separate essence: this means that the six perfections of non-action can adorn the One Vehicle.
If one refers to the teachings of skillful means, the six perfections serve as supporting vehicles; they are merely the perfections of practice.

Regarding the interpretation based on differences in meaning: from the perspective of principle (*li*), it is the One Vehicle; from the perspective of practice (*xiu*), it is the Six Perfections. Thus, they are said to be different.

Second, regarding the explanation of names as being designated in various places according to the sutra: *Śūraṅgama* is designated in terms of conduct; *Prajñā* in terms of wisdom; *Vajra* in terms of severance;
*Siṃhanāda* in terms of teaching; and *Buddhadhātu* in terms of cause. Therefore, it is said that it receives its name in various places.
"Non-common" (*asādhāraṇa*) refers to those that do not necessarily arise together with afflictions, such as vitarka and vicāra.
"Defiled" (*kliṣṭa*) refers to the arising of the five views and so forth, which are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

As the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states regarding the ten factors that arise: these refer to the ten [mental factors] consisting of sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), faith (*śraddhā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and concentration (*samādhi*).
Some say these are the ten abodes of the desire realm; others call them the ten abodes of sentient beings.
This refers to the three miserable realms as three, humans as one, and the six heavens as six; thus, they are called "ten."
First, regarding the clarification of bathing: the Tathāgata’s wisdom and capacity respond to those such as the various flying birds appearing before him; by beholding him, they attain liberation.

As for the scriptural passage asking, "Is the Buddha-nature not the self?", it means that the Tathāgata knows that the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to [the notion of] existence and do not delight in [the truth].
It is for the sake of severing [doubts] that I have taught: "I am the Buddha-nature," and thus one now attains the arousal of the bodhicitta.
To answer the question regarding the cultivation of the path, it means that one should not dogmatically cling to the idea that the Buddha-nature is without distinction;
rather, it is spoken of as having distinctions for the sake of sentient beings, just as it is said that there is a self (*ātman*).
As for the statement that "some regard me as non-self," this means that the essence of self and non-self is taught differently according to the capacities of sentient beings,
due to the four *siddhāntas*.
Regarding the mention of the Vajrapāṇi who is always present, there is no such statement in the preceding questions.
Regarding the phrase "like the initial moon, until it gradually becomes visible": sentient beings, being shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), cannot see the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Just as one cannot say that the initial moon does not exist because it has not yet appeared;

"gradually becoming visible" refers to the time when, through the cultivation of the path, one reaches the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), at which point it is like the moon’s manifestation—this is called "gradual seeing."
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha-nature is neither one, two, nor three," it is because the various masters of the past each held different views;
each grasped the meaning of a single gateway.
To cause one to realize the state beyond four through these four is the intent: a "gateway" is that which enables passage, and entering the principle through the gateway is precisely the "cause."
The four principles have no four names; therefore, it is said they are "not four. If one enters each through the gate of retribution, one does not enter into principle.
It is like a person asking about a bridge all day long—what benefit would that ever bring?

"Like one who does not see the elephant" means that while the four gates of entry into principle explained by our own school all attain the essence of the elephant, the various masters cling to partiality like the blind man's perception of the body;
thus they give rise to divergent views.
"To sever the afflictions between the two lands" means to sever the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

"To sever the ignorance of habitual tendencies" refers to the intention of connecting the distinct [stages] to the uninterrupted [path]. *Guaijiao* (乖較): *jiao* is pronounced as *jue* (with the initial *gu* of *gule* as its rhyme).

Regarding the statement that one should treat the three types of afflictions through the three contemplations as explained in the *Śāstra*, this is an interpretation by others that is not yet appropriate for that treatise.
For it merely employs loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the meditation on impurity (*aśubha*) to treat the afflictions of greed and hatred; thus, it is not truly consistent [with the intended meaning].

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) refutes the disease of grasping at intrinsic nature (svabhāva), while the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) refutes the disease of grasping at the provisional," this is the interpretation of the Madhyamaka masters.

That is to say, those who cling to and conceptualize intrinsic nature are refuted by the conventional truth; whereas those who merely posit provisional existence are refuted by true emptiness (śūnyatā). Once both the emptiness of intrinsic nature and the emptiness of characteristics are attained, the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) are thereby destroyed.
The two illnesses of "nature" and "provisionality" being removed is called the severing of afflictions; this refers specifically to the destruction of the affliction of ignorance.
As for the statement that "if one sees nature, these [afflictions] do not exist," it means that there are no śrāvakas who can see the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the contradiction with the sutras: the sutras state that one attains the vision of Buddha-nature by destroying the three delusions, not two.
How can this be made consistent? It means that only when all three types are destroyed and the nature is attained does it finally correspond to the sutras.

As for the distinct teaching’s entry into the common teaching, those who have severed afflictions and attained the vision of the Buddha-nature enter the first stage from the seventh stage within the common teaching;
there, they sever one grade of ignorance and see the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the statement that the first three types [of meditation] destroy delusions and so forth, this is based on the sense of sequential order.
Regarding the statement that the latter three types are contemplations, this is based on the sense of non-sequential order.

As for the previous analogies being applied to external objects, it means that within each of those preceding analogies, they are respectively applied to external objects, such as the striking of a ball and so forth.
For example, regarding the individual analysis of each member of the twelve links of dependent origination: within each of these twelve members, all twelve are present.
While this is generally categorized according to the three periods of time, the Buddha-nature likewise pervades all twelve members; it is for this reason that they are used as an analogy.

Regarding the "one hundred realms as the supporting direct and indirect causes and conditions": this refers to the twelve links of dependent origination within the three thousandfold world, which likewise possesses the three thousand.

As for the term "internal and external," its meaning encompasses many nuances; the interpretation offered by our own school differs from that of others, who explain it solely in terms of form (*rūpa*).

The mind takes both the internal and external as its objects; that is to say, the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses—both the basis (the dependent) and the correct (the true)—are all internal and external.
Therefore, it is said that there are many meanings.
Thus, "not grasping" means not grasping at prior fruits, because one thereby repays the causes from previous lives.

One interpretation states that the first seven days after conception constitute "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); however, this explanation is incorrect. Our current position is that "consciousness" refers to the very first moment [of rebirth].

At that time, the *rūpa* (form) still exists within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), where it seizes the discarded physical remains of the parents and enters into the midst of the two essences, red and white.
It is called "consciousness" (vijñāna). It is not only at seven days that it is first termed consciousness.
As for these "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) and the designation "sentient beings": "sentient beings" refers to a conventional designation (prajñapti), while "form" refers to form itself;
thus, they are called "name-and-form."
If it is argued that the subtle characteristics of arising constitute the consciousness-mind within the womb, this then uses the coarse characteristics outside the womb as an analogy;
for the subtle characteristics within the womb likewise possess the characteristics of arising and so forth.
There is as yet no "appropriator" (upādātṛ). The appropriator is a coarse characteristic.

Regarding the mind that acts first: this refers to the time when one is actually performing an action; it is capable of producing craving, grasping, and so forth, thereby bringing about future results.
Regarding internal and external phenomena: the medicines for the ears, mouth, and so forth are called "external," while the arising of conceptual discrimination is called "internal.
As for the transformation of names: the five aggregates of the present are transformed into birth, aging, and death in the future.
Those who do not possess painful sensation possess only pleasant sensation and neutral sensation.
Those who die as an embryo (kalala) are those who possess the four members [of dependent origination].

Regarding the statement that "those who go and return through the three realms ultimately possess the twelve," this means that although they have not yet fully possessed the twelve links of dependent origination, they possess the seeds thereof.

Those who do not sever [the roots] and are reborn in the desire realm all possess the twelve [links]. Therefore, they are likened to the Buddha-nature. Although there may be cases of possessing or not possessing it, in the end, it is always present.

As the Sūtra says: "Although one does not hear of its existence within the twelve divisions of the scriptures," this refers to the state prior to the opening [of the teaching]; it is only after the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra that [it is revealed].
Those of equal wisdom have not yet heard of the Buddha-nature. As explained previously regarding the five dharmas, extensive learning becomes increasingly superior through successive transmission.
Regarding the three additional matters that are not listed in the chapter and which, when combined, total thirty-six phrases, there are in fact only nine phrases in the text.
Within that which is neither suffering nor pleasure, there is only one [category]. Why, then, are two phrases still lacking? One should state: "What is suffering? What is pleasure?
What is neither non-suffering nor non-pleasure? and so forth; thus, it would constitute thirty-six phrases.
The Sūtra states, "to contemplate and understand": this means that the meaning of the preceding thirty-six phrases is none other than Buddha-nature;
it is the Dharma of the Three Truths of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the realm of the Tathāgata, and so forth.

The Sūtra states: "When the fire of afflictions is extinguished, one attains hearing and seeing. This should also be stated as: "At the time the fire is extinguished, one attains hearing and seeing. Why?
Because it is precisely at the moment the iron is red-hot that sentient beings perceive the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the latter two points on transforming others: as the sutra praises liberation and the teaching of sentient beings, these constitute transforming others.
Now, to clarify practicing with the mind of Great Nirvana means: to manifest the small as great, and when it is great, it is truly great.
Regarding the mutual implication of these meanings: it is simply because having few desires is itself contentment; because one is content, one is able to have few desires.
This clarifies the distinction between *nirvāṇa* and *vimukti*: *nirvāṇa* is a Sanskrit term, whereas *vimukti* is its Chinese translation.
Therefore, they are distinct.

Kaishan further states that "liberation" (*jie tuo*) means "to be without entanglement. This interpretation is untenable. How could there be a translation for "tuō" if it were not a transliteration of a foreign sound?
It is precisely because "liberation" (*jie tuo*) carries the meaning of being "without entanglement" (*wu lei*).
Regarding "the joy of precepts": a person who upholds the precepts knows the retribution of future lives and thus does not fear birth and death.
Therefore, the *Śīlasūtra* states that one can attain three kinds of joy; hence it is called the "joy of precepts."

Regarding the phrase "now provisionally juxtaposed": this text is not a formal commentary, hence it is called "provisional. It is intended to challenge others' interpretations by showing that their definitions of the essential nature (dharmatā) are untenable.
The statement "taking principle as the foundation" means that Nirvana is taken as the essence.
When I say, "None of them are so" (and so forth), I am now asking: with a mind of *nirvāṇa*, what meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) do they take as their essence?

Regarding the phrase in the Sūtra, "one who wears coarse woolen garments" (*cīvara*): the character 毳 (*chui*, pronounced *tian-niao* in the rhyme) refers to the fine hair of a sheep according to the *Sancang*;

the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the fine hair of a beast. The *Zhengshi* commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "In the sacrifice to the Four Quarters, the Mountains, and the Rivers, one wears *cīvara*. The *Zhu* sub-commentary says: "*Ji-cīvara* is woolen clothing."
Regarding the tenth dwelling, "both hearing-seeing and eye-seeing": this Buddha is the hearing, while these nine dwellings constitute the eyes.
As for those who do not attain it in other stages: if one refers to the various stages prior to the grounds according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), in all of them one has not yet seen.
Now, in this dwelling-ground, through realization, one attains both hearing-hearing and seeing-hearing. (End of four versions).
Section Two of the "Explanation of the Lion’s Roar" (End of Part Four, Beginning of Part One).

If one wishes to hear and see that which is to be seen with the eyes and maintained through upholding, this refers to practicing the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras with the mind of *nirvāṇa* and accomplishing five kinds of dharmas;
thus the teacher is able to see the Tathāgata’s single essence, the eternally abiding Buddha-nature.
It refers to those who attain the power of the Way through hearing and seeing—meaning hearing the preaching of the Dharma and seeing the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
Seeing the *rūpakāya* (form body) is weak; as the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* states:
"If one sees me by means of form, such a person walks upon a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is called "understanding" (*jie*).
"To know these skillful means" means that from the True Body (dharmakāya) arises the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya). This present body of mine is itself the Dharma-body;
therefore, it is said that "one sees the Buddha.
Regarding the first two actions of body and speech: if one sees the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, this is the eye [of wisdom].
This is seeing.
If one hears that all twelve divisions of the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata are the Mahāyāna, this is hearing and seeing.
When the sūtra asks, "For whom did he take birth? For whom does he preach the Dharma? and so forth, it means there is no sovereign master; thus one knows the Tathāgata.
To assume a body for the sake of sentient beings and to preach the Dharma for their sake is what is meant by "hearing and seeing.
That these factors mutually constitute the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) means that, regarding the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi, one employs the two contemplations as skillful means;

when viewed from the perspective of different times, one attains entry into the first bhūmi, which is called the "contemplation of equality" (*samatā-vipaśyanā*). Because this is able to accomplish the Dharma-body and is termed the "Middle Way," it is so designated.
The Sūtra states, "Based on these two kinds of causes and conditions," which refers to what was previously mentioned: hearing and seeing with the eyes, as well as contemplation and investigation.

As for the question posed by the person who is a *catur-apāśraya* (one of the four reliances), this clarifies that the appearance of the four reliances in the world involves internal birth and external maturation; thus, the question is asked because they are observed in relation to both ordinary beings and sages.
"Practicing these external traces" refers to "traces," meaning the traces of transformation.

"Deceitfully manifesting likes and dislikes, and so forth" means that they are already difficult to discern; this refers to the fact that their true nature is hard to distinguish from their outward appearance.
What is meant by "relying on these two matters"? It refers to seeing the physical body with the eyes and hearing the preaching of the Dharma, whereby one realizes that such a Māra is not an illusion.
As the Sūtra says: "If one acts for the sake of the True Dharma, cultivating and upholding the ultimate precepts with the mind of Great Nirvāṇa, one will immediately attain [it]."
This refers to seeing and hearing.

The Sūtra says, "A single root is deep and difficult to uproot. This "root" is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*); because one possesses faith, one is able to cultivate the three kinds of emptiness.
For this reason, it is difficult to uproot.
If one’s mind is free from regret and one’s upholding of the precepts is not shallow, all such acts constitute the mind of nirvana;

by practicing the precepts one has received, one will thus perceive the Buddha-nature without needing to seek it through deliberate effort. This is because even if one generates a formal vow to uphold them, one still cannot see the nature.
"Subsequently binding one side exclusively" means binding oneself exclusively to the extreme of either nirvana or impermanence.
When the sutra says, "Regarding those who are like the lighting of a lamp," the intended meaning is that [the self] is provisionally dependent upon causes, which are momentary and impermanent.
Regarding the phrase "well-obtained long time, short day of Śākyamuni": "long time" refers to thirty million years; "short day" refers to his entry into parinirvāṇa from dawn until midnight.

Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is cited as an illustration, stating that even durations as brief as a meal-time are not truly short, yet they all serve as skillful means (*upāya*) for the sake of sentient beings.
To preclude the objection that this would lead to an infinite regress: if one were to take thirteen phrases and treat them as causes for one another in succession, it would indeed be infinite.
Therefore, the present intention is to say that faith and listening to the Dharma serve as cause and effect for one another.
Regarding the ancient interpretation that the pot and its supporting stand mutually function as cause and effect: my current view is not so.

As the Sūtra says, the stand and the pot should not mutually function as cause and effect with one another. Why? Because if there are three pieces of wood, if even one is missing, the stand is not formed;
thus, they are successively dependent upon one another. One piece of wood is the cause and two pieces of wood are the effect.
Two pieces of wood serve as the cause, while one piece of wood serves as the effect; thus, they are mutually cause and effect. This is also called *xun-yu*.
According to the *Erya*, *xun* refers to the vertical and *yu* refers to the horizontal, but this is not the intended meaning here.
The scripture says, "standing with a *ju*. The character *ju* (pronounced *qí lǚ*) refers to an externalist's vessel that is round like a gourd and lacks a handle;
it is lifted by crossing three staffs over it. In various scriptures, it is sometimes called a "three-pronged *ju*" (*sān qí lì ju*) or a "three-cubit *ju*" (*sān zhàng lì ju*);
both refer to this same object.

Emperor Wu of Liang cited those who reject [this view], yet even the "thirsty bird" of today has not yet grasped this point. One must simply allow for the mutual functioning of cause and effect between the upper and lower levels;
they must not be treated as a mere linear succession. Thus, it is both the cause and the cause-of-cause, and both the fruit and the fruit-of-fruit, and so forth.
If the three periods of time were fixed, such that the past is the cause and the present is the effect, and so forth, then causes would certainly never be able to mutually serve as effects.
Regarding the inexhaustibility of saṃsāra:
for example, ignorance is the cause and volitional formations are the effect; volitional formations are the cause and ignorance is the effect.
Action is the cause; consciousness is the effect, and so forth.

As the Sūtra says, "That which gives birth can give birth to dharmas," this means that the Great Birth (*mahā-jāti*) can give birth to the Small Birth (*jāti-jāti*), yet the Great Birth itself cannot give birth to itself.
Therefore, it is by means of the "giver of birth"—that is, the Small Birth—that the Great Birth is further produced; the Great Birth does not arise from itself.

Because they arise dependently (*pratītyasamutpāda*). That which arises is capable of producing both the great and the small; the small can produce the great, and they mutually give rise to one another.

What fault is there in using this analogy? If we borrow from the Abhidharma of the Hīnayāna, the eight characteristics (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*) of the great and the small exist simultaneously without being lost.
Although the text here specifically mentions "arising" (*jāti*), it should likewise apply to "abiding" (*sthiti*), "change" (*anyathātva*), and "cessation" (*nirodha*).
It is called "severing" because it is a fruit that transcends all dependencies; since both extremes of affliction (*kleśa*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) do not arise, it is termed "severance.

Regarding the phrase "afflictions are called faults, and faults are further produced upon the afflictions": this means that afflictions are called faults, and furthermore, faults are produced upon the very substance of those afflictions. Thus it is said.
"Exceedingly excessive" (*guòguò*) means that just as a wicked person commits evil again after having already done so, it is likewise called "exceedingly excessive.
Regarding "the absence of a dependent cause": this refers to being beyond all dependence. As the sutra states, because there is neither beginning nor end, the beginning itself is the cause.
Since there is neither beginning nor end, it is said to be "beyond dependence."
Regarding the force of the phrasing: it means that *nirvāṇa* is ultimate. It is not something that comes from following after various non-characteristics (*animitta*), nor is it "not-not.

Because the intent of the formal objection was thus, the Tathāgata’s response remained as "five remain one," meaning that *nirvāṇa* is ultimately the absence of self (*anātman*) and the absence of what belongs to a self (*amama*), and so forth.
Regarding the analogy of the sun and moon being shrouded or dispersed: this means that when the moon is shrouded by clouds, it is not visible; yet when the clouds disperse, it appears.
The intent is that it is not the case that [the moon] is entirely non-existent.

"To a small degree it is so" means that while it is ultimately non-existent, it is merely the same as being non-existent due to a lack of causes; therefore, it is called "to a small degree. If one considers it from the perspective of existence...
The "fruit" (phala) refers to the complete portion.
As the Sūtra says regarding "worldly dharmas and nirvāṇa," it means that nirvāṇa is a supramundane dharma.
Why, then, would one take the six [objects] of the world as being non-obstructive?

The Sūtra states: "Sentient beings are the parents; this is called the cause of realization (*vijñapti-hetu*). Here, the parents are that which realizes, and sentient beings are that which is realized.
To briefly distinguish this: it is distinguished briefly within the context of non-discrimination; therefore, it is called inconceivable (*acintya*).
Furthermore,
regarding the phrase "subsequently, horizontal and vertical are relative" (and so forth), this means that viewing the fundamental substance directly is "horizontal," while the stage of faith,
in relation to the beginning, is "vertical."

Regarding the explanation of the productive cause (*janakahetu*) and the revealing cause (*vyañjakahetu*) from the perspective of meaning: the essence of *nirvāṇa* truly lacks both production and revelation.
This is because, unlike worldly objects which are produced by being brought into existence, [the essence of *nirvāṇa*] is capable of [being revealed] through [the removal of obscurations].
When worldly people say that these two are contradictory, their intention is that the dharma of nirvāṇa should not be treated as both arising-and-ceasing and permanent-and-impermanent simultaneously;
therefore, it is explained by way of the inconceivable.

Furthermore, regarding those who employ the *śūraṅgama-vidyā*: this refers to the non-manifestation of the skillful means of the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*, wherein the two birds of "permanence" and "impermanence" fly together. As for worldly people—
Why is it said that while birth is definitively "birth," one speaks of them as being simultaneous?
This is intended to show that even after having acquired wealth, it may be lost again; by citing this worldly analogy, it is meant to demonstrate that even death is not truly "death.
Fearing that in the supramundane Dharma, "birth" might likewise not be "birth," how could one speak of it as being "defeated"?
Regarding "the first is permanent and the second is impermanent": this refers to that which is not born appearing as born.
"Fully opening up both meanings" means opening up the two aspects of permanence and impermanence, and the two aspects of form and formlessness;

it is called having visibility and invisibility because the views and hearings of sentient beings and bodhisattvas differ. Thus, it is said there are "two meanings. Master Guan’s commentary states: "Since..."
The clouds are also not the bodies of sentient beings. As for "external," where in the world could Buddha-nature exist if it were neither internal nor external?
That would mean it has no nature at all.
This is like a bird deprived of its two wings; the intent is to refute Master Guan’s attempt to avoid the dilemma of being either internal or external. Just as a bird without wings cannot fly...
It is functional.
This dharma is precisely the conventional (prajñapti). That is to say, because the dharmas of the five aggregates arise from conditions, they are conventional.

Regarding "not being present in both truths simultaneously": this means that while abiding in the extremes, one is simultaneously within the two truths; therefore, it is said that one does not abide solely in the Middle Way.
The Way pervades both the ultimate and the conventional.
This inconceivable Dharma is three in being one, and one in being three.
As for the fact that emptiness itself is not external and is not the conventional truth: this inconceivable conventionality is discussed in terms of its oneness.
Third: Because the three are indeterminate and threefold, they are neither internal nor external; thus, it refutes the various masters.
This further establishes the meaning of the preceding [point]: because the three truths are inconceivable and simultaneously illumined, the "double negation" (neither...
nor) is not lost, and therefore it is not destroyed.

Furthermore, because it illuminates both simultaneously, it is said that "it is not lost. Since it is neither internal nor external, yet is both internal and external, it is called "not lost or destroyed.
That it is "provisionally named existent" means that it is called "existent" by relying upon sentient beings.
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha-nature and the Middle Way can all be understood": since one has already refuted both the internal and the external, this is called the Middle Way.
Within the sphere of the Buddha-nature, all places are simultaneously internal and external; therefore, it is said that they can be understood.

That milk is empty is because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since emptiness arises from conditions, milk is merely provisional; and since curd likewise arises from conditions, it too is empty.
As both arise from conditions, they possess nothing more than provisional names.
